AI.conclusion: The signal for code editing lives in the source code being edited itself; summaries and surrounding context contribute little. Compressed context offers significant token efficiency. A ~9% noise floor from temperature-0 inference should be accounted for in future benchmark evaluations.

title: A Generalized Deep Non-negative Matrix Factorization Approach for SAR Automatic Target Recognition
summary: The deep nonnegative matrix factorization (DNMF) technique is proposed to address the low interpretability of deep learning-based methods in extracting multilayer features from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) target samples. However, existing DNMF methods employ a layer-by-layer decomposition strategy, which is prone to causing error accumulation and local optimum, thereby hindering a consistent improvement in recognition accuracy as the number of layer increases. In this paper, a robust multilayer feature extraction method, termed generalized deep non-negative matrix factorization (G-DNMF), is proposed to address the above challenges in SAR automatic target recognition (ATR). The G-DNMF aims global optimality and derives the update rules for each parameter using lagrangian multiplier method. The new update formula indicates that both the DNMF method based on the encoding matrix and the mixing matrix are special cases of the proposed method, theoretically demonstrating the universality of proposed method. In general, the proposed method discards the layer-by-layer decomposition strategy, thereby effectively mitigating the risk of local optima and eliminating error accumulation, leading to a significant improvement in DNMF's multi-layer feature extraction capability. The experimental results, by presenting the feature images extracted from each layer by G-DNMF and the reconstructed original images, verified the proposed method's pure additive understanding of multi-layer features and demonstrated its interpretability. The experimental results based on MSTAR and OpenSARship datasets show that G-DNMF outperforms existing DNMF algorithms and their derivatives in terms of stability and recognition performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Generalized Deep Non-negative Matrix Factorization (G-DNMF) to overcome error accumulation and local optima issues in existing layer-by-layer DNMF methods for SAR target recognition, achieving superior stability and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing DNMF methods use a layer-by-layer decomposition strategy that causes error accumulation and local optima, hindering consistent accuracy improvements with deeper layers. The goal is robust multilayer feature extraction for SAR ATR with global optimality.
AI.method: G-DNMF discards the layer-by-layer decomposition strategy, derives update rules via Lagrangian multiplier method for global optimality, and generalizes both encoding-matrix-based and mixing-matrix-based DNMF as special cases.
AI.result: Experiments on MSTAR and OpenSARship datasets show G-DNMF outperforms existing DNMF methods and derivatives in stability and recognition performance. Feature and reconstruction images verify its interpretability and pure additive multi-layer feature understanding.
AI.conclusion: G-DNMF effectively mitigates local optima and eliminates error accumulation, significantly enhancing DNMF's multi-layer feature extraction capability for SAR ATR, with demonstrated universality and interpretability.

title: CHARM: Charge Calibration and Acoustic Rescue for LLM-based Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
summary: Sarcasm detection, the identification of discrepancies between literal and intended meaning, is a fundamental task in affective computing. However, zero-shot instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically over-predict the positive (sarcastic) class across the entire capability spectrum, while the prosodic cues humans rely on remain underexploited and transfer unevenly across languages. We introduce CHARM (Charge Calibration and Acoustic Rescue for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection), a training-free framework that couples two modules. Bidirectional Charge Calibration (BiCAL) steers the LLM toward opposing sarcastic and literal verdicts along a symmetric axis of charged prompts; the induced directional biases cancel by construction, and a simple aggregation recovers an unbiased pragmatic signal. Acoustic Late-Fusion Rescue (ALFR) then fuses the calibrated votes with prosodic descriptors and LLM-generated auditory-perception probes through a shallow classifier, actively down-weighting saturated text votes in favour of acoustic evidence. Without fine-tuning any backbone, BiCAL attains the highest reported zero-shot text-only Macro-F1 of 0.787 on MUStARD, while ALFR lifts weak backbones by up to +0.382 Macro-F1 on CMMA. A Stouffer meta-analysis confirms statistical significance on MUStARD and CMMA (Z = 13.89 and Z = 34.64, respectively; p < 10^-43). Our analysis further uncovers a cross-cultural prosodic decoupling: low-level acoustics fail to transfer across languages, whereas high-level perceptual abstractions remain robust. Together, these components yield an explainable, cross-lingual multimodal detector.

AI.tldr: CHARM is a training-free framework for multimodal sarcasm detection that combines Bidirectional Charge Calibration (BiCAL) to debias LLM predictions and Acoustic Late-Fusion Rescue (ALFR) to fuse text with acoustic evidence. It achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results (0.787 Macro-F1 on MUStARD) and reveals cross-cultural prosodic decoupling where low-level acoustics don't transfer across languages but high-level perceptual abstractions do.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot instruction-tuned LLMs systematically over-predict the sarcastic class, and prosodic cues humans rely on remain underexploited and transfer unevenly across languages. Existing methods require fine-tuning backbone models.
AI.method: Two-module training-free framework: (1) BiCAL steers LLM toward opposing sarcastic/literal verdicts via charged prompts, canceling directional biases through symmetric aggregation; (2) ALFR fuses calibrated text votes with prosodic descriptors and LLM-generated auditory-perception probes via a shallow classifier, down-weighting saturated text votes in favor of acoustic evidence.
AI.result: BiCAL achieves highest reported zero-shot text-only Macro-F1 of 0.787 on MUStARD; ALFR lifts weak backbones by up to +0.382 Macro-F1 on CMMA. Stouffer meta-analysis confirms significance (MUStARD: Z=13.89, CMMA: Z=34.64, p<10^-43). Cross-cultural prosodic decoupling identified.
AI.conclusion: CHARM yields an explainable, cross-lingual multimodal sarcasm detector without fine-tuning. Low-level acoustics fail to transfer across languages but high-level perceptual abstractions remain robust cross-culturally.

title: From Business Requirements to Test Assertions: Evaluating LLM-Generated Oracles on Real Bugs
summary: The oracle problem (determining the correct expected outcome for a test) remains a major bottleneck in automated testing, and is increasingly relevant as non-experts rely on AI-generated code they cannot reliably validate. We study whether large language models (LLMs) can generate generalizable test oracles directly from natural-language business requirements, without access to source code or example input-output pairs. We propose a reproducible, requirement-driven pipeline grounded in Defects4J. For each of 10 real bugs from Defects4J Lang (Bugs 1 and 3-11), we (i) extract behavioral changes via buggy/fixed diffs, (ii) manually translate the change into a business requirement, (iii) construct a requirement-derived oracle (REQ) as a gold standard, and (iv) prompt five LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Gemma-3n, Llama-3, Mistral-7B, and Qwen-3) to generate Java oracle code. We evaluate oracle correctness and generalization under two targets: agreement with REQ and agreement with the system under test (SUT), reporting macro-averaged accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. LLMs achieve non-trivial generalization but with substantial bug- and model-level variance. Generated oracles align more closely with REQ than with SUT, and correlations between requirement technicality/ambiguity ratings and oracle accuracy are weak with wide confidence intervals. No detectable linear relationship exists between requirement properties and oracle accuracy in this dataset, suggesting that pretraining coverage and the semantic specificity of the required behavior dominate oracle correctness. As a pilot proof of concept, these findings are preliminary and are intended to establish feasibility and motivate larger-scale empirical investigation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs can generate test oracles from natural-language business requirements alone (no code or I/O examples). Using a Defects4J-based pipeline with 10 real bugs and 5 LLMs, the authors find that generated oracles agree better with gold-standard requirements than with actual system behavior, and that requirement properties (technicality/ambiguity) are weakly correlated with oracle accuracy—suggesting pretraining coverage and behavioral semantics are the dominant factors. Results are preliminary but establish feasibility for larger studies.
AI.motivation: The oracle problem—determining correct expected test outcomes—remains a critical bottleneck in automated testing, especially as non-experts increasingly rely on AI-generated code they cannot reliably validate. The paper aims to explore whether LLMs can generate generalizable test oracles from natural-language business requirements alone, bypassing the need for source code or example input-output pairs.
AI.method: The authors propose a reproducible, requirement-driven pipeline built on Defects4J. For each of 10 real bugs from Defects4J Lang (Bugs 1 and 3–11): (i) extract behavioral changes via buggy/fixed diffs; (ii) manually translate changes into a business requirement; (iii) construct a gold-standard requirement-derived oracle (REQ); (iv) prompt five LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Gemma-3n, Llama-3, Mistral-7B, Qwen-3) to generate Java oracle code. Evaluation measures macro-averaged accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 under two targets: agreement with REQ and agreement with the system under test (SUT).
AI.result: LLMs achieve non-trivial generalization but with substantial bug- and model-level variance. Generated oracles align more closely with REQ than with SUT. Correlations between requirement technicality/ambiguity ratings and oracle accuracy are weak with wide confidence intervals. No detectable linear relationship exists between requirement properties and oracle accuracy in this dataset, suggesting pretraining coverage and semantic specificity of required behavior dominate oracle correctness.
AI.conclusion: These preliminary findings establish feasibility and motivate larger-scale empirical investigation. The results indicate that LLM-generated oracles from requirements are promising but depend more on pretraining coverage and behavioral semantics than on surface-level requirement properties.

title: Latent-Identity Tuning in Text-to-Image Personalization Models
summary: Generating and editing a person's face demands high precision, as even minor modifications can significantly alter a subject's perceived identity. Current personalization and editing methods built on general-purpose text-to-image models, however, often lack the precision required for fine-grained facial edits. We present a method for fine-grained identity tuning in text-to-image personalization models. Unlike standard image editing, which operates on a given image, identity tuning modifies the latent representation of a specific identity, enabling the generation of diverse images that consistently depict the same edited identity. To enable fine-grained latent identity tuning, we explore the latent space of a pre-trained, frozen encoder for text-to-image personalization. Our approach requires no additional training. Instead, it leverages the existing architecture of a frozen encoder to uncover latent semantic directions. This space consists of a set of latent tokens that play distinct roles in capturing different aspects of an identity and often correspond to specific spatial or semantic facial regions. We show that meaningful directions can be identified within this space and within subspaces defined by selected tokens, enabling localized, fine-grained, and semantically coherent edits. We validate our approach through qualitative and quantitative experiments that demonstrate diverse localized facial edits while preserving cross-image identity consistency. Project page at: https://garibida.github.io/IdentityTuning/

AI.tldr: A method for fine-grained identity tuning in text-to-image personalization models that edits the latent representation of a specific identity using a pre-trained frozen encoder, enabling localized facial edits without additional training.
AI.motivation: Current personalization and editing methods built on general-purpose text-to-image models lack the precision required for fine-grained facial edits, as even minor modifications can significantly alter a subject's perceived identity.
AI.method: The method explores the latent space of a pre-trained, frozen encoder for text-to-image personalization. It leverages existing architecture to uncover latent semantic directions within the space of latent tokens that capture different aspects of identity. Meaningful directions are identified within this space and within subspaces defined by selected tokens, enabling localized, fine-grained, semantically coherent edits without additional training.
AI.result: Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate diverse localized facial edits while preserving cross-image identity consistency.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables fine-grained identity tuning by manipulating latent semantic directions in a frozen encoder's space, achieving localized facial edits without extra training while maintaining identity consistency across images.

title: Closed-Loop Control with Rule-Aligned Small Language Models and Multi-Agent Self-Correction
summary: A key step toward autonomous industrial operation is the ability to create and reconfigure control policies from natural-language requirement specifications, with minimal or no manual redesign. In this setting, policy generation by AI agents can be a credible path when paired with a plant-aware validator (e.g., a digital twin) that can check generated candidate actions before execution. However, practical deployment is constrained by inference latency and compute footprint: large cloud-based models are often too slow, opaque, or data-sensitive for edge closed-loop use. This work investigates whether a compact Small Language Model (SLM) can be retrained for control reasoning and embedded in a validator-guided correction loop. We use a Qwen2.5-1.5B model aligned via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), combined with (i) an action agent, (ii) a symbolic/digital-twin-style validation layer, and (iii) a reprompting agent that iteratively steers outputs toward valid actions. In randomized thermal-control simulations (30 experiments with 500 steps each), the framework achieves 91.5% average action-alignment accuracy (86.3%--100% across cases) at 3.84\,s mean inference latency. Under symbolic re-mapping, it maintains a 95% in-range rate, indicating robust physical regulation despite reduced token-level agreement. These results support SLM+validator architectures as a practical path toward reconfigurable autonomous control at the edge.

AI.tldr: A Small Language Model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) fine-tuned via GRPO and paired with a validator-guided correction loop achieves 91.5% action-alignment accuracy and 3.84s mean inference latency in thermal-control simulations, demonstrating a practical path for edge-deployable autonomous control from natural-language specifications.
AI.motivation: To enable autonomous industrial operation with minimal manual redesign, where natural-language requirement specifications can generate control policies. Cloud-based large models are unsuitable due to latency, opacity, and data sensitivity, motivating the need for compact edge-deployable SLM-based solutions.
AI.method: Uses Qwen2.5-1.5B aligned via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), coupled with an action agent, a symbolic/digital-twin validation layer, and a reprompting agent that iteratively corrects outputs toward valid actions.
AI.result: In 30 randomized thermal-control simulations (500 steps each): 91.5% average action-alignment accuracy (86.3%–100% range), 3.84s mean inference latency, and 95% in-range rate under symbolic re-mapping.
AI.conclusion: SLM+validator architectures offer a credible, reconfigurable, and edge-deployable path for autonomous control, balancing accuracy, latency, and physical regulation robustness.

title: Reference-Based Distillation Detection in LLMs
summary: Model distillation -- training on outputs from stronger third-party models -- is widely used to boost performance, but raises concerns about unfair advantages and policy violations. This motivates a fundamental question: can we detect whether a model was distilled from another? We show that, while identifying a teacher model from a student in isolation is highly challenging, it becomes tractable in a reference-based setting: given a model and an earlier-generation checkpoint from the same lineage, we can identify the teacher model used to train the later checkpoint. We introduce a distillation detection method based on reference-based membership inference. By comparing how strongly a student model preferentially aligns with outputs from different candidate teachers relative to a reference checkpoint, our method identifies the most likely teacher and detects evidence of distillation. To handle unknown distillation pipelines such as hidden prompts, we infer proxy prompt templates directly from model outputs. We additionally identify a distinctive glyph-level signal specific to o1/o3 models. Evaluating distillation detection is challenging because modern model lineages are already heavily entangled. To address this, we develop a hybrid evaluation spanning both controlled distillation experiments and real-world models. Across both settings, our approach recovers the true teacher with near-perfect accuracy in single-teacher distillation scenarios, even when the underlying distillation pipeline is largely unknown. We further introduce statistical tests for both teacher attribution and distillation detection, and extend our framework to open-world settings where no teacher is guaranteed to be present among the candidates. Applying our method to contemporary models yields new evidence regarding potential distillation relationships involving QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reference-based membership inference method to detect whether a student model was distilled from a particular teacher model, achieving near-perfect accuracy in single-teacher scenarios and uncovering evidence of distillation relationships among contemporary models like QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS.
AI.motivation: Model distillation is widely used to boost performance but raises concerns about unfair advantages and policy violations, motivating the need to detect whether a model was distilled from another.
AI.method: A reference-based membership inference approach that compares how strongly a student model aligns with outputs from different candidate teachers relative to a reference checkpoint. Proxy prompt templates are inferred for unknown pipelines, and a glyph-level signal specific to o1/o3 models is identified.
AI.result: Near-perfect accuracy in identifying the true teacher in single-teacher distillation scenarios across both controlled experiments and real-world models. Statistical tests for teacher attribution and distillation detection are introduced, extending to open-world settings.
AI.conclusion: The method provides effective distillation detection and attribution, yielding new evidence about potential distillation relationships involving QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS.

title: Towards Real-World Wearable Motion Reconstruction
summary: The modern-day surge in popularity of wearable devices poses a fundamentally unique motion capture problem: reconstructing full-body movement from any set of sensing hardware worn at a given moment. Yet, most research efforts assume fixed sensor configurations (e.g. IMU suits or HMD-centric rigs) and cannot generalize across them. In contrast, we argue that motion capture should prioritize unobtrusive and lightweight devices such as smartphones, smartwatches, smart glasses, and smart insoles, and study the interplay between them. To this end, we make three contributions. First, we present a large-scale multi-modal dataset synchronizing these consumer-grade sensors with ground-truth 3D motion, spanning 50 diverse activities including everyday tasks, sports, and social interactions. Second, we propose WHIP, a baseline generative model that reconstructs motion from arbitrary subsets of available sensors, robustly handling missing modalities and producing physically plausible motions. Third, we conduct a systematic study of sensor complementarity, quantifying how different modalities complement one another. Code and dataset are available at https://vcai.mpi-inf.mpg.de/projects/WHIP/

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WHIP, a generative model for full-body motion capture from arbitrary subsets of consumer-grade wearable sensors (smartphones, smartwatches, smart glasses, smart insoles), along with a large multi-modal dataset of 50 activities, and a systematic analysis of sensor complementarity.
AI.motivation: Current motion capture research focuses on fixed sensor configurations (e.g., IMU suits, HMD-centric rigs) and cannot generalize across different sensing hardware. The authors argue for prioritizing unobtrusive, lightweight devices like smartphones, smartwatches, smart glasses, and smart insoles, studying how they interplay for full-body motion reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors present WHIP (a baseline generative model) that reconstructs full-body motion from arbitrary subsets of available sensors, robustly handles missing modalities, and produces physically plausible motions. They also collect a large-scale multi-modal dataset synchronizing consumer-grade sensors with ground-truth 3D motion across 50 diverse activities.
AI.result: The model demonstrates robust handling of missing modalities and produces physically plausible motions from arbitrary sensor subsets. The systematic study quantifies how different sensor modalities complement one another for motion reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues for a paradigm shift toward flexible, consumer-grade wearable motion capture that generalizes across varying sensor configurations, supported by a dataset, baseline model, and sensor complementarity analysis.

title: MusicMark: A Robust Generative Watermarking Framework for Music Generation
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
summary: AI music generation has rapidly advanced alongside commercial platforms, raising the need for reliable watermarking for provenance and attribution. However, existing audio watermarking research has largely focused on speech, and applying speech-oriented methods to music is challenging due to music's complex structure and rich acoustic texture. Most existing methods are post-hoc, adding imperceptible perturbations after generation rather than embedding watermarks as part of the content. This makes them fragile under transformations and especially vulnerable to neural codec re-synthesis, which can discard imperceptible residual signals. Moreover, since generation and watermarking are decoupled, the watermarking step can be bypassed or omitted, weakening provenance guarantees. To address these issues, we propose MusicMark, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative watermarking framework for music. Specifically, MusicMark embeds watermark messages into the semantic latent space during generation, incorporating the watermark as part of the musical content and ensuring robustness against diverse attacks, particularly neural codec re-synthesis. To this end, we introduce a watermark adapter into a diffusion-based generation model to embed watermark messages across denoising steps. The adapter and detector are trained with a joint objective that preserves fidelity by constraining watermarked latents close to their unwatermarked reference latents, while improving robustness through attack augmentations. Experiments demonstrate that MusicMark substantially outperforms post-hoc baselines across diverse attacks including neural codec re-synthesis, while maintaining comparable generation quality. We further introduce a cover-song attack, converting the singing voice while preserving musical content, and show that MusicMark remains more robust than post-hoc methods.

AI.tldr: MusicMark is the first generative watermarking framework for music that embeds watermarks directly into the semantic latent space during diffusion-based generation, achieving superior robustness over post-hoc methods, particularly against neural codec re-synthesis and cover-song attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing audio watermarking methods focus on speech and are post-hoc, making them fragile under transformations (especially neural codec re-synthesis) and easily bypassed, which weakens provenance guarantees for AI-generated music.
AI.method: MusicMark introduces a watermark adapter into a diffusion-based generation model to embed watermark messages across denoising steps. The adapter and detector are jointly trained with a fidelity-preserving constraint that keeps watermarked latents close to unwatermarked references, plus attack augmentations for robustness.
AI.result: MusicMark substantially outperforms post-hoc baselines across diverse attacks including neural codec re-synthesis and cover-song attacks, while maintaining comparable generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Generative watermarking (embedding during generation) is more robust and reliable than post-hoc methods for music provenance, and MusicMark provides a strong foundation for trustworthy AI music generation.

title: Partial Contracts Suffice: Sound, LLM-Inferred Regression Verification
summary: Software evolves continuously, yet ensuring that a patch preserves intended behavior without re-verifying an entire codebase remains difficult. Regression verification addresses this problem, but existing techniques require expensive whole-program reasoning or rely on manually written specifications that are rarely available in practice. We present the first contract-based regression verification tool. Contract soundness is ensured by proving all function versions match the behavior. The contract then verifies program flow via assume-guarantee. We ask whether a partial, caller-sufficient contract, rather than a full behavioral specification, is enough. On Frama-C-Problems we strengthen each inferred contract past what the caller needs and measure how much tighter it becomes. It barely moves: for most targets in every model the caller-sufficient contract is already the tightest the loop reaches, and our tightness comparator rates the partial and strengthened contracts equivalent for the large majority of targets it can compare. Partial-spec contracts thus capture nearly all the attainable tightness, so stopping at caller-sufficiency costs almost nothing. The regression check underneath is sound: on the third-party EqBench-C suite it never fabricates an equivalence, returning zero false proofs and reporting an unprovable difference instead. It also surfaced nine pairs that EqBench mislabels as equivalent, more than a concurrent tool reports. The contracts themselves are inferred automatically from the checker's own counterexamples, with no separate specification step; on Frama-C-Problems and the ANSSI X509 parser this reaches a verification rate comparable to tools AutoSpec and Preguss, while a passing result certifies at least as strong a property, which we call \emph{safety-preserving conditional equivalence}: enforcement plus caller-sufficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first contract-based regression verification tool that uses automatically inferred, caller-sufficient partial contracts to verify that patches preserve intended behavior. The contracts are sound, require no manual specifications, and achieve verification rates comparable to existing tools while providing a stronger property called safety-preserving conditional equivalence.
AI.motivation: Software evolves continuously, but ensuring patches preserve intended behavior without re-verifying the entire codebase is difficult. Existing regression verification techniques require expensive whole-program reasoning or manually written specifications that are rarely available in practice.
AI.method: The tool infers partial contracts automatically from the checker's own counterexamples, requiring no separate specification step. Contract soundness is ensured by proving all function versions match the behavior. The contracts then verify program flow via assume-guarantee reasoning. The approach uses "caller-sufficient" (partial) contracts rather than full behavioral specifications.
AI.result: On Frama-C-Problems, strengthening inferred contracts past what the caller needs barely tightens them; partial contracts already capture nearly all attainable tightness. On the EqBench-C suite, the tool never fabricates equivalence (zero false proofs) and reported nine pairs mislabeled as equivalent by EqBench. On Frama-C-Problems and ANSSI X509 parser, verification rates are comparable to AutoSpec and Preguss.
AI.conclusion: Partial-spec (caller-sufficient) contracts capture nearly all attainable tightness, so stopping at caller-sufficiency costs almost nothing. The regression check is sound. A passing result certifies safety-preserving conditional equivalence: enforcement plus caller-sufficiency.

title: Feedback-Coupled Memory Systems in Continuous Time
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures. Extends arXiv:2603.11560 to continuous time. Code: github.com/stevefatz95/fcms-continuous
summary: The Feedback-Coupled Memory Systems (FCMS) architecture formalizes closed-loop coordination through four abstract operators, two of which - the agent update operator $f_i$ and the environmental update operator $Ψ$ - are left axiomatically undefined in the original framework. To address this, $f_i$ is defined by Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), where agents update locally through a decentralized price mechanism and economic principles, and $Ψ$ is defined by the Coupled Memory Graph Process (CMGP), a non-Markovian framework where the environment is treated as a physical substrate that records and responds to trajectory history coherently without external forcing. The resulting continuous-time FCMS instantiation achieves Lyapunov global dissipativity governed by the computable threshold $4β^2 < 2ημγ^2$. This generalizes both the discrete FCMS stability condition $4ηβ^2 < γ$ and CMGP's physical bifurcation threshold $α_c = 1/K$, confirming that memory dissipation must outpace feedback gain as a universal organizing principle. Numerical simulation with $N=2$ agents and mean-field validation at $N=10^6$ confirm the stability threshold and the self-reinforcing coordination cascade that emerges when it is violated.

AI.tldr: The paper defines the two axiomatically undefined operators in FCMS architecture—f_i via Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI) and Ψ via Coupled Memory Graph Process (CMGP)—and proves a Lyapunov global dissipativity condition (4β² < 2ημγ²) that generalizes prior discrete and physical stability criteria, with numerical and mean-field validation showing a coordination cascade when the threshold is violated.
AI.motivation: The FCMS framework left two core operators—agent update f_i and environmental update Ψ—axiomatically undefined, limiting its applicability. This work resolves that gap by providing concrete mechanistic definitions grounded in economic principles (MBI) and non-Markovian physical memory dynamics (CMGP).
AI.method: f_i is defined via decentralized price mechanism and economic principles (Mechanism-Based Intelligence); Ψ is defined via Coupled Memory Graph Process, a non-Markovian framework treating the environment as a physical substrate recording trajectory history coherently. A continuous-time Lyapunov analysis derives the global dissipativity condition 4β² < 2ημγ².
AI.result: The derived condition generalizes both the discrete FCMS stability condition (4ηβ² < γ) and CMGP's physical bifurcation threshold (α_c = 1/K). Numerical simulation (N=2) and mean-field validation (N=10⁶) confirm the threshold and reveal a self-reinforcing coordination cascade when violated.
AI.conclusion: Memory dissipation must outpace feedback gain as a universal organizing principle for closed-loop coordination systems, with the unified threshold bridging discrete algorithmic stability and continuous physical bifurcation.

title: Depth-Entropy Guided Sampling for Training-Free LLM Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become the dominant paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but it requires expensive training, curated data, and reward signals. Recent work shows that sampling from sharpened base-model distributions at test time recovers much of the RL gain, yet existing methods rely solely on output-layer likelihoods and ignore the transformer's internal forward-pass dynamics. We introduce Depth-Entropy Guided Sampling (DEGS), a training-free, test-time method that exploits layer-wise entropy collapse as an intrinsic quality signal. We observe that stronger reasoners -- including RL-posttrained variants -- exhibit a distinctive "late collapse": logit-lens decoded entropy stays elevated until deeper layers before converging. We define a per-sequence collapse depth $D(\mathbf{x})$ and a joint objective $π(\mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x})^α\exp(βD(\mathbf{x}))$ that combines sequence likelihood with this depth-entropy structure, instantiated inside an MCMC power-sampling framework (DEGS-MCMC). Across three open-weight models and four reasoning benchmarks, this near-chance per-candidate signal compounds over the sampling trajectory into state-of-the-art training-free accuracy, with gains largest out of domain and on the harder splits -- exactly where likelihood alone falls short -- at single-digit-percent wall-clock overhead. DEGS narrowly trails an in-house GRPO reference on the math splits GRPO was trained for, yet surpasses it out of domain on GPQA for all three models, without any training, reward model, or labeled data.

AI.tldr: DEGS is a training-free, test-time method that uses layer-wise entropy collapse in transformers to improve reasoning, outperforming likelihood-only sampling and rivaling RL-trained models on out-of-domain tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time sampling methods only use output-layer likelihoods, ignoring internal transformer dynamics. Meanwhile, RL improves reasoning but requires expensive training, curated data, and reward signals. The authors aim to exploit intrinsic layer-wise entropy patterns as a free quality signal.
AI.method: DEGS defines per-sequence collapse depth D(x) from logit-lens decoded entropy, and combines it with sequence likelihood via a joint objective π(x) ∝ p(x)^α exp(βD(x)), instantiated inside an MCMC power-sampling framework (DEGS-MCMC).
AI.result: Across three open-weight models and four reasoning benchmarks, DEGS achieves state-of-the-art training-free accuracy with single-digit-percent overhead. It trails in-house GRPO on math splits but surpasses it out-of-domain on GPQA for all three models, with largest gains on harder splits where likelihood alone fails.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise entropy collapse is a cheap, effective intrinsic signal for test-time reasoning improvement. DEGS demonstrates that near-chance per-candidate signals can compound over sampling trajectories to match or exceed RL-trained models without any training, reward model, or labeled data.

title: Compression Asymmetry and Trajectory Binding in Noise-Anchored Diffusion Inversion
summary: Real-image diffusion inversion is governed by a tight quality-cost trade-off, with costs incurred in computation, storage, or per-image optimization. We study this trade-off through the forward Gaussian noise anchor that defines a diffusion trajectory and isolate two mechanisms behind effective stored-noise inversion. First, diffusion noise exhibits an element-wise compression asymmetry: int8 full-dimensional anchors preserve reconstruction, whereas low-dimensional subspace summaries are much less reliable, often collapsing even at comparable or smaller payloads; the element-wise over subspace ordering persists across five stored-noise inversion methods. Second, inversion is trajectory-bound and score-prior coupled: the matched forward anchor and a trained score network are both necessary, arguing against a purely algebraic-identity explanation. Together, these findings specify what to store and how to use it. They lead to Noise-Anchored Reverse Correction (NARC), a training-free inversion primitive that stores a single int8 latent anchor and reuses it with a fixed, noise-level-dependent anchor-weight schedule: strong anchoring when the reverse trajectory is noise-dominated, then relaxed anchoring as image detail emerges. On PIE-Bench++ with Stable Diffusion 1.5, NARC outperforms five modern non-exact baselines and improves PSNR by +3.24 dB over PnP DirectInv while using about 400x less inversion storage than PnP DirectInv. The compression asymmetry, anchor specificity, and editing plug-in also transfer to SDXL 1024^2.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the quality-cost trade-off in real-image diffusion inversion, identifying that element-wise int8 noise anchors preserve reconstruction much better than low-dimensional subspace summaries, and that inversion relies on both the matched forward anchor and trained score network. Based on these findings, the authors propose NARC, a training-free inversion method that stores a single int8 latent anchor with a noise-level-dependent weight schedule, achieving +3.24 dB PSNR improvement over PnP DirectInv on PIE-Bench++ while using ~400x less storage.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind stored-noise diffusion inversion and resolve the quality-cost trade-off that plagues existing methods, which incur high costs in computation, storage, or per-image optimization.
AI.method: The authors isolate two key mechanisms: (1) element-wise compression asymmetry, where int8 full-dimensional anchors maintain reconstruction quality while low-dimensional subspace summaries collapse; (2) trajectory-bound and score-prior coupled inversion requiring both the matched forward anchor and trained score network. They then propose NARC (Noise-Anchored Reverse Correction), a training-free primitive that stores a single int8 latent anchor and applies a noise-level-dependent anchor-weight schedule (strong anchoring early, relaxed anchoring later).
AI.result: NARC outperforms five non-exact baselines on PIE-Bench++ with SD 1.5, improving PSNR by +3.24 dB over PnP DirectInv while using ~400x less inversion storage. The compression asymmetry, anchor specificity, and editing plug-in transfer to SDXL 1024^2 as well.
AI.conclusion: Element-wise noise anchors (int8) are vastly superior to subspace summaries for diffusion inversion, and inversion is fundamentally trajectory-bound and score-coupled. NARC provides a practical, training-free solution that achieves state-of-the-art quality with drastically reduced storage requirements.

title: BeatEdit: Symbolic Music Generation as Explicit Editing
summary: Music creation is fundamentally a process of revision. Yet symbolic music generation remains dominated by paradigms that produce complete sequences from scratch, with limited support for selective modification. Edit-based methods have proven effective for text transformation tasks, but remain largely unexplored for symbolic music. We trace this absence to the representational level: conventional event-based music encodings lack the structural properties required by explicit music editing. In contrast, the BEAT encoding, a beat-grid-anchored representation originally designed for autoregressive generation, possesses structural properties amenable to editing. We propose BeatEdit, the first framework for symbolic music generation based on explicit edit operations, recasting generation as producing new content by editing a draft rather than synthesizing from scratch. BeatEdit comprises three complementary mechanisms along an axis of increasing edit density: per-token sequence tagging for error correction, iterative refinement for accompaniment editing, and tag-then-fill for segment completion. All these mechanisms share a single encoding and pre-trained backbone, achieving higher precision and perceptual quality than autoregressive and diffusion methods across all three tasks, while remaining efficient, with single-pass inference completing in under 100 ms. Cross-encoding evaluation further reveals that encoding design substantially influences editing effectiveness, with notable encoding-method interaction effects. Code is available at https://github.com/Haoyu-Gu/BeatEdit-code

AI.tldr: BeatEdit is the first framework for symbolic music generation based on explicit edit operations, using a beat-grid-anchored representation (BEAT encoding) to enable three editing mechanisms (per-token tagging, iterative refinement, tag-then-fill) that outperform autoregressive and diffusion methods across all tasks with single-pass inference under 100ms.
AI.motivation: Music creation is fundamentally a process of revision, yet symbolic music generation lacks support for selective modification. Edit-based methods are unexplored for symbolic music due to conventional event-based encodings lacking structural properties needed for editing.
AI.method: BeatEdit uses the BEAT encoding (a beat-grid-anchored representation) and comprises three complementary mechanisms: per-token sequence tagging for error correction, iterative refinement for accompaniment editing, and tag-then-fill for segment completion. All share a single encoding and pre-trained backbone.
AI.result: BeatEdit achieves higher precision and perceptual quality than autoregressive and diffusion methods across all three tasks, with efficient single-pass inference completing in under 100ms. Cross-encoding evaluation reveals that encoding design substantially influences editing effectiveness with notable encoding-method interaction effects.
AI.conclusion: Edit-based generation using BEAT encoding is effective for symbolic music, outperforming existing paradigms while being computationally efficient. Encoding design is a critical factor for editing effectiveness in music generation.

title: A Framework for Managing the Models of Engineered Quantum Systems
summary: Quantum technologies are maturing into systems that classical engineering must build, verify and maintain. The model-driven community has begun to respond with quantum-aware pipelines and languages, and the domain models these produce must be synchronised with the heterogeneous models created and owned by other communities. We argue that existing synchronisation approaches are insufficient for engineered quantum systems. A quantum system description captures superposition and entanglement, which a model transformation could remove undetected, while every structural check passes. To address this, we present the Quantum Systems Model Management (QSysMM) Framework, which guides the construction and synchronisation of the models of a quantum system into a digital single source of truth. The framework features four concerns: ontological, abstraction, composition and exposure, each given the treatment that engineered quantum systems require. Within this framework, we propose a Quantum Systems Modelling Language (QSysML) on the SysML v2 technology stack, and we close with a proposal that matures this synchronisation core into full model management for quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper argues existing model synchronisation approaches fail for quantum systems because they cannot detect loss of superposition and entanglement, and proposes QSysMM (Quantum Systems Model Management) Framework with QSysML language on SysML v2 stack to address this.
AI.motivation: Existing model synchronization approaches are insufficient for engineered quantum systems because they cannot detect when superposition and entanglement are inadvertently removed during model transformations, while all structural checks still pass.
AI.method: The QSysMM Framework is proposed, featuring four concerns: ontological, abstraction, composition, and exposure, each specifically tailored for engineered quantum systems. A Quantum Systems Modelling Language (QSysML) is built on the SysML v2 technology stack as the concrete realization.
AI.result: A framework (QSysMM) and a modelling language (QSysML) that enable construction and synchronization of quantum system models into a digital single source of truth, preventing undetected loss of quantum properties.
AI.conclusion: The synchronisation core should be matured into full model management for quantum systems, as existing approaches are inadequate for preserving quantum-specific properties like superposition and entanglement.

title: AGM-like Paraconsistent Partial Meet Abductive Expansion Operation
summary: In his 1996 doctoral thesis, Maurice Pagnucco created the first AGM-like abductive expansion operation. Taking his operation as a basis, as well as a taxonomy -- inspired by Atocha Aliseda -- responsible for highlighting and formalizing the main components of abductive reasoning, the main aim of this paper is to present a new paraconsistent AGM-like abductive expansion operation -- capable of assimilating contradictory explanatory hypotheses without trivialization and the consequent absurd epistemic state -- with its postulates and its transitively relational partial meet construction. To a large extent, the formal development presented in this paper was only made possible by the recent creation of the paraconsistent logic RCbr, an LFI (Logics of Formal Inconsistencies) that establishes properties especially relevant to belief revision contexts, in particular, the ability to be self-extensional -- i.e., to satisfy the replacement property. This is the first of two papers: the paraconsistent abductive expansion operation announced here -- which is part of a new system called AGMpabd -- despite bringing many interesting features, does not assign any relevant epistemic role to the paraconsistent operators of negation and consistency. Only in a second paper will an analogous paraconsistent abductive expansion operation -- which is part of another new system, AGMcircabd -- be enhanced in this direction. Nevertheless, to the best of my knowledge, the operation developed in this paper is the first of its kind in the AGM literature.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AGMpabd, the first paraconsistent AGM-like abductive expansion operation that can incorporate contradictory explanatory hypotheses without trivialization, built on Pagnucco's work and the logic RCbr.
AI.motivation: To create a paraconsistent abductive expansion operation capable of assimilating contradictory explanatory hypotheses without leading to trivialization or an absurd epistemic state, which was previously impossible in classical AGM frameworks.
AI.method: The operation is built upon Pagnucco's AGM-like abductive expansion and Aliseda's taxonomy of abductive reasoning components, formalized using the paraconsistent logic RCbr (an LFI) that satisfies the replacement property (self-extensionality). The paper provides postulates and a transitively relational partial meet construction for the new operation.
AI.result: The first paraconsistent AGM-like abductive expansion operation (AGMpabd) is formally developed with postulates and construction, capable of handling contradictions without trivialization. However, it does not assign any relevant epistemic role to paraconsistent negation and consistency operators.
AI.conclusion: This is the first of two papers; the current operation (AGMpabd) is a novel contribution to AGM literature as the first of its kind. A second paper (AGMcircabd) will enhance the operation by giving epistemic roles to paraconsistent operators of negation and consistency.

title: Low-Rank Attention Residuals
summary: Attention Residuals replace the fixed residual sum with depthwise attention over previous sub-layer outputs in large language models (LLMs), but use each output as both a full-dimensional key and value. This couples routing with representation and makes depth-routing scores scale with the hidden width $d$. We propose Low-Rank Attention Residuals (LR-AttnRes), which keep full-dimensional residual values while using $r$-dimensional keys, with $r \ll d$, for routing. Projected LR-AttnRes emits learned low-rank keys from existing output projections, decoupling routing from residual content and achieving the best validation loss among the variants tested. Sliced LR-AttnRes uses the last $r$ dimensions of each value as the routing key, removing the auxiliary key-projection path and reducing residual-side FLOPs while still improving performance. Comprehensive sweeps show that depthwise routing can be effective with far fewer dimensions than the model width. We release code and models to facilitate future research.

AI.tldr: LR-AttnRes improves attention residuals in LLMs by using low-rank keys for routing, decoupling routing from representation and reducing computational cost while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: Standard Attention Residuals in LLMs couple routing with representation by using full-dimensional outputs as both keys and values, making depth-routing scores scale with hidden width d. This is computationally inefficient and conceptually conflates what information to route (content) with where to route it (routing decision).
AI.method: Two variants proposed: (1) Projected LR-AttnRes — learns low-rank keys (r-dimensional, r ≪ d) from existing output projections to decouple routing from content; (2) Sliced LR-AttnRes — uses the last r dimensions of each value as the routing key, eliminating auxiliary key projection and further reducing FLOPs.
AI.result: Projected LR-AttnRes achieved the best validation loss among all variants tested. Sliced LR-AttnRes reduced residual-side FLOPs while still improving performance. Depthwise routing is effective with far fewer dimensions than model width.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank routing keys are sufficient for effective depthwise attention in LLMs, and decoupling routing from representation yields both efficiency and quality gains. Code and models are released.

title: Lifelong Representations: A Survey on Continual Self-Supervised Learning for Vision Models
comment: This work has been accepted for publication in IEEE EAIS 2026
summary: Traditionally, continual learning has assumed access to labeled data, yet many real-world applications -- such as lifelong robotics -- require models to adapt continuously from unlabeled streams. This has led to the development of continual self-supervised learning (CSSL), a rapidly growing area that lacks a dedicated, systematic review. In this work, we present a comprehensive survey of CSSL for vision, with connections to emerging vision-language settings. First, we analyze existing evaluation protocols and highlight inconsistencies that hinder fair comparison. We then examine why self-supervised objectives exhibit improved robustness to catastrophic forgetting, relating this to task-agnostic representations and smoother loss landscapes. Next, we organize existing methods into a unified taxonomy based on their forgetting-mitigation strategies, including distillation, replay, regularization, architectural approaches, model merging, and objective-level adaptation. Finally, we identify open challenges such as scalability and the need for fast adaptability. We argue that advancing CSSL requires moving beyond small-scale benchmarks towards continual pre-training paradigms for large-scale systems.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first comprehensive survey of continual self-supervised learning (CSSL) for vision, analyzing evaluation protocols, explaining robustness to catastrophic forgetting, proposing a unified taxonomy of methods, and identifying open challenges including the need for continual pre-training at scale.
AI.motivation: Real-world applications like lifelong robotics require models to adapt from unlabeled data streams, but CSSL lacked a dedicated systematic review despite its rapid growth.
AI.method: The survey analyzes evaluation protocols, examines self-supervised objectives' robustness, organizes methods into a unified taxonomy (distillation, replay, regularization, architectural approaches, model merging, objective-level adaptation), and identifies open challenges.
AI.result: Identified inconsistencies in evaluation protocols; explained that self-supervised objectives resist forgetting due to task-agnostic representations and smoother loss landscapes; proposed a unified taxonomy of mitigation strategies.
AI.conclusion: Advancing CSSL requires moving beyond small-scale benchmarks toward continual pre-training paradigms for large-scale systems.

title: Anysynth:Zero-Shot Instrument Cloning via In-Context Learning and Asymmetric Hierarchical Guidance
summary: Zero-shot instrument cloning aims to render an arbitrary [Target MIDI] sequence with the acoustic identity of an unseen instrument given only a short [Reference Audio, Reference MIDI] pair. Existing methods rely on pre-trained embeddings (e.g., CLAP) that compress the reference audio into a fixed-length vector, discarding fine-grained acoustic cues essential for faithful timbre reconstruction. We present Anysynth, an embedding-free neural synthesizer based on in-context flow matching. By conditioning a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) directly on the uncompressed reference audio and target MIDI, our model allows self-attention to dynamically retrieve acoustic details at generation time. Experiments show that \tool outperforms embedding-based and auto-regressive baselines in audio quality, timbre similarity, and melody adherence. Notably, the model exhibits prompt-length scaling: longer reference prompts yield steadily better timbre fidelity, a property absent in embedding-based systems. To optimize controllability, we further propose Asymmetric Hierarchical CFG, which structurally decouples MIDI and reference-timbre guidance based on their natural semantic-acoustic dependency. This asymmetric formulation avoids gradient conflicts and improves both note accuracy and timbre fidelity, pushing the boundary of expressive, zero-shot instrument cloning. Demo audios are available at https://anysynth-demo.github.io/

AI.tldr: Anysynth is an embedding-free neural synthesizer using in-context flow matching and Diffusion Transformer that achieves zero-shot instrument cloning by conditioning on uncompressed reference audio and target MIDI, outperforming embedding-based methods with prompt-length scaling and improved controllability via Asymmetric Hierarchical CFG.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot instrument cloning methods rely on pre-trained embeddings (e.g., CLAP) that compress reference audio into fixed-length vectors, discarding fine-grained acoustic cues essential for faithful timbre reconstruction.
AI.method: Anysynth uses an embedding-free approach based on in-context flow matching with a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) conditioned directly on uncompressed reference audio and target MIDI, enabling self-attention to dynamically retrieve acoustic details. It also proposes Asymmetric Hierarchical CFG to structurally decouple MIDI and reference-timbre guidance.
AI.result: Outperforms embedding-based and auto-regressive baselines in audio quality, timbre similarity, and melody adherence. Exhibits prompt-length scaling (longer reference prompts yield better timbre fidelity). Asymmetric Hierarchical CFG improves both note accuracy and timbre fidelity by avoiding gradient conflicts.
AI.conclusion: Anysynth pushes the boundary of expressive, zero-shot instrument cloning by preserving fine-grained timbre details through in-context conditioning and offering improved controllability through asymmetric guidance.

title: Model-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Quantum Networks
summary: Quantum networks are advancing towards larger and more operational infrastructures, yet their evaluation remains fragmented across heterogeneous physical platforms, simulators, protocols, and architectural abstractions. Current digital-twin studies for quantum networks mainly realise isolated capabilities or application-specific solutions rather than reusable system-level twins. This paper argues that Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) can provide a systematic basis for integrating and evolving these heterogeneous artefacts. It derives requirements for design-time evaluation and runtime synchronisation, and proposes a progression of architectures from code-driven and domain-model-driven solutions to point-to-point and hub-and-spoke integration. A conceptual implementation case study illustrates this using SysML v2, QKD kit, an EMF-based controller, and SeQUeNCe. The work provides a foundation for adaptable and interoperable digital twins for quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) to create adaptable and interoperable digital twins for quantum networks, addressing the fragmentation across heterogeneous platforms, simulators, and protocols.
AI.motivation: Quantum networks are advancing but their evaluation is fragmented across heterogeneous physical platforms, simulators, protocols, and architectural abstractions. Current digital-twin studies offer only isolated or application-specific solutions rather than reusable system-level twins.
AI.method: The paper derives requirements for design-time evaluation and runtime synchronization, proposes a progression of architectures (code-driven, domain-model-driven, point-to-point, hub-and-spoke), and presents a conceptual implementation case study using SysML v2, QKD kit, EMF-based controller, and SeQUeNCe.
AI.result: A foundation for adaptable and interoperable digital twins for quantum networks is established through MDE-based architecture progression.
AI.conclusion: Model-Driven Engineering provides a systematic basis for integrating and evolving heterogeneous artefacts in quantum network digital twins, enabling reusable system-level solutions.

title: Coresets Before Score Sets: Evaluation-Unsupervised Prompt Subset Selection for LLM Benchmarks
summary: We study LLM benchmark coreset selection: selecting a small subset of prompts over multiple benchmarks whose induced model scores and rankings approximate those obtained from the full benchmark suite. In evaluation-unsupervised benchmark coreset selection (our approach), the selection algorithm uses no model evaluation outcomes, and operates on a fine granularity by producing subsets of prompts over multiple benchmarks rather than producing a sub-collection of entire benchmarks. We use submodular subset selection, and we develop and evaluate many different submodular functions for this purpose, including determinantal point process (DPP) based approaches, submodular mutual information functions, and facility location-based functions. On a new large-scale suite of 35 heterogeneous benchmarks spanning five different capability categories, 18 frontier LLMs, and over 61K prompts, we find that the facility location (FL) function operating exclusively on inexpensive semantic prompt embeddings preserves LLM scores better than twelve separate score-based and diversity-based baselines, across a range of coreset budgets. Moreover, we show our proposed objective is not limited to the evaluation-unsupervised regime: in the setting where only a handful of whole benchmarks must be selected and a large amount of model scores are available, the same objective matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on the MMLU and MTEB leaderboards, while being substantially cheaper to compute. Together, our results suggest that submodularity, in general, is a strong and reliable tool for benchmark compression.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an evaluation-unsupervised benchmark coreset selection method using submodular subset selection (specifically facility location based on semantic embeddings) to select a small subset of prompts across multiple benchmarks. It outperforms baselines on 35 benchmarks with 18 LLMs and 61K+ prompts, and also matches/exceeds SOTA on MMLU and MTEB leaderboards at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLMs on large benchmark suites is computationally expensive. The authors aim to efficiently approximate full-benchmark evaluation results (model scores and rankings) using a small, carefully selected subset of prompts drawn across multiple benchmarks, without requiring any model evaluation outcomes during selection.
AI.method: The method is evaluation-unsupervised benchmark coreset selection using submodular subset selection. The authors develop and compare multiple submodular functions: DPP-based approaches, submodular mutual information functions, and facility location-based functions. The facility location function operates on inexpensive semantic prompt embeddings. The approach selects subsets of prompts at fine granularity (across benchmarks) rather than selecting entire benchmarks.
AI.result: On a large-scale suite of 35 heterogeneous benchmarks, 18 frontier LLMs, and 61K+ prompts, the facility location function on semantic embeddings preserves LLM scores better than twelve score-based and diversity-based baselines across various coreset budgets. In the whole-benchmark selection setting, it matches/outperforms SOTA on MMLU and MTEB leaderboards with lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Submodularity is a strong and reliable tool for benchmark compression, effective in both unsupervised (no model scores needed) and supervised (with available scores) regimes.

title: FedCausal-Dyn: A Causal-Dynamic Paradigm for Federated Learning under Dynamic Feature Drift
summary: This paper addresses the challenging problem of dynamic feature drift in federated learning, where data distributions evolve across clients and over time -- a common scenario in real-world applications like financial technology. Existing approaches often assume static drift, limiting their effectiveness in non-stationary environments. To overcome this, we propose \textbf{FedCausal-Dyn}, a novel federated learning framework built on a causal-dynamic paradigm. Its key innovation is \textit{causal-domain feature separation}, which disentangles domain-invariant causal features from spurious, domain-specific variations via specialized projection heads and adversarial training. This enables \textit{reliable and dynamic prototype aggregation}, weighting local class prototypes by estimated reliability before global aggregation. We further introduce \textit{causal-feature guided collaborative regularization}, unifying prototype contrastive alignment and domain invariance into a cohesive objective. Extensive experiments on three federated domain generalization benchmarks demonstrate that FedCausal-Dyn consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the highest average accuracy and the most stable results. Ablation studies confirm each component's critical contribution. Our work provides a robust and principled solution for federated learning under dynamic feature drift.

AI.tldr: FedCausal-Dyn is a federated learning framework that handles dynamic feature drift by separating causal (domain-invariant) features from spurious (domain-specific) variations, using reliability-weighted prototype aggregation and causal-feature guided collaborative regularization, achieving state-of-the-art results on domain generalization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing federated learning approaches assume static data drift, which is ineffective in real-world non-stationary environments like financial technology where data distributions evolve across clients and over time.
AI.method: (1) Causal-domain feature separation via projection heads and adversarial training to disentangle invariant causal features from spurious domain-specific variations; (2) Dynamic prototype aggregation weighted by estimated reliability; (3) Causal-feature guided collaborative regularization unifying prototype contrastive alignment and domain invariance.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on three federated domain generalization benchmarks, achieving the highest average accuracy and most stable results; ablation studies confirm each component's critical contribution.
AI.conclusion: FedCausal-Dyn provides a robust and principled solution for federated learning under dynamic feature drift.

title: Adversarially Guided Diffusion for LiDAR Range Image Synthesis
comment: Accepted at the 1st Workshop on Secure and Trustworthy AI (STAI 2026), co-located with the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD 2026)
summary: LiDAR semantic segmentation is a key perception task in autonomous driving, where false predictions can affect downstream planning and safety-critical decision-making. Although adversarial attacks, and specifically adversarial examples, have been widely studied for image classification and 3D point cloud segmentation, unrestricted adversarial examples remain largely unexplored in the space of 2D range images, which are projections of 3D point clouds. The proposed method is, to the best of our knowledge, the first diffusion-based unrestricted adversarial attack against 2D range-image segmentation, using adversarial guidance from a segmentation loss. By applying guidance directly during sampling, the method produces unrestricted adversarial examples that remain close to the learned LiDAR data manifold while inducing structured segmentation errors. Experiments on the SemanticKITTI dataset using RangeNet++ and CENet segmentation networks demonstrate that the attack provides adjustable degradation across guidance strengths and transfers across segmentation architectures. Compared with norm-bounded FGSM and SegPGD baselines, the proposed attack offers a distinct effectiveness-realism trade-off, achieving controllable white-box and transfer degradation while maintaining competitive distributional and visual realism.

AI.tldr: First diffusion-based unrestricted adversarial attack on 2D range-image LiDAR segmentation, using adversarial guidance from segmentation loss to produce realistic adversarial examples that induce structured errors while staying on the LiDAR data manifold.
AI.motivation: Adversarial attacks, especially unrestricted adversarial examples, are underexplored for 2D range-image LiDAR semantic segmentation, which is critical for autonomous driving safety and downstream planning.
AI.method: Applies adversarial guidance from a segmentation loss directly during diffusion sampling to generate unrestricted adversarial examples that remain close to the LiDAR data manifold.
AI.result: On SemanticKITTI with RangeNet++ and CENet, the attack achieves adjustable degradation across guidance strengths, transfers across architectures, and offers a controllable effectiveness-realism trade-off compared to FGSM and SegPGD baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diffusion-based approach produces more realistic unrestricted adversarial examples with competitive distributional and visual realism, offering a distinct trade-off between attack effectiveness and realism for 2D range-image segmentation.

title: Evidence Subspace Projection: Measuring How Much Evidence Explains Deepfake Detection in Self-Supervised Speech Models
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) models are widely used as feature extractors for state-of-the-art audio deepfake detection, but it remains unclear how to directly and quantitatively connect what SSL models capture to detection decisions. To address this gap, we propose Evidence Subspace Projection, a method that represents both evidence factors (e.g., attack category, codec, gender, transmission) and authenticity labels in a shared space constructed from SSL models' neuron activation patterns. By projecting the decision vector onto each evidence subspace, we obtain a scalar ratio that quantifies the explanatory power of each evidence type. We evaluate SSL models in raw, fine-tuned, and post-trained settings on multiple datasets. The results confirm findings from established studies, validating the proposed method, and reveal new insights into model behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Evidence Subspace Projection (ESP), a method to quantify how different evidence factors (attack category, codec, gender, transmission) influence SSL-based audio deepfake detection decisions by projecting decision vectors onto evidence subspaces derived from neuron activation patterns.
AI.motivation: SSL models are widely used for audio deepfake detection, but it remains unclear how to directly and quantitatively connect what SSL models capture to their detection decisions.
AI.method: Evidence Subspace Projection (ESP): represents evidence factors and authenticity labels in a shared space from SSL neuron activation patterns, then projects the decision vector onto each evidence subspace to obtain a scalar ratio quantifying explanatory power of each evidence type.
AI.result: Validates the method by confirming findings from established studies, and reveals new insights into model behavior across raw, fine-tuned, and post-trained SSL settings on multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: ESP provides a quantitative way to interpret SSL-based audio deepfake detection by attributing decisions to specific evidence factors.

title: Mitigating LLM Sycophancy in Code Smell Detection Using Evidence-Guided Reasoning Prompts
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code smell detection tasks due to their ability to interpret program semantics. However, their reliability in this context remains poorly explored, particularly under varying prompt conditions where model predictions may be influenced by external cues rather than code characteristics. One such limitation is sycophancy bias, where models tend to align their outputs with user-provided assumptions instead of performing objective analysis. In this paper, we present the first systematic empirical study of sycophancy bias in LLM-based code smell detection. Using the MLCQ dataset, we evaluate how different prompt framings like confirmation bias, contradictory hints, and false premises affect model predictions. Our results show that LLMs are highly sensitive to prompt variations, with Decision Flip Rates reaching up to 72% and False Alignment Rates exceeding 90%, indicating substantial instability and agreement with misleading prompts. To address this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Debiasing Prompting (EGDP), a structured prompting strategy that enforces evidence-first reasoning. EGDP reduces decision instability and improves robustness, lowering Decision Flip Rates to as low as 12% and False Alignment Rates to as low as 21%, while increasing reliance on structurally grounded evidence. Our findings demonstrate that sycophancy bias poses a critical threat to the reliability of LLM-based code smell detection, and that evidence-guided reasoning provides an effective and generalizable mitigation approach.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies sycophancy bias in LLM-based code smell detection, showing that LLMs are highly susceptible to misleading prompts (up to 72% Decision Flip Rate and 90% False Alignment Rate). The authors propose Evidence-Guided Debiasing Prompting (EGDP), which reduces flip rates to 12% and false alignment to 21%, demonstrating an effective mitigation strategy.
AI.motivation: The reliability of LLMs in code smell detection under varying prompt conditions remains poorly explored, particularly regarding sycophancy bias where models align with user-provided assumptions rather than performing objective analysis.
AI.method: Using the MLCQ dataset, the authors systematically evaluate sycophancy bias by introducing different prompt framings (confirmation bias, contradictory hints, false premises). They then propose Evidence-Guided Debiasing Prompting (EGDP), a structured prompting strategy enforcing evidence-first reasoning.
AI.result: LLMs show high sensitivity to prompt variations with Decision Flip Rates up to 72% and False Alignment Rates exceeding 90%. EGDP reduces Decision Flip Rates to as low as 12% and False Alignment Rates to as low as 21%, improving robustness and reliance on structural evidence.
AI.conclusion: Sycophancy bias poses a critical threat to the reliability of LLM-based code smell detection, and evidence-guided reasoning (EGDP) provides an effective and generalizable mitigation approach.

title: A Dynamic Scene Interaction Reasoning Framework for Scene-level Lane-Change Intention and Trajectory Prediction of Multiple Interacting Vehicles
summary: Safe motion planning in advanced driver-assistance systems and autonomous vehicles requires an accurate understanding of how the surrounding traffic scene is likely to evolve. However, many existing lane-change prediction methods remain centered on a single target vehicle, while multi-agent forecasting approaches often describe scene evolution only through future positions and provide limited explicit information about the maneuver associated with each vehicle. This study proposes a dynamic scene graph attention framework that predicts the lane-change intention and future trajectory of every relevant vehicle within a local traffic scene. The scene is represented as a time-varying interaction graph in which vehicles are modeled as nodes and their spatial and kinematic relationships are encoded through explicit edge features. Temporal graph-attention message passing captures evolving inter-vehicle dependencies and pre-maneuver cues, while an intention-guided decoder links each predicted maneuver to its corresponding future motion. A scene-level consistency objective further encourages compatible multi-vehicle futures. Experiments on the NGSIM I-80, NGSIM US-101, and highD datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines. DSiGAT achieves intention prediction accuracies of 90.12% and 90.97% on NGSIM I-80 and US-101, respectively, and reduces trajectory RMSE by up to 52.94% relative to the strongest baseline. It also produces lower inter-agent collision rates and joint displacement errors, indicating more coherent scene-level predictions. Ablation, sensitivity, robustness, and qualitative analyses further validate the contribution of the proposed components and the effectiveness of the scene-focused formulation.

AI.tldr: DSiGAT is a dynamic scene graph attention framework that jointly predicts lane-change intentions and future trajectories for all vehicles in a traffic scene, using temporal graph-attention message passing and scene-level consistency, outperforming baselines on NGSIM and highD datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing lane-change prediction methods focus on single target vehicles, while multi-agent forecasting approaches only predict future positions without explicit maneuver information. A unified framework for both intention and trajectory prediction of all relevant vehicles is needed.
AI.method: A dynamic scene graph attention framework where vehicles are nodes with explicit edge features encoding spatial/kinematic relationships. Temporal graph-attention message passing captures evolving inter-vehicle dependencies. An intention-guided decoder links predicted maneuvers to future motion, with a scene-level consistency objective for compatible multi-vehicle futures.
AI.result: Intention prediction accuracies of 90.12% (NGSIM I-80) and 90.97% (US-101). Trajectory RMSE reduced by up to 52.94% relative to the strongest baseline. Lower inter-agent collision rates and joint displacement errors.
AI.conclusion: The scene-focused formulation with explicit interaction modeling and scene-level consistency yields more coherent and accurate multi-vehicle predictions, validated through ablation, sensitivity, robustness, and qualitative analyses.

title: Mitigating Early Training Collapse in CTR Models
summary: Deep neural models for click-through rate prediction often exhibit a sharp decline in validation performance immediately after the first training epoch despite continued improvement in training loss. This instability restricts effective learning and limits model performance. In this study, we analyze this behavior using large-scale industrial datasets and evaluate practical mitigation strategies. While reducing the learning rate provides only incremental gains, controlling feature sparsity yields substantial improvements. Removing highly sparse features and aggregating infrequent feature values stabilizes training, extends useful learning beyond a single epoch, and improves both offline evaluation metrics and online system performance.

AI.tldr: Deep CTR prediction models suffer from validation performance collapse after the first epoch despite training loss improvement. Analysis on industrial datasets shows that controlling feature sparsity (removing sparse features, aggregating infrequent values) stabilizes training, enables multi-epoch learning, and improves offline/online metrics, while learning rate reduction offers only marginal benefits.
AI.motivation: To understand and mitigate the sharp decline in validation performance after the first training epoch in deep CTR prediction models, a phenomenon that restricts effective learning and limits model performance.
AI.method: Analyzed the instability using large-scale industrial datasets; evaluated practical mitigation strategies including reducing learning rate (incremental gains) and controlling feature sparsity via removing highly sparse features and aggregating infrequent feature values.
AI.result: Controlling feature sparsity substantially stabilizes training, extends useful learning beyond a single epoch, and improves both offline evaluation metrics and online system performance. Reducing learning rate provides only incremental gains.
AI.conclusion: Feature sparsity control is an effective practical strategy to overcome the first-epoch validation collapse in CTR models, enabling deeper training and better performance.

title: MVMGNN;Multi-View Masked Graph Neural Network for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis using Structural MRI
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder, and early diagnosis is of great significance for delaying disease progression and enabling timely intervention. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), which represents an intermediate clinical stage between cognitively normal aging and AD. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) provides detailed characterization of anatomical structures and plays an important role in AD-related brain analysis. However, existing sMRI-based brain network methods typically rely on a single graph construction strategy, limiting their ability to jointly capture spatial relationships and morphological similarities between brain regions.
