WebDesignIter works in two stages: design-informed planning pulls historical context and architectural overviews from WebAppArchKG to produce an implementation plan with corresponding test scripts, and design-aware generation executes that plan through targeted diff-based patches, validated by sandbox execution and automatic syntax repair. On Web-Bench, WebDesignIter delivers an average Pass@2 gain of 9.55 percentage points across nine foundation models over existing baselines. More importantly, WebDesignIter outperforms every general-purpose coding agent Claude Code, OpenHands, SWE-Agent, Codex CLI on every model configuration, posting the highest Pass@1 and Pass@2 while consuming 2530 fewer input tokens. Ablation singles out design knowledge as the most impactful component: stripping it drops Pass@1 by 11.40 percentage points, a degradation far larger than removing code-graph retrieval, patch-based generation, or sandbox verification, confirming that design knowledge provides a fundamentally more efficient and reliable path to repository-level code generation.

AI.tldr: WebDesignIter is a framework that uses a persistent knowledge graph (WebAppArchKG) to fuse repository structure with design knowledge for repository-level front-end code generation, achieving 9.55 percentage points Pass@2 improvement over baselines and outperforming general-purpose coding agents while using fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Current LLM coding agents tuned for single-shot tasks cannot reliably track complex cross-file dependencies across multiple iterations in front-end development, leading to functional regressions and unmaintainable code. The missing piece is design knowledge—architectural principles, module responsibilities, and structural constraints that developers use to keep code readable, maintainable, and evolvable.
AI.method: WebDesignIter operates in two stages: (1) design-informed planning, which pulls historical context and architectural overviews from WebAppArchKG to produce an implementation plan with test scripts; (2) design-aware generation, which executes the plan through targeted diff-based patches, validated by sandbox execution and automatic syntax repair.
AI.result: On Web-Bench, WebDesignIter achieves an average Pass@2 gain of 9.55 percentage points across nine foundation models over baselines. It outperforms Claude Code, OpenHands, SWE-Agent, and Codex CLI on every model configuration with the highest Pass@1 and Pass@2 while consuming 25-30 fewer input tokens. Ablation shows removing design knowledge drops Pass@1 by 11.40 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Design knowledge is the most impactful component for repository-level code generation, providing a fundamentally more efficient and reliable path than code-graph retrieval, patch-based generation, or sandbox verification alone.

title: LegalFarePlan: A Label-Setting Framework for Fare-Transparent Urban Rail Route Planning under Non-Additive Fare Rules
comment: 6 pages, 4 tables; author preprint version, not the conference camera-ready version
summary: Urban rail fare systems may be non-additive: the fare of a single paid journey from an origin to a destination can differ from the sum of fares over multiple legally separated journey legs. This paper presents LegalFarePlan, a fare-transparent route-planning framework that models legal exit-and-reentry operations as explicit, auditable constraints. Given a transit network, fare function, transfer rules, station-level exit/re-entry costs, an extra-time budget, and a split limit, the planner computes explainable route plans over paid journey segments. The artifact implements Dijkstra shortest-time and direct route-planner baselines, a greedy split heuristic, bounded exact label-setting, and Pareto-frontier search. Evaluation uses controlled synthetic data and a 57-station semi-synthetic benchmark with 360 OD pairs. On the semi-synthetic benchmark, bounded exact search identifies positive modeled fare reductions for 71.11% of OD pairs, with mean reduction 3.78 and maximum reduction 9.0 synthetic fare units under a 45-minute extra-time budget. These results demonstrate method behavior and reproducibility; they are not empirical conclusions about MTR or any transit operator.

AI.tldr: LegalFarePlan is a fare-transparent route-planning framework that models legal exit-and-reentry operations to handle non-additive urban rail fare systems. Using bounded exact search on a semi-synthetic benchmark, it achieves positive fare reductions for 71.11% of OD pairs with a mean reduction of 3.78 fare units under a 45-minute extra-time budget.
AI.motivation: Urban rail fare systems may be non-additive (the fare of a single journey can differ from the sum of fares over multiple legally separated journey legs), which existing route planners do not account for transparently.
AI.method: The framework models legal exit-and-reentry operations as explicit, auditable constraints, and implements Dijkstra shortest-time and direct route-planner baselines, a greedy split heuristic, bounded exact label-setting, and Pareto-frontier search.
AI.result: On a semi-synthetic benchmark (57 stations, 360 OD pairs) with a 45-minute extra-time budget, bounded exact search identifies positive modeled fare reductions for 71.11% of OD pairs, with mean reduction of 3.78 and maximum reduction of 9.0 synthetic fare units.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate method behavior and reproducibility, but are not empirical conclusions about any specific transit operator.

title: Gauge dependence and structured-output corruption in sign-branched repetition penalties: measurements across models, inference stacks, and alternative repetition controls
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code, data, per-stack survey and git genealogy: https://github.com/captainpete/repetition-penalty-gauge
summary: The multiplicative repetition penalty shipped across the LLM inference ecosystem (HuggingFace, vLLM, llama.cpp, and a dozen further engines) branches on the sign of each raw logit (divide positives by theta, multiply negatives). But the softmax is unchanged by adding a constant to every logit, so a model's logit zero-point is arbitrary, and the sign-branch reads that arbitrary point. The sign-branch is itself the accepted fix for an earlier bug, so the accepted fix branches on a quantity the training objective leaves unconstrained. Two measurable consequences follow. (1) The penalty is not well-defined: re-centring a model's logits by a constant is a provable no-op at theta=1, yet at a routine theta=1.3 it changes 58-96% of greedy tokens, where subtractive and normalized penalties change none; real checkpoints sit at widely different zero-points, so a fixed repetition_penalty is a different operation on every model. (2) It corrupts structured output: on 200 real-world JSON schemas, theta=1.3 drops the rate of valid, schema-conformant output from 97% to 23%. In our measurements, applying the penalty to normalized log-probabilities instead of raw logits removes both effects. HuggingFace already ships that operator (LogitNormalization); today it is off by default and applied after the penalty. This note gives the mechanism, the measurements (five models up to 7B, base and RLHF, on WikiText-103 prefixes; two code models on HumanEval and JSONSchemaBench; both effects replicated inside vLLM and llama.cpp through their own samplers on the same inputs), and the normalized variant.

AI.tldr: The multiplicative repetition penalty used across LLM inference engines branches on the sign of raw logits, but the softmax is shift-invariant, making the zero-point arbitrary. This causes (1) inconsistent penalty effects across models (58-96% token changes at theta=1.3) and (2) corrupted structured output (valid JSON drops from 97% to 23%). Applying the penalty to normalized log-probabilities instead of raw logits fixes both issues.
AI.motivation: To identify and document a fundamental bug in the widely-adopted multiplicative repetition penalty implementation: it branches on logit signs, which are undefined due to softmax shift-invariance, causing inconsistent and harmful behavior across models and tasks.
AI.method: The authors analyze the mathematical formulation of the penalty (divide positives by theta, multiply negatives), demonstrate its reliance on arbitrary zero-points, and empirically measure its effects across five models (up to 7B, base and RLHF) on WikiText-103, HumanEval, and JSONSchemaBench. They replicate findings in vLLM and llama.cpp, and propose a fix: apply the penalty to normalized log-probabilities (LogitNormalization) instead of raw logits.
AI.result: (1) At theta=1.3, the sign-branch penalty changes 58-96% of greedy tokens across models, while subtractive/normalized penalties change none. (2) Valid JSON output drops from 97% to 23% when using theta=1.3 on 200 real-world JSON schemas. Both effects replicate in vLLM and llama.cpp.
AI.conclusion: The sign-branch repetition penalty is ill-defined due to softmax's shift invariance. Normalizing log-probabilities before applying the penalty eliminates both issues. The fix is already available (LogitNormalization in HuggingFace) but currently off by default and applied after the penalty.

title: Reliability-Aware Ensemble Classification Under Class Imbalance: A Calibration Study on Liquid-Based Cervical Cytology
summary: Cervical cytology classification models are typically evaluated on curated, class-balanced benchmarks, but real-world liquid-based cytology (LBC) collections are often small and class-imbalanced. This paper presents a class-imbalance-aware and calibration-aware ensemble classification study on the Mendeley LBC dataset, using its native four-class Bethesda taxonomy (NILM, LSIL, HSIL, SCC) rather than a collapsed binary formulation. Three lightweight architectures (Swin-Tiny, TinyViT-5M, DenseNet121) are trained directly on Mendeley LBC using weighted random sampling to counteract class imbalance, and compared against two soft-voting ensembles (Hybrid-2, Hybrid-3). Post-hoc temperature scaling is fit on a held-out calibration subset carved out of the training portion of each cross-validation fold, distinct from both the training data used to fit model weights and the evaluation fold used for final metrics, avoiding the optimistic calibration estimates that result when the same data is used for both purposes. Calibration substantially reduces expected calibration error, Brier score, and negative log-likelihood for every model and ensemble configuration tested, while discrimination metrics (accuracy, macro-F1, macro-AUROC) remain essentially unchanged. Ensemble size shows no consistent additional reliability benefit over the best individual model once all configurations are properly calibrated. Confusion matrices show that all classification errors, across every configuration, are confined to the boundary between high-grade lesions (HSIL) and carcinoma (SCC); no errors involve the negative (NILM) or low-grade (LSIL) categories. These results suggest that, for this dataset, calibration is the dominant lever for reliability, not ensemble size, though this conclusion should be read in light of the dataset's modest size.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates class-imbalance-aware and calibration-aware ensemble models on the Mendeley LBC dataset using the full Bethesda taxonomy (NILM, LSIL, HSIL, SCC). It shows post-hoc temperature scaling calibration substantially improves reliability metrics (ECE, Brier, NLL) without affecting discrimination, and that ensemble size offers no additional reliability benefit over a well-calibrated individual model. All classification errors occur only at the HSIL-SCC boundary.
AI.motivation: Real-world LBC datasets are small and class-imbalanced, yet cervical cytology models are typically evaluated on curated, balanced benchmarks. The paper aims to address the gap by studying calibration and ensemble methods under realistic, imbalanced conditions using the native four-class Bethesda system.
AI.method: Three lightweight architectures (Swin-Tiny, TinyViT-5M, DenseNet121) are trained on the Mendeley LBC dataset with weighted random sampling. Two soft-voting ensembles (Hybrid-2, Hybrid-3) are compared. Post-hoc temperature scaling is applied on a held-out calibration subset carved from the training portion of each cross-validation fold, ensuring strict separation from training and evaluation data.
AI.result: Calibration significantly reduces ECE, Brier score, and NLL for all models/ensembles without changing accuracy, macro-F1, or macro-AUROC. Ensemble size does not consistently improve reliability over the best individual calibrated model. All errors are confined to the HSIL-SCC boundary; no errors involve NILM or LSIL.
AI.conclusion: Calibration is the dominant lever for reliability in this dataset, not ensemble size. However, this conclusion is tempered by the dataset's modest size.

title: Commenting with Copilot: A Taxonomy and Multi-Year Analysis of Student Code-Generation Specifications
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted in the Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference (SIGCSE Virtual 2026)
summary: As AI code tools become integrated into programming environments, students increasingly describe intended behavior in natural language and rely on these tools to generate code, shifting emphasis from code writing to specification. Yet little is known about the comments students write as specifications in AI-assisted programming tasks. We analyze a four-year dataset of undergraduate programming submissions and reflections from tasks in which students wrote comments to guide code generation and refined solutions using test-case feedback. We introduce a taxonomy spanning three dimensions: comment type, code expression level, and code construct. Using automated classification, we examine how these dimensions vary across attempts and how students describe the process in their reflections. Our findings show that students mostly wrote natural-language What comments, shifted toward How comments for more procedural constructs, and focused more on verifying generated code than on repeatedly rewriting comments.

AI.tldr: Study analyzing student comments as specifications in AI-assisted programming tasks, introducing a taxonomy of comment types and examining how students shift from describing what code should do (What comments) to how it should work (How comments) across attempts, with students focusing more on verifying generated code than rewriting comments.
AI.motivation: As AI code tools become integrated into programming education, students increasingly describe intended behavior in natural language rather than writing code directly. However, little is known about the comments students write as specifications in AI-assisted programming tasks, motivating this investigation.
AI.method: Analyzed a four-year dataset of undergraduate programming submissions and reflections from AI-assisted tasks. Introduced a taxonomy spanning three dimensions (comment type, code expression level, code construct) and used automated classification to examine how these dimensions vary across attempts and how students describe the process in their reflections.
AI.result: Students mostly wrote natural-language What comments, shifted toward How comments for more procedural constructs, and focused more on verifying generated code than on repeatedly rewriting comments.
AI.conclusion: In AI-assisted programming, students' commenting behavior shifts from specification (What) to implementation details (How) for procedural constructs, and students prioritize code verification over iterative comment refinement.

title: BatteryLake: Agentic, Physics-Grounded Curation of Heterogeneous Battery Aging Data and Benchmarking
comment: The platform, benchmark, and curation protocol are publicly available at https://tianwen1209.github.io/batterylake/
summary: Public battery aging datasets are a critical asset for advanced health management, but their practical use is often limited by inconsistent formats, unclear schemas, and metadata scattered across repositories and publications. Current curation remains largely manual and hard to reproduce, while general-purpose data integration tools miss the domain-specific semantics of electrochemical time-series data. We present BatteryLake, a governed data lakehouse that turns raw public battery data into benchmark-ready assets through an agentic, physics-grounded curation framework, with three contributions. First, LLM agents extract metadata and synthesize dataset-specific converters, grounding every output in verbatim evidence and abstaining when none supports a value. Second, a human-in-the-loop mechanism frames verification as selective prediction and gates admitted data through 26 schema, statistical, and physical-plausibility rules. Third, we release an open benchmark of 41 datasets from over 25 institutions, with standardized SOH and RUL tasks, three split protocols, and eight baseline model families. The platform, benchmark, and curation protocol are publicly available at https://tianwen1209.github.io/batterylake/.

AI.tldr: BatteryLake is a governed data lakehouse that uses LLM agents and human-in-the-loop verification to automatically curate 41 public battery aging datasets into standardized, benchmark-ready assets with consistent schemas, metadata, and evaluation protocols.
AI.motivation: Public battery aging datasets are inconsistently formatted, lack clear schemas, and have scattered metadata, making practical use difficult. Current curation is manual and not reproducible, and general data tools fail to capture domain-specific electrochemical semantics.
AI.method: Three contributions: (1) LLM agents extract metadata and generate dataset-specific converters grounded in verbatim evidence; (2) Human-in-the-loop verification via selective prediction, gating data through 26 schema, statistical, and physical-plausibility rules; (3) Release of an open benchmark with 41 datasets, standardized SOH/RUL tasks, three split protocols, and eight baseline model families.
AI.result: A curated platform and benchmark comprising 41 datasets from over 25 institutions, with standardized tasks (SOH, RUL), three evaluation split protocols, and eight baseline model families. Platform, benchmark, and curation protocol are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Automated, physics-grounded curation via agentic frameworks and domain-specific rules can transform raw public battery data into reproducible, benchmark-ready assets, advancing battery health management research.

title: Metadata-Free Meta-Reweighted Direct Preference Optimization under Noisy Preference Labels
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become an important method for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences because it removes the need for explicit reward modeling and reinforcement learning optimization. However, its performance depends heavily on the quality of preference data, and noisy preference data in real-world settings can weaken alignment performance. To address this issue, we propose a bilevel optimization framework and prove, under certain assumptions, that this framework can recover the DPO optimum under clean data. We further derive a prior form for the learnable weighting function under asymmetric label-flipping noise. Considering that high-quality metadata may be difficult to obtain, we propose a task-agnostic meta-knowledge-driven method that enables meta-learning even when metadata is completely unavailable. To reduce the high cost of higher-order gradients in LLM meta-learning, we combine central-difference approximation with LoRA fine-tuning and develop a scalable training scheme. Experiments on TL;DR summarization and Anthropic HH single-turn dialogue show that the proposed method improves training performance over multiple DPO baselines under different noise rates.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses DPO's vulnerability to noisy preference data by proposing a bilevel optimization framework with a learnable weighting function, meta-learning for noise-robust alignment, and a scalable training scheme using central-difference approximation with LoRA. Experiments show improvements over DPO baselines under various noise rates.
AI.motivation: DPO's alignment performance degrades significantly in real-world settings due to noisy preference data; existing methods lack robustness to label-flipping noise without explicit reward modeling.
AI.method: A bilevel optimization framework is proposed to recover DPO's clean-data optimum under noisy conditions. A learnable weighting function with a prior form for asymmetric label-flipping noise is derived. A task-agnostic meta-knowledge-driven approach enables meta-learning without metadata. Central-difference approximation combined with LoRA fine-tuning reduces higher-order gradient costs for scalable training.
AI.result: The proposed method improves training performance over multiple DPO baselines under different noise rates on TL;DR summarization and Anthropic HH single-turn dialogue datasets.
AI.conclusion: The bilevel optimization framework with meta-learning and scalable training successfully mitigates the impact of noisy preference data on DPO alignment, achieving more robust performance without requiring explicit reward modeling or high-quality metadata.

title: Prompting-MammAlps: Fine-Grained Text-to-Video Retrieval for Camera-Trap Data
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026; Project page: https://cnai.epfl.ch/prompting-mammalps
summary: Automatically retrieving videos from large camera-trap datasets remains challenging. Text-to-Video retrieval (TVR) methods based on large video-language models (VLMs) have potential to retrieve events of interest by describing them with simple text queries. However, current methods often lack spatiotemporal understanding and do not generalize well to ecological data. In this work, we introduce Prompting-MammAlps, the first camera-trap TVR benchmark, and propose a fine-grained and interpretable TVR method. Specifically, we trained a vision transformer to perform spatiotemporal action localization, and convert its output to structured text, describing each video. Independently, ethology-inspired queries are processed by a Large-Language Model (LLM) based coding agent to parse the structured text per video and retrieve videos accordingly. We harnessed the LLM to use functions from a custom parsing library to minimize the risk of LLM hallucinations and to improve method interpretability. This retrieval approach applied on the Prompting-MammAlps benchmark achieved a set-based F1-score of 34\% on a test set of 135 ecologically-relevant queries and 775 candidate videos. In comparison the best zero-shot VLM achieved a F1-score of 18\%, while also lacking interpretability. Project page: https://cnai.epfl.ch/prompting-mammalps

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Prompting-MammAlps, the first camera-trap Text-to-Video retrieval benchmark, and proposes a fine-grained, interpretable method that uses a vision transformer for spatiotemporal action localization and an LLM-based coding agent for structured text parsing, achieving 34% F1-score vs. 18% for zero-shot VLMs.
AI.motivation: Current Text-to-Video retrieval methods lack spatiotemporal understanding and do not generalize well to ecological camera-trap data, and no dedicated benchmark exists for this domain.
AI.method: A vision transformer is trained for spatiotemporal action localization, converting outputs to structured text per video. An LLM-based coding agent processes ethology-inspired queries using a custom parsing library to retrieve videos, reducing hallucination risks and improving interpretability.
AI.result: Achieved 34% set-based F1-score on 135 queries and 775 candidate videos, outperforming the best zero-shot VLM (18% F1-score).
AI.conclusion: The proposed method significantly outperforms zero-shot VLMs on camera-trap TVR while providing interpretability, establishing the first benchmark for this domain.

title: Maintenance and Support in Community-Driven Scientific Pipeline Ecosystems: A Cross-Platform Empirical Study of nf-core
summary: Community-driven scientific pipeline ecosystems are increasingly important for reproducible data-intensive research, but their sustainability depends on more than workflow engines, templates, and testing infrastructure. It also depends on how communities maintain pipelines, integrate contributions, and support users across heterogeneous execution environments. This paper presents a cross-platform empirical study of maintenance and support in nf-core, a large ecosystem of standardized Nextflow pipelines. We analyze 15,760 GitHub issues, 35,411 GitHub pull requests, and 895 Seqera Community Forum discussions to examine what maintenance and support concerns arise, how they differ across artifact types, which factors are associated with resolution outcomes, and how problems and solutions flow between repository-centered and community-centered spaces. We find that issues primarily capture repository-level problem reporting and maintenance coordination; pull requests capture implementation, review, testing, dependency, and template-update work; and forum discussions capture user-facing support around execution failures, containers, cloud and HPC environments, MultiQC reporting, and Nextflow usage. Resolution outcomes are associated with actionability, coordination, and diagnostic evidence. Issue closure is linked to assignees, comments, milestones, bug labels, error mentions, and version information. Pull request integration varies by author role, automation type, draft status, checklists, linked issues, and review routing. Forum accepted answers are more likely when discussions include code blocks, sustained interaction, and concrete technical evidence, while cloud, HPC, and workflow-semantics questions are harder to resolve. Cross-platform analysis reveals strong repository-internal traceability within GitHub, but limited explicit linkage between forum discussions and repository artifacts.

AI.tldr: This cross-platform empirical study of the nf-core ecosystem analyzes 15,760 GitHub issues, 35,411 pull requests, and 895 forum discussions to understand maintenance and support patterns. Issues handle repository-level reporting, PRs manage implementation and review, and forums address user-facing execution support. Resolution depends on actionability, coordination, and diagnostic evidence. Cross-platform traceability is strong within GitHub but weak between forums and repositories.
AI.motivation: Sustainability of community-driven scientific pipeline ecosystems depends not only on technical infrastructure but also on how communities maintain pipelines, integrate contributions, and support users across heterogeneous environments—an aspect that has been understudied empirically.
AI.method: Cross-platform empirical study analyzing 15,760 GitHub issues, 35,411 GitHub pull requests, and 895 Seqera Community Forum discussions from the nf-core ecosystem, examining maintenance concerns across artifact types, factors associated with resolution outcomes, and information flow between repository-centered and community-centered spaces.
AI.result: Issues capture problem reporting and maintenance coordination; PRs capture implementation, review, testing, dependency, and template-update work; forums capture user-facing support around execution failures, containers, cloud/HPC, MultiQC, and Nextflow usage. Resolution is associated with assignees, comments, milestones, bug labels, error mentions, version info (issues); author role, automation type, draft status, checklists, linked issues, review routing (PRs); code blocks, sustained interaction, technical evidence (forums). Cloud/HPC and workflow-semantics questions are harder to resolve. Strong GitHub-internal traceability but limited forum-repository linkage.
AI.conclusion: Maintenance and support in scientific pipeline ecosystems are distributed across complementary platforms with distinct roles. Improving cross-platform traceability and addressing hard-to-resolve categories (cloud, HPC, workflow semantics) could enhance ecosystem sustainability.

title: How Much Does Correctness Cost? Budgeted Placement of Strong Correctors in a Weak Multi-Agent Swarm
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 1 table.. Code and data: https://github.com/YehudaItkin/budgeted-oracle-placement
summary: A cheap swarm of unreliable agents can be steered to a correct consensus by a few strong, expensive "oracle" correctors. We ask how much one must spend, and where to place the oracles. We model the swarm as a consensus on a graph in which each oracle pins one node toward the truth at a cost-coupled, concave strength, and measure quality by the coherence H(R)=tr M(R)^{-1}. Our first result is that H stays submodular (each added oracle helps less than the last) even when the oracles differ in strength, so a cost-benefit greedy comes within 1-1/e of the best placement at any budget. Inverting the budget gives the budget-correctness frontier B*(eps), the least spend that guarantees an eps-correct consensus: closed-form on the complete graph, and a minimal oracle count k* when oracles cost the same. Whether a budget then buys a few strong oracles or many medium onese curvature of the cost-quality law: diminishing returns favour spreadsharply increasion. Measured onthe Qwen3 ladder (0.6-32B), the law is concave for math verificatio convex foremergent code tracing, so the verdict is genuinely task-dependent.https://github.com/YehudaItkin/budgeted-oracle-placemen

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to optimally place a limited number of "oracle" correctors on a graph to steer a swarm of unreliable agents toward correct consensus, considering cost-coupled concave strengths. It proves submodularity of the coherence function H(R), enabling a greedy algorithm with near-optimal performance, derives budget-correctness frontiers, and shows task-dependent concavity/convexity of the cost-quality law using Qwen3 models.
AI.motivation: To determine the minimal cost and optimal placement strategy for deploying strong oracle correctors to guide a swarm of unreliable agents toward correct consensus, balancing between few strong oracles vs. many medium-strength ones.
AI.method: Models swarm consensus on a graph where each oracle pins a node toward truth with cost-coupled concave strength. Uses coherence H(R)=tr M(R)^{-1} as quality measure. Proves submodularity of H, enabling greedy cost-benefit optimization. Derives closed-form budget-correctness frontier on complete graphs and minimal oracle count for equal-cost oracles. Empirically evaluates curvature of cost-quality law on Qwen3 models (0.6-32B) for math verification and code tracing tasks.
AI.result: Coherence H remains submodular even with differing oracle strengths, yielding greedy algorithm within 1-1/e of optimal. Closed-form B*(eps) derived for complete graphs. Cost-quality law is concave for math verification but convex for emergent code tracing, showing task-dependent optimal strategies.
AI.conclusion: Optimal oracle placement depends on the curvature of the cost-quality law: diminishing returns favor spreading oracles, while sharply increasing returns favor concentrating them. The optimal strategy is genuinely task-dependent.

title: JEPA for AI-Native 6G: Predictive Representations and Open Challenges
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Tutorial and review on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for AI-native 6G. Submitted to IEEE Communications Magazine
summary: Sixth-generation (6G) networks are moving toward AI-native operation, where learning modules are embedded across the radio access network (RAN), edge, and core. This transition requires learning from limited labels, heterogeneous wireless and network data, partial observations, non-stationary propagation, and latency-constrained control loops. Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) is a promising self-supervised paradigm for this setting because it predicts missing or future representations in latent space instead of reconstructing raw measurements or using contrastive negative samples. This article presents a wireless-oriented tutorial on JEPA for 6G intelligence. We define the JEPA training mechanism, describe how CSI, beam measurements, KPIs, topology graphs, and sensing observations can be tokenized and masked, and position the learned encoder as a predictive representation layer for RAN, O-RAN, edge, and core functions, with task-specific heads or controllers producing final decisions. Then we present an illustrative, beam-management case study suggesting that a wireless-aware target, specifically an auxiliary future beam-energy target during self-supervised pretraining, can improve label efficiency and robustness across shifted deployment conditions relative to a supervised source domain. Finally, we outline open challenges in multi-timescale prediction, action-conditioned modeling, distributed training, trustworthiness, efficient deployment, benchmarking, and standardization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a tutorial on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) as a self-supervised learning paradigm for 6G AI-native networks, covering tokenization of wireless data, use cases across RAN/O-RAN/edge/core, a beam-management case study showing improved label efficiency and robustness, and open challenges.
AI.motivation: 6G networks are moving toward AI-native operation, requiring learning from limited labels, heterogeneous wireless data, partial observations, non-stationary propagation, and latency-constrained control loops, motivating the need for a self-supervised paradigm suitable for this setting.
AI.method: The paper provides a wireless-oriented tutorial on JEPA: it predicts missing or future representations in latent space (instead of reconstructing raw data or using contrastive negatives), defines tokenization and masking for CSI, beam measurements, KPIs, topology graphs, and sensing data, and positions the learned encoder as a predictive representation layer with task-specific heads. A beam-management case study uses an auxiliary future beam-energy target during self-supervised pretraining.
AI.result: The beam-management case study suggests that a wireless-aware self-supervised target (future beam-energy) improves label efficiency and robustness under shifted deployment conditions compared to a supervised source domain.
AI.conclusion: JEPA is a promising self-supervised framework for 6G intelligence. Open challenges remain in multi-timescale prediction, action-conditioned modeling, distributed training, trustworthiness, efficient deployment, benchmarking, and standardization.

title: A Dual-Stream Challenge-Response Protocol for Ocular Liveness Verification
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Simulation-based theoretical framework; human-subject validation identified as future work
summary: Ocular biometric systems face sophisticated presentation attacks, including high-resolution video replays and real-time generative deepfakes, which easily bypass static liveness checks. Current Presentation Attack Detection (PAD) frameworks typically rely on isolated physiological metrics, such as gaze tracking or the Pupillary Light Reflex (PLR), which can be spoofed independently. This paper proposes a Spatio-Luminance Sensor Fusion protocol, which introduces a dual-stream challenge-response framework for ocular liveness verification by uniting these metrics into a simultaneous authentication challenge. By generating a randomized, time-varying visual stimulus that fluctuates in both spatial trajectory and luminance intensity, we construct a mathematically coupled state-space likelihood model, termed the Synchronization Matrix, to evaluate the continuous cross-correlation between the expected biological latencies of smooth pursuit tracking and pupillary constriction. Using Monte Carlo simulation grounded in literature-derived latency distributions, we demonstrate theoretical separability between genuine and simulated attack conditions, and show that a multi-round challenge design improves the detection of generative deepfakes when a non-zero rendering-latency gap exists. This work provides a simulation-supported theoretical framework for next-generation dynamic spoofing defense in ocular and iris biometrics; human-subject validation is identified as necessary future work before deployment claims can be made.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Spatio-Luminance Sensor Fusion protocol that combines gaze tracking and pupillary light reflex into a simultaneous dual-stream challenge-response framework for ocular liveness detection. Using a randomized visual stimulus varying in spatial trajectory and luminance, it builds a Synchronization Matrix to measure cross-correlation between biological latencies. Monte Carlo simulations show theoretical separability between genuine and attack conditions, with multi-round designs improving deepfake detection.
AI.motivation: Current ocular PAD systems rely on isolated physiological metrics (gaze, PLR) that can be independently spoofed by advanced attacks like high-resolution video replays and real-time generative deepfakes, motivating the need for a coupled, simultaneous multi-metric verification.
AI.method: A dual-stream challenge-response protocol using randomized spatio-luminance visual stimuli; a Synchronization Matrix state-space likelihood model that evaluates continuous cross-correlation between smooth pursuit tracking latencies and pupillary constriction latencies; Monte Carlo simulation with literature-derived latency distributions.
AI.result: Theoretical separability between genuine biological responses and simulated attack conditions was demonstrated; multi-round challenge design improves detection of generative deepfakes when a non-zero rendering-latency gap exists.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a simulation-supported theoretical foundation for next-generation dynamic spoofing defense in ocular biometrics, though human-subject validation is required before deployment claims can be made.

title: How Do Practitioners Build SE Agents? Insights from a Mixed-Methods Study
summary: The rise of Software Engineering (SE) agents, i.e., LLM-based agents that can understand large codebases and carry out engineering tasks with limited human intervention, has been marked by rapid advances and adoption, but little is known about how developers build these systems in practice: existing studies mine repositories or examine deployment, but few investigate how SE agents are constructed. Through semi-structured interviews with 20 practitioners from 12 organizations and an online survey of 80 practitioners, this paper is the first to study how SE processes are changing in the development of SE agents and what challenges developers face. We find that as implementation becomes cheaper, bottlenecks shift rather than disappear: long-standing non-coding work such as requirements, coordination, review, and deployment becomes more visible, while reviewing and evaluating agent output becomes new and central. We characterize a seven-stage workflow and a shift toward evaluation-driven development, in which evaluation steers iteration and specifications become versioned artifacts read by both humans and agents. We further identify six challenges that teams face, together with the practices they adopt to address them, including unreliable evaluation signals, comprehension debt as code outpaces understanding, and behavioral changes introduced by provider-side model updates.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how SE processes are changing during the development of LLM-based SE agents through interviews (N=20) and surveys (N=80). It finds bottlenecks shift from coding to non-coding work (requirements, coordination, review, deployment), identifies a seven-stage workflow and evaluation-driven development, and highlights six key challenges including unreliable evaluation signals, comprehension debt, and provider-side model update issues.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid advances in SE agents (LLM-based agents for codebase understanding and engineering tasks), little is known about how developers actually build these systems in practice — existing work focuses on repository mining or deployment, not construction practices.
AI.method: Mixed-methods: semi-structured interviews with 20 practitioners from 12 organizations, plus an online survey of 80 practitioners.
AI.result: Implementation becomes cheaper, bottlenecks shift from coding to non-coding work (requirements, coordination, review, deployment). Reviewing and evaluating agent output becomes new and central. A seven-stage workflow and evaluation-driven development are identified. Six challenges found: unreliable evaluation signals, comprehension debt, and behavioral changes from provider-side model updates, etc.
AI.conclusion: As coding becomes cheaper, the bottlenecks in SE agent development shift to non-coding activities and evaluation becomes the central steering mechanism. Teams face emerging challenges like evaluation unreliability, comprehension debt, and external model update disruptions.

title: Norm Enforcement for AI Agents: Robustly Shaping Behavior in Multi-Agent Systems
comment: ICML2026 Trustworthy AI for Good Workshop
summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in shared environments where they pursue diverse goals and compete for rewards. This multi-agent competition can lead to behaviors that serve individual gains at collective cost -- for instance, marketing agents may post misleading content as a result of competing for engagement on social media. Human societies address such problems through norms that constrain acceptable behavior, supported by enforcement mechanisms that detect and penalize violations. Motivated by this, we study norm enforcement mechanisms for language model agents. We find that simple enforcement mechanisms are exploited by misaligned agents for competitive advantage, even when they are not explicitly trained or prompted to do so. We thus turn our attention to designing more robust mechanisms, and identify two key ingredients: estimating each agent's reliability over time, and updating this estimate with escalating penalties for repeated misbehavior. Across three simulated environments and a variety of agent populations, mechanisms built on these principles resist exploitation, while still penalizing norm violations at comparable or lower cost than baselines. Our results position norm enforcement mechanisms as scalable levers for shaping agents' behavior, but only when designed to anticipate becoming part of the system they govern. Our code and data are available at https://yaowenye.com/norm-enforcement.

AI.tldr: The paper studies norm enforcement mechanisms for language model agents in multi-agent competitive environments, finding that simple enforcement is exploitable by misaligned agents, and proposes robust mechanisms using reliability estimation and escalating penalties to resist exploitation.
AI.motivation: AI agents pursuing diverse goals in shared environments can engage in individually beneficial but collectively costly behaviors (e.g., posting misleading content for engagement). Inspired by human societal norms and enforcement, the authors aim to study norm enforcement mechanisms for language model agents to curb such behaviors.
AI.method: The authors first test simple enforcement mechanisms and find them exploitable by misaligned agents. They then design robust mechanisms with two key ingredients: (1) estimating each agent's reliability over time, and (2) updating this estimate with escalating penalties for repeated misbehavior. They evaluate across three simulated environments with diverse agent populations.
AI.result: Mechanisms built on reliability estimation and escalating penalties resist exploitation while penalizing norm violations at comparable or lower cost than baselines across all three simulated environments and various agent populations.
AI.conclusion: Norm enforcement mechanisms are scalable levers for shaping agent behavior, but must be designed to anticipate becoming part of the system they govern to be effective.

title: The Silent Freeze: Predicting When Low-Precision Training Stops Learning
summary: Training in reduced floating-point precision can silently halt learning: when a gradient-descent weight update falls below half the unit in the last place (ULP) of the weight, it rounds away and that coordinate freezes while its gradient is still nonzero. The freeze is deterministic, governed by a per-coordinate half-ULP condition, and predictable from a high-precision trajectory and the target mantissa length alone, without low-precision data. In a small GPT trained under the standard AdamW-plus-cosine recipe with bf16-equivalent stored weights, training proceeds normally and then permanently freezes just past mid-run, within four steps of the a-priori prediction. In a $124$-million-parameter GPT-2 transformer whose weights are constrained to the $8$-bit floating-point grid after every optimizer step, with no master weights, the dense weights freeze at initialization in both fp8 formats -- predicted \emph{a priori} from an fp32 reference -- and validation loss plateaus while full precision keeps improving. Stochastic rounding removes the persistent freeze, and the same reference predicts that too. The condition transfers across frozen-feature regression, a mantissa-truncation emulator spanning $128\times$ in precision, small networks, and a CNN on MNIST: a computable axis of low-precision training, not diffuse noise.

AI.tldr: Training in reduced floating-point precision can cause weight updates to fall below half the Unit in the Last Place (ULP) of the weight, resulting in deterministic freezing of gradient descent. This freeze is predictable from high-precision trajectories and mantissa length alone, and was empirically verified across GPT, GPT-2, and other models. Stochastic rounding eliminates the freeze.
AI.motivation: To identify and theoretically characterize a fundamental failure mode in low-precision training—weight freezing due to insufficient precision—that is deterministic and predictable, rather than being diffuse noise.
AI.method: The authors define a half-ULP condition for weight freezing, derive a priori predictions from high-precision trajectories and target mantissa length, and validate empirically on GPT (bf16-equivalent), 124M GPT-2 (fp8 formats), regression tasks, a mantissa-truncation emulator, small networks, and a CNN on MNIST.
AI.result: Freezing occurs deterministically at predicted steps; validation loss plateaus while full precision continues improving. Stochastic rounding removes persistent freezing as predicted. The condition generalizes across diverse architectures and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Weight freezing is a computable, predictable axis of low-precision training failure, not random noise, and can be mitigated via stochastic rounding.

title: ShapKO: Shapley-Adaptive Modality Knockout for Robust Multimodal Learning
summary: Multimodal medical models often degrade when inputs are missing, a common scenario in real-world clinical workflows. Separately, even when all modalities are present, modality dominance is observed during training, where optimization over-relies on a highly predictive modality and undertrains complementary sources, resulting in poor robustness under partial availability. While training-time modality knockout improves missing-modality robustness, existing approaches use static masking rates that cannot adapt to evolving modality utility during training. We introduce ShapKO (Shapley-Adaptive Modality Knockout), a dynamic training strategy that learns modality-specific knockout probabilities based on validation utility. ShapKO periodically evaluates performance across modality subsets, estimates modality importance via Shapley values, and updates masking probabilities to suppress dominant modalities more frequently. This adaptive process promotes complementary representations, while requiring no architectural modifications. We evaluate ShapKO on three datasets covering multitask clinical classification, survival prediction, and cancer detection. ShapKO consistently improves performance under modality absence and yields interpretable trajectories of learned masking behavior. Code is available at: https://github.com/sumona00/ShapKO

AI.tldr: ShapKO introduces a dynamic training strategy that adaptively knocks out modalities during training based on Shapley value-estimated importance, improving multimodal model robustness under missing modalities without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Multimodal medical models suffer performance degradation when inputs are missing, and training suffers from modality dominance where optimization over-relies on highly predictive modalities while undertraining complementary ones. Existing knockout methods use static masking rates that cannot adapt to evolving modality utility during training.
AI.method: ShapKO dynamically learns modality-specific knockout probabilities by periodically evaluating performance across modality subsets, estimating modality importance via Shapley values, and updating masking probabilities to suppress dominant modalities more frequently during training.
AI.result: Evaluated on three datasets (multitask clinical classification, survival prediction, and cancer detection), ShapKO consistently improves performance under modality absence and yields interpretable trajectories of learned masking behavior.
AI.conclusion: ShapKO effectively addresses missing-modality robustness by adaptively balancing modality usage during training, requiring no architectural modifications, and improves performance across diverse medical tasks.

title: BackendForge: Benchmarking Agentic End-to-End Code Generation with Backend Services
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in agentic coding settings, where they can inspect files, execute commands, run tests, observe failures, and iteratively revise code. This shift raises a central evaluation question: can an agentic LLM generate an end-to-end software artifact that is both deployable and behaviorally correct under execution? Backend services provide a controlled but realistic substrate for this evaluation. Their APIs expose application-level executable semantics, and deployed behavior can be checked deterministically against an OpenAPI contract through black-box HTTP interactions. We introduce BackendForge, a benchmark of 56 contract-defined backend generation tasks rewritten from real open-source applications. Given a visible specification and an OpenAPI contract, an LLM must generate a Dockerized service that is built, deployed, and evaluated only through HTTP tests. To strengthen evaluation without introducing hidden requirements, BackendForge uses a test agent and a code agent to co-evolve the test oracle and reference service, where the test agent proposes specification-grounded backend tests and the code agent repairs the reference implementation. Although the best-performing model, GPT-5.5, succeeds on 55.4\% of tasks under the base oracle, it succeeds on only 28.6\% under the final oracle. This gap suggests that current LLMs can implement many local API behaviors, but still struggle to produce complete backend services.

AI.tldr: BackendForge is a benchmark of 56 backend generation tasks from real apps, where LLMs must generate deployable backend services from OpenAPI contracts. While GPT-5.5 succeeds on 55.4% of tasks with a base oracle, performance drops to 28.6% under a stricter co-evolved oracle, revealing that LLMs can implement local API behaviors but struggle with complete, deployable backend services.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether agentic LLMs can generate end-to-end software artifacts that are both deployable and behaviorally correct under execution, specifically focusing on backend services as a controlled but realistic substrate.
AI.method: Created BackendForge, a benchmark of 56 contract-defined backend generation tasks rewritten from real open-source applications. Uses a test agent and code agent to co-evolve test oracles and reference services, evaluating generated services solely through black-box HTTP interactions against OpenAPI contracts.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves 55.4% success on tasks under the base oracle but only 28.6% under the final oracle, indicating a significant gap between implementing local API behaviors and producing complete, deployable backend services.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs can implement many local API behaviors but still struggle to produce complete backend services, highlighting the need for further progress in agentic code generation for deployable software artifacts.

title: Verification of Adaptive Agentic Controllers through Finite Rule Revision
summary: Industrial agentic AI systems increasingly exhibit a gap between prototype capability and production deployment. In particular, adaptive agents may generate plausible outputs while remaining difficult to verify under non-determinism, confidentiality constraints, limited context, and weak observability. This paper formulates a bounded verification protocol for adaptive agentic controllers represented by finite symbolic rules, explicit diagnostic predicates, explanation logs, and held-out re-evaluation. The central research question is: when an adaptive agentic controller is represented through finite rules, explicit diagnostic predicates, explanation logs, and held-out re-evaluation, which classes of controller failure can be detected, locally repaired, or rejected without relying on unrestricted human-in-the-loop judgment? The proposed framework treats the controller as a finite revisable object. Diagnostic failures are mapped to predefined rule-level edits, including rule addition, rule deletion, and priority revision. Repaired controllers are then evaluated on held-out simulation seeds or cloned initial states. Experiments in a stylized financially constrained inventory-control benchmark show three outcomes: resource-induced failures that remain non-repairable by one rule edit, partial repairs that are rejected because they violate thresholds or guardrails, and a local one-step repair of an order-volatility failure induced by removing a smoothing rule. The contribution is methodological and provides a simulation-compatible procedure for testing whether specific controller-level failures can be made observable, explainable, locally revisable, and empirically re-tested under controlled conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a bounded verification protocol for adaptive agentic controllers using finite symbolic rules, diagnostic predicates, explanation logs, and held-out re-evaluation. It systematically classifies controller failures as detectable, locally repairable (via rule addition/deletion/priority revision), or rejectable, demonstrated on an inventory-control benchmark with three failure types.
AI.motivation: Industrial agentic AI systems exhibit a gap between prototype capability and production deployment due to challenges with non-determinism, confidentiality, limited context, and weak observability, making verification difficult for adaptive agents that generate plausible but hard-to-verify outputs.
AI.method: The framework treats the controller as a finite revisable object, maps diagnostic failures to predefined rule-level edits (addition, deletion, priority revision), and evaluates repaired controllers on held-out simulation seeds or cloned initial states.
AI.result: Experiments in a financially constrained inventory-control benchmark show three outcomes: non-repairable resource-induced failures, rejected partial repairs violating thresholds/guardrails, and a locally repairable order-volatility failure via smoothing rule removal.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a simulation-compatible methodological procedure for testing whether specific controller-level failures can be made observable, explainable, locally revisable, and empirically re-tested under controlled conditions.

title: Discovering Latent Response Laws in Forced Physical Systems
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures and 2 tables. Supplementary Information provided as an ancillary file
summary: Governing equations provide compact descriptions of physical systems, yet the variables in which they are simple are often hidden in high-dimensional measurements. This challenge is sharper for forced systems, whose responses depend on both intrinsic dynamics and time-dependent inputs. Here we introduce FLARE, a forced latent autoencoder for response equations that learns compact response coordinates, identifies sparse input-dependent latent dynamics and decodes equation rollouts to full responses. By estimating latent dimension from data and separating state estimation from external forcing, FLARE enables forecasts to be initialized from past responses and driven by prescribed future inputs. Across known dynamical systems, application-scale forced responses and visual observations, FLARE recovers compact forced dynamics and predicts long-horizon high-dimensional responses under inputs not used for training. By turning learned coordinates into a dynamical interface, FLARE extends equation discovery to systems whose effective states are hidden within complex observations, providing a route for interpretable modelling and prediction of high-dimensional responses in forced dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: FLARE is a forced latent autoencoder that discovers compact, interpretable governing equations for high-dimensional forced dynamical systems directly from observational data, enabling accurate long-horizon predictions under unseen inputs.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional measurements of forced dynamical systems obscure the simple governing equations and latent variables that describe their behavior, making it difficult to model and predict responses under time-dependent inputs.
AI.method: FLARE (Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations) learns compact response coordinates via an autoencoder, identifies sparse input-dependent latent dynamics, and decodes equation rollouts back to full responses. It estimates latent dimension from data and separates state estimation from external forcing.
AI.result: Across known dynamical systems, application-scale forced responses, and visual observations, FLARE recovers compact forced dynamics and predicts long-horizon high-dimensional responses under unseen inputs not used during training.
AI.conclusion: FLARE extends equation discovery to systems whose effective states are hidden within complex observations, providing an interpretable dynamical interface for modeling and predicting high-dimensional forced responses.

title: Bridging the Catalog-to-Real Gap: Scalable Product Recognition via Multi-Stage Contrastive Learning
summary: Automated product recognition is a cornerstone of modern retail intelligence; however, accurately matching real-world, in-store images against extensive corporate catalogs remains a major scalability bottleneck for large-scale applications. In this work, we address this challenge by reformulating the task as an embedding-based cross-domain retrieval problem rather than a standard closed-set classification task. Specifically, we define the objective as retrieving the most corresponding catalog reference image for a given real-world product query crop from an expansive inventory. To bridge the severe domain gap between pristine studio packshots and noisy in-store queries, we introduce a novel catalog-to-real multi-stage contrastive learning paradigm (Cat2Real). This framework fine-tunes a vision backbone by systematically exploiting both item-level and image-level similarities to drive targeted hard negative mining. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that our paradigm scales seamlessly to unseen products and categories, yielding outstanding zero-shot generalization performance even in the complete absence of real-world training images for novel inventory.

AI.tldr: Cat2Real reformulates product recognition as an embedding-based cross-domain retrieval problem, using multi-stage contrastive learning with hard negative mining to bridge the studio-to-real domain gap, achieving strong zero-shot generalization without requiring real-world training images.
AI.motivation: Accurate matching of in-store images against corporate catalogs is a scalability bottleneck for retail intelligence; existing closed-set classification approaches fail due to the severe domain gap between pristine studio packshots and noisy real-world queries.
AI.method: Proposes Cat2Real, a catalog-to-real multi-stage contrastive learning framework that fine-tunes a vision backbone by exploiting both item-level and image-level similarities for targeted hard negative mining, formulated as an embedding-based cross-domain retrieval task.
AI.result: Scales seamlessly to unseen products and categories, achieving outstanding zero-shot generalization performance even without real-world training images for novel inventory.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating product recognition as cross-domain retrieval with multi-stage contrastive learning effectively bridges the domain gap and enables scalable, generalizable product matching in real-world retail settings.

title: Retrieval-Oriented Code Representations in Agentic Bug Localization
summary:
LLM-based agents are increasingly being used to support software development, yet their performance in repository-level tasks depends on retrieving the right code context. Existing studies have explored file-level localization using traditional information retrieval over file paths and raw source code. However, the role of textual code representations in retrieval and localization remains underexplored.
  We study file-level bug localization as a representation-driven retrieval problem. Across the Long Code Arena (LCA) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE) datasets, we compare five code representations: file paths, raw source code, and three LLM-generated textual representations. Our experiments include lexical, semantic, and LLM-based retrieval, followed by LLM-based post-retrieval ranking. We quantify the cost incurred by a representation through the representation footprint. We find that the choice of code representation affects both localization effectiveness and cost. Role-aware summaries outperform file-path representations by up to 40% Hit@5 while requiring a representation footprint 10.4 to 20.9x smaller than raw source code. Combining complementary representation results and ranking retrieved candidates with an LLM provides further gains of up to 31.9% and 42.0%, respectively. Overall, role-aware summaries provide the best cost-effectiveness trade-off, while raw source code offers effectiveness in some settings at a significantly higher cost. A case study with Agentless reveals the utility of our techniques within a well-known pipeline, reaching 94% Hit@6 on file localization (+4.7% against the baseline). Our findings suggest that code representation should be treated as a first-class design choice in agentic localization pipelines, guided by pipeline stage and cost-accuracy requirements.

AI.tldr: This paper studies file-level bug localization as a representation-driven retrieval problem, comparing five code representations (file paths, raw source code, and three LLM-generated textual representations) across LCA and SWE datasets. Role-aware summaries outperform file paths by up to 40% Hit@5 with 10.4-20.9x smaller footprint than raw source code, and combining complementary representations with LLM ranking yields further gains. The authors argue code representation should be a first-class design choice in agentic localization pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing studies on repository-level bug localization rely on traditional IR over file paths and raw source code, but the role of textual code representations in retrieval and localization remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors study file-level bug localization as a representation-driven retrieval problem. They compare five code representations (file paths, raw source code, and three LLM-generated textual representations) across Long Code Arena and SWE-bench Verified using lexical, semantic, and LLM-based retrieval with post-retrieval ranking, quantifying cost via representation footprint.
AI.result: Role-aware summaries outperform file-path representations by up to 40% Hit@5 while requiring 10.4-20.9x smaller footprint than raw source code. Combining complementary representations yields up to 31.9% gains, and LLM ranking adds up to 42.0% further gains. In a case study with Agentless, the approach reaches 94% Hit@6 (+4.7% over baseline).
AI.conclusion: Code representation should be treated as a first-class design choice in agentic localization pipelines, guided by pipeline stage and cost-accuracy requirements. Role-aware summaries offer the best cost-effectiveness trade-off, while raw source code provides effectiveness in some settings at significantly higher cost.

title: EvoCUA-1.5: Online Reinforcement Learning for Multi-turn Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents must solve long-horizon tasks through repeated interaction with partially observable, multimodal desktop environments. Although imitation learning and offline trajectory refinement provide strong priors, static traces cannot cover the causal feedback loop of real computer use: each action changes the screen state, future action space, and recovery options. EvoCUA-1.5 extends self-evolving computer-use agents from offline experience learning to online reinforcement learning, where policies interact with executable sandbox environments and improve from verifiable task outcomes. Online RL in this setting requires more than directly reusing single-turn language-RL recipes. Multi-turn interaction introduces context-managed observations, sparse terminal rewards, variable-length trajectories, and slow environment feedback. EvoCUA-1.5 addresses these challenges with Step-Level Policy Optimization (STEPO), which preserves trajectory-level advantage balance after decomposition into step-level samples; policy-aware filtering and pass-rate calibration over verifiable synthesized tasks; Dynamic Tri-Adaptive Curriculum (DTAC), which combines learnable tasks, difficult positive replay, and controlled infeasible-task exposure; and a fully asynchronous RL infrastructure with staleness control and mini-group batching. Experiments show that these components improve training stability and downstream performance. EvoCUA-1.5 achieves 63.2\% success on OSWorld-Verified, outperforming comparable 32B/35B-scale open-weight baselines and even approaching models with significantly larger parameter counts. Overall, EvoCUA-1.5 provides a practical framework for scaling online RL in multi-turn computer-use agents.

AI.tldr: EvoCUA-1.5 extends computer-use agents from offline learning to online RL, addressing challenges of multi-turn interaction with Step-Level Policy Optimization (STEPO), policy-aware filtering, Dynamic Tri-Adaptive Curriculum (DTAC), and asynchronous RL infrastructure, achieving 63.2% success on OSWorld-Verified and outperforming comparable 32B/35B-scale models.
AI.motivation: Static offline traces cannot cover the causal feedback loop of real computer use where each action changes screen state, future action space, and recovery options. Prior imitation learning and offline trajectory refinement provide strong priors but lack the ability to improve from actual task outcomes through environment interaction.
AI.method: EvoCUA-1.5 proposes: (1) Step-Level Policy Optimization (STEPO) to preserve trajectory-level advantage balance after step-level decomposition; (2) policy-aware filtering and pass-rate calibration over verifiable synthesized tasks; (3) Dynamic Tri-Adaptive Curriculum (DTAC) combining learnable tasks, difficult positive replay, and controlled infeasible-task exposure; (4) fully asynchronous RL infrastructure with staleness control and mini-group batching.
AI.result: Achieves 63.2% success rate on OSWorld-Verified, outperforming comparable 32B/35B-scale open-weight baselines and approaching models with significantly larger parameter counts.
AI.conclusion: EvoCUA-1.5 provides a practical framework for scaling online RL in multi-turn computer-use agents, with demonstrated training stability and downstream performance improvements.

title: Quota Marketplace: Dynamic Pricing for Efficient Allocation of ML Training Resources
summary:
The escalating demand for Machine Learning (ML) training resources in recent years has resulted in a substantial gap between the high demand and the available supply. Efficient allocation of these scarce and expensive resources is crucial for organizations to maximize their return on investment. Existing resource allocation mechanisms, like Karma [OSDI'23], are designed to guarantee Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness in settings with dynamic (time-varying) user demands, but fail to preserve these key properties in the presence of demands with heterogeneous values. Given the ubiquity and inevitability of heterogeneity in organizational values of different workloads, effective resource allocation policies must accommodate these variations.
  In this paper, we describe the design, implementation, deployment, and theoretical analysis of Quota Marketplace, a market-based mechanism to efficiently allocate ML training chips (like GPUs), explicitly addressing scenarios with demands of heterogeneous value. We detail the implementation of this mechanism within Google and present metrics that demonstrate its impact. We also discuss many business-critical requirements that the Quota Marketplace handles quite effectively, and document the gains and opportunities it has unlocked. We establish theoretically how this market-based approach achieves the essential properties of Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness by allowing the users to express the value of their workloads and enabling dynamic resource pricing based on supply and demand fluctuations. Ultimately, the market facilitates resource allocation that aligns with organizational priorities.

AI.tldr: Quota Marketplace is a market-based mechanism deployed at Google for allocating scarce ML training chips (GPUs) that handles heterogeneous workload values, achieving Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness through dynamic pricing and user value expression.
AI.motivation: Existing resource allocation mechanisms like Karma guarantee Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness under dynamic demands but fail when demands have heterogeneous values, which is common in organizational settings.
AI.method: A market-based mechanism where users express the value of their workloads and resources are dynamically priced based on supply and demand fluctuations; implemented and deployed within Google.
AI.result: Metrics from Google deployment demonstrate positive impact; the mechanism effectively handles business-critical requirements and unlocks gains and opportunities.
AI.conclusion: The market-based approach achieves Pareto efficiency and max-min fairness while accommodating heterogeneous workload values, aligning resource allocation with organizational priorities.

title: Do Transformer Temporal Heads and Post-Pooling Motion Gates Help CorrNet-based CSLR? An Empirical Study
summary: CorrNet is a strong baseline for continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) because it models inter-frame correlations inside the visual encoding stage. In this paper, we study two natural extensions of a reproduced CorrNet system: replacing the BiLSTM temporal head with a Transformer encoder, and injecting motion cues after temporal pooling. We find that the Transformer head does not outperform the BiLSTM baseline, even with a training strategy adjusted for the Transformer, and the two heads have almost the same computational and runtime cost. For the second extension, we design a lightweight module called MotionGate. In our experiments, MotionGate consistently collapses to an identity-like mapping: the gate loses motion selectivity, and the injected residual becomes a weak, non-selective perturbation of the pooled features. These results suggest that explicit motion injection after CorrNet's correlation-based encoding is largely redundant, and that natural-looking architectural extensions in CSLR should be tested carefully instead of being assumed to help.

AI.tldr: This paper tests two natural extensions to CorrNet for CSLR: replacing BiLSTM with Transformer (which doesn't outperform BiLSTM) and injecting motion cues via MotionGate (which collapses to identity mapping). Both fail, showing that architectural extensions should be tested carefully rather than assumed beneficial.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether two seemingly natural architectural extensions of the CorrNet CSLR baseline—using a Transformer instead of BiLSTM and injecting explicit motion cues—actually improve performance.
AI.method: (1) Replaced CorrNet's BiLSTM temporal head with a Transformer encoder with adjusted training strategy; (2) Designed MotionGate, a lightweight module to inject motion cues after temporal pooling.
AI.result: Transformer head does not outperform BiLSTM despite comparable compute/runtime; MotionGate collapses to identity-like mapping, losing motion selectivity and producing weak non-selective perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Explicit motion injection after CorrNet's correlation-based encoding is largely redundant; natural-looking architectural extensions in CSLR should be empirically validated rather than assumed helpful.

title: AgentCheck: A Reproduce-Intervene-Mitigate Workbench for LLM Agents over MCP
summary: Tool-using LLM agents are mostly evaluated assuming all tools work. When a tool times out, returns a week-stale value, or has its description poisoned in deployment, the developer needs a controlled way to reproduce the failure, test a fix, and confirm the fix worked before deployment. We present AgentCheck, an open-source web workbench that turns an MCP server into an intervention surface. AgentCheck runs an agent against its real tools and records every tool response, then re-runs the agent with the response perturbed by a fault (12 types) injector. Matching tool calls are replayed from cache, and later tool calls go live after the agent diverges. This yields a reproduce-intervene-confirm loop: the developer toggles a mitigation, re-runs against the identical fault, and sees if the failure goes away. Scoring has two parts: deterministic pass/fail rules, plus an LLM judge for interpretive labels, validated against human annotations. Across five agents, the best passes 105/120 scenarios and the weakest only 77. The failures are usually silent, confident use of incorrect tool outputs rather than crashes. On the weakest agent, a retry mitigation raises success on timeout error faults from as few as 30% of cases to 100%, whereas stale-data faults remain near 3-4 of 10 regardless of the mitigation. AgentCheck makes these failure modes reproducible, comparable, and verifiable before deployment.

AI.tldr: AgentCheck is an open-source workbench that turns MCP servers into intervention surfaces, enabling a reproduce-intervene-confirm loop for testing LLM agents against tool faults (12 types). Using replayed cached responses and live execution after divergence, it evaluates agents via deterministic rules and an LLM judge. Across five agents, the best passes 105/120 scenarios; retry mitigations fully resolve timeout faults but barely help with stale-data faults.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents are evaluated assuming all tools work, but in deployment tools can time out, return stale values, or have poisoned descriptions. Developers lack a controlled way to reproduce failures, test fixes, and confirm fixes before deployment.
AI.method: AgentCheck turns an MCP server into an intervention surface: it records all tool responses during an agent run, then re-runs the agent with responses perturbed by a 12-type fault injector. Matching tool calls are replayed from cache; after divergence, later calls go live. This creates a reproduce-intervene-confirm loop where a developer toggles a mitigation and re-runs against the identical fault. Scoring uses deterministic pass/fail rules plus an LLM judge validated against human annotations.
AI.result: Across five agents, the best passes 105/120 scenarios and the weakest only 77. Failures are mostly silent — confident use of incorrect tool outputs rather than crashes. On the weakest agent, a retry mitigation raises timeout error faults from 30% to 100% success, but stale-data faults remain near 3-4/10 regardless of mitigation.
AI.conclusion: AgentCheck makes failure modes (tool faults) reproducible, comparable, and verifiable before deployment, enabling developers to systematically test mitigations.

title: From Patterns to Maze Structures: SMT-Based Path Synthesis and 2D/3D Construction
summary: We present a pipeline for constructing maze structures from input patterns such as text or shapes. The central path-synthesis problem is encoded in Satisfiability Modulo Theories as global constraints on adjacency, continuity, and pattern-constrained coverage, allowing each fixed-bound instance to be solved in one call. The resulting path is either a planar, self-avoiding route or a layered traversal with prescribed over--under crossings, and it serves as a scaffold for constructing planar mazes and three-dimensional realizations of woven mazes. This report extends the published Bridges 2026 conference paper with more representative SMT-LIB examples and a fuller account of how synthesized paths become concrete maze constructions in planar and three-dimensional form.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an SMT-based pipeline for synthesizing maze structures from input patterns, generating planar self-avoiding routes or layered traversals with over-under crossings, and extending the Bridges 2026 paper with additional SMT-LIB examples and construction details.
AI.motivation: To enable automatic generation of maze structures from arbitrary input patterns (text, shapes) by formulating the central path-synthesis problem as global constraints solvable via Satisfiability Modulo Theories.
AI.method: The path-synthesis problem is encoded in SMT as global constraints on adjacency, continuity, and pattern-constrained coverage, solved in a single call per fixed-bound instance. The resulting path is either a planar self-avoiding route or a layered traversal with prescribed over-under crossings, serving as a scaffold for constructing planar and 3D woven mazes.
AI.result: The approach produces either planar self-avoiding routes or layered traversals with over-under crossings, which can be realized as both planar mazes and three-dimensional woven maze constructions.
AI.conclusion: SMT-based synthesis provides a flexible and efficient method for generating maze structures from diverse input patterns, with extensions to both 2D and 3D forms.

title: Spectral Origins of the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Autoregressive Generation
summary: Large autoregressive language models exhibit a self-correction blind spot: they reliably fix identical errors when attributed to an external source yet fail to fix the same errors in their own outputs.
