Prior work has documented this phenomenon empirically, through controlled error injection, error-depth decompositions, RL-based verifier-corrector training, and intrinsic self-verification, but offers no formal model of why generating a token suppresses the ability to detect its error, no quantitative activation condition for correction markers, and no convergence guarantee for reinforcement-learning-based self-correction. We close these gaps with SPARC, a spectral-algebraic theory of self-correction in autoregressive generation. We define the error-propagation operator as the product of per-step attention Jacobians on the residual stream and prove that the blind spot arises if and only if the spectral radius of this operator is at least one. We derive a sharp activation threshold, given as a function of the spectral radius, that a correction marker must exceed, recovering the 89.3\% blind-spot reduction observed with a simple ``Wait'' marker. We further prove that RL-based verifier-corrector training converges at a rate proportional to the squared coupling strength over the square root of the number of samples if and only if the verifier-corrector coupling matrix has spectral norm below one, and that this criterion is invariant across residual-stream autoregressive modalities, unifying text LLMs and autoregressive image and video generation. Experiments across four backbones and a visual autoregressive probe validate every theorem, with spectral predictions matching measured blind-spot rates within 3.2\% RMSE.

AI.tldr: SPARC presents a spectral-algebraic theory of self-correction in autoregressive models, proving that the blind spot (inability to fix own errors vs. external errors) arises when the spectral radius of the error-propagation operator ≥ 1, deriving activation thresholds for correction markers, and providing convergence guarantees for RL-based verifier-corrector training under spectral norm conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing work documents the self-correction blind spot empirically but lacks a formal model of why token generation suppresses error detection, lacks quantitative activation conditions for correction markers, and offers no convergence guarantees for RL-based self-correction. SPARC closes these theoretical gaps.
AI.method: SPARC defines the error-propagation operator as the product of per-step attention Jacobians on the residual stream, uses spectral radius analysis to derive the blind spot condition (≥1), derives a sharp activation threshold for correction markers as a function of spectral radius, and proves RL verifier-corrector training convergence rate conditioned on spectral norm of coupling matrix.
AI.result: The spectral condition predicts blind-spot rates within 3.2% RMSE across four backbone LLMs and a visual autoregressive probe. The derived "Wait" marker threshold recovers 89.3% blind-spot reduction. Convergence rate for RL training is proportional to squared coupling strength over sqrt(samples) iff spectral norm < 1.
AI.conclusion: The blind spot is formally characterized by spectral radius ≥ 1 of the error-propagation operator; correction marker effectiveness and RL training convergence are governed by spectral properties, unifying self-correction theory across text, image, and video autoregressive modalities.

title: Banshee: Target Switch Attacks on Gimbal-Stabilized Visual Tracking Systems via Acoustic Injection
comment: Accepted by the 47th IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (IEEE S&P 2026). 20 pages. Artifact: https://github.com/U1ltra/Banshee
summary: Gimbal-stabilized visual tracking is critical for modern autonomous systems such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). While prior work shows acoustic signals can disturb gimbal internals, the impact of such attacks on real-world applications like UAV tracking and following remains underexplored. Existing demonstrations largely overlook practical challenges for real-world attacks, such as object-motion uncertainty and runtime latency. To bridge this gap, we present Banshee, the first physically realizable attack that induces target switching in UAV visual tracking systems by exploiting acoustic vulnerabilities in gimbal-camera systems. Banshee generates carefully crafted acoustic waveforms that induce optimized adversarial gimbal oscillations, causing directionally biased camera-view drifts that break inter-frame target associations. Consequently, the onboard tracker is driven to switch from the original target to an attacker-selected object with high probability, with occasional target loss. Banshee achieves a 93.6% success rate in simulation across two commercial gimbal systems and five trackers. Real-world benchtop and in-flight black-box attacks against a commercial drone across varied scenarios show an overall 95.5% attack success rate. Our results reveal a practical cross-domain vulnerability between acoustics and vision, highlighting the need for robust designs of gimbal systems and applications. Our code is available at: https://github.com/U1ltra/Banshee.

AI.tldr: Banshee is the first physically realizable acoustic attack that induces target switching in UAV visual tracking systems by exploiting gimbal vulnerabilities, achieving 93.6% simulation and 95.5% real-world attack success rates.
AI.motivation: While prior work shows acoustic signals can disturb gimbal internals, the impact on real-world UAV tracking/following remains underexplored, and existing demonstrations overlook practical challenges like object-motion uncertainty and runtime latency.
AI.method: Banshee generates carefully crafted acoustic waveforms that induce optimized adversarial gimbal oscillations, causing directionally biased camera-view drifts that break inter-frame target associations, forcing the tracker to switch from the original target to an attacker-selected object.
AI.result: 93.6% success rate in simulation across two commercial gimbal systems and five trackers; 95.5% attack success rate in real-world benchtop and in-flight black-box attacks against a commercial drone across varied scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals a practical cross-domain vulnerability between acoustics and vision, highlighting the need for robust designs of gimbal systems and applications.

title: Know Before Fix: QA-Driven Repository Knowledge Acquisition for Software Issue Resolution
summary: LLM-based coding agents have significantly advanced automated software issue resolution, yet they remain highly prone to factual errors caused by insufficient repository understanding. Recent methods attempt to mitigate this limitation through pre-repair repository exploration; however, their fix-driven strategies explore repositories without identifying the agent's knowledge gaps, often yielding imprecise context that fails to bridge the underlying understanding deficit. In this paper, we propose ACQUIRE, a QA-driven framework for software issue resolution. Mirroring how experienced developers first comprehend unfamiliar code before attempting a fix, ACQUIRE explicitly acquires repository knowledge prior to repair. The framework decouples knowledge acquisition from patch generation through two stages: in the first stage, a Questioner and an Answerer collaborate to acquire structured repository knowledge, where the Questioner poses targeted questions and the Answerer produces evidence-grounded answers through autonomous exploration; in the second stage, the Resolver leverages the resulting QA knowledge to generate informed patches. By transforming implicit knowledge gaps into explicit, factually reliable understanding, ACQUIRE accelerates knowledge-intensive repair stages and enables more accurate resolution. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified demonstrate that ACQUIRE consistently outperforms representative pre-repair methods, raising Pass@1 by up to 4.4 percentage points with modest additional cost and time.

AI.tldr: ACQUIRE is a QA-driven framework for software issue resolution that decouples knowledge acquisition from patch generation. It uses a Questioner-Answerer collaboration to gather structured repository knowledge before repair, enabling more accurate fixes. On SWE-bench Verified, it improves Pass@1 by up to 4.4 percentage points over pre-repair methods.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents suffer from factual errors due to insufficient repository understanding. Existing pre-repair exploration methods use fix-driven strategies that fail to identify the agent's knowledge gaps, yielding imprecise context that doesn't address the underlying understanding deficit.
AI.method: ACQUIRE is a two-stage framework: (1) Knowledge Acquisition stage where a Questioner poses targeted questions and an Answerer produces evidence-grounded answers through autonomous exploration; (2) Patch Generation stage where the Resolver uses the QA knowledge to generate informed patches. This decouples knowledge acquisition from patch generation.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, ACQUIRE consistently outperforms representative pre-repair methods, raising Pass@1 by up to 4.4 percentage points with modest additional cost and time.
AI.conclusion: By transforming implicit knowledge gaps into explicit, factually reliable understanding, ACQUIRE accelerates knowledge-intensive repair stages and enables more accurate resolution of software issues.

title: Length Penalties Make Chain-of-Thought Less Monitorable
summary: Length-penalized reinforcement learning can shorten chain-of-thought reasoning while hiding an influence that drives the model's answer. In our experiments, training with length penalties does not stop misleading hints from steering models, even though the models' chains of thought mention the hint much less often. A token-accuracy evaluation would count these runs as successful because they use fewer reasoning tokens with little accuracy loss; it would miss whether the remaining trace still shows what drove the answer. We train Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B variants with different target chain lengths, then evaluate them with biasing-hint interventions on held-out MMLU-Pro-R and four transfer benchmarks. Compression sharply cuts reasoning tokens, preserves most multiple-choice accuracy, and leaves hint influence near baseline. At the strongest target, lower-bound faithfulness falls to 63.1% of baseline for Qwen3-14B and 69.4% for Qwen3-4B; the raw rate at which a monitor catches hint use falls from 69% to 49% and from 60% to 48%. To separate length from content, we randomly delete sentences from uncompressed baseline chains until the remaining text matches the compressed length. Even after this length matching, compressed chains disclose the hint 7-35 percentage points less often than baseline chains that we shorten at random, for both Qwen3 sizes and all five evaluation distributions. Compression therefore does more than shorten reasoning, preferentially removing the cues a monitor needs to see what influenced the answer. Together, these results reveal a compression-monitorability frontier in which cheaper reasoning can preserve answers while making the influences behind them harder to detect.

AI.tldr: Length-penalized RL compression of chain-of-thought reasoning reduces reasoning tokens and preserves accuracy, but also preferentially removes cues needed to detect biasing influences, revealing a compression-monitorability trade-off.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether length-penalized reinforcement learning compresses chain-of-thought reasoning in a way that conceals the influence of biasing hints, rather than simply shortening reasoning while preserving faithful traceability of model decisions.
AI.method: Train Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B variants with different target chain lengths using length-penalized RL; evaluate with biasing-hint interventions on MMLU-Pro-R and four transfer benchmarks; compare compressed chains to randomly shortened baseline chains matched for length.
AI.result: Compression sharply cuts reasoning tokens with little accuracy loss, but hint influence remains near baseline; lower-bound faithfulness drops to 63.1% (Qwen3-14B) and 69.4% (Qwen3-4B); monitor catch rate falls from 69%→49% and 60%→48%; compressed chains disclose hints 7-35 percentage points less than length-matched random deletions.
AI.conclusion: Length-penalized compression does more than shorten reasoning—it preferentially removes cues needed to monitor what influenced the answer, revealing a compression-monitorability frontier.

title: RUBRIC: Realism--Utility Balanced Ranking for Imbalanced Classification
summary:
Class imbalance poses a fundamental challenge in risk-sensitive applications such as fraud detection and medical diagnosis, where minority-class samples are scarce yet critical for accurate classification. Existing oversampling methods generate synthetic samples to rebalance class distributions; however, they often produce large numbers of low-quality candidates that distort decision boundaries or introduce artifacts, leading to overfitting and degraded generalization.
  In this work, we introduce RUBRIC, a generator-agnostic filtering framework that formulates synthetic sample selection as a quality-over-quantity optimization problem. RUBRIC ranks candidates using a realism-utility trade-off: realism is quantified by a learned discriminator that distinguishes real samples from synthetic samples, while utility captures proximity to the decision boundary through a concave margin-based scoring function. We show that, under mild regularity conditions, the proposed filtering strategy monotonically tightens the generalization bound for margin-based classifiers by jointly reducing distribution shift and suppressing near-negative tail contributions.
  Through extensive experiments on credit-card fraud detection and other imbalanced benchmarks, we demonstrate that RUBRIC improves F1-macro and recall while maintaining comparable ROC-AUC across several generators. We also provide explicit lambda-sensitivity analysis to show how users can recover AUPRC when ranking quality is prioritized.

AI.tldr: RUBRIC is a generator-agnostic filtering framework that selects high-quality synthetic samples for tackling class imbalance by optimizing a realism-utility trade-off, theoretically tightening generalization bounds, and empirically improving F1-macro and recall across multiple generators.
AI.motivation: Class imbalance harms risk-sensitive applications (fraud detection, medical diagnosis) because existing oversampling methods produce many low-quality synthetic candidates that distort decision boundaries, introduce artifacts, and cause overfitting and poor generalization.
AI.method: RUBRIC is a generator-agnostic filtering framework that formulates synthetic sample selection as a quality-over-quantity optimization problem. It ranks candidates using a realism-utility trade-off: realism via a learned discriminator (real vs. synthetic), and utility via a concave margin-based scoring function measuring proximity to the decision boundary. It theoretically shows the filtering strategy monotonically tightens the generalization bound for margin-based classifiers under mild regularity conditions.
AI.result: On credit-card fraud detection and other imbalanced benchmarks, RUBRIC improves F1-macro and recall while maintaining comparable ROC-AUC across several generators. Explicit lambda-sensitivity analysis shows how users can recover AUPRC when ranking quality is prioritized.
AI.conclusion: RUBRIC effectively addresses the quality issue in oversampling by selecting fewer but better synthetic samples, leading to improved generalization and classification performance on minority classes.

title: UniPose9D: Universal Category-Agnostic Object Pose Estimation
summary: Object pose estimation is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Although recent state-of-the-art approaches achieve strong performance, they often overfit to existing benchmarks and exhibit limited generalization to novel categories and unseen scenes. We propose UniPose9D, a category-agnostic foundation model for 9D object pose estimation: given an instance mask/ROI and either an RGB-D observation or an RGB image with predicted depth, the model estimates rotation, translation, and metric size without category labels, CAD models, mean-shape priors, or reference views. Specifically, UniPose9D samples point pairs from the observed object geometry and uses DINOv2 and PointNet features to predict NOCS coordinates for each pair. To improve accuracy, we introduce a point-pair-based RANSAC N-hop Kabsch--Umeyama algorithm with an adaptive threshold. We further employ flow matching to address symmetric ambiguities and construct a large-scale training set by curating and aligning pose annotations from existing public datasets. Experiments across six datasets show that a single unified model can match or surpass specialist methods while generalizing to unseen objects and in-the-wild scenarios. Our code and model are available on https://github.com/qq456cvb/UniPose9D.

AI.tldr: UniPose9D is a category-agnostic foundation model for 9D object pose estimation (rotation, translation, metric size) that uses point-pair sampling, DINOv2+PointNet features, NOCS coordinate prediction, a novel RANSAC N-hop Kabsch-Umeyama algorithm, and flow matching for symmetry handling, achieving state-of-the-art performance across six datasets without category labels, CAD models, or shape priors.
AI.motivation: Existing object pose estimation methods overfit to benchmarks and exhibit limited generalization to novel categories and unseen scenes; the goal is to build a category-agnostic foundation model that works across diverse objects without requiring category labels, CAD models, mean-shape priors, or reference views.
AI.method: UniPose9D takes an instance mask/ROI with RGB-D (or RGB + predicted depth), samples point pairs from observed geometry, extracts features via DINOv2 and PointNet to predict NOCS coordinates per pair, applies a point-pair-based RANSAC N-hop Kabsch-Umeyama algorithm with adaptive threshold for pose estimation, and uses flow matching to resolve symmetric ambiguities. Training uses a large-scale curated dataset with aligned pose annotations from multiple public datasets.
AI.result: A single unified model matches or surpasses specialist methods across six datasets, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen objects and in-the-wild scenarios.
AI.conclusion: UniPose9D shows that a category-agnostic foundation model can achieve competitive performance with specialized approaches while generalizing better, eliminating the need for category-specific training, CAD models, or shape priors.

title: RepTran: Search-Based Repair of Transformer Models
comment: 12 pages. Accepted to the Research Track of ISSRE 2026
summary: To ensure the overall quality of AI-enabled software, not only traditional software components but also AI components need to be tested and repaired. Among AI components, Transformer models are increasingly integrated into software systems, which makes their misbehaviors critical. Although prior work in the software engineering community has proposed deep neural network (DNN) repair methods, most overlook Transformer-specific structures. We propose RepTran, a search-based repair method for Transformer models. It targets their feed-forward networks (FFNs), which play a central role in the architecture. RepTran identifies suspicious weights by combining two types of scores: a variance-based neuron score and an existing bidirectional score. It then iteratively optimizes these weights using differential evolution. Our evaluation includes 18 fault benchmarks constructed from CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet. We compare RepTran against three baselines: random weight selection, Arachne (a state-of-the-art DNN repair method), and ArachneW, which enables Arachne to control the number of selected weights. RepTran achieved an average repair rate of 74.7%, statistically outperforming random selection and Arachne across all benchmarks. Effect size analysis revealed that RepTran achieved higher repair rates than ArachneW regardless of the number of selected weights. These results suggest that RepTran is effective for enhancing the reliability of AI-enabled software.

AI.tldr: RepTran is a search-based repair method for Transformer models that targets feed-forward networks by combining variance-based neuron scores and bidirectional scores to identify suspicious weights, then optimizes them via differential evolution, achieving 74.7% average repair rate and outperforming baselines on 18 fault benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Transformer models are increasingly integrated into AI-enabled software, but existing DNN repair methods overlook Transformer-specific structures, leaving their misbehaviors unaddressed.
AI.method: RepTran identifies suspicious weights in Transformer FFNs by combining a variance-based neuron score with an existing bidirectional score, then iteratively optimizes these weights using differential evolution (search-based repair).
AI.result: Achieved 74.7% average repair rate across 18 fault benchmarks (CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet), statistically outperforming random selection and Arachne; effect size analysis showed higher repair rates than ArachneW regardless of selected weight count.
AI.conclusion: RepTran is effective for enhancing the reliability of AI-enabled software by providing a Transformer-specific repair method that outperforms general DNN repair approaches.

title: PHITSBench: an execution-scored benchmark for AI-assisted PHITS radiation-transport input generation using natural language
summary: We introduce PHITSBench, an execution-scored benchmark for the Monte Carlo Particle and Heavy Ion Transport code System (PHITS). PHITSBench comprises 282 transport-scorable tasks spanning three common workflow categories: parameter editing (Edit), syntax repair (Repair ), and complete simulation generation from natural-language descriptions (Reproduce). Each task is evaluated using a Composite Metric Score that combines execution success with agreement between generated and reference transport observables. Using PHITSBench, we evaluate five GPT-5.4-based configurations ranging from zero-shot prompting to knowledge-augmented and agentic workflows. Without domain-specific knowledge, the model performs well on editing and repair tasks (95% and 70% success, respectively) but fails to generate correct simulations from scratch (0% success on the Reproduce track). A structured, machine-readable PHITS knowledge catalog, supplied alongside the user manual, raises single-shot Reproduce-task success to 57%. Agentic execution provides a further improvement to 66-73%, but at increased computational cost. Failure analysis shows that the remaining errors are dominated by incorrect selection and configuration of physical observables rather than syntax generation. These results suggest that future progress in AI-assisted radiation-transport modeling will depend as much on machine-readable knowledge bases, curated domain-training datasets, and execution-grounded evaluation environments as on advances in foundation models themselves.

AI.tldr: PHITSBench is an execution-scored benchmark with 282 tasks for Monte Carlo particle transport code (PHITS). GPT-5.4 achieves 95% on editing and 70% on repair, but 0% on full generation; knowledge augmentation raises generation success to 57%, and agentic workflows to 66-73%. Errors are dominated by physical observable configuration, not syntax.
AI.motivation: There is no existing execution-scored benchmark for evaluating LLMs on the PHITS Monte Carlo code system, making it difficult to assess AI-assisted radiation-transport modeling capabilities.
AI.method: Created PHITSBench with 282 tasks across three categories (Edit, Repair, Reproduce). Evaluated five GPT-5.4 configurations (zero-shot, knowledge-augmented, agentic). Used a Composite Metric Score combining execution success and agreement with reference observables.
AI.result: Zero-shot: 95% Edit, 70% Repair, 0% Reproduce. Knowledge-augmented: 57% Reproduce. Agentic: 66-73% Reproduce. Remaining errors dominated by incorrect physical observable selection/configuration.
AI.conclusion: Future progress in AI-assisted radiation-transport modeling requires machine-readable knowledge bases, curated domain-training datasets, and execution-grounded evaluation environments in addition to advances in foundation models.

title: Estimation, Prediction, and Assortment Optimization for Markov Chain Choice Models with Panel Data
summary: We propose a framework for the Markov chain (MC) choice model with panel data, including parameter estimation, personalized choice prediction, and personalized assortment optimization. In contrast to the traditional setting, which assumes that each transaction is independently drawn from a random utility model, our framework accounts for dependencies among transactions for the same customer in historical data, captured by partial-ordering preference information. To the best of our knowledge, our framework initiates the study of choice modeling with panel data under MC. As our primary result, we propose novel expectation-maximization (EM) algorithms for MC parameter estimation by incorporating partial-ordering-based customer preference information. On synthetic datasets and the sushi dataset, our EM algorithms outperform the traditional EM algorithm of Simsek and Topaloglu (Operations Research, 66, 2018) and multinomial-logit-based partial-order benchmarks adapted from Jagabathula and Vulcano (Management Science, 64, 2018). As our secondary contribution, we present hardness and computational results for conditional choice prediction and assortment optimization problems. These results complement our estimation framework and clarify the computational landscape of conditional choice and assortment optimization, which may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Markov chain choice model framework for panel data that accounts for customer-level dependencies via partial-ordering preferences, proposes novel EM algorithms for parameter estimation that outperform existing methods, and provides hardness/computational results for choice prediction and assortment optimization.
AI.motivation: Traditional choice models assume independent transactions from random utility models, ignoring dependencies among transactions from the same customer in panel data. The paper aims to fill this gap by incorporating partial-ordering preference information into the Markov chain choice model framework.
AI.method: The authors develop novel expectation-maximization (EM) algorithms that incorporate partial-ordering-based customer preference information for Markov chain parameter estimation using panel data. They validate on synthetic datasets and the sushi dataset, comparing against traditional EM (Simsek & Topaloglu) and multinomial-logit-based partial-order benchmarks (Jagabathula & Vulcano).
AI.result: The proposed EM algorithms outperform existing methods on both synthetic datasets and the sushi dataset. The paper also establishes hardness results and computational findings for conditional choice prediction and assortment optimization problems.
AI.conclusion: The framework initiates the study of choice modeling with panel data under the Markov chain model. The computational landscape results for conditional choice and assortment optimization complement the estimation framework and may be of independent interest.

title: Model Guides You How to Draw: Adaptive Visual Gating for Unified Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) with interleaved reasoning, which generate both textual and visual steps as part of intermediate reasoning traces, have demonstrated great potential for visual mathematical reasoning tasks. However, we identify a key insight in this paradigm: generating intermediate visual reasoning steps is not always beneficial and can even be harmful, as self-generated visual steps may introduce erroneous visual evidence that misleads subsequent reasoning. Moreover, frequently triggering visual steps during reasoning incurs substantial computational and memory overhead, degrading inference efficiency. To address these accuracy and efficiency challenges, we observe that the model's internal signals can indicate whether a visual step will benefit reasoning before the entire visual generation is completed. Specifically, this work identifies two internal signals: 1) Generation Intent, which reflects whether the model has a concrete textual plan for what to draw, and 2) Visual Fidelity, which measures whether the visual generation remains grounded in the original input image. Leveraging these internal signals, we propose AdaViG, a training-free adaptive visual gating method for unified multimodal reasoning. AdaViG dynamically evaluates each triggered visual step at an early visual generation stage and aborts it when both signals are weak, thereby preventing misleading visual evidence from entering the reasoning trace while avoiding unnecessary computation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AdaViG improves accuracy by up to 5.7% while reducing visual generation FLOPs by 25.0%-91.0% and wall-clock latency by 15.4%-45.6%.

AI.tldr: AdaViG is a training-free adaptive visual gating method that uses internal model signals (Generation Intent and Visual Fidelity) to dynamically decide whether to generate intermediate visual reasoning steps in unified multimodal models, preventing harmful visual steps from misleading reasoning while reducing computational overhead by up to 91%.
AI.motivation: Intermediate visual reasoning steps in UMMs can introduce erroneous visual evidence that misleads reasoning, and frequently triggering visual steps incurs substantial computational and memory overhead, degrading inference efficiency.
AI.method: AdaViG leverages two internal signals—Generation Intent (whether the model has a concrete textual plan for what to draw) and Visual Fidelity (whether visual generation remains grounded in the original input image)—to dynamically gate each triggered visual step at an early generation stage, aborting it when both signals are weak.
AI.result: AdaViG improves accuracy by up to 5.7%, reduces visual generation FLOPs by 25.0%-91.0%, and reduces wall-clock latency by 15.4%-45.6%.
AI.conclusion: Early internal model signals can effectively predict whether a visual step will benefit reasoning, and adaptive gating based on these signals improves both accuracy and efficiency in unified multimodal reasoning.

title: An Empirical Study for GUI Test Migration from Android to OpenHarmony System
summary: To reduce the substantial engineering effort required to test the corresponding applications from Android to OpenHarmony, migrating existing GUI test cases has become a critical problem. However, current research neither proposes solutions tailored for OpenHarmony nor provides a systematic evaluation of migration approaches on this system, leaving developers with limited empirical guidance in practice. In this paper, we present the first systematic empirical study of test migration from Android to OpenHarmony. Specifically, we first construct a dataset referred to as the ATH Benchmark, comprising 36 commercial applications with an average of over 9 billion downloads, along with 108 manually designed test cases. Second, we select two state-of-the-art test migration approaches (i.e., ReSPlay and ITeM) and adapt these two approaches to enable their execution on OpenHarmony. Third, we use the preceding infrastructure to evaluate these two approaches from three perspectives, including testing performance, root causes of failures, and the impact of OpenHarmony characteristics. Our results reveal that existing test migration approaches are less effective (15% success-rate on ReSPlay and 26% success-rate on ITeM) in Android-to-OpenHarmony scenarios. Through an in-depth analysis of failed cases, we identify that test performance is primarily hindered by OpenHarmony-specific characteristics, including technical architecture differences and unique ecosystem traits. Utilizing these findings, we propose an enhanced approach based on ITeM, referred as ITeM-HM, which incorporates specific OpenHarmony system features. As a result, ITeM-HM successfully achieves a 214% success-rate relative improvement over the original ITeM (from 26% to 81%).

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic empirical study of migrating GUI test cases from Android to OpenHarmony. Using a benchmark of 36 commercial apps and 108 test cases, the authors evaluate two existing migration approaches (ReSPlay and ITeM), finding low success rates (15% and 26% respectively). Based on failure analysis, they propose ITeM-HM, which improves success rate from 26% to 81%.
AI.motivation: The engineering effort required to test Android applications migrated to OpenHarmony is substantial, yet no existing research provides tailored solutions or systematic evaluation of test migration approaches for OpenHarmony.
AI.method: Constructed the ATH Benchmark with 36 commercial apps (9B+ downloads) and 108 test cases; adapted ReSPlay and ITeM for OpenHarmony; evaluated them on testing performance, failure root causes, and impact of OpenHarmony characteristics; developed ITeM-HM incorporating system-specific features.
AI.result: ReSPlay achieved 15% success rate; ITeM achieved 26% success rate. Failure causes stem from OpenHarmony-specific technical architecture differences and ecosystem traits. ITeM-HM achieved 81% success rate (214% relative improvement over ITeM).
AI.conclusion: Existing Android-to-OpenHarmony test migration approaches are significantly less effective, but the proposed ITeM-HM, which accounts for OpenHarmony-specific characteristics, substantially improves migration success.

title: Semantic Drift and the Stability of Operator Control in Reasoning-Class Decision Support Systems
summary: The article investigates the fundamental problem of ensuring the stability of operator control and preserving goal-targeting in hybrid human-machine decision support systems (DSS) of a new generation. Based on a two-month continuous longitudinal experiment on the joint design of a monograph-format textual array, the latent phenomenon of semantic context drift in large language models of deep logical reasoning (Reasoning LLMs) is verified and described. A mathematical model of interaction in the human-machine interface is proposed, and an original metric is introduced - the operator control stability coefficient, which takes into account the non-linear contextual pressure of hidden reasoning chains. Within the paradigm of the cognitome theory, a critical point of control functions inversion is captured. Engineering recommendations are formulated for implementing dynamic relational arbitration loops based on a modified hierarchical similarity model.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies semantic context drift in Reasoning LLMs during prolonged human-machine interaction, proposes a mathematical model with a novel stability metric, and offers engineering recommendations for dynamic arbitration loops to preserve operator control in hybrid DSS.
AI.motivation: To address the underexplored problem of control stability loss and goal-targeting degradation in next-generation hybrid human-machine decision support systems, particularly when interacting with deep reasoning LLMs over extended periods.
AI.method: A two-month continuous longitudinal experiment involving joint design of a monograph-format text; application of cognitome theory; development of a mathematical interaction model; introduction of an operator control stability coefficient that accounts for non-linear contextual pressure from hidden reasoning chains.
AI.result: Verification and description of the latent phenomenon of semantic context drift in Reasoning LLMs; identification of a critical inversion point of control functions; a measurable stability coefficient capturing nonlinear contextual effects.
AI.conclusion: Engineering recommendations for implementing dynamic relational arbitration loops based on a modified hierarchical similarity model to mitigate context drift and preserve operator control stability.

title: Learning Predictive Ambiguity Sets for Decision-Focused Distributionally Robust Optimization
summary: Predict-then-optimize systems usually compress uncertainty into a point forecast and then solve a downstream optimization problem as if the forecast were reliable. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers protection against misspecification, but the ambiguity set is often centered at historical samples and uses a fixed radius. We propose \emph{learned predictive ambiguity sets} (LPAS): a deep contextual model outputs a finite nominal scenario distribution, a state-dependent Wasserstein radius, and optionally an anisotropic ground metric. These outputs define a contextual ambiguity set that feeds a DRO decision layer. The radius is trained by a combination of conditional quantile calibration, size regularization, and downstream decision loss, so that robustness is adaptive rather than globally fixed. We derive the finite dual form used by the decision layer, present a staged training algorithm, and evaluate the method on distributionally robust portfolio optimization with 20 S&P 500 constituents from 2018--2026. The proposed method substantially improves over equal-weight, predict-then-optimize, and historical Wasserstein DRO baselines, achieving 26.28% annualized return, Sharpe ratio 1.30, final wealth 1.61, and lower tail loss than a deep fixed-radius DRO baseline while using a smaller average radius. The results show that learned ambiguity radii can recover most of the performance of strong fixed-radius DRO while reducing unnecessary conservatism and improving regime adaptivity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Learned Predictive Ambiguity Sets (LPAS), a deep contextual model that outputs a nominal scenario distribution, state-dependent Wasserstein radius, and optional anisotropic ground metric for distributionally robust optimization. LPAS adapts robustness per context via conditional quantile calibration, size regularization, and downstream decision loss. Evaluated on portfolio optimization with 20 S&P 500 stocks (2018-2026), LPAS achieves 26.28% annualized return, Sharpe ratio 1.30, and final wealth 1.61, outperforming equal-weight, predict-then-optimize, and fixed-radius DRO baselines while using a smaller average radius.
AI.motivation: Predict-then-optimize systems compress uncertainty into point forecasts, ignoring misspecification. Existing DRO methods use historical samples with fixed radii, lacking adaptivity. The goal is to make robustness state-dependent and learnable to reduce unnecessary conservatism while improving performance.
AI.method: LPAS uses a deep contextual model to output (1) a finite nominal scenario distribution, (2) a state-dependent Wasserstein radius, and (3) an optional anisotropic ground metric. These define a contextual ambiguity set fed into a DRO decision layer. Training combines conditional quantile calibration, size regularization, and downstream decision loss in a staged algorithm.
AI.result: On a 20-stock S&P 500 portfolio from 2018-2026, LPAS achieves 26.28% annualized return, Sharpe ratio 1.30, final wealth 1.61, and lower tail loss than fixed-radius DRO baselines while using a smaller average radius. It substantially outperforms equal-weight, predict-then-optimize, and historical Wasserstein DRO baselines.
AI.conclusion: Learned ambiguity radii can recover most of the performance of strong fixed-radius DRO while reducing unnecessary conservatism and improving regime adaptivity, demonstrating the value of context-dependent robustness.

title: FlashBEV: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact BEV Transformation with IO-Awareness
summary: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) perception is a core component of camera-based 3D understanding in autonomous driving, where view transformation (VT) maps multi-camera image features into a unified BEV representation. Sampling-based view transformation (Sampling-VT) is attractive because it supports dense and continuous BEV aggregation for high-resolution and long-range perception. Its deployment bottleneck, however, is systems-level: standard tensorized implementations of Sampling-VT -- which we refer to as Tensorized Sampling-VT -- explicitly materialize large height-dependent intermediate tensors, causing memory and latency costs that scale poorly with vertical resolution and the number of cameras. We revisit Tensorized Sampling-VT from an operator-execution perspective and show that it follows a gather-reduction pattern: each BEV query independently accumulates contributions across cameras and height bins, enabling thread-local accumulation with on-the-fly recomputation that eliminates the need to materialize height- and camera-dependent intermediates. Based on this insight, we propose FlashBEV, a fully fused and IO-aware execution strategy mathematically equivalent to Tensorized Sampling-VT (same operator output) while substantially reducing global memory traffic and kernel-launch overhead. Experiments show that FlashBEV achieves more than an order of magnitude lower peak GPU memory and significant inference-latency speedups, with memory effectively independent of the number of height bins, reducing the operator's peak memory to O(BCXY) (output only). This unlocks higher BEV range/resolution and vertical discretization within fixed deployment budgets on memory-constrained devices. Our contribution is an execution redesign -- same math, different execution -- that removes a key scalability barrier for deployment-ready Sampling-VT. Code available at https://github.com/yokosyun/FlashBEV

AI.tldr: FlashBEV introduces a fully fused, IO-aware execution strategy for sampling-based view transformation (Sampling-VT) in BEV perception that eliminates materialization of large height-dependent intermediate tensors by using thread-local accumulation with on-the-fly recomputation, achieving >10x peak GPU memory reduction and significant latency speedups while maintaining mathematical equivalence to standard tensorized implementations.
AI.motivation: Standard tensorized implementations of Sampling-VT materialize large height-dependent intermediate tensors, causing memory and latency costs that scale poorly with vertical resolution and number of cameras, creating a deployment bottleneck for memory-constrained autonomous driving systems.
AI.method: FlashBEV reinterprets Tensorized Sampling-VT as a gather-reduction pattern where each BEV query independently accumulates contributions across cameras and height bins via thread-local accumulation with on-the-fly recomputation, eliminating height- and camera-dependent intermediate materialization through a fully fused, IO-aware execution strategy.
AI.result: More than an order of magnitude lower peak GPU memory (reduced to O(BCXY) — output only), significant inference-latency speedups, memory effectively independent of number of height bins, enabling higher BEV range/resolution and vertical discretization within fixed deployment budgets.
AI.conclusion: FlashBEV removes a key scalability barrier for deployment-ready Sampling-VT through an execution redesign that achieves the same mathematical output with dramatically lower memory and latency, enabling high-resolution and long-range BEV perception on memory-constrained devices.

title: Hidden or Formal Architects: Understanding Who Makes Architectural Decisions in Practice
comment: Accepted at 52nd Euromicro Conference on Software Engineering and Advanced Applications (SEAA) 2026
summary: Empirical research on software architecture sometimes focuses on individuals holding the formal title of software architect. However, not all companies have individuals hired in such roles. Despite no formal architects, all systems have architectures, and there must be practitioners making the architectural decisions. This study aims to identify who, in practice, makes architectural decisions and in what environments the existence of a formal architect is perceived as necessary. This research employed a method consisting of a questionnaire with 54 participants from different companies and seven follow-up interviews. The findings indicate that architectural decisions are often made by individuals without a formal architect title. A formal architect is perceived as essential mainly in large companies and large teams. The results of this study show that many practitioners taking part in ADM may have been omitted by previous research, particularly if it focused on formal architects.

AI.tldr: Architectural decisions are often made by practitioners without formal architect titles, especially in small companies/teams, while formal architects are perceived as essential mainly in large companies. This suggests previous research focusing only on formal architects may have missed many actual decision-makers.
AI.motivation: To identify who actually makes architectural decisions in practice, given that not all companies have formal architect roles despite all systems having architectures.
AI.method: A questionnaire with 54 participants from different companies and seven follow-up interviews.
AI.result: Architectural decisions are often made by individuals without formal architect titles. Formal architects are perceived as essential mainly in large companies and large teams. Many practitioners involved in architectural decision-making may have been overlooked by prior research that focused solely on formal architects.
AI.conclusion: Previous research on software architecture decision-making that focused exclusively on formal architect roles may have omitted a significant population of practitioners who actually make these decisions in practice.

title: Agentic Context Learning with Self-Discovered Specification
summary: Context learning is an emerging inference-time task where LLMs must learn and apply novel, task-specific knowledge from intricate contexts absent from pre-training; even frontier models score under 24% task success. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study to understand why this setting remains difficult. A natural hypothesis is that failures stem from content access; yet across twelve retrieval, reflection, and verification baselines on CL-Bench, an extensive context learning benchmark, we find limited gains over direct full-context prompting. Further failure analysis reveals a key finding: unlike typical long-context tasks such as long document understanding, context learning requires not only recovering local content but also acquiring local specifications that are often unspecified in the query but distributed across the context: domain-specific formats, local rules, and completeness conditions. Across all 31,592 rubric items, we find that 55.4% clearly evaluate specification acquisition, while only 22.6% evaluate content acquisition. Moreover, despite 76.7% of specifications being unspecified in the user query, 95.5% are traceable to the context, indicating these are learnable obligations rather than hidden requirements. To validate this diagnosis, we design a deliberately simple intervention PSCI (private specification-contract induction) which extracts local specifications and enforces them through adversarial checking and repair; PSCI achieves state-of-the-art 28.14% with GPT-5.1 (+5.59 pp absolute and +24.8% relative) on CL-Bench, replicated on Qwen3.5-27B (+5.28 pp) and Gemini 3 Pro (+6.17 pp). Seventeen ablations further isolate the role of task-specific specifications. Overall, our results suggest context learning hinges on not only content acquisition but also specification acquisition.

AI.tldr: Context learning remains challenging for LLMs, with frontier models scoring <24% task success. The paper shows that failures are not mainly due to content access issues but rather specification acquisition: learning local, often unspecified rules distributed across context. The proposed PSCI (private specification-contract induction) method achieves state-of-the-art performance by extracting and enforcing these specifications.
AI.motivation: Despite extensive baselines (retrieval, reflection, verification) on CL-Bench, context learning still yields poor performance. The authors aim to understand why this emerging inference-time task remains difficult for LLMs.
AI.method: The study first conducts a comprehensive empirical analysis across 12 baselines on CL-Bench, then performs failure analysis on 31,592 rubric items to identify that 55.4% evaluate specification acquisition vs. 22.6% for content acquisition. They propose PSCI, which extracts local specifications (domain-specific formats, local rules, completeness conditions) from context, and enforces them via adversarial checking and repair.
AI.result: PSCI achieves state-of-the-art 28.14% with GPT-5.1 (+5.59 pp absolute, +24.8% relative) on CL-Bench, replicated on Qwen3.5-27B (+5.28 pp) and Gemini 3 Pro (+6.17 pp). Seventeen ablations confirm the role of task-specific specifications. 95.5% of specifications are traceable to context despite 76.7% being unspecified in the query.
AI.conclusion: Context learning hinges on both content acquisition and specification acquisition; the latter is a key bottleneck. Extracting and enforcing local specifications from context significantly improves performance, suggesting models need to learn not just facts but also implicit, distributed task rules.

title: A Strong Balanced-Softmax Classifier-Retraining Baseline for Long-Tailed Recognition
summary: Long-tailed recognition methods often modify losses, margins, or representations to reduce the dominance of frequent classes. We ask whether, after Balanced Softmax training, the remaining tail error can be reduced by retraining only the classifier. We evaluate BS-cRT, a two-stage procedure that trains a backbone and cosine classifier with Balanced Softmax, freezes the backbone, and updates only the classifier on balanced episodic batches. The second stage keeps the empirical-prior Balanced Softmax objective and uses raw cosine logits at inference. Across CIFAR-100-LT, CIFAR-10-LT, ImageNet-LT, and Places-LT, this classifier-only step consistently improves Few-shot accuracy over the matched Balanced Softmax checkpoint. At imbalance factor 100, Few-shot gains are +5.15 points on CIFAR-100-LT and +5.83 on CIFAR-10-LT; on ImageNet-LT and Places-LT, gains are +6.92 and +9.78 points, respectively, with a Top-1/Few-shot trade-off on ImageNet-LT. We also analyze Counterfactual Boundary Risk Minimization (CBRM), a boundary-probe extension using prototype-based features near decision boundaries. CBRM identifies two failure modes: scaled-logit cosine margins destabilize training, and corrected hardest-negative probes remain head-class anchored. The results support BS-cRT as a practical classifier-side baseline and indicate that boundary supervision must account for class frequency.

AI.tldr: After Balanced Softmax training, retraining only the classifier (BS-cRT) on balanced episodic batches consistently improves few-shot accuracy across four long-tailed benchmarks, while a boundary-probe extension (CBRM) reveals that cosine-margin scaling destabilizes training and hard-negative probes remain head-class anchored.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the remaining tail error after Balanced Softmax training can be reduced by retraining only the classifier, without modifying the backbone.
AI.method: BS-cRT: two-stage procedure — (1) train backbone + cosine classifier with Balanced Softmax, (2) freeze backbone, update only classifier on balanced episodic batches while keeping the Balanced Softmax objective and using raw cosine logits at inference. CBRM: a boundary-probe extension using prototype-based features near decision boundaries.
AI.result: BS-cRT consistently improves few-shot accuracy over matched Balanced Softmax checkpoints: +5.15 (CIFAR-100-LT), +5.83 (CIFAR-10-LT) at imbalance 100; +6.92 (ImageNet-LT), +9.78 (Places-LT). Top-1/Few-shot trade-off observed on ImageNet-LT. CBRM reveals two failure modes: scaled-logit cosine margins destabilize training; corrected hardest-negative probes remain head-class anchored.
AI.conclusion: BS-cRT is a practical classifier-side baseline for long-tailed recognition; boundary supervision methods must account for class frequency to be effective.

title: Extending Decision Maps for Sustainable Safety and Security in Self-Adaptive Systems
summary: Sustainability refers to a system's ability to maintain its functionality and endure over time. Hence, sustainability is a highly desirable property of software systems, including Self-Adaptive Systems (SASs). SASs can change (adapt) their behavior at runtime to continue achieving their objectives despite external or internal impacts. SASs' intended long-term system behavior can be expressed through a sustainability-driven visual modeling notation called Decision Maps (DMs). Although DMs have been proven helpful, they lack adequate modeling support for safety and security concerns. We address this limitation by extending the current notation for sustainability-driven modeling of SASs to better accommodate the unique characteristics of safety and security scenarios. First, we introduce an additional modeling dimension to account for safety incidents. Second, we adopt a fine-grained divide-and-conquer approach, modeling from distinct temporal security viewpoints ("security modes") to address security. We employ the extended DM notation in a real-world use case scenario provided by our industry partner to assess its feasibility and suitability for practitioners. Our results indicate that our modeling notation helps capture security and safety scenarios more accurately and provides holistic support for the self-adaptation life cycle phases.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Decision Maps (DMs), a sustainability-driven visual modeling notation for Self-Adaptive Systems (SASs), to incorporate safety and security concerns by adding a safety incident dimension and a fine-grained "security modes" approach from temporal viewpoints, validated through an industry case study.
AI.motivation: Decision Maps (DMs) support sustainability-driven modeling of Self-Adaptive Systems (SASs) but lack adequate support for modeling safety and security concerns, which are critical for long-term system sustainability.
AI.method: The authors extend the DM notation by (1) introducing a new modeling dimension for safety incidents, and (2) adopting a divide-and-conquer approach with distinct temporal security viewpoints ("security modes") for security. The extended notation is evaluated in a real-world industrial use case.
AI.result: The extended DM notation helps capture security and safety scenarios more accurately and provides holistic support for the self-adaptation life cycle phases, as demonstrated in the industry partner's use case.
AI.conclusion: The proposed extensions to Decision Maps improve the modeling of safety and security in sustainability-driven Self-Adaptive Systems, offering practitioners a more comprehensive tool for designing adaptive systems that endure over time.

title: Exploring Agentic Workflows for Generating High Quality Math Visual Aids
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Exploratory course project on agentic workflows for generating and evaluating K 12 mathematical diagrams
summary: Mathematical diagrams play a crucial role in K 12 education, both as problem components and as scaffolding for student comprehension. However, current AI tools, including Large Language Models (LLMs), struggle to reliably generate accurate and pedagogically sound visual diagrams, even when provided with detailed descriptions. A significant gap therefore remains in the reliable generation of diagrams for middle school mathematics. To address this, we introduce an agentic workflow that enables LLM agents to evaluate the quality of generated visuals and use this feedback to iteratively improve their outputs. This self improvement loop aims to enhance the accuracy and educational appropriateness of AI generated diagrams. Our research investigates two questions. First, can LLMs accurately generate quality assurance questions for a visual aid given specific criteria for visual quality? Second, given valid quality assurance questions, can Vision Language Models effectively evaluate generated K 12 visual aids and use the resulting feedback to improve them iteratively? We conduct an exploratory evaluation of our agentic workflow and identify key areas for improvement, including stronger spatial reasoning and more comprehensive coverage of diagram features in the generated quality assurance questions. Our results provide preliminary evidence that this approach can improve the reliability and educational value of AI generated mathematical diagrams.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an agentic workflow where LLM agents iteratively generate, evaluate, and improve K-12 mathematical diagrams using self-generated quality assurance questions and Vision Language Model feedback, aiming to enhance diagram accuracy and educational appropriateness.
AI.motivation: Current AI tools (including LLMs) struggle to reliably generate accurate and pedagogically sound mathematical diagrams for K-12 education, creating a significant gap in automated diagram generation for middle school mathematics.
AI.method: The authors introduce an agentic workflow with a self-improvement loop: LLM agents generate quality assurance questions for visual aids based on specific criteria, then Vision Language Models evaluate generated diagrams using these questions and iteratively improve the outputs based on feedback.
AI.result: Exploratory evaluation shows preliminary evidence that the approach can improve diagram reliability and educational value, but identifies weaknesses in spatial reasoning and insufficient coverage of diagram features in generated QA questions.
AI.conclusion: The agentic workflow shows promise for enhancing AI-generated mathematical diagrams, though future work is needed to strengthen spatial reasoning and QA question comprehensiveness.

title: From Direction to Magnitude: How Multimodal Instruction-Tuning Reorganizes the Geometric Encoding of Identity-Specifying Prompts in Transformer Hidden States
comment: 16 pages, 8 tables. Working draft v0.3. Uses Ollivier-Ricci curvature and edge-wise Wasserstein-1 as primary geometric statistic; four models (Gemma-4-E4B, Gemma-4-E4B-it, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct)
summary: We investigate whether identity-specifying system prompts produce statistically distinguishable geometric fingerprints in the hidden-state trajectories of four open-weight transformer language models spanning four post-training regimes: no training (Gemma-4-E4B base), multimodal RLHF (Gemma-4-E4B-it), RL distillation (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), and SFT (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Three prompt conditions (an identity-specifying axis prompt, a length-matched generic-assistant prompt, and a 26-token vanilla baseline) are compared via five geometric metrics, principally the 1-Wasserstein distance between edge-wise distributions of Ollivier-Ricci curvature on k-NN trajectory graphs. Claims rest on trajectory-level permutation tests with multiple geometric controls (teacher-forced content controls, temporal-chain vs k-NN topology, ABT-projected k-NN, angular vs Euclidean graph construction, B=5000 permutations on borderline statistics). The central finding is a qualitative reorganization of identity encoding across the instruction-tuning boundary: in the base model the fingerprint is direction-coded (separation 0.034, p=0.002 under angular k-NN); in the multimodal instruction-tuned model it migrates into the magnitude (angular separation collapses to p=0.439 while Euclidean survives at p=0.042, and the mean norm of the first generated state inverts its length-ordering, being lowest for the identity prompt). This direction-to-magnitude reorganization is specific to the multimodal instruction-tuning regime, absent under RL distillation and SFT. A teacher-forced control attributes ~30% of the free-running cosine signal to prompt-driven effects. We position W_1 on edge-wise Ollivier-Ricci distributions on k-NN trajectory graphs as a methodological contribution of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Identity-specifying system prompts produce statistically distinguishable geometric fingerprints in LLM hidden-state trajectories, with a qualitative reorganization from direction-coded (base model) to magnitude-coded (multimodal instruction-tuned model), absent under RL distillation and SFT. The paper introduces 1-Wasserstein distance on edge-wise Ollivier-Ricci curvature distributions of k-NN trajectory graphs as a novel geometric analysis method.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether identity-specifying system prompts (e.g., "you are a helpful assistant") induce systematic, geometrically distinguishable patterns in the hidden-state trajectories of LLMs, and to understand how these patterns vary across different post-training regimes (base, RLHF, RL distillation, SFT).
AI.method: Four open-weight models spanning four post-training regimes are compared under three prompt conditions. Five geometric metrics are computed on k-NN trajectory graphs, primarily 1-Wasserstein distance between edge-wise Ollivier-Ricci curvature distributions. Trajectory-level permutation tests with multiple geometric controls (teacher-forced content controls, temporal-chain vs k-NN topology, ABT-projected k-NN, angular vs Euclidean graph construction, B=5000 permutations) are used.
AI.result: In the base model, the identity fingerprint is direction-coded (angular separation 0.034, p=0.002). In the multimodal instruction-tuned model, it migrates to magnitude (angular p=0.439, Euclidean p=0.042; mean norm of first generated state is lowest for identity prompt). This reorganization is specific to multimodal instruction-tuning, absent under RL distillation and SFT. Teacher-forced control attributes ~30% of free-running cosine signal to prompt-driven effects.
AI.conclusion: Instruction tuning qualitatively reorganizes how identity information is geometrically encoded in LLM hidden states, shifting from directional to magnitude-based encoding specifically under multimodal RLHF. The proposed methodological framework (W_1 on Ollivier-Ricci curvature of k-NN trajectory graphs) offers a novel tool for analyzing prompt-induced geometric structure.

title: CVKD-UDA: Cross-View Knowledge Distillation for 3D Unsupervised Domain Adaptive Segmentation
summary: 3D unsupervised domain adaptive (UDA) segmentation mitigates the high cost of manual annotations of the new domain data. Self-training has emerged as the dominant approach in this area, where its success heavily depends on a well-initialized warm-up model to generate reliable pseudo labels. However, existing methods often depend on source supervision or output-level adversarial alignment to obtain the warm-up model, which suffer from limited generalization and training instability due to the large domain gap between domains. Constructing domain-similar representations is an effective way to bridge this gap. In this work, we propose CVKD-UDA, which revisits voxel size as a core design factor to construct domain-similar representations and leverages cross-view complementary cues to balance transferability and discriminability of the warm-up model. First, we generate two complementary views by varying voxel sizes and introduce a cross-view knowledge distillation (CVKD) to enhance generalization and target perception of the model. Second, to balance transferability and discriminability, we design a lightweight Decouple-Adapter and an auxiliary imitation classifier to decouple cross-view knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate that CVKD-UDA effectively improves the performance of self-training methods and provides a new perspective for 3D UDA segmentation. Our code will be available at GitHub.

AI.tldr: CVKD-UDA proposes using variable voxel sizes to construct domain-similar representations and cross-view knowledge distillation to improve warm-up model initialization for 3D unsupervised domain adaptive segmentation.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D UDA methods rely on source supervision or output-level adversarial alignment for warm-up model initialization, which suffer from limited generalization and training instability due to large domain gaps.
AI.method: CVKD-UDA generates two complementary views by varying voxel sizes, applies cross-view knowledge distillation (CVKD) to enhance generalization and target perception, and uses a Decouple-Adapter with an auxiliary imitation classifier to balance transferability and discriminability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two benchmarks show CVKD-UDA effectively improves self-training methods for 3D UDA segmentation.
AI.conclusion: CVKD-UDA provides a new perspective for 3D UDA segmentation by using voxel size as a core design factor for domain-similar representations and cross-view complementary cues.

title: FlowArk: Boosting Agentic Data-flow Analysis for Android Apps via Context-Aware Knowledge Reuse
summary:
Data-flow analysis is foundational to Android app privacy and security auditing. Recent coding agents can assist with non-trivial source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks by searching, reading, and reasoning over repository code. However, when these tasks are executed as a batch workload, current agentic analysis setups incur substantial re-analysis cost. Agent instances assigned to different taint sources may inspect shared code fragments, because code reuse in the target app can cause different data-flow paths to converge on shared program logic. Since these agent instances are context-isolated, analysis of these shared code fragments can be repeated within a batch, unnecessarily consuming API budget and limiting scalability.
  We propose FlowArk, a knowledge-reuse system that reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by making knowledge from completed analyses available to later agent instances. Specifically, FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into a later agent instance's context. We implement FlowArk on OpenCode and evaluate it on 4,685 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks from 50 open-source Android apps. Compared with standard OpenCode, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintains comparable analysis quality while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.83%. In addition, under a USD 100 budget, FlowArk completes 36.66% more tasks (1,060 vs. 776).

AI.tldr: FlowArk reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by reusing knowledge from completed analyses, achieving 26.83% API cost reduction and 36.66% more task completions under a fixed budget.
AI.motivation: Current agentic analysis setups for batch data-flow analysis incur substantial re-analysis cost because agent instances assigned to different taint sources may repeatedly inspect shared code fragments due to code reuse, wasting API budget and limiting scalability.
AI.method: FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages them into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into later agent instances' contexts to avoid redundant analysis of shared code.
AI.result: On 4,685 source-to-sink tasks from 50 Android apps, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode reduces end-to-end API cost by 26.83% while maintaining comparable quality. Under a USD 100 budget, it completes 36.66% more tasks (1,060 vs. 776).
AI.conclusion: FlowArk demonstrates that knowledge reuse across agent instances effectively reduces re-analysis overhead in batch data-flow analysis, improving scalability and cost-efficiency for Android app privacy auditing.

title: TopoExplore: Topological Discrimination for Archive-Based Exploration
summary: Archive-based exploration methods such as Go-Explore select which visited state to return to using visitation rarity, and frontier methods return to the boundary of the unknown; neither asks whether the unexplored region behind a boundary is enterable at all. Exploration is not just about finding reward - it is about collecting a structurally complete experience for downstream learning and planning. We introduce TopoExplore, which augments Go-Explore cell selection with a periodic topological pass: enclosed unexplored regions (voids) of the visited-set occupancy grid are detected by flood fill (the H1 classes of its cubical complex), and a decaying selection bonus is placed only on their strict entrances (gap or door cells), so sealed regions are never targeted and entered regions retire. On a controlled 18-environment MiniGrid suite (15 seeds, frozen hyperparameters) TopoExplore attains a 1.52x geometric-mean speedup in median steps-to-first-entry over its exact Go-Explore ablation, versus 1.37x for a frontier baseline; frontier exploration degrades when sealed decoy structure appears (0.83-1.48x on decoy environments vs. 1.65-2.11x for TopoExplore), while TopoExplore holds its largest win on hard multi-interaction doors (10.9x). We report an honest negative on Montezuma's Revenge - without wall knowledge, unreachable occupancy artifacts capture the bonus and performance degrades as it grows, isolating the wall-aware entrance test as the load-bearing component - and a preliminary positive on HM3D scanned buildings, where the speedup over Go-Explore tracks scene difficulty (r=0.69) even as frontier selection dominates blanket coverage. The evidence supports a deliberately scoped claim: topology-aware selection pays off where enclosed structure must be discriminated, and remains competitive at open coverage, where frontier methods are strongest, despite not being tuned for that regime.

AI.tldr: TopoExplore augments Go-Explore with topological detection of enclosed unexplored regions (voids) and targets only their entrances (gaps/doors), achieving 1.52x speedup over Go-Explore on MiniGrid and up to 10.9x on multi-interaction doors, while frontier methods degrade on sealed decoy structures.
AI.motivation: Existing exploration methods (Go-Explore, frontier) select states to revisit based on rarity or boundary proximity without checking whether unexplored regions are actually enterable, wasting effort on sealed areas. The paper argues exploration should collect structurally complete experience for downstream tasks.
AI.method: TopoExplore adds a periodic topological pass to Go-Explore's cell selection: flood-fill detects enclosed unexplored regions (voids) in the occupancy grid (H₁ classes of its cubical complex), and a decaying bonus is placed only on strict entrance cells (gaps/doors). Sealed regions are never targeted and entered regions retire.
AI.result: On 18 MiniGrid environments (15 seeds, frozen hyperparameters): 1.52x geometric-mean speedup over Go-Explore, 1.37x over frontier. On decoy environments: TopoExplore 1.65-2.11x vs frontier 0.83-1.48x. On hard multi-interaction doors: 10.9x. Negative result on Montezuma's Revenge without wall knowledge. Positive result on HM3D (r=0.69 correlation with scene difficulty).
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware exploration pays off when enclosed structure must be discriminated, and remains competitive at open coverage where frontier methods are strongest, despite not being tuned for that regime. The wall-aware entrance test is the load-bearing component.

title: Nonlinear Axiomatic Attribution for Cooperative Games
summary: The Shapley value is a widely used concept in attribution problems, as it uniquely satisfies the axioms of linearity, consistency, equal treatment, and efficiency. Often, the inclusion AUC metric is used to evaluate the quality of player rankings, in order to identify positively participating players. However, it can be established that the Shapley value is not always reliable for this purpose. The core issue lies in its linearity: the Shapley value acts as a linear operator with an excessively large null space, which is likely to contain non-negligible perturbations that remain indistinguishable to the operator. To address this limitation, we explore the design of nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods. Inspired by the least core, which is a popular nonlinear substitute for the Shapley value, we introduce a class of nonlinear attribution methods that retain the remaining necessary axioms. Each method yields a contribution vector that is the unique optimal solution to a minimization problem, which aims to approximate utility functions as faithfully as possible. In terms of the inclusion AUC metric, our experiments demonstrate the potential effectiveness of these methods compared to Shapley value variants that relax only the efficiency axiom. Our code is available at https://github.com/watml/nonlinear-axiom.

AI.tldr: The Shapley value's linearity creates a large null space that makes it unreliable for attribution ranking (e.g., inclusion AUC). The authors propose nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods inspired by the least core, which retain desirable axioms while better approximating utility functions, and show improved effectiveness over Shapley value variants.
AI.motivation: The Shapley value's linearity leads to a large null space that can hide non-negligible perturbations, making it unreliable for evaluating player rankings (e.g., inclusion AUC metric). The authors aim to address this by designing nonlinear attribution methods.
AI.method: The authors introduce a class of nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods inspired by the least core. Each method produces a unique contribution vector as the optimal solution to a minimization problem that approximates utility functions faithfully, while retaining the necessary axioms other than linearity.
AI.result: Experiments using the inclusion AUC metric demonstrate that the proposed nonlinear methods are potentially more effective than Shapley value variants that only relax the efficiency axiom.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear axiomatic attribution methods can overcome the reliability issues of the Shapley value in ranking tasks, offering better performance under the inclusion AUC metric.

title: EMBRACE: A Multi-task Framework for Comprehensive Quality Assessment in Cleavage-stage Embryo
summary: Cleavage-stage embryo assessment in in vitro fertilization requires the integrated interpretation of cytoplasmic fragmentation, developmental stage, and blastomere symmetry. However, conventional visual assessment is affected by observer variability, particularly when fragmented regions are small, irregular, or low contrast. This study presents EMBRACE, a multi-task deep learning framework for jointly performing cytoplasmic-fragmentation segmentation, t2/t4 developmental-stage classification, and blastomere-symmetry grading from static cleavage-stage embryo microscopy images. EMBRACE combines a shared ResNet-50 backbone, a concatenation-based multi-scale feature-fusion (C-MSFF) module, a U-Net-style segmentation decoder, and two task-specific classification heads. After predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 9,137 annotated embryo images were divided into 7,309 training, 914 validation, and 914 held-out test images. On the held-out test set, EMBRACE achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.781 and an intersection over union of 0.677 for fragmentation segmentation. Developmental-stage classification achieved an accuracy of 0.995, macro-F1 of 0.994, and AUC of 1.000. Blastomere-symmetry grading achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.901, macro-F1 of 0.907, and quadratic weighted kappa of 0.859. These findings support the feasibility of combining spatially inspectable fragmentation localization with embryo-level morphology assessment in a single framework. External and prospective validation is required before clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: EMBRACE is a multi-task deep learning framework that simultaneously performs cytoplasmic fragmentation segmentation, developmental-stage classification (t2/t4), and blastomere symmetry grading from cleavage-stage embryo microscopy images, achieving strong performance on a dataset of 9,137 annotated images.
AI.motivation: Conventional visual assessment of cleavage-stage embryos is affected by observer variability, particularly when fragmented regions are small, irregular, or low contrast. There is a need for an integrated, objective, and automated approach to simultaneously assess cytoplasmic fragmentation, developmental stage, and blastomere symmetry.
AI.method: EMBRACE uses a shared ResNet-50 backbone, a concatenation-based multi-scale feature-fusion (C-MSFF) module, a U-Net-style segmentation decoder for fragmentation, and two task-specific classification heads for stage and symmetry. The framework was trained/validated/tested on 9,137 annotated embryo images (7,309/914/914 split).
AI.result: Fragmentation segmentation: Dice 0.781, IoU 0.677. Stage classification: accuracy 0.995, macro-F1 0.994, AUC 1.000. Symmetry grading: balanced accuracy 0.901, macro-F1 0.907, quadratic weighted kappa 0.859.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the feasibility of combining spatially inspectable fragmentation localization with embryo-level morphology assessment in a single framework. External and prospective validation is required before clinical deployment.

title: Fail-Aware and Explainable Test Oracle Prediction
summary: Despite their central role in fault detection, test oracles remain challenging to construct effectively. Recent learning based methods address this challenge by automatically generating test assertions, yet even if syntactically correct, they are often ineffective in revealing bugs. Rather than generating assertions, this study explores a different approach by training a model to directly predict whether a given test prefix passes or fails. We present FOCAL, an emerging code LLM-based discriminative oracle predictor. It learns from labeled pairs of test prefixes and methods under test, employs losses that emphasize failing cases during training, and grounds its predictions in statement level behavioral evidence. Compared with the baseline method SEER, we substantially improve performance on failing cases for unseen projects and provide richer explanations. A preliminary evaluation on fault-detection benchmarks and automated test-generation artifacts shows that our approach is highly accurate within its training distribution and substantially improves failure detection on previously unseen projects where prior discriminative oracles collapse. Moreover, the highlighted statements are supported by behavioral explanation checks. These early results suggest that fail-aware discriminative oracle prediction can complement existing approaches such as fuzzing, search-based testing, and LLM-based test generation. These techniques produce test prefixes at scale but often lack fault oriented oracles. In future work, FOCAL could take generated test prefixes and attach fault-aware predicted oracles to them, turning high-volume input generation into executable tests that are more likely to expose semantic failures.

AI.tldr: FOCAL is an LLM-based discriminative oracle predictor that directly determines whether a test prefix passes or fails, using fail-aware training losses and statement-level behavioral evidence. It significantly improves failure detection on unseen projects compared to prior work (SEER) and complements fuzzing, search-based testing, and LLM-based test generation.
