AI.motivation: Test oracles are central to fault detection but difficult to construct. Existing learning-based assertion generation methods produce syntactically correct assertions that are often ineffective at revealing bugs. The authors aim to bypass assertion generation and directly predict test outcomes (pass/fail) from test prefixes.
AI.method: FOCAL is a code LLM-based discriminative oracle predictor that: (1) learns from labeled pairs of test prefixes and methods under test; (2) employs loss functions that emphasize failing cases during training; (3) grounds predictions in statement-level behavioral evidence; and (4) provides richer explanations compared to the baseline SEER.
AI.result: FOCAL achieves high accuracy within its training distribution and substantially improves failure detection on unseen projects where prior discriminative oracles collapse. The highlighted statements are supported by behavioral explanation checks.
AI.conclusion: Fail-aware discriminative oracle prediction can complement fuzzing, search-based testing, and LLM-based test generation by attaching fault-aware predicted oracles to generated test prefixes, turning high-volume input generation into executable tests more likely to expose semantic failures.

title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?
summary: Automated failure attribution uses LLMs to identify where and why agentic systems fail. As agents become more capable, their failures become subtler, making automated attribution increasingly important. We introduce Who&When Pro, a large-scale benchmark for automated failure attribution in agentic systems. Using a strictly controlled pipeline that injects a failure only after exactly replaying a successful prefix, we construct 12,326 failed trajectories with golden labels across 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks covering various scenarios. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct extensive experiments and analyses, revealing systematic patterns in how models attribute failures across modalities, protocols, and model families, and providing empirical guidance for future automated failure attribution systems.

AI.tldr: Who&When Pro is a large-scale benchmark (12,326 failed trajectories) for automated failure attribution in agentic systems, covering 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks, with systematic analysis of attribution patterns across models and protocols.
AI.motivation: As agentic systems become more capable, their failures become subtler, making automated failure attribution crucial for identifying where and why failures occur.
AI.method: Constructed 12,326 failed trajectories with golden labels using a strictly controlled pipeline that injects a failure only after exactly replaying a successful prefix, spanning 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks.
AI.result: Revealed systematic patterns in how different models attribute failures across modalities, protocols, and model families, providing empirical guidance for future automated failure attribution systems.
AI.conclusion: Automated failure attribution is increasingly important for capable agents, and the proposed benchmark along with empirical findings offers guidance for building such systems.

title: Serving the Long Tail: Training-Free LLM Candidate Generation for Vacation Rental Marketplaces
comment: Accepted at TSMO 2026 workshop, co-located with KDD 2026; 9 pages
summary: Vacation rental marketplaces face a structural imbalance on the supply side: a small fraction of properties receive most user interactions, while the long tail of new, niche, and seasonal listings generates too little behavioral signal for collaborative filtering to serve effectively. At Vrbo, item-based k-nearest neighbors (IBKNN) is a core candidate generation channel, but leaves tens of thousands of properties with no candidates and produces weak neighborhoods for sparsely interacted ones. We present a training-free, LLM-based candidate generation pipeline that complements IBKNN using static property metadata alone. An off-the-shelf LLM synthesizes diverse semantic queries per property, a pre-trained text encoder embeds them, and an approximate nearest-neighbor index retrieves candidates from an 11.7M-property catalog. A Union fusion strategy merges these with IBKNN while preserving the behavioral channel's ordering, guaranteeing no degradation on well-served properties, and a downstream learning-to-rank model re-scores the fused pool. Evaluated on 1.6M focal properties, the system extends candidate coverage to tens of thousands of properties IBKNN cannot reach, delivers its largest gains on the long-tail segment where behavioral methods are weakest, and matches or beats IBKNN at every K on shared properties. A downstream learning-to-rank stage further lifts the fused pool, yielding a complete candidate generation and re-ranking stack that serves the long tail without regressing well-served properties. We additionally show that Union fusion collapses the recall gap between a 3B open-weights LLM and frontier API-based models from 27-46% to under 1%, supporting self-hosted small-model deployment at marketplace catalog scale.

AI.tldr: Vrbo presents a training-free LLM-based candidate generation pipeline that uses property metadata to generate semantic queries, complements IBKNN via Union fusion, extends candidate coverage to long-tail properties, and closes the recall gap between small open-weights LLMs and frontier models.
AI.motivation: Vacation rental marketplaces suffer from supply-side imbalance where long-tail properties (new, niche, seasonal) lack behavioral signals, making collaborative filtering (IBKNN) ineffective. Tens of thousands of Vrbo properties have no candidates or weak neighborhoods.
AI.method: An off-the-shelf LLM synthesizes diverse semantic queries per property from static metadata; a pre-trained text encoder embeds them; an approximate nearest-neighbor index retrieves candidates from an 11.7M-property catalog. Union fusion merges these candidates with IBKNN preserving behavioral ordering, then a downstream learning-to-rank model re-scores the fused pool.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1.6M focal properties: extends candidate coverage to tens of thousands of previously unreachable properties, delivers largest gains on long-tail segments, matches/beats IBKNN at every K. Union fusion collapses recall gap between 3B open-weights LLM and frontier API models from 27-46% to under 1%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LLM-based candidate generation with Union fusion and learning-to-rank re-scoring provides a complete stack serving the long tail without regressing well-served properties, and enables self-hosted small-model deployment at marketplace catalog scale.

title: LFD: Enabling Real-World Lensless Face Recognition with a Large-Scale Dataset
summary: Face recognition is a ubiquitously used computer vision task that has a wide range of applications ranging from everyday smartphone biometrics to high-stakes security systems. Most face recognition systems rely on traditional cameras, which often suffer from limitations such as bulky form factors, high costs, and limited privacy protection. To address these limitations, lensless cameras have emerged as an alternative. Lensless cameras use thin optical encoders, enabling smaller size, lower cost, and greater design flexibility. These cameras are typically paired with reconstruction algorithms that convert raw captures into recognizable images. However, reconstructed images often contain artifacts, and the reconstruction methods struggle to generalize well to real-world conditions. Furthermore, existing face datasets do not account for the artifacts present in lensless images. To address this issue, we introduce the Lensless Face Dataset (LFD). LFD comprises 21,080 lensless raw measurements, reconstructions, and standard images of faces captured under diverse lighting, angle, and distance. Our key contributions are: (1) Real-world lensless face data: LFD focuses on capturing a diverse face dataset with varying levels of artifacts introduced under different environments; (2) In-the-wild captures: 4,976 images are captured in outdoor settings with varying intensities of natural light and different background patterns; (3) Multiple lensless devices: LFD includes face images collected from three different types of lensless cameras, each with a unique optical encoder. We use this hardware diversity to demonstrate generalization across different lensless cameras. Through comprehensive evaluations and analysis, we show that LFD effectively captures shared features and artifacts across different lensless imaging devices, making it a valuable dataset for advancing lensless face recognition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Lensless Face Dataset (LFD), a comprehensive real-world dataset of 21,080 face images captured by three different lensless cameras under diverse conditions, designed to advance lensless face recognition by addressing the lack of lensless-specific training data and generalization challenges.
AI.motivation: Lensless cameras offer advantages like compact size, low cost, and privacy protection for face recognition, but reconstructed images suffer from artifacts and reconstruction methods generalize poorly to real-world conditions. Existing face datasets do not account for lensless image artifacts, hindering progress in this area.
AI.method: The authors constructed LFD with 21,080 face samples including raw lensless measurements, reconstructions, and standard images from three different lensless camera types. Data was collected under diverse lighting, angles, distances, and includes 4,976 outdoor (in-the-wild) captures to ensure real-world variability.
AI.result: LFD effectively captures shared features and artifacts across different lensless imaging devices. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate the dataset's value for advancing lensless face recognition and generalization across hardware.
AI.conclusion: LFD fills a critical gap by providing a diverse, multi-device lensless face dataset that enables better generalization and benchmarking for lensless face recognition systems.

title: Understanding the Impact of AI Code Assistants on Security API Usage: An Empirical Study
comment: Accepted for publication at the 29th International Symposium on Research in Attacks, Intrusions and Defenses (RAID 2026)
summary: AI code assistants are transforming software development, but their implications for software security remain a major concern, particularly in the context of security APIs. These APIs are critical for safeguarding software systems, yet their complexity often leads to incorrect use and serious vulnerabilities. Developing an evidence-based understanding of how AI assistants influence developers' use of these APIs is therefore essential for informing effective mitigation strategies. While a few user studies have examined the broader impact of AI assistants on software vulnerabilities, the use of security APIs remains unexplored from a developer-centered perspective. This study addresses this gap by presenting the first empirical investigation into how AI code assistants affect professional developers' use of security APIs. We conducted a study with 44 developers who completed security API programming tasks with and without GitHub Copilot assistance. Our findings show that, while Copilot improves functional correctness and marginally reduces certain insecure patterns, it does not significantly improve secure API usage. We also found that developers rarely raised security concerns when engaging with Copilot, and many did not recognize that their final implementations remained insecure. Finally, we offer recommendations for enhancing security awareness among developers and propose future research directions to support safer AI-assisted software development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first empirical study with 44 developers investigating how GitHub Copilot affects professional developers' use of security APIs. Results show Copilot improves functional correctness and marginally reduces some insecure patterns, but does not significantly improve secure API usage, and developers rarely recognize security concerns when using the AI assistant.
AI.motivation: AI code assistants are transforming software development but their impact on software security, particularly regarding complex security APIs, remains a major concern. Prior studies examined broader vulnerability impacts but no developer-centered research explored security API usage specifically. This gap motivated the need for evidence-based understanding to inform mitigation strategies.
AI.method: Conducted a controlled study with 44 professional developers who completed security API programming tasks both with and without GitHub Copilot assistance. Compared outcomes across conditions to assess functional correctness, secure API usage patterns, and developer awareness of security concerns.
AI.result: Copilot improved functional correctness and marginally reduced certain insecure patterns. However, it did not significantly improve secure API usage. Developers rarely raised security concerns when interacting with Copilot, and many did not recognize that their final implementations remained insecure.
AI.conclusion: AI code assistants like Copilot offer functional benefits but do not adequately address security API challenges. Recommendations include enhancing security awareness among developers and pursuing future research directions to support safer AI-assisted software development.

authors: Jose Luis Lima de Jesus Silva
title: A Symbolic Neural CPU for Quantization-Simulated Writeback and Interpretable Program Execution
summary: Neural networks can learn algorithmic input-output mappings, but trusting a learned executor requires more than a correct final answer because the state transitions that produce it are usually hidden. To make those transitions visible, we introduce a trace-supervised symbolic neural CPU, a factorized learned execution architecture that combines recurrent control, an explicit operation router over a fixed differentiable arithmetic-logic unit bank, destination-masked register writeback, complete trajectory supervision and matched fixed-point replay. The model exposes the selected operation, source and destination registers, register trajectory, memory signals and writeback semantics at every step. On the principal 16-wide benchmark, the non-quantized executor reproduces reference execution exactly, while the eight-bit quantization-simulated executor preserves the symbolic operation path through programs of 1,000 instructions. When the same execution is evaluated against a matched fixed-point replay, the residual numerical drift disappears, showing that it comes from a mismatch between continuous and low-precision reference semantics rather than from execution failure. We compare recurrent, Transformer, temporal-convolution, temporal graph-inspired and state-space controllers, and the ablations show that operation-gate supervision is necessary for an inspectable execution path. Hidden-opcode memory-pressure tasks expose the remaining limits in delayed state use and temporal binding. We also extend the interface with ValueMemory, hybrid adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire controllers, candidate-constrained symbolic control trained through behaviour cloning and actor-critic reinforcement learning, and an RV32I base-integer semantic bridge. Together, these results establish a trace-verifiable framework for interpretable, low-precision and controllable neural execution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a trace-supervised symbolic neural CPU that makes hidden state transitions in neural execution visible, achieving exact reproduction of reference execution on a 16-wide benchmark, with quantization preserving symbolic paths through 1,000-instruction programs. The framework includes multiple controller architectures, ablation studies showing operation-gate supervision is necessary for inspectable execution, and extensions like ValueMemory, hybrid adaptive LIF controllers, and an RV32I semantic bridge.
AI.motivation: Neural networks can learn algorithmic mappings, but the hidden state transitions that produce the final answer cannot be inspected or trusted. The authors aim to make these transitions visible to enable verifiable, interpretable neural execution.
AI.method: Factorized learned execution architecture with recurrent control, an explicit operation router over a fixed differentiable ALU bank, destination-masked register writeback, complete trajectory supervision, and matched fixed-point replay. Compared recurrent, Transformer, temporal-convolution, temporal graph-inspired, and state-space controllers.
AI.result: Non-quantized executor reproduces reference execution exactly on the 16-wide benchmark; 8-bit quantization-simulated executor preserves symbolic operation path through 1,000-instruction programs. Residual numerical drift is from continuous/low-precision reference mismatch, not execution failure. Operation-gate supervision is necessary for inspectable execution paths.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a trace-verifiable framework for interpretable, low-precision, and controllable neural execution, with remaining limits in delayed state use and temporal binding under hidden-opcode memory-pressure tasks.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Data-Parallel Gibbs Sampling
summary: Inverse Reinforcement Learning recovers reward functions from expert demonstrations, but standard formulations assume that all demonstrations come from a single expert. When demonstrations are pooled from multiple experts with distinct preferences, parametric methods recover an averaged reward that fits no individual expert well. We implement Nonparametric Bayesian Inverse Reinforcement Learning with a Dirichlet Process prior over reward functions, allowing the number of latent reward types to be inferred jointly with the rewards themselves. Inference uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler combining a Chinese Restaurant Process update for cluster assignments with a Metropolis-Hastings update for reward weights, and soft value iteration as the inner planning routine. We evaluate on a 10x10 ObjectWorld grid with two and three ground-truth reward types. The serial sampler recovers K=2 with Adjusted Rand Index of 1.000, substantially outperforming a Maximum Entropy IRL baseline (ARI=0.000). Extension to K=3 shows that the sampler correctly identifies the number of clusters in all runs; assignment ARI of 0.48-0.58 reflects behavioral overlap between expert types that persists across grid instantiations, revealing that reliable K=3 evaluation on ObjectWorld requires controlled object placement rather than random seeding. We further parallelize the sampler across CPU cores using Ray on HPC hardware, achieving a peak speedup of 4.79x at 8 workers, and characterize a throughput-versus-accuracy tradeoff arising from the consensus merge heuristic used during state aggregation. Code and a containerized environment are available at https://github.com/dasashreeya/np_bayes_irl.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Nonparametric Bayesian Inverse Reinforcement Learning approach using a Dirichlet Process prior to infer multiple latent reward types from pooled multi-expert demonstrations, without assuming a single expert. The method uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler with Chinese Restaurant Process and Metropolis-Hastings updates, achieving perfect cluster recovery (ARI=1.000) for K=2 on ObjectWorld and correctly identifying K=3 across all runs. A parallelized implementation on HPC achieves 4.79x speedup with 8 workers, with a throughput-accuracy tradeoff from consensus merging.
AI.motivation: Standard IRL assumes single-expert demonstrations; when data is pooled from multiple experts with distinct preferences, parametric methods recover an average reward that fits no individual expert well.
AI.method: Nonparametric Bayesian IRL with Dirichlet Process prior over reward functions; collapsed Gibbs sampler combining Chinese Restaurant Process for cluster assignment, Metropolis-Hastings for reward weights, and soft value iteration as inner planning routine; parallelized with Ray on HPC.
AI.result: For K=2, serial sampler recovers K=2 with ARI=1.000 vs. MaxEnt IRL baseline ARI=0.000. For K=3, sampler correctly identifies cluster count in all runs; assignment ARI of 0.48-0.58 due to behavioral overlap. Parallelization achieves 4.79x speedup at 8 workers.
AI.conclusion: Nonparametric Bayesian IRL effectively infers both the number of expert types and their reward functions from pooled multi-expert demonstrations, outperforming standard parametric methods. Parallelization is effective but introduces a throughput-accuracy tradeoff from consensus merging.

title: DynaFilter: Cloud-driven Dynamic Filtering for Satellite Edge Intelligence
comment: 15 pages, 23 figures, accepted by ACM MobiCom 2026
summary: Modern satellite edge systems, including those performing remote sensing tasks such object detection and tracking, are characterized by severely limited bandwidth and intermittent connections, making continuous data transmission to the cloud impractical. Existing edge-cloud systems, however, either require heavy pre-processing before analysis, for instance, full decompression of imagery data, or transmit all compressed data regardless of relevance. To address these challenges, we design DynaFilter, a dynamic filtering technique that enables satellite edge devices to perform selective region-of-interest (RoI) inference directly in the compressed-domain, without full decompression. Our key insight is that low-level compression syntax, specifically DC coefficients/AC energy in JPEG images and motion vectors in video streams, exhibits strong correlations with high-level semantic queries. By establishing a precise mapping between cloud query semantics and multimodal compressed-domain features, DynaFilter enables the edge to identify and transmit only relevant data associated to RoIs. Extensive evaluations show that DynaFilter reduces the total volume of pixel data for decoding and subsequent inference by 1.6x-7.1x for images, and achieves 92.0% bandwidth savings for video streams compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, it decreases energy consumption by 43.1-88.6% on target devices and achieves a 1.6x-3.0x speedup in inference latency.

AI.tldr: DynaFilter is a dynamic filtering technique for satellite edge systems that enables selective region-of-interest inference directly in the compressed-domain (JPEG/Video), leveraging correlations between compression syntax and semantic queries to reduce data transmission, bandwidth usage, energy consumption, and inference latency.
AI.motivation: Satellite edge systems suffer from limited bandwidth and intermittent connections, making continuous data transmission to the cloud impractical. Existing edge-cloud systems either require heavy pre-processing (e.g., full decompression) before analysis or transmit all compressed data regardless of relevance.
AI.method: DynaFilter establishes a precise mapping between cloud query semantics and multimodal compressed-domain features (DC coefficients/AC energy in JPEG, motion vectors in video streams). It enables edge devices to perform selective RoI inference directly in the compressed domain without full decompression, filtering and transmitting only relevant data.
AI.result: Reduces pixel data volume for decoding/inference by 1.6x-7.1x for images, achieves 92.0% bandwidth savings for video streams, decreases energy consumption by 43.1-88.6%, and achieves 1.6x-3.0x speedup in inference latency compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: DynaFilter effectively addresses bandwidth and energy constraints in satellite edge systems by enabling compressed-domain selective inference, demonstrating significant improvements in data efficiency, energy consumption, and latency.

title: Predicting Program Comprehension with Foundation Models of Human Cognition
summary: Software engineering depends on the ability of developers to understand code, yet predicting how they do so remains an open challenge despite decades of research. Existing approaches rely either on simplified proxy measures that limit accuracy or on non-trivial measurements requiring elaborate experimental setups that are difficult to scale and apply in practice. In contrast, recent work in psychology suggests an alternative perspective: Instead of modeling task-specific phenomena directly, human behavior can be captured through cognitive regularities learned from large-scale behavioral data. This idea treats complex human behavior as the observable outcome of underlying cognitive processes that manifest consistently across tasks and domains. In this paper, we explore this perspective in the context of program comprehension. We evaluate Centaur, a foundation model trained on 160 general psychological experiments, on 9 previously published program-comprehension studies. We assess how well its predicted response distributions align with human response data and compare Centaur's performance to its base model, Llama 3.1. To better understand the source of its performance, we conduct ablation studies to isolate the contribution of different sources of information, such as the code artifacts, task-related context, and prior trials and participant responses. In a nutshell, we find that Centaur more closely aligns with human response patterns than its base model, is significantly less reliant on information from prior trials and responses, and benefits more from task-related information. These findings suggest that behavioral patterns learned from general psychological data can transfer to complex software engineering tasks such as program comprehension. More broadly, they point toward foundation models of human cognition as a basis for modeling developer behavior in software engineering.

AI.tldr: Centaur, a foundation model trained on general psychological experiments, better predicts human program comprehension behavior than its base model Llama 3.1, suggesting behavioral patterns from psychology can transfer to software engineering tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing code comprehension prediction approaches either use oversimplified proxy measures (limited accuracy) or require elaborate experimental setups (difficult to scale). The authors seek a middle ground by leveraging cognitive regularities learned from large-scale behavioral data.
AI.method: Evaluated Centaur (trained on 160 psychological experiments) on 9 program-comprehension studies, comparing its response distributions to human data and against Llama 3.1. Conducted ablation studies to isolate contributions from code artifacts, task context, and prior trial/response information.
AI.result: Centaur aligns more closely with human response patterns than Llama 3.1, relies less on prior trial/response information, and benefits more from task-related context.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral patterns learned from general psychological data transfer to complex software engineering tasks, suggesting foundation models of human cognition can serve as a basis for modeling developer behavior.

title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
summary: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AgentAbstain, the first systematic framework for evaluating whether LLM-based agents know when to abstain from acting, and AbstainGen, an automated pipeline for generating paired should-act/should-abstain tasks. The best agent achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy, and abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving ability.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain from action, posing real risks such as unintended irreversible actions under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures.
AI.method: Proposes AgentAbstain, a paired-task benchmark with 263 tasks across 42 sandbox environments covering 8 abstention scenarios (pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery). Also introduces AbstainGen, an automated pipeline for synthesizing sandbox environments and generating paired tasks with deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges.
AI.result: The best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy. Abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability. Identifies failure modes like post-hoc abstention where agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers.
AI.conclusion: Scaling task-solving alone will not close the abstention gap; the community needs dedicated methods for improving agentic abstention. The framework and automated pipeline enable ongoing evaluation with fresh, contamination-resistant task instances.

title: Remembering Distinct Items, Not Tokens: A Learnable Dirichlet-Process Cache Between State-Space Models and Attention
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Companion paper on event-log applications forthcoming
summary: Fixed-state sequence models compress an unbounded past into a bounded state, which caps their associative recall at roughly the state dimension; attention escapes the cap by keeping a key-value entry for every token, at quadratic compute and a cache that grows with the sequence. We study the middle ground: a sparse cache that allocates a slot only when an input is novel, so its size tracks the number of distinct items rather than the number of tokens. The allocation rule is the DP-means clustering rule, the small-variance limit of a Dirichlet-process mixture, used not as latent-variable inference but as the key-value memory operator for a deep recurrent backbone. We develop it in two forms, a static cache with a fixed concentration and a surprise-adaptive variant whose concentration follows the recent novelty rate. On a controlled associative-recall benchmark with redundancy we show that the cache matches full-attention recall while storing only the distinct items, that it dominates a fixed-budget eviction cache on the recall-versus-size frontier, and that on a state-space backbone it answers both a recall query and a long-range aggregate at the lowest memory of any model tested. The allocation is learnable end to end: a two-parameter novelty-threshold gate trained on the task loss alone recovers the rule exactly, whereas an over-parameterized gate fails, so the operative ingredient is the inductive bias rather than capacity. The evidence is a family of controlled mechanism studies at modest scale, with the distinct-items property confirmed on four real streams (recommendation, systems logs, clinical events, and insurance claims); a real-backbone, real-corpus language validation is pursued in a companion study.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes sparse cache models that use DP-means clustering as a key-value memory operator to allocate slots only for novel inputs, enabling associative recall matching full attention while storing only distinct items, with memory tracking distinct item count rather than token count.
AI.motivation: Fixed-state sequence models have capped associative recall limited by state dimension, while attention mechanisms escape this cap but suffer from quadratic compute and growing cache size. The authors seek a middle ground with a sparse cache that tracks distinct items rather than all tokens.
AI.method: The method uses DP-means clustering (the small-variance limit of Dirichlet-process mixtures) as a key-value memory operator for deep recurrent backbones. Two variants are developed: a static cache with fixed concentration and a surprise-adaptive variant whose concentration follows recent novelty rate. The allocation is learnable end-to-end via a two-parameter novelty-threshold gate.
AI.result: On controlled associative-recall benchmarks with redundancy, the cache matches full-attention recall while storing only distinct items, dominates fixed-budget eviction caches on recall-versus-size frontier, and achieves lowest memory usage on state-space backbones for both recall queries and long-range aggregates. The distinct-items property is confirmed on four real data streams.
AI.conclusion: The sparse cache approach effectively bridges the gap between fixed-state models and attention by using clustering-based allocation, with the inductive bias of the DP-means rule being the key ingredient (a two-parameter gate recovers it exactly while over-parameterized gates fail).

title: WeaveEarth: Structured Evidence Construction and Reasoning for Training-Free UHR Remote Sensing Understanding
summary: Ultra-High-Resolution (UHR) remote sensing image understanding requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to capture both the global scene layout and sparse yet task-critical local details under limited computational budgets. Existing methods mainly follow two paradigms. One is passive perception, which relies on resolution expansion or token compression and may therefore discard fine-grained details. The other is active perception, which depends on multi-round zooming and search, but suffers from high latency, contextual fragmentation, and error accumulation. We argue that a more effective path toward UHR understanding lies not in accessing more, but in organizing better. To this end, we propose WeaveEarth, a training-free framework that reformulates UHR understanding as a problem of structured evidence construction and reasoning under global context constraints. Specifically, WeaveEarth first employs Global-Aware Evidence Construction to select a compact, low-redundancy, and spatially complementary Minimal Support Evidence Set. It then introduces Structured Evidence Reasoning, which weaves local evidence, spatial metadata, and relative topology into a unified reasoning interface, thereby enhancing the VLM's ability to perform global-local joint reasoning. Extensive experiments show that WeaveEarth consistently outperforms strong baselines and existing UHR methods across multiple UHR remote sensing benchmarks and multiple frozen VLM backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/XianZhi-Ma/WeaveEarth.

AI.tldr: WeaveEarth is a training-free framework for Ultra-High-Resolution remote sensing image understanding that reformulates the problem as structured evidence construction and reasoning under global context constraints, outperforming existing methods across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing UHR remote sensing understanding methods (passive perception via resolution expansion/token compression and active perception via multi-round zooming/search) struggle with discarding fine-grained details or suffering from high latency, contextual fragmentation, and error accumulation. The paper argues that a more effective path lies in organizing information better rather than accessing more.
AI.method: WeaveEarth is a training-free framework with two key components: (1) Global-Aware Evidence Construction, which selects a compact, low-redundancy, spatially complementary Minimal Support Evidence Set; and (2) Structured Evidence Reasoning, which weaves local evidence, spatial metadata, and relative topology into a unified reasoning interface for global-local joint reasoning.
AI.result: WeaveEarth consistently outperforms strong baselines and existing UHR methods across multiple UHR remote sensing benchmarks and multiple frozen VLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Organizing information better (structured evidence construction + reasoning under global context constraints) is more effective than simply accessing more information for UHR remote sensing understanding. Code is publicly available.

title: From GUI Tests to Conversational Interaction: A New Perspective on App-Specific Voice Assistants
summary:
Voice assistants are widely deployed on mobile platforms, yet most are designed as system-level services that remain poorly aligned with application-specific behavior. As a result, enabling voice interaction at the app level requires developers to manually reimplement application logic, leading to high development and maintenance costs.
  We propose an LLM-driven approach to automating the development of app-specific voice assistants by repurposing GUI test code, which encodes behavior-preserving, executable specifications of application functionality. In this paper, we present a perspective in which large language models reinterpret GUI tests as bridges between application behavior and conversational interaction. By transforming test methods into app-specific VA artifacts, such as voice intents, capability descriptions, and executable action plans, our approach grounds voice assistants directly in existing application logic rather than external specifications.
  We illustrate this vision through AppVA, a research prototype on Android. Our preliminary results across five open-source applications suggest that GUI test code can be reused beyond testing, enabling the synthesis of app-specific voice assistants and highlighting a broader research direction at the intersection of software testing, interaction design, and LLM-enabled automation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using LLMs to transform GUI test code into app-specific voice assistants, enabling automated voice interaction at the application level without manual reimplementation.
AI.motivation: Current voice assistants are system-level services poorly aligned with app-specific behavior, requiring developers to manually reimplement application logic for voice interaction, which incurs high development and maintenance costs.
AI.method: The approach uses large language models to reinterpret GUI test code (which encodes behavior-preserving executable specifications) as bridges between application behavior and conversational interaction. LLMs transform test methods into app-specific VA artifacts including voice intents, capability descriptions, and executable action plans.
AI.result: Preliminary results with the AppVA Android prototype across five open-source applications demonstrate that GUI test code can be reused beyond testing to synthesize app-specific voice assistants.
AI.conclusion: GUI test code can serve as a foundation for automating app-specific voice assistant development, opening a broader research direction at the intersection of software testing, interaction design, and LLM-enabled automation.

title: From ambiguous utterances to governed reuse classes: canonicalization, quotient invariance, and conditional decidability
summary: Semantic caching defines answer reuse on embedding similarity: two utterances share a stored answer when a similarity score clears a threshold, with no notion of authorization, versioning, or of what makes two demands the same. This note changes the object on which reuse is defined: in a governed domain, reuse should operate on a mathematically characterized quotient of resolved conversational demands, not on a similarity heuristic. Three independently defined relations on resolved utterances -- reading identity, resolution identity, and reuse identity -- form a refinement chain, strict under realized nondegeneracy conditions checkable on deployment logs; the pipeline's outputs are invariant along the chain, and reuse identity is exactly the kernel of the resolution map into the governed answer partition, so the reuse quotient is the utterance-side object that partition induces, not a relabeling of it. Reuse identity licenses the governed query key and its certified answer space; reuse of a particular answer requires resolution identity or an applicability certificate. The supporting layer is stated at exactly the strength proved: exact-denotation normal forms; join aggregation as a design operator, with closure-stable cells characterizing no-escape; total computability of the full pipeline relative to an untrusted proposal layer; policy admissibility for arbitrary proposers -- and provably not factual grounding or intent fidelity; and elicitation terminating after finitely many informative replies, sound under target consistency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes replacing semantic similarity-based caching with a mathematically rigorous quotient of resolved conversational demands, defined by three strictly refined identity relations (reading, resolution, reuse) that ensure governed answer reuse is invariant, computable, and policy-admissible.
AI.motivation: Semantic caching lacks notions of authorization, versioning, and formal equivalence for reuse. In governed domains, heuristic similarity thresholds are insufficient; a principled, mathematically characterized reuse structure is needed.
AI.method: Defines three identity relations (reading, resolution, reuse) forming a strict refinement chain under nondegeneracy conditions. Reuse identity equals the kernel of the resolution map into the governed answer partition, inducing a reuse quotient. Pipeline uses exact-denotation normal forms, join aggregation with closure-stable cells, and total computability relative to an untrusted proposer layer.
AI.result: Reuse identity licenses the query key and certified answer space; answer reuse requires resolution identity or an applicability certificate. The pipeline is totally computable, policy-admissible, and elicitation terminates in finitely many informative replies under target consistency.
AI.conclusion: Governed answer reuse should operate on a mathematically characterized quotient of resolved demands, not similarity heuristics. The framework is provably not about factual grounding or intent fidelity, but about policy-admissible reuse in governed domains.

title: SMETA-ZSL:Semantic Meta-Alignment for Zero-Shot Threat Classification
summary: Cybersecurity systems must adapt rapidly to emerging threats. However, labeled data for new threat categories is unavailable when those threats first appear. Generalized zero-shot learning offers a natural solution by enabling recognition of unseen classes through auxiliary semantic knowledge rather than labeled examples. Large language models are particularly promising in this setting because they can convert unstructured CTI reports into semantic prototypes for emerging threats. However, applying language-driven zero-shot learning to cybersecurity is difficult due to strong semantic overlap between threat descriptions, heterogeneity between behavioral attributes and text, severe class imbalance, and open-set conditions where unseen threats are unknown during training. We propose SMETA-ZSL, that learns semantic prototypes from overlapping language descriptions through contrastive finetuning, aligns behavioral features through episodic meta-learning and knowledge distillation, and performs adaptive routing for generalization across seen-unseen classes. Across 7 benchmarks, SMETA-ZSL delivers the strongest overall generalized zero-shot performance under the strictest inductive setting, surpassing prior methods by 10.8 points on average, with gains up to 18.1 points. Github:https://github.com/Security-And-Intelligence-Lab-UTEP/SMETA-ZSL

AI.tldr: SMETA-ZSL is a generalized zero-shot learning framework for cybersecurity that uses contrastive finetuning of LLMs to generate semantic prototypes from CTI reports, aligns behavioral features via episodic meta-learning and knowledge distillation, and performs adaptive routing for seen-unseen class generalization, outperforming prior methods by 10.8 points on average across 7 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Cybersecurity systems must adapt to emerging threats, but labeled data for new threat categories is unavailable at first appearance. Generalized zero-shot learning with LLMs offers a solution by using unstructured CTI reports as semantic prototypes, though challenges include semantic overlap, heterogeneity, class imbalance, and open-set conditions.
AI.method: SMETA-ZSL: (1) learns semantic prototypes from overlapping language descriptions via contrastive finetuning of LLMs; (2) aligns behavioral features through episodic meta-learning and knowledge distillation; (3) performs adaptive routing for generalization across seen and unseen classes.
AI.result: Across 7 benchmarks under the strictest inductive setting, SMETA-ZSL surpasses prior methods by 10.8 points on average, with gains up to 18.1 points in generalized zero-shot performance.
AI.conclusion: SMETA-ZSL provides the strongest overall generalized zero-shot performance for cybersecurity threat recognition, demonstrating that language-driven semantic prototype learning with contrastive finetuning, meta-learning alignment, and adaptive routing effectively handles the key challenges of zero-shot learning in this domain.

title: TextGaze: Prompting Gaze Target Estimation with Textual Scene Cues
comment: Accepted by IJCAI 2026. All contents are available at: https://github.com/idremo/TextGaze-IJCAI2026
summary: Gaze target estimation aims to infer the position of a person's gaze within a scene. Within mainstream design logic, multi-branch methods require extra supervision and annotations, while streamlined designs prioritize low-level visual saliency over true gaze intent. The former leads to a high annotation burden and hinders domain transfer, whereas the latter causes misalignment between predicted attention and actual gaze targets. To address this issue, we propose TextGaze, a unified cross-modal architecture that leverages a Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) as scalable semantic guidance to balance the two design paradigms. The model extracts visual features from a frozen encoder and utilizes an LVLM to obtain gaze-aligned textual cues. We design a transformer-based fusion module with hierarchical text supervision to preserve task semantics. Lightweight decoding heads enable the joint prediction of gaze heatmaps and in-/out-of-frame status. We evaluate our method on four mainstream datasets, and the results show competitive performance across key metrics with robust cross-dataset generalisation without extra fine-tuning. Overall, we provide a streamlined alternative to traditional designs and highlight the potential of LVLMs as accessible auxiliary guidance for gaze estimation.

AI.tldr: TextGaze is a unified cross-modal architecture using Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) as semantic guidance for gaze target estimation, achieving competitive performance and robust cross-dataset generalization without extra fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing gaze target estimation methods suffer from a trade-off: multi-branch designs require costly extra supervision and annotations hindering domain transfer, while streamlined designs prioritize low-level visual saliency over true gaze intent, causing misalignment.
AI.method: TextGaze extracts visual features from a frozen encoder, uses an LVLM to obtain gaze-aligned textual cues, and employs a transformer-based fusion module with hierarchical text supervision to preserve task semantics. Lightweight decoding heads jointly predict gaze heatmaps and in-/out-of-frame status.
AI.result: Evaluated on four mainstream datasets, TextGaze shows competitive performance across key metrics and robust cross-dataset generalization without extra fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: TextGaze provides a streamlined alternative to traditional gaze estimation designs and highlights the potential of LVLMs as accessible auxiliary semantic guidance.

title: TerraRepair: A Tool-Grounded LLM Agent for Infrastructure-as-Code Repair
comment: The paper has been peer reviewed and accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 20th International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2026)
summary: Background: Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scanners detect cloud misconfigurations in Terraform and other IaC languages before deployment, but repairing the flagged configurations remains largely manual. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based repair approaches can repair some findings, but may hallucinate unsupported constructs or suppress warnings without fixing the issue. Aims: We study whether tool grounding can improve LLM-based Terraform repair, and when a finding should be escalated because the required deploymnet-specific context is not availble. Method: We present TerraRepair, a prototype of a tool-grounded LLM agent for Terraform repair with structured escalation. TerraRepair retrieves dependency context from Terraform references, consults the installed provider schema, and re-runs the scanner before returning a candidate repair. Then teh required context is absent, TerraRepair escalates instead of fabricating a plausible fix. Results: We evaluate our tool on two vulnerable-by-design Terraform repositories using two IaC security scanners, Checkov and Trivy, across AWS, Azure, and GCP. On the combined AWS benchmark, TerraRepair improves scanner-verified fix rates from 26.6% to 78.4% on Checkov and from 44.8% to 72.4% on Trivy, compared with a controlled one-shot baseline. It repairs are labelled as correct under a majority-vote protocol. Conclusions: These emerging results show that tool grounding can substantially improve scanner-verified LLM-based IaC repair on the studied benchmarks, while missing deployment-specific context remains the main knowledge boundary for full autonomy.

AI.tldr: TerraRepair is a tool-grounded LLM agent for Terraform infrastructure repair that retrieves dependency context and provider schemas, re-runs scanners, and escalates when deployment-specific context is missing. On AWS benchmarks, it improves scanner-verified fix rates from 26.6% to 78.4% (Checkov) and 44.8% to 72.4% (Trivy) compared to a one-shot LLM baseline.
AI.motivation: IaC scanners detect cloud misconfigurations in Terraform but repairing flagged configurations remains largely manual. Existing LLM-based repair approaches may hallucinate unsupported constructs or suppress warnings without fixing issues.
AI.method: TerraRepair is a tool-grounded LLM agent that retrieves dependency context from Terraform references, consults installed provider schemas, re-runs the scanner before returning a candidate repair, and escalates when deployment-specific context is absent instead of fabricating a fix.
AI.result: On the combined AWS benchmark, TerraRepair improved scanner-verified fix rates from 26.6% to 78.4% on Checkov and from 44.8% to 72.4% on Trivy compared to a one-shot baseline.
AI.conclusion: Tool grounding substantially improves scanner-verified LLM-based IaC repair on studied benchmarks, but missing deployment-specific context remains the main knowledge boundary for full autonomy.

title: MAG: A Web-Agent Benchmark and Harness for Multimodal Action and Guide Generation
comment: 8 pages main text, 21 pages total including appendices; 11 figures, 7 tables, 2 algorithms. Benchmark, harness, and model checkpoints to be released
summary: Digital Adoption Platforms (DAPs) are embedded overlays widely used on web systems to guide users through operations inside a page, helping them get started with unfamiliar interfaces quickly. Completing a real task, however, rarely means clicking a few buttons on a single page: it takes a sequence of actions that unfolds across changing page states. Prior studies have also treated automated web agent actions and guide text generation as two separate problems, and most of them feed models textual page representations such as the DOM or accessibility trees rather than the rendered screens that humans actually operate on. In this work we introduce MAG, the first benchmark that unifies task execution and guide writing into a single Multimodal Action and Guide task, with two grounding schemes over screenshots: Set-of-Mark element selection and raw pixel coordinates. We further build a complete harness for this compound task, covering annotation with LLM assistance and human verification, training, evaluation in live environments, and joint metrics for actions and guides. With this harness we evaluate frontier API models and open multimodal models, and report detailed analyses. Finally, we design a GRPO training method augmented with expert trajectories, which nearly doubles the success rate of a supervised 9B agent (from 6.9% to 13.2%) and improves guide quality at the same time. Even the strongest model completes fewer than 40% of the tasks, leaving ample room for future research.

AI.tldr: MAG is a benchmark unifying task execution and guide writing for digital agents via multimodal (screenshot-based) grounding, with a GRPO training method that nearly doubles a 9B model's success rate.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats web agent actions and guide text generation as separate problems, uses textual page representations (DOM/accessibility trees) instead of rendered screenshots, and lacks a unified benchmark for real-world multi-step tasks across changing page states.
AI.method: MAG introduces a Multimodal Action and Guide task with two grounding schemes (Set-of-Mark element selection and raw pixel coordinates), a full harness (LLM-assisted annotation + human verification, training, live evaluation, joint metrics), and a GRPO training method augmented with expert trajectories.
AI.result: GRPO augmented with expert trajectories nearly doubles success rate of a supervised 9B agent (from 6.9% to 13.2%) while improving guide quality; strongest model still completes <40% of tasks.
AI.conclusion: MAG reveals a large gap in current multimodal agents for compound task execution and guide generation, with ample room for future improvement.

title: A Foundation Model for Multimodal Event Sequences in Financial Applications
summary: Predictive modeling is a core component of modern financial services, where a wide range of tasks are traditionally addressed using separate models trained on manually engineered tabular features. This task-specific approach limits reuse and makes it difficult to fully exploit heterogeneous data sources such as transaction histories and digital interaction signals. In this paper, we present an approach based on pretraining a foundation transformer model on multimodal sequences of user events. Events from multiple data sources are unified into a single chronological sequence, enabling early fusion of heterogeneous modalities and learning of general-purpose representations via a next-event prediction objective. These representations are combined with existing engineered user features, on top of which lightweight neural models are trained for multiple downstream tasks. The proposed system outperforms traditional task-specific models while reducing development overhead. The approach was deployed in production at one of the biggest banks in Eastern Europe, resulting in measurable improvements in business metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a foundation transformer model pretrained on multimodal sequences of user events for predictive modeling in financial services. It unifies heterogeneous data sources (e.g., transaction histories, digital signals) into chronological event sequences, uses next-event prediction for pretraining, and combines learned representations with engineered features to train lightweight downstream models. Deployed at a major Eastern European bank, it outperforms traditional task-specific models and improves business metrics.
AI.motivation: Traditional financial predictive modeling relies on separate task-specific models trained on manually engineered tabular features, which limits reuse and fails to fully exploit heterogeneous data sources like transaction histories and digital interaction signals.
AI.method: A foundation transformer model is pretrained on multimodal sequences of user events via next-event prediction. Events from diverse sources are unified into a single chronological sequence for early fusion of modalities. Learned representations are combined with existing engineered features, and lightweight neural models are trained for multiple downstream tasks.
AI.result: The proposed system outperforms traditional task-specific models while reducing development overhead. It was deployed in production at one of the largest banks in Eastern Europe, yielding measurable improvements in business metrics.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining a transformer foundation model on unified multimodal event sequences is an effective and scalable approach for financial predictive modeling, enabling better performance, model reuse, and reduced engineering cost compared to task-specific tabular models.

title: FlowPainter: Inpainting Optical Flow via Confidence-Guided Completion
summary: Existing optical flow methods broadly follow two paradigms: iterative optimization and diffusion-based estimation. Iterative methods, exemplified by RAFT, achieve high accuracy through recurrent refinement, but remain challenged by large displacements and complex motion. Diffusion-based methods introduce generative modeling and show promise in such ambiguous regions. However, existing diffusion models usually denoise the entire dense flow field from Gaussian noise, including simple regions where reliable motion can already be estimated by a lightweight network. This increases the denoising burden and may cause slow convergence and unstable training. To address this issue, we introduce FlowPainter, a diffusion-based optical flow framework that reformulates dense-flow generation as confidence-guided soft inpainting. FlowPainter employs a lightweight confidence-aware network to predict a rough flow and a pixel-wise confidence mask, distinguishing reliable simple regions from uncertain hard regions. The resulting simple-flow prior is used for confidence-based initialization and further injected into iterative denoising through confidence-gated residual guidance. With dynamically decaying guidance strength, FlowPainter stabilizes early denoising while preserving the flexibility of the diffusion model for late-stage detail refinement. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, including Sintel, KITTI, and Spring, show that FlowPainter achieves strong accuracy under comparable training settings and converges more efficiently than existing diffusion-based optical flow methods, with notable gains on challenging benchmark splits. Our approach offers a practical way to integrate reliable discriminative priors with diffusion-based refinement for optical flow estimation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mya012/FlowPainter.

AI.tldr: FlowPainter reformulates diffusion-based optical flow estimation as confidence-guided soft inpainting, using a lightweight network to predict a coarse flow and confidence mask that initializes and guides iterative denoising, improving convergence and accuracy on challenging motion regions.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based optical flow methods denoise the entire dense flow field from Gaussian noise, including simple regions where motion can be easily estimated by a lightweight network. This increases denoising burden, causing slow convergence and unstable training.
AI.method: FlowPainter introduces: (1) a lightweight confidence-aware network to predict a rough flow and pixel-wise confidence mask, distinguishing reliable simple regions from uncertain hard regions; (2) confidence-based initialization using the simple-flow prior; (3) confidence-gated residual guidance that injects the prior into iterative denoising; (4) dynamically decaying guidance strength to stabilize early denoising while preserving diffusion flexibility for late-stage refinement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Sintel, KITTI, and Spring benchmarks show strong accuracy under comparable training settings, more efficient convergence than existing diffusion-based optical flow methods, and notable gains on challenging benchmark splits.
AI.conclusion: FlowPainter offers a practical way to integrate reliable discriminative priors with diffusion-based refinement for optical flow estimation, improving both accuracy and training efficiency.

title: Knowledge-Guided Synthetic Bug Feedback for LLM-Based Unit Test Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for unit test generation, but executable tests do not necessarily reveal real defects. This paper studies how historical real-bug mechanisms can be transformed into executable feedback targets for LLM-based unit test generation. The proposed framework constructs structural and semantic representations of real-bug records, retrieves mechanisms applicable to a focal method, and instantiates them as synthetic bugs that guide iterative test enhancement. We evaluate the approach on method-level real-bug detection tasks from Defects4J and show that mechanism-guided synthetic-bug feedback improves real-bug detection over execution-, coverage-, mutation-, knowledge-, and search-based baselines. The results suggest that organizing real-bug mechanisms as retrievable and executable feedback targets is an effective way to guide generated tests toward bug-triggering inputs and behavioral oracles.

AI.tldr: LLMs can generate unit tests, but executable tests don't guarantee defect detection. This paper proposes using historical real-bug mechanisms as feedback targets for LLM-based test generation. The framework extracts structural/semantic bug representations, retrieves relevant mechanisms, and instantiates synthetic bugs to iteratively guide test improvement. Evaluated on Defects4J, the approach outperforms execution-, coverage-, mutation-, knowledge-, and search-based baselines in detecting real bugs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based unit test generation produces executable tests but fails to reliably reveal real defects. The gap is that generated tests often pass on buggy code rather than trigger failures, calling for feedback signals that capture how real bugs actually manifest.
AI.method: The framework (1) constructs structural and semantic representations from historical real-bug records, (2) retrieves mechanisms relevant to a given focal method, and (3) instantiates them as synthetic bugs that provide feedback to iteratively refine LLM-generated tests toward bug-triggering inputs and behavioral oracles.
AI.result: On Defects4J method-level real-bug detection tasks, mechanism-guided synthetic-bug feedback improves real-bug detection accuracy compared to baselines including execution-based, coverage-based, mutation-based, knowledge-based, and search-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Organizing real-bug mechanisms as retrievable and executable feedback targets is an effective strategy for guiding LLM-generated unit tests to detect real defects.

title: Looped State-Space Language Models with Adaptive Exit-State Selection
summary: Recent work on looped language models suggests that many reasoning problems benefit from greater computational depth rather than from additional independent parameters. Existing studies, however, focus almost exclusively on Transformer backbones, leaving open whether this principle also applies to state-space language models. We investigate Looped Mamba and Looped Hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures, which repeatedly apply a shared Mamba (or hybrid) block to introduce explicit finite-depth recurrent computation. On two controlled reasoning tasks-Mano (modular-arithmetic manipulation) and p-hop induction-Looped Mamba consistently outperforms parameter-matched non-looped baselines and, in several settings, matches or exceeds non-looped models of equal effective depth. We then extend the study to language model pre-training under matched iso-parameter and iso-FLOPs protocols, which jointly disentangle the effects of parameter sharing and effective depth: looped models remain competitive on downstream benchmarks with substantially fewer distinct parameters, although deeper non-looped models retain an advantage in validation perplexity under strict iso-FLOPs comparisons. Finally, we adapt Ouro's two-stage exit gate to Looped Mamba for threshold-controlled selection among recurrent-step outputs. Since all recurrent steps are still executed, the selected exit step represents prediction depth rather than reduced wall-clock computation. At the scales studied, adaptive exit-state selection improves downstream performance at intermediate depths, while actual inference-time savings require additional state-handling mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether looped (weight-shared) architectures benefit state-space models (Mamba) and hybrid Mamba-Transformer models, showing that Looped Mamba outperforms parameter-matched non-looped baselines on reasoning tasks and remains competitive on language model pre-training with fewer parameters, though deeper non-looped models have an advantage in strict iso-FLOPs perplexity comparisons. The authors also adapt a two-stage exit gate for adaptive depth selection.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the principle that reasoning problems benefit from greater computational depth (via looping/recurrent computation) rather than additional independent parameters, which has been established for Transformer backbones, also applies to state-space language models like Mamba.
AI.method: The authors design Looped Mamba and Looped Hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures that repeatedly apply a shared block. They evaluate on Mano (modular arithmetic manipulation) and p-hop induction reasoning tasks, then extend to language model pre-training under iso-parameter and iso-FLOPs protocols. They also adapt Ouro's two-stage exit gate for adaptive recurrent-step output selection.
AI.result: Looped Mamba consistently outperforms parameter-matched non-looped baselines on reasoning tasks and matches/exceeds non-looped models of equal effective depth. In pre-training, looped models remain competitive on downstream benchmarks with fewer distinct parameters, though deeper non-looped models retain validation perplexity advantages under strict iso-FLOPs. Adaptive exit-state selection improves downstream performance at intermediate depths but actual inference savings require additional mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The benefit of looped architectures generalizes beyond Transformers to state-space models for reasoning tasks. However, in large-scale pre-training, the parameter-efficiency advantage of looping is partially offset by perplexity gains from deeper non-looped models under equal compute budgets. Adaptive exit selection shows promise but requires further state-handling mechanisms for practical inference speedup.

title: Optimizing ARDL Models for Retail Sales Forecasting and Fair Pricing
summary: Pricing food products to balance profitability with consumer welfare is a central challenge for retailers. Dynamic pricing is widely used to maximize revenue, yet most pricing models optimize business objectives while overlooking consumer fairness. This paper studies the risk of consumer exploitation under dynamic food pricing in Canada and proposes a methodology that embeds fairness constraints directly into retail sales forecasting. We model total retail trade sales with a log--log Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) specification, in which the coefficient on a product price is a sales elasticity, and pose the pricing problem as maximizing forecast sales subject to price bounds anchored to the Consumer Price Index (CPI). We solve this problem with both Linear Programming (LP) and Simulated Annealing (SA), under single-product and multi-product configurations. A key finding is that the fitted nominal elasticities are positive. As a result, an unconstrained sales-maximizer would push every price to its upper bound, and the CPI ceiling is the safeguard that prevents this. Simulated Annealing instead settles on conservative, interior prices that lower consumer cost while still meeting the sales target. We benchmark forecast accuracy against naive, seasonal-naive, ARIMA, and SARIMA baselines, and a CPI-deflated re-specification shows that the positive nominal elasticities are largely an inflation-driven artifact. The result is a transparent, fairness-aware pricing framework.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a fairness-aware dynamic pricing framework for food products in Canada, using ARDL modeling with CPI-anchored price constraints. It finds that unconstrained optimization leads to maximum pricing, while Simulated Annealing achieves lower consumer costs with maintained sales targets.
AI.motivation: Dynamic pricing models typically optimize profitability but overlook consumer fairness, risking consumer exploitation. The paper addresses the need to embed fairness constraints directly into retail pricing to balance profitability with consumer welfare.
AI.method: The authors use a log-log ARDL specification to model retail sales with price elasticity, formulate the pricing problem as maximizing forecast sales subject to CPI-anchored price bounds, and solve it using Linear Programming (LP) and Simulated Annealing (SA) under single-product and multi-product configurations. Forecast accuracy is benchmarked against naive, seasonal-naive, ARIMA, and SARIMA models.
AI.result: Fitted nominal elasticities are positive, meaning unconstrained optimization pushes prices to upper bounds. The CPI ceiling acts as a safeguard against this. Simulated Annealing yields conservative, interior prices that reduce consumer costs while meeting sales targets. Positive nominal elasticities are identified as an inflation-driven artifact through CPI-deflated re-specification.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a transparent, fairness-aware pricing framework that integrates consumer welfare constraints into dynamic food pricing, demonstrating that socially responsible pricing is achievable without sacrificing sales targets.

title: REVA-PO: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning for Chest X-ray Report Generation
summary: Automated chest X-ray report generation has recently benefited from reinforcement learning (RL) and large language models. However, RL training often suffers from instability or limited exploration due to fixed Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization and a static reference policy that accumulates KL pressure over time. We propose Response-Weighted and Validation-Anchored Policy Optimization (REVA-PO), a RL framework that stabilizes long-term training via Response-Weighted Regularization (RER) and Validation-Anchored Policy Reset (VAPR). RER dynamically adjusts per-response KL weights based on advantage and reference-policy entropy, relaxing constraints for high-quality responses while tightening them for low-quality ones. Complementarily, VAPR periodically synchronizes the reference and current policies to the best validation checkpoint, resetting accumulated regularization pressure to expand the viable exploration space. To ensure a robust starting point, we employ a three-stage pipeline consisting of warm-up training, classifier-guided supervised fine-tuning, and RL. Extensive evaluations on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray demonstrate that REVA-PO sets new state-of-the-art benchmarks in both linguistic quality and clinical accuracy. Notably, BLEU-4 improves by 5.1% on MIMIC-CXR and 3.6% on IU-Xray, while CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1 scores increase by 4.5% and 12.8%, respectively, over prior leading methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/LiGuo12/REVA_PO/.

AI.tldr: REVA-PO is a novel RL framework for automated chest X-ray report generation that addresses training instability through response-weighted KL regularization and validation-anchored policy resets, achieving new SOTA on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray with BLEU-4 improvements of 5.1% and 3.6%, and CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1 gains of 4.5% and 12.8%.
AI.motivation: RL training for chest X-ray report generation suffers from instability and limited exploration due to fixed KL regularization and a static reference policy that accumulates KL pressure over time, hindering long-term training effectiveness.
AI.method: Proposes REVA-PO with two components: (1) Response-Weighted Regularization (RER) that dynamically adjusts per-response KL weights based on advantage and reference-policy entropy, and (2) Validation-Anchored Policy Reset (VAPR) that periodically synchronizes reference and current policies to the best validation checkpoint. Uses a three-stage pipeline: warm-up training, classifier-guided supervised fine-tuning, and RL.
AI.result: On MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, REVA-PO achieves SOTA in both linguistic quality and clinical accuracy. BLEU-4 improves by 5.1% on MIMIC-CXR and 3.6% on IU-Xray. CheXpert F1 improves by 4.5% and RadGraph F1 by 12.8% over prior leading methods.
AI.conclusion: REVA-PO effectively stabilizes long-term RL training for medical report generation through dynamic regularization and policy reset mechanisms, setting new benchmarks and demonstrating the effectiveness of the approach.

title: ThinkLog: Leveraging Reasoning for Log Statement Generation
summary: Runtime logs are an important source of information that supports software maintenance. To obtain useful logs, developers spend significant effort identifying appropriate log locations, assigning correct severity levels, and writing concise yet informative messages. Therefore, end-to-end automated log statement generation can help reduce this burden, and prior work has proposed many methods for this task. However, existing methods still exhibit limited accuracy. To address this problem, we propose ThinkLog, an LLM-based end-to-end log statement generation method. The core idea of ThinkLog is to incorporate reasoning that helps LLMs make decisions about log insertion, severity level assignment, and message generation, thereby improving log statement generation accuracy. ThinkLog injects reasoning into prompts as few-shot examples and guides LLMs to generate appropriate log statements. Evaluated on 9,619 Java methods extracted from public GitHub repositories, ThinkLog achieves 20.55% log statement generation accuracy, representing a 15.4% improvement over the best existing method. Moreover, these improvements were achieved at approximately 50% of the inference cost (USD) compared to the best existing method. These results show that leveraging reasoning is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve the accuracy of end-to-end log statement generation.

AI.tldr: ThinkLog improves end-to-end log statement generation accuracy by 15.4% over existing methods (to 20.55%) using reasoning-augmented LLM prompts with few-shot examples, while reducing inference cost by ~50%.
AI.motivation: Developers spend significant effort on manual log statement generation (identifying locations, severity levels, writing messages), and existing automated methods still exhibit limited accuracy.
AI.method: ThinkLog incorporates reasoning into prompts via few-shot examples to guide LLMs in making decisions about log insertion, severity level assignment, and message generation.
AI.result: Evaluated on 9,619 Java methods from public GitHub repositories, ThinkLog achieves 20.55% log statement generation accuracy, a 15.4% improvement over the best existing method, at ~50% of the inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging reasoning is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve the accuracy of end-to-end log statement generation.

title: Dynamic Agent Skills: A Lifecycle Survey and Taxonomy of Evolving Skill Libraries
summary: Large language model agents increasingly store reusable procedures outside the model. These reusable procedures are often called \emph{skills}: they may be code functions, natural-language instructions, SKILL.md packages, workflow graphs, or learned adapters that a future agent can retrieve and invoke. This taxonomy-driven survey asks how such skill libraries change over time. Across a $124$-paper $2023$--$2026$ audit set, we synthesize dynamic skill systems as \emph{lifecycle-managed, verified, evolving artifact stores}: agents collect evidence from interaction, propose skill updates, verify and admit candidates, organize them for retrieval and composition, repair or prune stale entries, and govern sharing through provenance and rollback. We organize the literature around three survey tools. First, a $\text{six}$-sense taxonomy distinguishes the structurally different artifacts called ``skills'' in current papers. Second, an $\text{eight}$-stage lifecycle architecture identifies the recurring design decisions behind evidence acquisition, proposal, verification/admission, storage, retrieval/composition, maintenance, distillation/portability, and governance. Third, a lightweight skill-record schema and $\text{ten}$-operator vocabulary provide common terms for comparing library updates without elevating them into a separate method contribution. Using this structure, we synthesize evidence-graded patterns with explicit caveats: admission and repair are repeatedly important, verifier quality materially affects skill-aware RL, flat retrieval can degrade as libraries grow, and current benchmarks still under-report library trajectories, usage--utility gaps, and safety surfaces. We close with concrete reporting standards and open problems for evaluating dynamic skills as changing libraries rather than static prompt or tool collections.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys 124 papers (2023-2026) on dynamic skill libraries for LLM agents, proposing a six-sense taxonomy of skill types, an eight-stage lifecycle architecture for skill evolution, a ten-operator vocabulary for comparing library updates, and identifies key patterns (importance of admission/repair, verifier quality effects, flat retrieval degradation) with open problems and reporting standards.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly store reusable procedures (skills) externally, but the literature lacks a unified framework for understanding how these skill libraries evolve over time — existing work treats skills as static artifacts rather than dynamic, lifecycle-managed stores.
AI.method: A taxonomy-driven survey of 124 papers (2023-2026) synthesizing dynamic skill systems as lifecycle-managed, verified, evolving artifact stores.
