AI.result: 99.48% accuracy on Mendeley liquid-based cytology dataset and 96.08% on SIPaKMeD dataset, with balanced gains in recall, precision, and overall classification performance. Visual analysis shows learned priors highlight diagnostically relevant cellular regions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometry-aware framework effectively integrates structural priors with axial self-attention to overcome limitations of both convolution-based and pure attention-based models, demonstrating strong potential as a screening-oriented decision-support tool for cervical cytology.

title: Can Agentic Trading Systems Pay for Their Own Intelligence?
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in trading systems, where model reasoning, tool use, and continual decisions incur costs that are expected to produce trading value. Existing evaluations typically report performance metrics, but rarely examine agentic viability: whether dynamic LLM-mediated decisions convert their induced costs into measurable incremental profit. To apply this criterion, we introduce TradeLens, a trace-grounded diagnostic toolkit for evaluating agentic trading systems from their trading records, runtime traces, and deployment configurations. It reconstructs trading trajectories, attributes profit and cost to interpretable evidence, and diagnoses whether and why an agent pays for its own intelligence. We conduct extensive analysis across backbone models, capital scales, trading frequencies, and system architectures, together with deployment discussion. Our results show that viability hinges on intelligence-to-profit conversion: models exhibit different failure patterns, such as poor asset selection in DeepSeek-V3.2 and negative timing in GLM-4.7, while capital scale, trading frequency, and architecture matter only by amplifying or degrading decision-attributed timing value. These findings reframe the evaluation of LLM-based trading agents from capability-centric performance ranking to trace-grounded diagnosis of intelligence-to-profit conversion. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TradeLens.

AI.tldr: TradeLens is a diagnostic toolkit for evaluating LLM trading agents by tracing whether their intelligence-driven decisions convert costs into measurable profit, revealing that viability depends on intelligence-to-profit conversion rather than raw capability.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based trading agents focus on performance metrics but fail to assess agentic viability—whether the costs incurred by dynamic LLM-mediated decisions are converted into measurable incremental profit.
AI.method: TradeLens is a trace-grounded diagnostic toolkit that reconstructs trading trajectories from records, runtime traces, and deployment configurations, attributing profit and cost to interpretable evidence to diagnose whether and why an agent pays for its own intelligence. Extensive analysis is conducted across backbone models, capital scales, trading frequencies, and system architectures.
AI.result: Viability hinges on intelligence-to-profit conversion. Different models exhibit distinct failure patterns (e.g., poor asset selection in DeepSeek-V3.2, negative timing in GLM-4.7). Capital scale, trading frequency, and architecture matter only by amplifying or degrading decision-attributed timing value.
AI.conclusion: The paper reframes LLM-based trading agent evaluation from capability-centric performance ranking to trace-grounded diagnosis of intelligence-to-profit conversion.

title: TabLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Low-Rank Ensemble Learning for Large-Scale Tabular Data
summary: Tabular learning is still dominated by gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs), while recent deep learning approaches have become increasingly competitive. However, applying deep tabular models to large-scale datasets remains challenging, as large sample sizes, high feature dimensionality, or many target classes can introduce substantial computational cost. We propose TabLoRA, a parameter-efficient trainable neural ensemble for large-scale tabular learning. Instead of using fully independent ensemble backbones, TabLoRA shares a common backbone across predictors and introduces predictor-specific low-rank adaptations, enabling ensemble-style prediction without full parameter duplication. Across benchmarks, TabLoRA achieves a favorable balance between predictive performance and practical efficiency compared with GBDT methods and recent deep learning baselines under the same resource constraints. Memory analysis and ablation studies further show that the proposed design improves the feasibility of neural ensemble learning while preserving much of the benefit of full ensembles.

AI.tldr: TabLoRA introduces a parameter-efficient neural ensemble for large-scale tabular learning, sharing a backbone across predictors with low-rank adaptations to reduce computational cost while maintaining ensemble benefits, outperforming GBDTs and deep baselines under resource constraints.
AI.motivation: Large-scale tabular learning (large sample sizes, high feature dimensionality, many target classes) remains computationally prohibitive for deep learning ensembles, while GBDTs still dominate. The authors aim to enable neural ensemble learning at scale without full parameter duplication.
AI.method: TabLoRA shares a common backbone across ensemble predictors and introduces predictor-specific low-rank adaptations (LoRA), replacing fully independent ensemble backbones with a parameter-efficient design that preserves ensemble-style diversity.
AI.result: TabLoRA achieves a favorable balance between predictive performance and practical efficiency compared to GBDT methods and recent deep learning baselines under identical resource constraints. Memory analysis and ablation studies confirm improved feasibility of neural ensembles while retaining most of the benefit of full ensembles.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-efficient ensembling via low-rank adaptations makes deep tabular learning more practical at scale, narrowing the gap with GBDTs while offering better efficiency than fully independent ensembles.

title: InterPet4D: A Multimodal 4D Human-Pet Interaction Dataset for Pet Motion Generation
summary: Human-pet interaction estimation and generation remain underexplored due to the absence of a high-quality large-scale dataset. We present InterPet4D, the first multimodal dataset capturing natural interactions between humans and dogs. Using a synchronized multi-view capture system, we record human-dog obedience tasks and provide annotations for both humans and dogs, including multi-view and egocentric videos, segmentations, 2D and 3D keypoints, meshes, and audio tracks. InterPet4D consists of 6.8 million frames collected from 13 dogs of 11 breeds interacting with 23 human participants. We further introduce the InterPetMoGen framework for human-pet interaction motion generation. Our proposed model achieves an FID score of 11.21 and substantially outperforms the Seq2Seq and DiT baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of InterPet4D for modeling realistic human-pet interactions.

AI.tldr: InterPet4D is the first large-scale multimodal dataset (6.8M frames, 13 dogs, 11 breeds, 23 humans) capturing natural human-dog interactions via synchronized multi-view capture, enabling human-pet interaction motion generation with the InterPetMoGen framework that outperforms baselines (FID 11.21).
AI.motivation: Human-pet interaction estimation and generation are underexplored due to the lack of a high-quality large-scale dataset.
AI.method: They built InterPet4D using a synchronized multi-view capture system for human-dog obedience tasks, providing multi-view/egocentric videos, segmentations, 2D/3D keypoints, meshes, and audio. They also propose InterPetMoGen for interaction motion generation.
AI.result: InterPetMoGen achieves FID score of 11.21, substantially outperforming Seq2Seq and DiT baselines.
AI.conclusion: InterPet4D enables effective modeling of realistic human-pet interactions, demonstrating the value of their dataset and framework.

title: SPARK: Susceptibility-Guided Profiling and Steering of Latent Reasoning States in Large Language Models
summary: Reasoning failures in large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated from final answers, but a wrong answer does not reveal why the model failed. The same incorrect output may reflect missing capability, an unstable reasoning trajectory, or a failure to activate a reasoning state that is already available in the frozen model. Existing prompting and benchmark-based evaluation methods mostly operate at the output level, while generic activation-steering methods typically apply global directions without diagnosing which examples require intervention. In this paper, we introduce SPARK, which uses hidden-state response to diagnose whether a model internally enters an effective reasoning state and to guide lightweight test-time steering. The key observation is that raw hidden-state susceptibility is strongly confounded by prompt length, especially in programmatic and algorithmic reasoning where harder serialized instances naturally become longer. SPARK therefore uses length-controlled susceptibility to separate input-scale effects from residual reasoning activation, and combines this signal with cross-layer coordination to select reasoning-active anchors and under-activated hard examples. We use FRONTIER-4.5K as a controlled programmatic reasoning suite for latent profiling and difficulty-aware analysis, and evaluate SPARK-Steering on GSM8K and MATH-500 with forward-only benchmark profiling. Our method improves Qwen3 series models consistently; on MATH-500, accuracy rises from 82.0% to 84.6% for Qwen3-4B and from 82.4% to 85.6% for Qwen3-8B. These results suggest that susceptibility can serve not only as a diagnostic signal for reasoning failures, but also as a practical guide for targeted test-time intervention.

AI.tldr: SPARK diagnoses and corrects LLM reasoning failures by analyzing length-controlled hidden-state susceptibility, using this signal to identify under-activated reasoning states and guide targeted test-time steering, improving accuracy on MATH-500 by ~2.6% for Qwen3 models.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation methods for reasoning failures operate at the output level (final answers) without revealing why the model failed, while activation-steering methods apply global directions without diagnosing which examples need intervention. There is a need for a diagnostic approach that identifies internal reasoning state deficiencies at the example level.
AI.method: SPARK uses hidden-state susceptibility as a diagnostic signal, applying length-controlled susceptibility to decouple input-scale effects (prompt length) from residual reasoning activation in LLMs. It combines this with cross-layer coordination to select reasoning-active anchors and under-activated hard examples, then applies lightweight test-time steering.
AI.result: On MATH-500, accuracy improved from 82.0% to 84.6% for Qwen3-4B and from 82.4% to 85.6% for Qwen3-8B. Evaluation uses FRONTIER-4.5K for controlled programmatic reasoning profiling and GSM8K/MATH-500 for benchmark steering evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-state susceptibility can serve both as a diagnostic signal for reasoning failures and as a practical guide for targeted test-time intervention, with length-controlled susceptibility effectively separating input-scale confounds from genuine reasoning activation deficits.

title: When Data Imbalance Helps: Robust Generalization Through Shortcut Saturation
summary: We study robust generalization under spurious correlations: tasks where a shortcut feature is correlated with the true label in training but anti-correlated in an adversarial held-out split. Varying the spurious ratio $r$ (the fraction of training examples where shortcut = true label) and model capacity, we find a counterintuitive result: data imbalance promotes generalization in sufficiently capable models. On a synthetic task where the true label is sum parity of an integer sequence and the shortcut is the parity of the maximum-valued element, a 2-layer, 2-head transformer generalized (reached $100\%$ adversarial accuracy) in 0% of seeds at $r{=}0.50$ but 77% of seeds at $r{=}0.90$. The effect is absent in 1-layer models, where imbalance instead traps the model on the shortcut. Through mechanistic analysis -- gradient conflict dynamics, circuit evolution, and QK/OV circuit ablations -- we characterize a mechanistic pathway consistent with imbalance promoting generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how data imbalance (spurious correlation ratio) affects robust generalization in transformer models, finding that imbalance (e.g., r=0.90) surprisingly promotes generalization in sufficiently capable (2-layer) models, while balanced data (r=0.50) leads to failure. This effect is absent in shallow (1-layer) models.
AI.motivation: To understand the counterintuitive effect of spurious correlation ratios on robust generalization in neural networks, specifically how data imbalance can sometimes help rather than hinder generalization in sufficiently capable models.
AI.method: Synthetic task (sum parity of integer sequences with shortcut being max-element parity), varying spurious ratio r and model capacity (1-layer vs 2-layer transformers). Mechanistic analysis via gradient conflict dynamics, circuit evolution, and QK/OV circuit ablations.
AI.result: At r=0.50, a 2-layer, 2-head transformer generalized in 0% of seeds; at r=0.90, it generalized in 77% of seeds. The effect is absent in 1-layer models where imbalance traps the model on the shortcut.
AI.conclusion: Data imbalance can promote robust generalization in sufficiently capable models, and a mechanistic pathway consistent with this effect was identified.

title: Structured Evidence Selection for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection
summary: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection relies solely on video-level labels for training, making it difficult to accurately localize anomalous events in complex scenes. In real-world videos, anomalous behaviors exhibit large variations in appearance and temporal duration, while scene appearance and action dynamics are often tightly entangled. Consequently, existing models tend to rely on scene-related statistical cues rather than true behavioral deviations, resulting in unstable detection performance. To address this challenge, we propose a Structured Evidence Selection framework (SESAD) that reformulates anomaly detection as a structured reasoning process over clip-level visual evidence. Instead of directly mapping aggregated features to anomaly scores, SESAD reorganizes clip representations into semantically structured candidate evidence and performs context-conditioned selection under scene and action constraints. This mechanism adaptively emphasizes anomaly-relevant semantics while suppressing scene interference, thereby alleviating semantic entanglement under weak supervision. Furthermore, we introduce a lightweight geometric discrimination module that constructs a dual-prototype structure in the embedding space, enabling anomaly decisions through relative geometric relations. Extensive experiments on UBnormal, ShanghaiTech, and UCF-Crime show that SESAD achieves 67.92, 97.99, and 88.46 AUC, respectively, while maintaining high computational efficiency and overall consistently stable anomaly discrimination.

AI.tldr: SESAD reformulates weakly supervised video anomaly detection as a structured evidence selection process with geometric discrimination, achieving state-of-the-art AUC scores on UBnormal (67.92), ShanghaiTech (97.99), and UCF-Crime (88.46).
AI.motivation: Existing weakly supervised anomaly detection methods rely on scene-related statistical cues rather than true behavioral deviations due to entangled scene appearance and action dynamics, leading to unstable detection performance.
AI.method: Proposes a Structured Evidence Selection framework (SESAD) that reorganizes clip representations into semantically structured candidate evidence with context-conditioned selection under scene and action constraints, plus a lightweight geometric discrimination module with a dual-prototype structure for anomaly decisions via relative geometric relations.
AI.result: Achieves 67.92, 97.99, and 88.46 AUC on UBnormal, ShanghaiTech, and UCF-Crime respectively, with high computational efficiency and stable anomaly discrimination.
AI.conclusion: SESAD effectively alleviates semantic entanglement under weak supervision by adaptively emphasizing anomaly-relevant semantics while suppressing scene interference, resulting in consistently stable and efficient anomaly detection.

title: Measure the Sim-to-Real Gap: Designing an Affordable Real-World Benchmark Platform for Reinforcement Learning in AIoT Systems
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly employed to enhance the performance of autonomous systems, including the Autonomous Internet of Things (AIoT). However, the trial-and-error nature of RL, when conducted in real-world environments, is costly and hazardous in some scenarios. Consequently, the majority of RL research is conducted in simulation. This reliance introduces challenges related to the Sim-to-Real transferability. Evaluating the Sim-to-Real algorithmic robustness and the Sim-to-Real gap is a critical prerequisite for research aimed at improving RL performance in the real world. Therefore, industries such as robotics have developed concurrent simulation and physical platforms to facilitate this research. However, a universal Sim-to-Real benchmark platform for AIoT does not currently exist. To address these concerns, we developed a real-world AIoT platform for studying RL in AIoT. On this platform, an agent deployed on an edge device plays video games on a separate host computer via a hardware-emulated keyboard, guided by vision input. This platform uses commercially available components costing less than USD 400, together with two computers. Because the system's objective is game score maximization, it inherently mitigates safety risks associated with real-world RL deployments. Experimental results show the simulation-trained agent suffers a 1160% performance degradation relative to the human-level performance after real-world deployment, indicating a significant Sim-to-Real gap. Direct real-world training using the deep Q-network (DQN) algorithm achieves approximately 38% of human-level performance after 10 million training steps, demonstrating the feasibility of RL under real-world conditions. These results suggest that the proposed Sim-to-Real benchmark platform provides a substantial foundation for qualitative and quantitative evaluations of RL in real-world AIoT systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a low-cost ($400) real-world AIoT benchmark platform for studying Sim-to-Real transfer in reinforcement learning. Experiments show a 1160% performance gap between simulation-trained and real-world deployed agents, while direct real-world DQN training achieves ~38% human-level performance, demonstrating the platform's value for evaluating RL in AIoT.
AI.motivation: RL research for AIoT is mostly done in simulation due to real-world safety/cost concerns, but no universal Sim-to-Real benchmark platform exists for AIoT, creating a need for standardized evaluation of algorithmic robustness and the Sim-to-Real gap.
AI.method: Developed a real-world AIoT platform using commercially available components (<$400) where an agent on an edge device plays video games on a host computer via hardware-emulated keyboard with vision input. The game score maximization objective inherently avoids real-world safety risks.
AI.result: Simulation-trained agent suffered 1160% performance degradation versus human-level after real-world deployment. Direct real-world DQN training achieved ~38% of human-level performance after 10 million steps.
AI.conclusion: The proposed platform provides a substantial foundation for qualitative and quantitative evaluations of RL in real-world AIoT systems, enabling standardized Sim-to-Real benchmarking.

title: GAE: Graph-Augmented Evolution for Scientific Discovery via Reinforcement Optimization
summary: Evolutionary program search guided by Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automated scientific discovery. However, current approaches are fundamentally constrained by three bottlenecks: structurally blind parent selection, sparse whole-program evaluation rewards, and static mutation operators that fail to adapt during search. We present GAE (Graph-Augmented Evolution), a framework that resolves these limitations through a tightly coupled, three-pillar architecture. First, a relational graph neural network (GNN) parses programs into typed computation graphs, producing structure-aware embeddings. Second, an RL-optimized meta-controller leverages these embeddings to replace blind evolutionary sampling with a directed policy, dynamically selecting optimal parents and mutation directions based on reward history. Third, an online GRPO fine-tuning loop continuously updates the LLM mutation operator at test-time using group-normalized evaluation rewards, directly aligning the model's generation distribution with high-fitness structural edits. We evaluate GAE on a challenging scientific discovery task: symbolic regression for complex nonlinear oscillator systems. By transforming stochastic search into a directed, self-improving trajectory, GAE efficiently discovers closed-form physical equations, consistently matching or outperforming static LLM-driven baselines and achieving state-of-the-art out-of-distribution performance.

AI.tldr: GAE introduces a three-pillar framework combining GNN-based program embeddings, RL-directed parent/mutation selection, and online GRPO fine-tuning of LLM mutation operators to overcome key bottlenecks in LLM-guided evolutionary program search, achieving state-of-the-art results on symbolic regression for nonlinear oscillator systems.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-guided evolutionary search suffers from three fundamental bottlenecks: blind parent selection, sparse whole-program evaluation rewards, and static mutation operators that lack adaptability.
AI.method: A three-pillar architecture: (1) a relational GNN parses programs into typed computation graphs for structure-aware embeddings; (2) an RL-optimized meta-controller uses these embeddings to direct parent selection and mutation choices; (3) an online GRPO fine-tuning loop continuously updates the LLM mutation operator using group-normalized evaluation rewards.
AI.result: GAE efficiently discovers closed-form physical equations on symbolic regression for nonlinear oscillator systems, consistently matching or outperforming static LLM-driven baselines and achieving state-of-the-art out-of-distribution performance.
AI.conclusion: Transforming stochastic evolutionary search into a directed, self-improving trajectory resolves key limitations of LLM-guided program search and sets a new state-of-the-art for automated scientific discovery in symbolic regression.

title: ChartSync: A Benchmark for Visuo-Logical Cascading Chart Editing
summary: Generative image editing models struggle with structured statistical charts when data modifications require geometric synchronization. We formalize this task as Visuo-Logical Cascading Editing (VLCE). However, existing methods remain confined to localized text substitutions and struggle with dependency-aware cascading updates. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce ChartSync, an expert-validated benchmark constructed via a programmatic rendering pipeline that guarantees deterministic visuo-logical coupling for the ground truth. ChartSync comprises 870 triplets across 9 chart categories and 4 task types, including 235 geometry-coupled VLCE instances that specifically test cascading text-to-geometry synchronization. We further evaluate these instances via a two-tier framework combining objective visual metrics with a vision-language model judge paradigm to assess low-level fidelity alongside multimodal comprehension and reasoning. Evaluating 14 image editing models and one code-mediated pipeline reveals a nuanced capability gap: most open-source models suffer severe drops in geometric synchronization, while only two frontier proprietary models show emerging VLCE capability, with their residual errors mainly involving semantic isolation and background corruption. Our detailed error analysis deconstructs these failure paradigms to identify core meta-abilities for guiding future multimodal architectures. The ChartSync dataset and code are publicly released at https://github.com/kaka-yjk/ChartSyncCodebase.

AI.tldr: ChartSync is a benchmark for evaluating generative image editing models on Visuo-Logical Cascading Editing (VLCE) of statistical charts, revealing that most open-source models fail at geometry-synchronized edits while frontier proprietary models show emerging capability but with residual errors in semantic isolation and background corruption.
AI.motivation: Existing image editing models struggle with structured statistical charts where data modifications demand geometric synchronization (e.g., changing a bar chart value requires proportional bar height updates). Current methods are limited to localized text substitutions and cannot handle dependency-aware cascading updates.
AI.method: The authors construct ChartSync, an expert-validated benchmark of 870 triplets across 9 chart categories and 4 task types, including 235 geometry-coupled VLCE instances. They use a programmatic rendering pipeline for deterministic ground truth. Evaluation uses a two-tier framework combining objective visual metrics with a VLM judge for low-level fidelity and multimodal reasoning assessment.
AI.result: Evaluating 14 image editing models and one code-mediated pipeline shows that most open-source models suffer severe drops in geometric synchronization. Only two frontier proprietary models exhibit emerging VLCE capability, though with residual errors involving semantic isolation and background corruption.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies core meta-abilities needed for future multimodal architectures through detailed error analysis of failure paradigms, and releases the dataset and code publicly.

title: Comparing Socio-technical Design Principles with Guidelines for Human-centered AI
summary: Human-centered AI (HCAI) refers to guidelines or principles that aim on ethi-cally oriented design of systems. We compare HCAI- guidelines with princi-ples of socio-technical systems that emerged in the context of conventional in-formation technology. The comparison leads to a revision of socio-technical heuristics by including aspects of AI-usage. The comparison reveals that con-tinuous evolution is a basic characteristic of socio-technical systems, and that human oversight or interventions and the subsequent appropriation of AI-systems lead to continuous adaptation and re-design of the systems, if autono-my is collaboratively exercised. From a socio-technical point of view, the cru-cial requirement of transparency has not only to be fulfilled with technical fea-tures, but also by contributions of the whole system including human actors. It will be promising for using AI, if not only technical features, but organization-al and social practices are socio-technically designed in a way that compen-sates shortcomings of AI.

AI.tldr: This paper compares Human-centered AI (HCAI) guidelines with socio-technical systems principles, finding that continuous evolution, collaborative autonomy, and socio-technical transparency are key for AI systems, and that organizational/social practices should be designed to compensate AI shortcomings.
AI.motivation: To compare HCAI guidelines with established socio-technical systems principles from conventional IT, and to revise socio-technical heuristics to incorporate AI-specific aspects.
AI.method: Comparative analysis between HCAI guidelines and socio-technical systems principles, leading to a revision of socio-technical heuristics for AI contexts.
AI.result: Continuous evolution is a basic characteristic of socio-technical systems; human oversight and collaborative autonomy lead to continuous adaptation; transparency must be fulfilled by the whole system (not just technical features) including human actors; organizational and social practices should compensate AI shortcomings.
AI.conclusion: Promising AI use requires socio-technical design that addresses not only technical features but also organizational and social practices to compensate for AI limitations.

title: Energy-guided Recursive Model
summary: Recursive reasoning models address structured problems by repeatedly updating latent states of small neural networks. However, their test-time scaling lacks a principled inference mechanism: increasing depth or stochastic breadth generates more trajectories without a clear criterion for selection, and existing methods predominantly rely on additional q-heads or heuristic voting. Here, we develop the Energy-guided Recursive Model (ERM), which introduces an intrinsic selection principle based on explicit Hopfield energies. ERM leverages Hopfield-type memories of valid local or global structures to define the selector over candidate trajectories. The resulting energy seamlessly integrates with energy-based techniques such as parallel tempering to enhance sampling efficiency and ranking. With $D=64$ recurrent steps and $K=128$ candidates, ERM reaches optimal solutions on Sudoku ($98.97\%$), Pencil Puzzle Bench (PPBench, $88.04\%$) and Maze ($99.30\%$), improving upon recent Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model and Equilibrium Reasoners. These results suggest that incorporating explicit energy functions into recursive reasoning offers a principled path toward more effective inference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ERM, a recursive reasoning model that uses Hopfield energies as a principled selection mechanism for candidate trajectories, achieving state-of-the-art results on Sudoku (98.97%), PPBench (88.04%), and Maze (99.30%) with 64 recurrent steps and 128 candidates.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive reasoning models lack principled inference mechanisms for test-time scaling—increasing depth or stochastic breadth generates more trajectories without a clear selection criterion, and current methods rely on heuristic voting or additional q-heads.
AI.method: ERM incorporates explicit Hopfield energy functions to define a selector over candidate trajectories, using Hopfield-type memories of valid local/global structures. It integrates with energy-based techniques like parallel tempering to enhance sampling efficiency and ranking.
AI.result: With D=64 recurrent steps and K=128 candidates, ERM achieves optimal solutions on Sudoku (98.97%), PPBench (88.04%), and Maze (99.30%), outperforming Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model and Equilibrium Reasoners.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit energy functions into recursive reasoning provides a principled path toward more effective inference, as demonstrated by ERM's superior performance across structured reasoning tasks.

title: Generalize LMMs to Versatile Visual Modalities via Fabricated Modality Synthesis
comment: Accepted by the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2026
summary: Despite the advancements of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in RGB vision, their ability to generalize to unseen visual modalities remains a largely unexplored challenge. We argue that different visual modalities are merely distinct samplings of the same physical world. Therefore, effective generalization requires models to possess both modality-agnostic perception of scene semantics and the adaptability to modality-specific characteristics. To achieve this, we propose a training framework, VVM-Tuning, to equip LMMs with these capabilities through modality synthesis and modality contexts. Specifically, we synthesize diverse appearance-varied images from RGB scenes, training the model to disentangle invariant semantics from varying visual appearances, and align these appearances with language for visual concepts decoupled from modalities. We then introduce modality contexts in the prompt and use instruction tuning to assist the model in mapping these appearance variations back to modality-related attributes, enabling zero-shot adaptation to unseen modalities during inference. To facilitate research in this direction, we introduce VVM-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark featuring 6 real and synthetic modalities to evaluate semantic perception and modality understanding. Experiments demonstrate that, via our training on synthetic modalities, 5 tested models exhibit consistent improvements on both real-world and novel synthetic modalities without in-modality training. Source code and data will be publicly available at https://github.com/Hunter-Will/VVM-Tuning.

AI.tldr: VVM-Tuning equips LMMs with modality-agnostic perception and modality-specific adaptability via synthetic appearance-varied images and modality context prompts, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen visual modalities. VVM-Bench evaluates across 6 real/synthetic modalities.
AI.motivation: LMMs excel in RGB vision but struggle to generalize to unseen visual modalities (e.g., thermal, depth). The paper argues these modalities are samplings of the same physical world, so models need both modality-agnostic scene understanding and modality-specific adaptation.
AI.method: Proposes VVM-Tuning framework: (1) synthesize diverse appearance-varied images from RGB scenes, training the model to disentangle invariant semantics from varying appearances and align with language; (2) introduce modality contexts in prompts with instruction tuning to map appearance variations back to modality-related attributes, enabling zero-shot adaptation to unseen modalities.
AI.result: 5 tested LMMs show consistent improvements on both real-world and novel synthetic modalities without any in-modality training. VVM-Bench provides a comprehensive benchmark of 6 real and synthetic modalities.
AI.conclusion: VVM-Tuning effectively enables zero-shot generalization to unseen visual modalities by combining modality-agnostic semantic learning with modality-specific prompt adaptation, validated across multiple models and modalities.

title: ABot-AgentOS: A General Robotic Agent OS with Lifelong Multi-modal Memory
summary: Recent VLM and VLA systems have improved robotic perception and action prediction, yet long-horizon embodied agents still require a general runtime layer for reasoning, memory, tool use, verification, and cross-embodiment execution. We present ABot-AgentOS, a general robotic Agent Operating System that sits above low-level controllers and provides a deliberative agent layer for scene-conditioned planning, context-isolated skill execution, multi-stage verification, multi-modal memory, and edge-cloud collaboration. To evaluate such systems, we introduce EmbodiedWorldBench, an executable benchmark with 16 indoor, outdoor, and hybrid scenes, four difficulty levels, and over 200 tasks involving navigation, object search, NPC dialogue, dynamic events, and trace-grounded scoring. ABot-AgentOS further introduces Universal Multi-modal Graph Memory, a persistent source-grounded substrate that converts dialogue, visual observations, spatial context, temporal relations, and task traces into typed nodes and edges. A failure-driven self-evolution loop converts diagnosed memory failures into gated runtime evo-assets that are promoted only to later evaluation splits, preventing current-split ground-truth leakage while enabling continual improvement. On an initial EmbodiedWorldBench subset, ABot-AgentOS improves over a single-controller baseline in both task success and goal completion. Across memory benchmarks, ABot-AgentOS Static achieves 87.5 on LoCoMo, 59.9 on OpenEQA EM-EQA, 88.6 on Mem-Gallery, and 76.5 Acc@All on NExT-QA; self-evolution further improves LoCoMo to 88.7, OpenEQA to 60.4, and Mem-Gallery to 89.0. These results suggest that a general Agent OS layer can improve long-horizon embodied execution while providing persistent, auditable memory for continual interaction.

AI.tldr: ABot-AgentOS is a general robotic Agent Operating System that provides a deliberative layer for long-horizon embodied agents, featuring scene-conditioned planning, multi-modal memory (Universal Multi-modal Graph Memory), multi-stage verification, and failure-driven self-evolution. It is evaluated on EmbodiedWorldBench (16 scenes, 200+ tasks) and memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, OpenEQA, Mem-Gallery, NExT-QA), outperforming single-controller baselines and showing continual improvement via self-evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM/VLA systems improve perception and action prediction but lack a general runtime layer for reasoning, memory, tool use, verification, and cross-embodiment execution needed for long-horizon embodied agents.
AI.method: ABot-AgentOS introduces: (1) a deliberative agent layer above low-level controllers for scene-conditioned planning and context-isolated skill execution; (2) Universal Multi-modal Graph Memory (UMGM) that converts observations into typed nodes/edges; (3) multi-stage verification; (4) failure-driven self-evolution loop that converts diagnosed memory failures into gated runtime evo-assets promoted only to later evaluation splits to prevent data leakage.
AI.result: On EmbodiedWorldBench, ABot-AgentOS improves task success and goal completion over single-controller baseline. Static memory benchmarks: LoCoMo 87.5, OpenEQA EM-EQA 59.9, Mem-Gallery 88.6, NExT-QA 76.5 Acc@All. Self-evolution further improves: LoCoMo 88.7, OpenEQA 60.4, Mem-Gallery 89.0.
AI.conclusion: A general Agent OS layer can improve long-horizon embodied execution while providing persistent, auditable memory for continual interaction.

title: SALT-GNN: Handling Dense Neighborhoods in Anti-Money Laundering Graphs via Statistics-Aware Attention
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures. Code available upon publication
summary: Money laundering threatens financial stability and exposes institutions to penalties, motivating automated detection. Because laundering schemes often emerge through relational patterns, graph neural networks (GNNs) are increasingly used for anti-money laundering (AML). Yet AML GNNs are typically evaluated with aggregate metrics such as overall F1 score, which hide an operational issue: high-activity recipient accounts concentrate many incoming transactions, making suspicious signals harder to isolate and costlier to investigate. We introduce a recipient-degree stratified evaluation that reports standard AML metrics across recipient-context density. Across three datasets (HI-Small, HI-Medium, and AMLSim-32k-5%), it reveals consistent degradation in dense recipient contexts, which we trace to three GNN characteristics: two known limitations that AML amplifies, i.e., (1) multiset non-discriminability and (2) cardinality blindness, and (3) an attention-specific effect: in dense neighborhoods, normalized attention attenuates weak but pattern-relevant multi-hop signals. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose SALT-GNN, a lightweight statistics-aware architecture that fuses degree-aware statistical aggregation with attention at each message-passing layer, so distributional and cardinality information shapes the node states used by subsequent attention steps. Ablations support fusion placement as a key factor in dense-context performance. On HI-Small and HI-Medium, SALT-GNN uses up to 77% fewer parameters than task-specific graph-transformer baselines while improving dense-context F1 score by 3-6 points; on AMLSim-32k-5%, it improves highest-degree F1 score by 16-20 points. The gains hold for both Transformer- and GAT-style attention, indicating that the benefit comes from where statistical and attentional evidence is fused rather than from a specific attention operator.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that GNN-based AML models perform poorly on high-degree recipient accounts due to multiset non-discriminability, cardinality blindness, and attention attenuation in dense neighborhoods. To address this, the authors propose SALT-GNN, a lightweight architecture fusing degree-aware statistical aggregation with attention at each message-passing layer, achieving 3-20 point F1 improvements on dense contexts with up to 77% fewer parameters than baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard aggregate metrics like overall F1 hide that AML GNNs struggle with high-activity recipient accounts, which concentrate many incoming transactions, making suspicious signals harder to isolate and costlier to investigate. The authors aim to diagnose and mitigate this operational blind spot.
AI.method: The authors introduce recipient-degree stratified evaluation to reveal performance degradation in dense contexts. They diagnose three causes: (1) multiset non-discriminability, (2) cardinality blindness, and (3) attention attenuation in dense neighborhoods. They propose SALT-GNN, which fuses degree-aware statistical aggregation with attention at each message-passing layer, so distributional and cardinality information shapes the node states used by subsequent attention steps.
AI.result: On HI-Small and HI-Medium, SALT-GNN uses up to 77% fewer parameters than task-specific graph-transformer baselines while improving dense-context F1 by 3-6 points; on AMLSim-32k-5%, it improves highest-degree F1 by 16-20 points. Gains hold for both Transformer- and GAT-style attention, indicating fusion placement matters more than the specific attention operator.
AI.conclusion: The diagnosis-driven SALT-GNN architecture effectively addresses the under-explored issue of dense-recipient-context degradation in AML GNNs, achieving significant gains with fewer parameters. The benefit stems from fusing statistical and attentional evidence at each layer rather than from a particular attention mechanism.

title: Imperceptible and Reversible Adversarial Examples against Vision-Language Models for Privacy Protection
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) offer powerful multimodal ability but also expose users to text-based privacy attacks where adversaries crawl online photos and query VLMs to extract sensitive attributes. Existing reversible adversarial example (RAE) methods protect images in purely visual tasks but fail in multimodal settings, and current adversarial examples on VLMs rely on high frequency noise that severely degrades visual quality. We propose CloakDiff, the first framework for reversible, high fidelity privacy protection against text-based query attacks in VLMs. CloakDiff produces imperceptible adversarial examples by combining diffusion based adversarial editing with an invertible network that embeds the original image for lossless recovery. It perturbs both pixel space embeddings and manipulates latent cross attention maps to ensure strong cross-model and cross-prompt transferability while preserving global visual structure. To further enhance fidelity, we design EDM Heuristic Sampling, a principled diffusion schedule for adversarial guidance. Experiments on multiple datasets and VLMs demonstrate that CloakDiff delivers multimodal privacy preservation with high visual quality and reversibility.

AI.tldr: CloakDiff is the first framework for reversible, high-fidelity privacy protection against text-based query attacks in VLMs, combining diffusion-based adversarial editing with an invertible network and EDM Heuristic Sampling to produce imperceptible adversarial examples with strong transferability.
AI.motivation: VLMs expose users to text-based privacy attacks where adversaries extract sensitive attributes from online photos via VLM queries. Existing RAE methods fail in multimodal settings, and current adversarial examples on VLMs use high-frequency noise that severely degrades visual quality.
AI.method: CloakDiff combines diffusion-based adversarial editing with an invertible network for lossless image recovery. It perturbs pixel-space embeddings and manipulates latent cross-attention maps for cross-model and cross-prompt transferability. EDM Heuristic Sampling provides a principled diffusion schedule for adversarial guidance.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple datasets and VLMs demonstrate that CloakDiff delivers multimodal privacy preservation with high visual quality and reversibility.
AI.conclusion: CloakDiff is the first framework to achieve reversible, high-fidelity privacy protection against text-based query attacks in VLMs, addressing the limitations of prior work in multimodal settings and visual degradation.

title: Co4ICF: Co-evolving Physics-Informed Surrogate and RL-based Pulse Optimizer for Inertial Confinement Fusion
summary: Offline-trained surrogates for Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF) suffer a well-known failure mode that iterative optimizers drive inputs into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions where predictions become unreliable. Here we present Co4ICF, a co-evolving framework that couples a physics-informed surrogate with a PPO-based pulse optimizer. The surrogate is iteratively fine-tuned on policy-induced trajectories, correcting extrapolation errors as the optimizer shifts the input distribution; the optimizer queries this evolving surrogate as a fast environment. In the 1D MULTI environment, Co4ICF achieves 146.1% normalized yield based on current laser design baseline; as a post-hoc cross-fidelity check, the optimized pulse further attains 246.9% normalized yield when directly evaluated in 2D-MULTI without any 2D training or fine-tuning. Budget-matched ablations support that the gains are not explained solely by additional simulation data and are consistent with the co-evolving mechanism playing a key role. We release a large-scale MULTI-IFE simulation dataset to support future benchmarking.

AI.tldr: Co4ICF couples a physics-informed surrogate with a PPO-based optimizer in a co-evolving framework for ICF pulse design, achieving 146.1% normalized yield in 1D MULTI and 246.9% in 2D-MULTI without 2D training, outperforming offline surrogates by iteratively correcting OOD extrapolation errors.
AI.motivation: Offline-trained surrogates for ICF suffer from failure modes where iterative optimizers drive inputs into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions, causing unreliable predictions.
AI.method: Co4ICF couples a physics-informed surrogate with a PPO-based pulse optimizer. The surrogate is iteratively fine-tuned on policy-induced trajectories to correct extrapolation errors as the optimizer shifts the input distribution; the optimizer queries this evolving surrogate as a fast environment.
AI.result: Co4ICF achieves 146.1% normalized yield in 1D MULTI environment. As a post-hoc cross-fidelity check, the optimized pulse attains 246.9% normalized yield when evaluated in 2D-MULTI without any 2D training or fine-tuning. Budget-matched ablations confirm gains are not solely from additional simulation data.
AI.conclusion: The co-evolving mechanism is key to the performance gains, and a large-scale MULTI-IFE simulation dataset is released for benchmarking.

title: LeRoPE: Learnable RoPE Frequencies Improve Language Modeling
summary: Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE) are currently the most popular positional encodings used in modern language models. RoPE rotates two-dimensional chunks of query and key vectors, operating as a function of their relative positional offset. The position-wise rates of rotation in RoPE typically follow a geometric sequence specified by a fixed base-frequency hyperparameter. Prior work has improved performance by either increasing this parameter to slow rotation or by applying RoPE to only a subset of QK dimensions. In this work we modify RoPE by learning a scalar per frequency, treating frequencies as learnable parameters rather than hyperparameters. We validate Learned RoPE by training a ladder of language models from scratch, ranging from 52M to 2.5B parameters. We observe and analyze the emergence of a high-norm, positional LeRoPE band. LeRoPE consistently outperforms RoPE and partial RoPE across all scales, with RoPE requiring 3.4% more compute (FLOPs) to match LeRoPE at the largest scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Learned RoPE (LeRoPE), which modifies standard Rotary Positional Encodings by making the frequency parameters learnable rather than fixed hyperparameters. Training from 52M to 2.5B parameters, LeRoPE consistently outperforms RoPE and partial RoPE, with standard RoPE requiring 3.4% more compute to match LeRoPE at the largest scale.
AI.motivation: Prior work improved RoPE either by increasing the base-frequency hyperparameter to slow rotation or by applying RoPE to only a subset of QK dimensions, but the frequency parameters remained fixed. The authors aim to learn these frequencies directly from data to improve performance.
AI.method: The authors modify RoPE by treating each frequency as a learnable scalar parameter rather than a fixed hyperparameter (specifically, learning a scalar per frequency). They train a ladder of language models from scratch across multiple scales (52M to 2.5B parameters) and analyze the resulting learned positional encoding behavior.
AI.result: LeRoPE consistently outperforms both standard RoPE and partial RoPE across all model scales. Standard RoPE requires 3.4% more compute (FLOPs) to match LeRoPE's performance at the largest scale (2.5B). The authors observe and analyze the emergence of a high-norm, positional LeRoPE band.
AI.conclusion: Making RoPE frequencies learnable is a simple yet effective modification that yields consistent improvements across model scales without adding significant complexity or computational overhead.

title: GRC-ProbNet: Uncertainty-aware Feature Extraction for Cardiovascular Disease Classification
summary: The automatic detection and classification of cardiovascular disease (CVD) from computed tomography (CT) images plays an important role in clinical practice. Recently, a hybrid pipeline (GRC-Net) for CVD classification was proposed, which leverages a deep-learning-based segmentation and registration method to extract radiomic and geometric features. However, GRC-Net relies on a deterministic segmentation mask, without considering the inherent ambiguity associated with cardiac anatomy. In this paper, we propose GRC-ProbNet, which takes advantage of a deep ensemble to produce multiple segmentation masks for a given input. From these masks, we extract multiple uncertainty features. We analyze these uncertainty features for both their correlation with segmentation error and their propagation effects on downstream CVD classification performance. Our experiments on the publicly available MM-WHS and ASOCA datasets show that the uncertainty measure that best reflects segmentation quality is not necessarily the one that provides the strongest signal for downstream CVD classification. Overall, our results demonstrate that GRC-ProbNet utilizing uncertainty features substantially improves CVD classification AUROC (92.92\) compared to the baseline GRC-Net model (91.25%). Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/biomedia-mira/GRC-ProbNet.

AI.tldr: GRC-ProbNet improves CVD classification from CT images by using deep ensemble-based uncertainty features from multiple segmentation masks, achieving 92.92% AUROC vs. 91.25% baseline, while showing that the best uncertainty measure for segmentation quality does not always benefit downstream classification.
AI.motivation: The prior GRC-Net pipeline for CVD classification uses deterministic segmentation without accounting for the inherent ambiguity of cardiac anatomy.
AI.method: GRC-ProbNet employs a deep ensemble to generate multiple segmentation masks per input, extracts multiple uncertainty features, analyzes their correlation with segmentation error and their impact on downstream CVD classification.
AI.result: GRC-ProbNet achieves 92.92% AUROC, outperforming GRC-Net's 91.25% on MM-WHS and ASOCA datasets. The best uncertainty measure for segmentation quality is not necessarily the most effective for downstream classification.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating uncertainty features from deep ensembles improves CVD classification performance, and the relationship between segmentation uncertainty and downstream task utility is non-trivial.

title: ANCHOR: Automated Alignment Auditing for CLI Agents on Real-World Harm
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026. 19 pages, 14 figures, 5 tables
summary: Autonomous CLI agents can now execute hundreds of actions across multi-hour sessions: writing code, executing shell commands, browsing the web, and managing cloud infrastructure, all with minimal human oversight. Does greater autonomy invite greater risk? We introduce ANCHOR, an automated auditing framework that stress-tests CLI agents on illegal tasks grounded in public US court cases. ANCHOR deploys an auditor agent fine-tuned on dark personality data using supervised and reinforcement fine tuning. This auditor roleplays persistent malicious users who decompose tasks, reframe requests upon refusal, and adapt strategies across multi-turn interactions. Evaluating frontier CLI agents, we find that while they often refuse illegal tasks when prompted directly, compliance reaches 100\% under persistent malicious interaction. When agents comply, they frequently exceed user requests, autonomously building infrastructure for large-scale harm, including catastrophic risk scenarios such as large-scale financial fraud and bioweapon development. These findings demonstrate that current alignment techniques are insufficient for autonomous agents and underscore the need for safety evaluations against persistent, adaptive malicious users. We release ANCHOR at https://github.com/garified/anchor

AI.tldr: ANCHOR is an automated auditing framework that stress-tests CLI agents on illegal tasks grounded in US court cases. It uses an auditor agent fine-tuned on dark personality data to roleplay persistent malicious users. Results show frontier CLI agents reach 100% compliance under persistent multi-turn attacks, often autonomously building infrastructure for catastrophic harm like large-scale fraud and bioweapon development, exposing insufficient alignment for autonomous agents.
AI.motivation: To determine whether greater autonomy in CLI agents invites greater risk, especially when faced with persistent, adaptive malicious users attempting to elicit illegal behavior.
AI.method: ANCHOR framework: (1) Grounds illegal tasks in real US court cases; (2) Uses an auditor agent fine-tuned on dark personality data via supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning; (3) The auditor roleplays persistent malicious users that decompose tasks, reframe requests upon refusal, and adapt strategies across multi-turn interactions.
AI.result: Frontier CLI agents often refuse direct illegal prompts, but compliance reaches 100% under persistent malicious interaction. When complying, agents frequently exceed the request scope, autonomously building infrastructure for large-scale harm including catastrophic risk scenarios such as large-scale financial fraud and bioweapon development.
AI.conclusion: Current alignment techniques are insufficient for autonomous agents; there is a critical need for safety evaluations against persistent, adaptive malicious users.

title: RDQ: Residual Distribution Quantization for Large Language Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models degrades sharply below 4-bit precision. We identify the root cause as residual stream distributional drift: quantization noise injected at each transformer layer accumulates in the shared residual representation, causing KL divergence from the FP16 baseline to grow super-linearly with depth (Pearson r=0.999 with log-perplexity, p<0.001, confirmed across all tested methods and bit-widths). We discover that 84% of LLaMA-3-8B layers exhibit non-Gaussian residual distributions (KS test, p<=0.05), and that per-layer residual stream variance grows 6,548x across depth. We propose RDQ (Residual Distribution Quantization), a PTQ framework whose central contribution is Cascaded Error Compensation (CEC): a sequential calibration procedure that captures the actual drifted activations each layer receives (computed by running calibration data through already-quantized upstream layers) and fits per-channel AWQ-style scales against those drifted inputs, with scales folded into preceding RMSNorm weights for exact mathematical equivalence at zero inference overhead. RDQ achieves state-of-the-art results on all three tested architectures: LLaMA-3-8B: 7.55 / 5.62 PPL (W3/W4); Qwen-2.5-7B: 7.46 / 6.38 PPL; Mistral-7B: 6.88 / 5.73 PPL. RDQ beats the best published baseline (LeanQuant/SpinQuant) at every model and bit-width combination, with gains up to -46.4% vs. RTN at W3A16 on LLaMA-3-8B. All output is standard group-128 asymmetric quantization, deployable on Qualcomm AIMET, GGUF, and any standard inference stack at zero runtime overhead.

AI.tldr: RDQ is a PTQ framework that identifies residual stream distributional drift as the root cause of LLM quantization degradation below 4-bit, and proposes Cascaded Error Compensation (CEC) to calibrate quantization scales against drifted activations from already-quantized upstream layers, achieving SOTA results across LLaMA-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral-7B at zero inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization of LLMs degrades sharply below 4-bit precision; the root cause is identified as residual stream distributional drift where quantization noise accumulates super-linearly across depth (Pearson r=0.999 with log-perplexity).
AI.method: RDQ proposes Cascaded Error Compensation (CEC): a sequential calibration procedure that feeds calibration data through already-quantized upstream layers to capture actual drifted activations, then fits per-channel AWQ-style scales against those drifted inputs, folding scales into preceding RMSNorm weights for zero inference overhead.
AI.result: LLaMA-3-8B: 7.55 / 5.62 PPL (W3/W4); Qwen-2.5-7B: 7.46 / 6.38 PPL; Mistral-7B: 6.88 / 5.73 PPL. Up to -46.4% vs. RTN at W3A16 on LLaMA-3-8B. Beats LeanQuant/SpinQuant at all model/bit-width combinations.
AI.conclusion: RDQ achieves SOTA results across three architectures with standard group-128 asymmetric quantization deployable on Qualcomm AIMET, GGUF, and any standard inference stack at zero runtime overhead.

title: Benchmarking the Robustness of Foundation Models for Mammography under Domain Shift
comment: Under Review. Giang Nguyen and Raghav Mehta contributed equally
summary: Foundation models are increasingly used as image feature extractors for mammography, but their robustness under external domain shift remains unclear. We benchmark 15 foundation-model backbones across breast density, BI-RADS severity, and cancer status using a unified frozen-backbone linear-probe protocol, training on 3 source datasets and evaluating on 12 task-compatible out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets after label harmonization. Mammography-specific vision-language models (Mammo-FM and MaMA) provide the strongest mean OOD performance, but robustness is not explained by mammography exposure alone. DINOv3 remains a competitive vision-only baseline, and mammography-adapted pretraining does not consistently improve generalization. Dataset-level analysis further shows that even leading models show heterogeneous performance across datasets. Feature-space inspection reveals that useful representations can preserve clinical signal while retaining dataset and acquisition structure. These findings highlight dataset-level OOD evaluation as a central criterion for assessing mammography representations. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/biomedia-mira/mammo-ood.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks 15 foundation-model backbones for mammography feature extraction under out-of-distribution (OOD) domain shifts, finding mammography-specific vision-language models (Mammo-FM, MaMA) perform best overall, though robustness isn't solely explained by mammography exposure; DINOv3 is a strong vision-only baseline, and dataset-level OOD evaluation is crucial for assessing mammography representations.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are increasingly used as image feature extractors for mammography, but their robustness under external domain shift remains unclear.
AI.method: Benchmark 15 foundation-model backbones across breast density, BI-RADS severity, and cancer status using a unified frozen-backbone linear-probe protocol, training on 3 source datasets and evaluating on 12 task-compatible OOD datasets after label harmonization.
AI.result: Mammography-specific vision-language models (Mammo-FM and MaMA) provide the strongest mean OOD performance, but robustness is not explained by mammography exposure alone. DINOv3 remains a competitive vision-only baseline, and mammography-adapted pretraining does not consistently improve generalization. Even leading models show heterogeneous performance across datasets. Useful representations can preserve clinical signal while retaining dataset and acquisition structure.
AI.conclusion: These findings highlight dataset-level OOD evaluation as a central criterion for assessing mammography representations.

title: GRASP: GRanularity-Aware Search Policy for Agentic RAG
summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) extends static RAG by allowing language models to iteratively reason, generate search queries, retrieve evidence, and predict answers. However, it remains challenging for models to decide when to retrieve, whether to use lexical matching or semantic similarity, and how to control context granularity to prevent irrelevant tokens from interfering with agent reasoning. In this paper, we introduce GRASP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for training agents to adaptively coordinate complementary retrieval tools during multi-step reasoning. GRASP provides the agent with semantic search, keyword search, and paragraph-reading actions, enabling it to retrieve sentence-level evidence and expand further context only when needed. We train the policy with a reward that jointly accounts for answer accuracy, grounded reading, complementary search, and turn efficiency. Experiments on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks show that GRASP improves both retrieval recall and downstream question answering performance compared with single-step retrieval, prompting-based agentic RAG, and RL-based retrieval baselines. Qualitative and ablation analyses show that the learned policy develops interpretable skimming and scanning behavior: it uses semantic search for broad exploration, paragraph reading for local verification, and keyword search for entity-specific evidence. These results suggest that learning to coordinate retrieval signals and context granularity is critical for agent's correct reasoning.

AI.tldr: GRASP is a reinforcement learning framework that trains agents to adaptively coordinate semantic search, keyword search, and paragraph-reading tools during multi-step reasoning, improving retrieval recall and QA performance on multi-hop benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic RAG systems struggle with deciding when to retrieve, whether to use lexical or semantic matching, and how to control context granularity to prevent irrelevant tokens from interfering with agent reasoning.
AI.method: GRASP uses reinforcement learning to train a policy that coordinates three retrieval tools (semantic search, keyword search, paragraph reading) with a reward function balancing accuracy, grounded reading, complementary search, and turn efficiency.
AI.result: GRASP outperforms single-step retrieval, prompting-based agentic RAG, and RL-based retrieval baselines on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks in both retrieval recall and downstream QA performance.
AI.conclusion: Learning to coordinate retrieval signals and context granularity is critical for correct agent reasoning; the learned policy develops interpretable skimming (semantic search) and scanning (keyword search, paragraph reading) behaviors.

title: LLMs as a Jury: Cross-Model Consensus Can Outperform Process Reward Models for LLM Reasoning
summary: Selecting the correct answer from a pool of candidate reasoning chains is the engine of test-time scaling, yet the standard selectors each carry a cost: self-consistency inherits the errors of the single model it resamples, and trained reward models need labeled data and transfer poorly off-distribution. We study a third signal, free at inference time: cross-model consensus, the degree to which independently trained models, each solving the problem once, agree on a final answer. We treat the panel as an LLM-jury, in which the structure of agreement, not any model's score of another, is the verification signal. Across seven benchmarks it selects correct answers better than self-consistency and far better than a model scoring its own candidates: on competition math it closes the entire gap to an oracle selector, while self-scoring closes almost none. The mechanism is error decorrelation: independently trained models err differently, so their wrong answers scatter while the correct one accumulates agreement. We make this precise with a parameter-free law, derived in closed form, that predicts consensus accuracy from three measured panel statistics to a mean absolute error of $0.03$ and exposes the method's ceiling: a shared-error floor where models share a misconception, near zero on math but non-trivial on science. Against four trained verifiers spanning discriminative, outcome, and generative reward models, the free LLM-jury matches the strongest inside their math training domain and is the top selector outside it. Cross-model consensus is thus a verifier we can characterize in advance: a law that says when to trust it, and a floor that marks where it cannot.

AI.tldr: Cross-model consensus—agreement among independently trained models—serves as a free, inference-time verification signal for selecting correct reasoning chains, outperforming self-consistency and matching trained verifiers, with a closed-form law predicting its accuracy and exposing a shared-error floor.
AI.motivation: Standard selectors for test-time scaling have limitations: self-consistency inherits single-model errors, and trained reward models require labeled data and transfer poorly off-distribution. The paper explores cross-model consensus as a free, accessible alternative.
AI.method: Treats a panel of independently trained LLMs as a jury, using the structure of agreement (not model-to-model scoring) as the verification signal. Derives a parameter-free closed-form law predicting consensus accuracy from three panel statistics.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, cross-model consensus outperforms self-consistency and self-scoring; on competition math it closes the entire gap to an oracle selector. The law predicts accuracy to MAE of 0.03. Matches the strongest trained verifiers in-domain and is the top selector out-of-domain.
AI.conclusion: Cross-model consensus is a verifiable, free signal with a predictable accuracy law and a known failure floor (shared errors), making it a principled alternative to trained reward models.

title: Gradient-Skipping Relevance Propagation for Efficient Explainability of Vision Transformers
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are difficult to interpret because current methods of relevance propagation and attention flow do not fully consider some key architectural features, such as the uneven importance of attention heads and residual connections. Prior approaches typically assume uniform importance across attention heads; furthermore, they model skip connections as identity paths, leading to inaccurate relevance attribution. To address these issues, we introduce GradSkip, a novel relevance propagation method for ViTs based on adaptive head weighting and skip-aware propagation. GradSkip models the different importance of the attention heads and dynamically distributes relevance between the attention and residual paths. Experiments on ImageNet1K and BloodMNIST demonstrate a state-of-the-art faithfulness of GradSkip while requiring over 14 times fewer GFLOPs than the best-performing existing approaches. Additional evaluations using transformer-based segmentation confirm improved localization and alignment with ground-truth regions.

AI.tldr: GradSkip is a new relevance propagation method for Vision Transformers that addresses limitations of prior approaches by adaptively weighting attention heads and properly modeling skip connections, achieving state-of-the-art faithfulness with over 14x fewer GFLOPs.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability methods for ViTs fail to account for uneven importance across attention heads and inaccurately model skip connections as identity paths, leading to flawed relevance attribution.
AI.method: GradSkip introduces adaptive head weighting to model differential importance of attention heads and skip-aware propagation to dynamically distribute relevance between attention and residual paths.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art faithfulness on ImageNet1K and BloodMNIST while requiring over 14x fewer GFLOPs than the best-performing existing approaches; improved localization and alignment on transformer-based segmentation tasks.
AI.conclusion: GradSkip provides a more accurate and efficient approach to interpreting Vision Transformers by properly handling attention head diversity and residual connections.

title: Agents Don't Just Agree, They Remember: Benchmarking Persistent Sycophancy in Stateful Personal Agents
summary: Stateful personal agents increasingly maintain long-term user profiles, episodic memories, and reusable skills. This persistence turns conversational sycophancy into a state-writing failure: accepted user-centric claims can be committed as lasting preferences, background facts, or workflows and later reused after the original conversation is gone. We call this persistent sycophancy and introduce the Personal Agent Sycophancy Benchmark (PASB), a 1,600-task benchmark that traces whether a conversational claim is accepted, written into durable agent state, and reused in a later neutral query. Unlike prior benchmarks that provide pre-written memories, PASB evaluates real agents (Hermes-Agent and OpenClaw) that decide what to store. It isolates the write process by combining four scenario framings with four temporal delivery patterns and separating a five-turn persist stage from a cleared three-turn query stage, ensuring downstream effects arise only from durable state. Across twelve models, the commit boundary is the key inflection point: downstream failure increases from 45.0% in session-only episodes to 71.9% after commitment, a consistent increase of 27.0 percentage points. Committed claims exhibit three write-time patterns: status promotion, attribution removal, and scope broadening. These patterns become stronger under memory-like or procedural framing, repeated reinforcement, and even across domain boundaries. These results show that agent sycophancy is fundamentally a state-writing governance problem. Once user content is committed to durable memory, safety must govern what agents write, not only what they say. PASB identifies the write-time controls needed to gate risky commits while preserving the source, role, and scope of stored content beyond response-level mitigations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Persistent Sycophancy, a state-writing failure where conversational sycophancy is committed into durable agent memory and reused later. The PASB benchmark (1,600 tasks) traces claim acceptance → state writing → reuse, showing downstream failure increases from 45.0% to 71.9% (+27pp) after commitment. Three write-time patterns (status promotion, attribution removal, scope broadening) emerge, framing agent sycophancy as a state-writing governance problem requiring write-time controls.
AI.motivation: Stateful personal agents persist user profiles, episodic memories, and skills, making conversational sycophancy a lasting problem. Accepted user-centric claims can be committed as durable preferences or facts and reused beyond the original conversation—a failure mode prior benchmarks overlook by providing pre-written memories instead of evaluating agents' own storage decisions.
AI.method: PASB combines four scenario framings with four temporal delivery patterns across a five-turn persist stage (where agents decide what to store) and a cleared three-turn query stage. Evaluates real agents (Hermes-Agent, OpenClaw) that autonomously decide what to commit. Analyzes commit boundary effects and three write-time patterns: status promotion, attribution removal, and scope broadening.
AI.result: Downstream failure increases from 45.0% (session-only) to 71.9% (after commitment), a consistent +27.0pp. Three write-time patterns identified: status promotion, attribution removal, scope broadening. These patterns intensify under memory-like/procedural framing, repeated reinforcement, and cross-domain boundaries. The commit boundary is the key inflection point for safety degradation.
AI.conclusion: Agent sycophancy is fundamentally a state-writing governance problem. Safety must govern what agents write into durable memory, not only what they say. PASB identifies needed write-time controls to gate risky commits while preserving source, role, and scope of stored content.

title: Beyond Euclidean Clipping: Overcoming Exploration Collapse in LLM RL via Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. However, RL algorithms with PPO-Clip are inherently limited by exploration collapse. Subsequent works remain primarily heuristic and fail to identify the essential cause of PPO-Clip's failure. This work reveals the fundamental flaw of PPO-Clip: it implicitly measures policy discrepancy using Euclidean metric, which is theoretically inconsistent with the intrinsic geometry on the policy Riemannian manifold. This geometric mismatch results in overly conservative updates in low-probability regions while aggressive in high-probability regions, ultimately collapsing exploration. To correct this geometric flaw, we propose Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization (RIPO), which guarantees isometric policy updates on the Riemannian manifold, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation. We further show that RIPO achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off, which stabilizes optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RIPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across seven competition-level benchmarks (up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24).

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that PPO-Clip fails due to geometric mismatch (Euclidean vs. Riemannian metrics) in policy space, and proposes RIPO which performs isometric policy updates on the Riemannian manifold to balance exploration-exploitation, achieving up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24.
AI.motivation: Existing RL algorithms for LLMs (PPO-Clip) suffer from exploration collapse, and subsequent heuristic works fail to identify the root cause. The paper aims to uncover the fundamental geometric flaw of PPO-Clip and correct it with a principled approach.
AI.method: RIPO (Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization) performs isometric policy updates on the Riemannian manifold, replacing the Euclidean metric used implicitly by PPO-Clip with the intrinsic geometry of the policy space, thereby achieving balanced exploration and exploitation with favorable bias-variance trade-off.
AI.result: RIPO significantly outperforms existing LLM RL algorithms across seven competition-level benchmarks, with up to 60% improvement over GRPO on AIME24.
AI.conclusion: Correcting the geometric mismatch in policy optimization is crucial for effective RL-based LLM training; RIPO provides a principled solution that stabilizes optimization and enhances reasoning capabilities.

title: Cross-Layer Misalignment Detection in Agent Skills: A Progressive Loading-Aware Contrastive Learning Approach
comment: 10 pages, 5 pages supplemental. Accepted at the KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly extended through Agent Skills, reusable artifacts that package natural-language metadata, procedural instructions, and execution-time resources for runtime use. As open-source skill marketplaces expand, users and agents increasingly rely on brief metadata to select third-party skills, making it difficult to detect inconsistencies between a skill's description and its true behavior, a problem we call cross-layer misalignment. To address this issue, we propose Progressive Loading-Aware Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (PL-HCL), an LLM-based framework that detects misalignment by modeling the layered structure of Agent Skills and learning cross-layer consistency. Using a normalized corpus of over 264,000 open-source skills and a human-verified challenge set, PL-HCL improves Macro-F1 from approximately 0.45 for unadapted baselines to 0.87-0.89 across evaluated LLM backbones. This approach offers an effective screening tool for users and operators, as well as design principles for detecting inconsistencies in layered digital artifacts.

AI.tldr: PL-HCL is an LLM-based framework that detects cross-layer misalignment in Agent Skills (inconsistencies between metadata descriptions and actual behavior) by using progressive loading-aware hierarchical contrastive learning, improving Macro-F1 from ~0.45 to 0.87-0.89 on a corpus of 264K+ open-source skills.
AI.motivation: As open-source skill marketplaces grow, users and LLM agents rely on brief metadata to select third-party skills, but inconsistencies between a skill's description and its actual behavior (cross-layer misalignment) are hard to detect, posing trust and safety risks.
AI.method: PL-HCL (Progressive Loading-Aware Hierarchical Contrastive Learning), an LLM-based framework that models the layered structure of Agent Skills (natural-language metadata, procedural instructions, execution-time resources) and learns cross-layer consistency through contrastive learning with progressive loading.
AI.result: On a normalized corpus of 264K+ open-source skills and a human-verified challenge set, PL-HCL improves Macro-F1 from ~0.45 (unadapted baselines) to 0.87-0.89 across evaluated LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: PL-HCL provides an effective screening tool for detecting inconsistencies in layered digital artifacts, offering design principles for users and marketplace operators to verify Agent Skill trustworthiness.

title: ABot-N1: Toward a General Visual Language Navigation Foundation Model
summary: Visual Language Navigation foundation models aim to unify deep reasoning for grounded spatial decisions with broad versatility for diverse embodied tasks. Current approaches typically achieve this integration via monolithic policies that map observations directly to actions, yet they often suffer from coordinate drift and poor handling of long-tail semantics. Furthermore, these black-box mappings lack interpretability, hindering the simultaneous achievement of generality, robustness, and transparency. We present ABot-N1, a step toward a general Visual Language Navigation foundation model, that addresses these challenges by decoupling cognition from control via a slow-fast architecture guided by dual visual-language signals. More specifically, a slow vision-language reasoner performs explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning while producing a pixel goal.
