A single policy is post-trained via RL across diverse PDE families (hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic, incompressible-flow).
AI.result: RLVP improves over both pre-trained and supervised-only baselines on PDE benchmarks, shows zero-shot improvement transfer to held-out PDEs, and a smaller LLM post-trained with RLVP can outperform prompting a frontier model on in-distribution PDE solver generation.
AI.conclusion: The trained policy exhibits compositionality in numerical motifs, recombining stencils, time-stepping schemes, and boundary-handling primitives learned from training PDEs into solvers for unseen PDE problems.

title: Why Domain Matters: Domain-Aware Benchmarking of Underwater Object Detection and Annotation Quality
summary: Underwater object detection is strongly affected by domain shift, where performance can vary significantly across different locations, habitats, and deployment conditions. However, detector performance is typically evaluated using aggregate metrics that hide failures in specific environments, while existing domain generalization benchmarks often rely on synthetic variations that do not reflect real-world conditions. We introduce a framework that characterizes underwater images by appearance, scene composition, and acquisition geometry to assign domain labels. Using this framework, we perform the first systematic study of how domain factors influence both human annotation quality in underwater object detection datasets and deep learning-based detector performance, revealing substantial domain-dependent discrepancies. By incorporating physically meaningful domain labels, domain shift becomes something we can characterize, measure, benchmark, and act on. We highlight how this can be used to guide data collection and annotation, design more informative benchmarks, and assess detector robustness across diverse underwater environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for characterizing underwater image domains by appearance, scene composition, and acquisition geometry, and systematically studies how domain factors affect both human annotation quality and deep learning-based detector performance, revealing substantial domain-dependent discrepancies.
AI.motivation: Underwater object detection suffers from domain shift that degrades performance across different environments, yet current evaluation relies on aggregate metrics that obscure failures in specific conditions, and existing domain generalization benchmarks use synthetic variations that poorly reflect real-world underwater scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that assigns domain labels to underwater images based on three factors: appearance, scene composition, and acquisition geometry. They use this framework to systematically study how domain factors impact both human annotation quality and deep learning-based detector performance.
AI.result: The study reveals substantial domain-dependent discrepancies in both human annotation quality and detector performance across different underwater environments.
AI.conclusion: By incorporating physically meaningful domain labels, domain shift becomes characterizable, measurable, and actionable, enabling better data collection and annotation strategies, more informative benchmarks, and improved assessment of detector robustness across diverse underwater environments.

title: LOGOS: A Living Logic for AI Agent Teams That Evolve With Humans
summary: AI agents are evolving from answer engines into persistent teams that use tools, delegate work, learn from experience, and modify the artifacts that shape their future behavior. The defining question for deployment is no longer merely what agents can do, but who controls what they are allowed to become. We introduce logos, a pluggable layer for self-evolution and governance that strengthens existing multiagent frameworks rather than replacing them. logos compiles heterogeneous multimodal inputs, including documents, images, audio, tables, databases, APIs, and human instructions into versioned agent packs containing agents, tools, knowledge, tests, permissions, and policies. During operation, it transforms agent activity into portable, auditable event traces and applies fail-closed verification across frameworks and backends. Every learned prompt, memory, skill, tool, role, or workflow remains an untrusted release candidate until held-out execution evidence, human-controlled policy, and explicit authorization permit its promotion. This architecture enables "verifiable human-agent loop engineering": agents can act, ask, learn, and propose improvements, while humans can steer objectives, permissions, approvals, and irreversible actions without interrupting continuous operation. logos provides a living logic for accountable automation. Agents may evolve at machine speed, but only evidence and human authority can close the loop.

AI.tldr: Logos introduces a pluggable governance layer for multiagent frameworks that compiles multimodal inputs into versioned agent packs, transforms activity into auditable traces, and enforces fail-closed verification, treating all learned artifacts as untrusted release candidates until validated by evidence and human authorization.
AI.motivation: The key question for deploying AI agents has shifted from capability ("what can agents do?") to control ("who controls what agents are allowed to become"), requiring a systematic approach to agent self-evolution and governance.
AI.method: Logos compiles heterogeneous multimodal inputs into versioned agent packs with agents, tools, knowledge, tests, permissions, and policies; transforms agent activity into portable auditable event traces; applies fail-closed verification across frameworks; and enforces that all learned artifacts (prompts, memories, skills, tools, roles, workflows) remain untrusted release candidates until validated by execution evidence, human-controlled policy, and explicit authorization.
AI.result: An architecture for "verifiable human-agent loop engineering" where agents act, ask, learn, and propose improvements while humans steer objectives, permissions, approvals, and irreversible actions without interrupting continuous operation.
AI.conclusion: Logos provides a living logic for accountable automation where agents evolve at machine speed, but only evidence and human authority can close the loop.

title: ARMOR: Stabilizing On-Policy LLM RL with Off-Policy Anchor Samples
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet the training process remains notoriously fragile. In this work, we investigate a critical source of this instability: over-optimization, where models exploit training heuristics at the expense of generalizable reasoning. While reverse KL regularization is the standard defense against such degradation, our analysis reveals that it is often insufficient in this regime, as it fails to ensure comprehensive coverage of the reference distribution. To address this, we propose ARMOR (Anchor Rollout and Mixed Optimization for RL), a framework that shifts the paradigm from passive penalty to active sample stabilization. ARMOR comprises two key components: (1) Anchor Rollout, which leverages off-policy data from the reference policy to preserve established solution patterns; and (2) Mixed Optimization, which reformulates the policy objective to enable controlled exploration without relying on auxiliary losses. Extensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks validate that ARMOR effectively mitigates validation collapse, enabling sustained performance improvements over extended training horizons.

AI.tldr: ARMOR introduces Anchor Rollout and Mixed Optimization to stabilize RL training for LLMs by preventing over-optimization and validation collapse, outperforming standard reverse KL regularization.
AI.motivation: RL-based training of LLMs suffers from instability due to over-optimization, where models exploit training heuristics and lose generalizable reasoning. Reverse KL regularization, though standard, fails to provide sufficient coverage of the reference distribution.
AI.method: ARMOR consists of two components: (1) Anchor Rollout — using off-policy data from the reference policy to preserve established solution patterns; (2) Mixed Optimization — reformulating the policy objective for controlled exploration without auxiliary losses, shifting from passive penalty to active sample stabilization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks show ARMOR effectively mitigates validation collapse and enables sustained performance improvements over extended training horizons.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from passive reverse KL regularization to active sample stabilization via ARMOR provides a more robust training paradigm for RL-based LLM reasoning improvement.

title: DiffUE: Enhancing Utility-Unlearnability Trade-off of Unlearnable Examples via Diffusion Autoencoders
comment: To appear at the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2026
summary: AI models are increasingly trained on personal images scraped from social media and public platforms, often without consent, leading to serious privacy violations, such as unauthorized facial recognition and targeted advertising. To counter this, researchers have developed unlearnable examples (UEs), images modified with imperceptible noise to prevent AI models from extracting meaningful information. However, existing UE methods primarily rely on pixel-space noise, which can be bypassed by relearning strategies such as adversarial training, image transformation, and compression. While some techniques improve robustness, they often come at the expense of significant degradation in image utility and perceptual quality. In this paper, we introduce DiffUE to overcome these limitations by injecting noise into the semantic space of images instead of the pixel space. Instead of corrupting pixel values, DiffUE modifies high-level semantic features of images, ensuring robust unlearnability while preserving visual quality and utility. By leveraging a diffusion-based autoencoder framework to manipulate semantic features, DiffUE generates purposeful, natural-looking modifications that effectively resist advanced relearning strategies. Extensive experiments on four datasets, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CelebA-HQ, and ImageNet, as well as a subjective user study, demonstrate that DiffUE significantly enhances the trade-off between image quality and unlearnability, offering a more robust and effective solution for safeguarding personal data in an increasingly exploitative AI landscape.

AI.tldr: DiffUE introduces a diffusion-based autoencoder that injects noise into the semantic feature space of images (rather than pixel space) to create unlearnable examples that resist advanced relearning strategies while preserving visual quality.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearnable examples (UEs) add pixel-space noise that can be bypassed by relearning strategies (adversarial training, image transformation, compression), and robust pixel-based methods degrade image utility and perceptual quality.
AI.method: DiffUE uses a diffusion-based autoencoder to modify high-level semantic features of images instead of corrupting pixel values, generating natural-looking, purposeful modifications that resist advanced relearning strategies.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CelebA-HQ, and ImageNet, plus a subjective user study, show DiffUE significantly improves the trade-off between image quality and unlearnability.
AI.conclusion: DiffUE offers a more robust and effective solution for safeguarding personal data by producing unlearnable examples with preserved visual quality that resist sophisticated adversarial relearning attacks.

title: First-Order Modal Logic in HOL: Deep and Shallow Embeddings with Automated Faithfulness (Extended Preprint)
comment: 21 pages. Extended version, with a source-code appendix, of a paper accepted at ARQNL 2026 (International Workshop on Automated Reasoning in Quantified Non-Classical Logics). The full Isabelle/HOL development is included as ancillary files
summary:
We extend, in Isabelle/HOL, the deep-and-shallow embedding methodology of our prior work from propositional to first-order modal logic (FML) with constant-domain Kripke semantics. Three embeddings of FML into classical higher-order logic (HOL) are provided side by side: a deep embedding, a heavyweight maximal-shallow embedding, and a lightweight minimal-shallow embedding. The minimal-shallow embedding is presented as an Isabelle/HOL locale, parametrised by an accessibility relation, a world-indexed interpretation, a universe of worlds, and a variable assignment; the locale form admits a global faithfulness theorem, stating that quantifying over all minimal-shallow interpretations recovers exactly deep validity.
  A central technical contribution is a mechanisation, for FML under constant-domain Kripke semantics, of the (countable) downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem, which underpins the automation of our faithfulness proof between the deep and minimal-shallow embeddings. Deploying it inside an extension of the minimal-shallow locale resolves the surjectivity problem that arises against an uncountable domain of individuals -- where the locale's variable assignment, having countable domain V = nat, cannot be surjective onto the domain -- and thereby yields faithfulness over the full domain.
  Since prior work treats only the propositional fragment, we develop here the substitution machinery (free/bound-variable predicates, the fresh-variable function, capture-avoiding substitution, alphabetic renaming, the substitutability predicate, the substitution lemma, and size-based induction principles) needed for the first-order quantifiers.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a deep-and-shallow embedding methodology from propositional to first-order modal logic (FML) in Isabelle/HOL, providing three embeddings (deep, heavyweight maximal-shallow, lightweight minimal-shallow) and mechanizing the downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem to prove faithfulness between them, along with first-order substitution machinery.
AI.motivation: To extend prior work on deep-and-shallow embedding methodology from propositional to first-order modal logic, enabling faithful theorem proving for FML with constant-domain Kripke semantics in Isabelle/HOL.
AI.method: Three embeddings of FML into classical HOL are provided: deep embedding, heavyweight maximal-shallow embedding, and lightweight minimal-shallow embedding (as a parametrised Isabelle/HOL locale). The countable downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem is mechanized for FML under constant-domain semantics to resolve surjectivity issues in faithfulness proofs. First-order substitution machinery (free/bound variables, substitution, renaming, etc.) is developed.
AI.result: The minimal-shallow embedding locale admits a global faithfulness theorem where quantifying over all minimal-shallow interpretations recovers deep validity. The Löwenheim-Skolem theorem resolves the surjectivity problem against uncountable domains, yielding faithfulness over the full domain.
AI.conclusion: The methodology successfully extends to first-order modal logic with constant-domain semantics, providing mechanized faithfulness proofs and necessary first-order logical infrastructure.

title: EvidentialRAG: Quantifying and Mitigating Information Conflict in Multi-Source Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Evidential Deep Learning
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds large language models in external evidence, but most pipelines still treat retrieved passages as deterministic and mutually consistent context. In open information environments, retrieved sources may disagree because of temporal drift, source error, ambiguity, or genuine uncertainty. This paper introduces ERAG, an uncertainty-aware RAG framework that converts retrieved chunks into probabilistic evidence before generation. A lightweight evaluator extracts candidate claims and maps chunk-level support to Dirichlet evidence. A conflict-preserving Dempster-Shafer fusion rule then transfers unresolved disagreement into epistemic uncertainty rather than normalizing it away. The generator is routed to direct answering, conflict-aware answering, or abstention according to the fused uncertainty score. Experiments on CRAG, ConflictQA, and MuSiQue show that ERAG remains competitive with the strongest matched baseline on standard question answering while improving behavior under conflict. On the CRAG ambiguous subset, hallucination decreases from 45.3% for Corrective RAG to a human-calibrated estimate of 34.8%, conflict resolution increases from 35.2% to 51.2%, and expected calibration error improves to 0.122. These results suggest that evidential modeling is a practical mechanism for trustworthy information processing in foundation-model-based retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: ERAG is an uncertainty-aware RAG framework that models retrieved passages as probabilistic evidence using Dirichlet distributions and Dempster-Shafer fusion, enabling the system to detect and handle conflicting information by routing to direct answering, conflict-aware answering, or abstention, reducing hallucination on ambiguous queries from 45.3% to 34.8%.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG pipelines treat retrieved passages as deterministic and mutually consistent, ignoring that sources may disagree due to temporal drift, source error, ambiguity, or genuine uncertainty, leading to hallucination when conflicts are present.
AI.method: ERAG uses a lightweight evaluator to extract candidate claims and map chunk-level support to Dirichlet evidence, then applies a conflict-preserving Dempster-Shafer fusion rule that transfers unresolved disagreement into epistemic uncertainty rather than normalizing it away; the generator is routed to direct answering, conflict-aware answering, or abstention based on the fused uncertainty score.
AI.result: On CRAG, ConflictQA, and MuSiQue, ERAG matches the strongest baseline on standard QA while improving conflict handling. On CRAG ambiguous subset: hallucination reduced from 45.3% (Corrective RAG) to 34.8%, conflict resolution increased from 35.2% to 51.2%, and expected calibration error improved to 0.122.
AI.conclusion: Evidential modeling is a practical mechanism for trustworthy information processing in foundation-model-based retrieval systems, enabling uncertainty-aware behavior under conflicting evidence.

title: Benchmarking UAV-based Vehicle Re-Identification under Simulated Weather Conditions
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Multimedia Analysis and Pattern Recognition (MAPR 2026)
summary: UAV-based vehicle re-identification (ReID) has emerged as a promising technique for traffic surveillance, urban monitoring, and public-safety applications thanks to the flexible viewpoints and wide-area coverage provided by unmanned aerial vehicles. However, despite recent progress on UAV-based vehicle ReID benchmarks, the robustness of existing methods under adverse weather remains insufficiently studied. This is important because weather degradation can significantly affect the fine-grained appearance cues required for reliable vehicle matching in aerial imagery, especially under small object scale, viewpoint variation, and complex backgrounds. In this paper, we present a controlled comparative study of three representative recent vehicle ReID methods, namely CLIP-ReID, MSINet, and AdaSP, on two UAV-based benchmarks, VRU and UAV-VeID. To ensure consistent robustness evaluation, we generate synthetic foggy and rainy variants of both datasets using an analytical weather-effect pipeline while preserving the original identities and data splits. All methods are then trained and evaluated under matched clean, foggy, and rainy conditions. Experimental results show that adverse weather consistently degrades retrieval performance across both datasets, with rain causing larger drops than fog in nearly all settings. Among the evaluated methods, AdaSP demonstrates the strongest robustness, achieving 93.0% and 88.5% mAP on VRU-Large, and 88.7% and 76.2% mAP on UAV-VeID-Test under foggy and rainy conditions, respectively. Overall, our findings show that simulated adverse weather substantially increases the difficulty of UAV-based vehicle ReID, reveals clear robustness differences among recent methods, and highlights the need for weather-aware model design and evaluation protocols in future aerial ReID research. The code is released at https://github.com/tranminhvu945/Benchmarking-ReID.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a controlled comparative study of three UAV-based vehicle ReID methods (CLIP-ReID, MSINet, AdaSP) under synthetic foggy and rainy conditions on VRU and UAV-VeID benchmarks, finding that weather degrades performance (rain > fog), AdaSP is most robust, and advocating for weather-aware model design.
AI.motivation: While UAV-based vehicle ReID has advanced, the robustness of existing methods under adverse weather conditions remains insufficiently studied, despite weather degradation significantly affecting fine-grained appearance cues critical for reliable vehicle matching in aerial imagery.
AI.method: Three representative ReID methods (CLIP-ReID, MSINet, AdaSP) are evaluated on two UAV benchmarks (VRU, UAV-VeID). Synthetic foggy and rainy variants are generated via an analytical weather-effect pipeline while preserving identities and data splits. All methods are trained and tested under matched clean, foggy, and rainy conditions.
AI.result: Adverse weather consistently degrades retrieval performance; rain causes larger drops than fog. AdaSP shows strongest robustness: 93.0%/88.5% mAP on VRU-Large and 88.7%/76.2% mAP on UAV-VeID-Test under foggy/rainy conditions respectively.
AI.conclusion: Simulated adverse weather substantially increases the difficulty of UAV-based vehicle ReID, reveals clear robustness differences among recent methods, and highlights the need for weather-aware model design and evaluation protocols in future aerial ReID research.

title: SETA: Scaling Environments for Terminal Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly shifting toward agents that solve tasks through diverse interfaces, including web and graphical user interfaces (GUIs). Among these, the terminal command line provides a text-based, general-purpose interface, covering tasks from system operations to data science and machine learning. However, scaling terminal-agent training remains challenging, as it requires diverse and coherent task instructions, executable environments, and reliable verification, while lacking naturally grounded supervision data. In this work, we propose SETA, a scalable framework for generating verifiable terminal environments for reinforcement learning (RL). The framework consists of two pipelines sharing a unified verification mechanism: SETA-Synth converts diverse sources into standardized RL environments, and SETA-Evol further expands from existing environments with adaptive control of difficulty and diversity. Together, we construct and release SETA-Env, the largest open-source verifiable terminal RL dataset to date, containing over 4,500 environments. We evaluate our dataset by training Qwen3-8B with GRPO on SETA-Env, achieving 12% pass rate on Terminal-Bench 2.0, the best reported result for an RL-trained model at the 8B scale. We further observe gains on DeepSeek-V4-Flash under the same terminal agent harness, with pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 improving from 40% to 43% and pass@5 improving from 54% to 58%. These results demonstrate that SETA- Env provides high-quality training environments for terminal agents and serves as a valuable resource for advancing research on terminal-based agent learning.

AI.tldr: SETA is a scalable framework for generating verifiable terminal command-line environments for reinforcement learning, producing SETA-Env (4,500+ environments), the largest open-source terminal RL dataset. Training Qwen3-8B with GRPO on it achieves 12% pass rate on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (best reported for 8B RL models), and also improves DeepSeek-V4-Flash's pass@1 from 40% to 43%.
AI.motivation: Scaling terminal-agent training is challenging due to the need for diverse, coherent task instructions, executable environments, reliable verification, and the lack of naturally grounded supervision data.
AI.method: Proposes SETA, a scalable framework with two pipelines (SETA-Synth for converting diverse sources into standardized RL environments, SETA-Evol for expanding from existing environments with adaptive difficulty/diversity control) unified by a shared verification mechanism, producing SETA-Env, a dataset of over 4,500 verifiable terminal RL environments.
AI.result: Training Qwen3-8B with GRPO on SETA-Env achieves 12% pass rate on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (best reported for 8B RL-trained models). DeepSeek-V4-Flash improves from 40% to 43% pass@1 and 54% to 58% pass@5 under the same terminal agent harness.
AI.conclusion: SETA-Env provides high-quality training environments for terminal agents and serves as a valuable resource for advancing research on terminal-based agent learning.

title: Learning from Noise: Effective-Rank Collapse and Out-of-Distribution Rejection in Restricted Boltzmann Machines
summary: Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) represent data by shaping an energy landscape over visible and hidden configurations, but their discriminative use is fragile under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs: samples outside the training distribution can be absorbed into one of the learned class basins rather than rejected. Here, we analyze this failure mode through the spectrum of the induced visible--visible interaction $J=WW^{T}$, where \(W\) is the visible--hidden weight matrix. Relative to a Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix reference, conventional training spreads spectral weight into many weak, bulk-compatible directions, increasing the effective rank of $J$. When auxiliary random binary images are assigned to a rejection label during training, the learned interaction undergoes effective-rank collapse: weak bulk-like modes are depleted, spectral weight concentrates into fewer dominant eigendirections, and the effective rank of $J$ approaches that of the empirical data covariance matrix. The resulting RBM rejects structured OOD image datasets while preserving MNIST classification accuracy, showing that random auxiliary exposure can reshape both the interaction spectrum and the free-energy landscape of an energy-based classifier.

AI.tldr: RBMs fail under OOD inputs because their visible-visible interaction matrix J=WW^T spreads spectral weight into many weak directions; training with random auxiliary images as rejection labels causes effective-rank collapse of J, concentrating spectral weight into dominant eigendirections, which enables OOD rejection while preserving classification accuracy.
AI.motivation: RBMs are fragile under out-of-distribution inputs because samples outside the training distribution can be absorbed into learned class basins rather than rejected; the paper aims to understand and fix this failure mode.
AI.method: Analyze the failure mode via the spectrum of the visible-visible interaction matrix J=WW^T relative to a Marchenko-Pastur random-matrix reference; propose training with auxiliary random binary images assigned to a rejection label to reshape the interaction spectrum.
AI.result: Conventional training spreads spectral weight into many weak bulk-compatible directions, increasing effective rank. Random auxiliary exposure causes effective-rank collapse: weak modes are depleted, spectral weight concentrates into fewer dominant eigendirections, and effective rank approaches that of the empirical data covariance matrix.
AI.conclusion: Random auxiliary exposure reshapes both the interaction spectrum and free-energy landscape of an energy-based classifier, enabling OOD rejection while preserving in-distribution (MNIST) accuracy.

title: Anomalous Frame Detection by Grouping Frame Similarities between Two Videos Computed by Vision-Language Model to Extract Expert Workers' Unique Actions
summary: Maintenance of critical infrastructures, such as railways and power plants, is essential for operational safety and reliability. However, the declining number of skilled maintenance workers poses a serious challenge to sustaining these operations, highlighting the need to effectively transfer expert know-how to less experienced workers. Although traditional interview-based approaches have been used to elicit maintenance skills, they struggle to capture know-how that experts themselves may not consciously recognize. To address this gap, we proposed a method that detects anomalous frames of candidate actions including know-how by comparing a video of manual-based work with that of expert maintenance workers. In a simulated maintenance experiment involving a distribution board, our method targeted 11 types of actions not described in the manual and achieved a 66.9% extraction rate, marking a 50-percentage-point improvement over conventional techniques. These findings underscore the effectiveness of our approach in revealing hidden maintenance knowledge, thereby contributing to enhanced skill transfer and workforce development in critical infrastructure maintenance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to extract hidden expert maintenance know-how by detecting anomalous actions in worker videos compared to manual-based work, achieving 66.9% extraction rate for undocumented actions—a 50-percentage-point improvement over conventional methods.
AI.motivation: The declining number of skilled maintenance workers in critical infrastructures (railways, power plants) creates a need to transfer expert know-how to less experienced workers. Traditional interview-based methods fail to capture tacit knowledge that experts themselves may not consciously recognize.
AI.method: The method detects anomalous frames of candidate actions (including know-how) by comparing videos of manual-based work with videos of expert maintenance workers performing the same task.
AI.result: In a simulated distribution board maintenance experiment, the method targeted 11 types of undocumented actions and achieved a 66.9% extraction rate, a 50-percentage-point improvement over conventional techniques.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively reveals hidden maintenance knowledge, contributing to enhanced skill transfer and workforce development in critical infrastructure maintenance.

title: Incremental Transformer for Surrogate-Based Inverse Design of Geopolymer Mixtures
summary: Small-data inverse design is challenging in engineering informatics when observations are heterogeneous, mixed-type, and constrained by physical relations among design variables. This work proposes a topology-aware surrogate framework guided by an Incremental Transformer (INCRT) for physics-constrained inverse design, applied to geopolymer mixture design. The method integrates intrinsic-dimensionality analysis, mixed-variable design-space representation, tabular surrogate prediction, INCRT-based manifold rationalisation, and constrained inverse optimisation. Using a public benchmark of fly-ash and slag-based geopolymer concrete mixtures with compressive-strength and carbon-emission targets, the high-dimensional design space proves strongly redundant, organising around fewer effective mixture regimes. Compressive strength requires nonlinear tabular surrogates, while carbon emission is largely determined by composition and well recovered by regularised linear models. INCRT thus acts not as a replacement for tabular predictors but as a rationalisation layer providing prototype regimes and a manifold-support score for inverse design. Three strategies are compared: unconstrained surrogate optimisation, physics-constrained optimisation, and topology-aware physics-constrained optimisation. Unconstrained optimisation can match target strength but may yield physically invalid or off-manifold candidates; physics-only constraints do not always ensure data support. The topology-aware strategy yields candidates balancing target compliance, carbon reduction, physical admissibility, and proximity to the learned feasible manifold. The framework aims not to replace experimental validation but to support screening of credible candidate mixtures from small, mixed, physically constrained engineering datasets.

AI.tldr: Proposes INCRT, a topology-aware surrogate framework with an Incremental Transformer for physics-constrained inverse design from small, heterogeneous, mixed-type engineering data, demonstrated on geopolymer mixture design. The method combines intrinsic-dimensionality analysis, mixed-variable representation, tabular prediction, manifold rationalisation via INCRT, and constrained optimisation. Results show that a topology-aware strategy (using INCRT's prototype regimes and manifold-support scores) outperforms unconstrained and physics-only constrained optimisation in balancing target strength, carbon reduction, physical validity, and data-support proximity.
AI.motivation: Small-data inverse design is challenging when observations are heterogeneous, mixed-type, and constrained by physical relations among design variables. Existing surrogate-based methods often fail to ensure physical admissibility and data-support proximity simultaneously.
AI.method: The framework integrates: (1) intrinsic-dimensionality analysis to identify redundancy in high-dimensional design spaces; (2) mixed-variable design-space representation; (3) tabular surrogate prediction (nonlinear for compressive strength, regularised linear for carbon emission); (4) INCRT-based manifold rationalisation to extract prototype regimes and manifold-support scores; (5) constrained inverse optimisation. Three strategies are compared: unconstrained surrogate optimisation, physics-constrained optimisation, and topology-aware physics-constrained optimisation.
AI.result: The high-dimensional design space is strongly redundant, organising around fewer effective mixture regimes. Compressive strength requires nonlinear surrogates; carbon emission is well captured by regularised linear models. INCRT acts as a rationalisation layer, not a predictor replacement. The topology-aware strategy yields candidates that best balance target compliance, carbon reduction, physical admissibility, and proximity to the learned feasible manifold.
AI.conclusion: The topology-aware framework (INCRT) effectively supports credible candidate screening for inverse design from small, mixed, physically constrained engineering datasets. It is not a replacement for experimental validation but a tool to prioritise promising candidates.

title: Conditional Optimal Bridge for Riemannian Activation Steering
summary: Activation steering offers a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language models at inference time. While many existing methods implicitly optimize a log-density-ratio objective between desired and undesired activation distributions, they do so heuristically rather than deriving it from a principled optimization problem. Moreover, these methods produce query-independent steering directions that can degrade performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. We introduce \textsc{Cobras} (Conditional Optimal Bridge for Riemannian Activation Steering), which addresses both limitations by casting activation steering as a Schrödinger Bridge on the residual-stream hypersphere. This formulation yields, to our knowledge, the first principled derivation of the log-density-ratio steering objective from a well-posed optimization problem. Solving the bridge via entropic optimal transport and extracting the probability flow ODE recovers the widely used density-ratio gradient as a special case when the Sinkhorn potentials are uniform. Crucially, the Schrödinger potentials are evaluated at the current activation, making the resulting steering direction inherently query-adaptive. Empirically, across four models and three alignment axes (helpfulness, truthfulness, and detoxification), \textsc{Cobras} consistently outperforms prior activation steering baselines while avoiding the OOD degradation commonly observed in existing methods. The code can be found at https://github.com/arshandalili/cobras.

AI.tldr: Cobras formulates activation steering as a Schrödinger Bridge on the residual-stream hypersphere, providing a principled derivation of the log-density-ratio steering objective and producing query-adaptive steering directions that avoid OOD degradation, outperforming prior methods across multiple models and alignment axes.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods heuristically optimize a log-density-ratio objective without a principled formulation, and produce query-independent steering directions that degrade performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution inputs.
AI.method: Cobras casts activation steering as a Schrödinger Bridge on the residual-stream hypersphere, solved via entropic optimal transport. Extracting the probability flow ODE recovers the density-ratio gradient as a special case under uniform Sinkhorn potentials. The Schrödinger potentials are evaluated at the current activation, making steering directions query-adaptive.
AI.result: Across four models and three alignment axes (helpfulness, truthfulness, detoxification), Cobras consistently outperforms prior activation steering baselines while avoiding OOD degradation common in existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The Schrödinger Bridge formulation provides the first principled derivation of the log-density-ratio steering objective from a well-posed optimization problem, and query-adaptive steering via entropic optimal transport yields superior performance without OOD degradation.

title: End-to-End Real-Time Drone-Based Person Detection Framework Using Deep Learning
summary: In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones have gained rapid response in terms of security, search and rescue (SAR), border surveillance, etc. Existing monitoring frameworks often struggle to maintain detection consistency when targets undergo significant scale variations due to altitude changes, leading to critical information gaps. To address this issue, this work proposes an integrated real-time detection pipeline for detecting targets through the wireless live drone video feed. Build upon YOLOv8-nano architecture, extensive flight experiments were conducted to determine the detection performance across multiple flight altitudes. Trained on VisDrone2019 dataset, the results of YOLOv8-nano model achieves 57.4%, 41%, 44.8% and 20.3% in precision, recall, mAP and mAP50:95 respectively. While demonstrating on real environment, this analysis revealed that the algorithm achieves near-total detection reliability at altitudes between 16 and 25 meters with the detection frame rate consistently maintained above 41 FPS and reaching a peak of 50 FPS. However, the goal of this work is to enable real-time person detection from an aerial platform via wireless transmission. This approach effectively addresses the dual challenges of identifying targets at varying scales and ensuring near-to-accurate localization during aerial observation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a real-time UAV-based person detection pipeline using YOLOv8-nano trained on VisDrone2019, achieving near-total detection reliability at 16-25m altitudes (41-50 FPS) with precision 57.4%, recall 41%, mAP 44.8%, and mAP50:95 20.3%.
AI.motivation: Existing monitoring frameworks struggle to maintain detection consistency when targets undergo significant scale variations due to altitude changes, creating critical information gaps for UAV-based security, SAR, and border surveillance applications.
AI.method: An integrated real-time detection pipeline built upon YOLOv8-nano architecture processes wireless live drone video feed. The model was trained on the VisDrone2019 dataset, and extensive flight experiments across multiple altitudes evaluated detection performance.
AI.result: YOLOv8-nano achieved 57.4% precision, 41% recall, 44.8% mAP, and 20.3% mAP50:95. Near-total detection reliability was observed at 16-25m altitudes with frame rates consistently above 41 FPS, peaking at 50 FPS.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively addresses the dual challenges of identifying targets at varying scales and ensuring near-to-accurate localization during aerial observation, enabling real-time person detection from an aerial platform via wireless transmission.

title: Learning Linear Temporal Specifications from Demonstrations with Uncertainty
comment: This paper has been accepted by the ACC2026 (American Control Conference)
summary: Learning temporal logic specifications from system demonstrations is essential for tasks such as formal verification and controller synthesis, especially in safety-critical domains. Existing approaches typically assume demonstrations are correct or only affected by misclassification errors. In practice, however, system traces are often uncertain or incomplete due to sensor faults, measurement errors, or data loss. We present a framework for learning minimal Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas from demonstrations with uncertainty. Our approach models uncertainty via Hamming distance to generate possible estimates around each observed trace, which are grouped with constraints requiring that at least one trace per group is consistent with the learned formula. Our problem is then reduced to an equivalent Pseudo-Boolean Optimization. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art LTL learning approaches and show that it recovers specifications that more closely align with ground-truth formulas under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for learning minimal LTL formulas from uncertain/incomplete system demonstrations by modeling uncertainty via Hamming distance and reducing the problem to Pseudo-Boolean Optimization, outperforming existing methods in recovering ground-truth specifications under uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Existing LTL learning approaches assume demonstrations are correct or only affected by misclassification errors, but real-world system traces are often uncertain or incomplete due to sensor faults, measurement errors, or data loss. This work addresses the need for a robust framework that handles such uncertainty in temporal logic specification learning.
AI.method: The framework models uncertainty using Hamming distance to generate possible estimates around each observed trace. These estimates are grouped with constraints requiring at least one trace per group to be consistent with the learned formula. The problem is reduced to an equivalent Pseudo-Boolean Optimization problem to find minimal LTL formulas.
AI.result: The method recovers specifications that more closely align with ground-truth formulas under uncertainty compared to state-of-the-art LTL learning approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively handles uncertainty in system demonstrations for LTL learning, producing more accurate specifications in the presence of sensor faults, measurement errors, or data loss.

title: LLM-PDESR: Robust PDE Discovery via Subdomain Weighted Residuals and LLM-Guided Symbolic Hypothesis Generation
summary: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from noisy observational data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning. Traditional symbolic regression (SR) methods often struggle to identify accurate equations within vast combinatorial search spaces, largely due to their inability to incorporate essential domain-specific prior knowledge. Furthermore, reliance on pointwise evaluations and discrete finite differences inherently amplifies high-frequency noise, creating deceptive fitness landscapes that derail the optimization process. To resolve these bottlenecks, we propose LLM-PDESR, a framework that integrates the structural hypothesis generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) with a mathematically rigorous evaluation environment. By employing C^4-continuous quintic splines for robust differentiation and subdomain weighted residuals as natural low-pass filters, our approach effectively mitigates the fitness landscape distortion that plagues existing methods. A Pareto-driven feedback loop then enables the LLM to iteratively refine candidate equations, balancing predictive accuracy with structural parsimony. We evaluate LLM-PDESR on 23 canonical PDEs and five structurally novel equations (including a multivariate system) specifically designed to preclude dataset memorization and test true discovery capabilities. Demonstrating real-world applicability, the framework successfully extracts a consistent structural skeleton for an interpretable 1D dynamical surrogate (1D-CACE) directly from noisy ERA5 reanalysis data. Extensive experiments and out-of-distribution testing confirm that LLM-PDESR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methodologies in structural recovery, noise resilience, and the avoidance of spurious complexity and equation bloat.

AI.tldr: LLM-PDESR integrates Large Language Models with C^4-continuous quintic spline differentiation and subdomain weighted residuals to discover governing PDEs from noisy observational data, outperforming existing methods on 23 canonical and 5 novel PDEs, and successfully extracting an interpretable surrogate from real-world ERA5 reanalysis data.
AI.motivation: Traditional symbolic regression methods for PDE discovery struggle with vast combinatorial search spaces, inability to incorporate domain-specific prior knowledge, and fitness landscape distortion caused by noise amplification from pointwise evaluations and finite differences.
AI.method: LLM-PDESR combines LLMs for structural hypothesis generation with a rigorous evaluation environment using C^4-continuous quintic splines for robust differentiation and subdomain weighted residuals as natural low-pass filters, guided by a Pareto-driven feedback loop that balances accuracy with parsimony.
AI.result: Evaluated on 23 canonical PDEs and 5 structurally novel equations (including a multivariate system) designed to prevent dataset memorization; successfully extracted a consistent structural skeleton for a 1D dynamical surrogate (1D-CACE) from noisy ERA5 data; significantly outperformed state-of-the-art in structural recovery, noise resilience, and avoidance of spurious complexity.
AI.conclusion: LLM-PDESR effectively addresses key bottlenecks in PDE discovery by combining LLM-guided hypothesis generation with mathematically robust evaluation, achieving superior noise resilience, structural accuracy, and real-world applicability compared to existing methods.

title: WasteAssistant: Regulation-Guided Visual Question Answering Framework for Intelligent Waste Segregation and Sustainable Managemen
summary: Efficient waste segregation is critical for sustainable urban management and environmental governance. Existing automated systems are limited by single-modality visual processing, insufficient contextual understanding, and weak regulatory alignment. To address these issues, we propose a language-guided vision-AI framework that integrates vision-language models and multimodal large language models for joint visual-linguistic reasoning. This framework implements a visual question answering paradigm aligned with India's Solid Waste Management Rules 2016. We construct a new WasteVQA dataset with 13,500 question-answer pairs across 21 waste categories. Experiments show that the BLIP-based model achieves a BLEU score of 0.8291 and a BERTScore of 0.9273, outperforming traditional CNN-based methods. This work improves source-level segregation accuracy, ensures regulatory compliance, and supports scalable deployment for municipal and citizen-facing waste management, promoting multimodal AI in sustainable urban infrastructure. The source code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/Khushkataruka/WasteAssistant

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a language-guided vision-AI framework integrating vision-language models and multimodal LLMs for waste segregation, using a VQA paradigm aligned with India's SWM Rules 2016. A new WasteVQA dataset (13,500 QA pairs, 21 categories) is introduced. The BLIP-based model achieves BLEU 0.8291 and BERTScore 0.9273, outperforming traditional CNN methods.
AI.motivation: Existing automated waste segregation systems are limited by single-modality visual processing, insufficient contextual understanding, and weak regulatory alignment, making them inadequate for effective sustainable urban management and environmental governance.
AI.method: A language-guided vision-AI framework integrating vision-language models (VLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for joint visual-linguistic reasoning, implemented via a visual question answering (VQA) paradigm aligned with India's Solid Waste Management Rules 2016. A new WasteVQA dataset with 13,500 QA pairs across 21 waste categories was constructed.
AI.result: The BLIP-based model achieves a BLEU score of 0.8291 and a BERTScore of 0.9273, outperforming traditional CNN-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework improves source-level segregation accuracy, ensures regulatory compliance, supports scalable deployment for municipal and citizen-facing waste management, and promotes multimodal AI in sustainable urban infrastructure.

title: SVR-R1: Bootstrapping Multi-modal Reasoning with Self-verification in Reinforcement Learning
summary: We introduce Self-Verified Reasoner (SVR-R1), a multi-turn RL framework that turns a model's own verification into a learning signal for multimodal reasoning. For each query, the model proposes an answer using the same weights, and issues a binary self-verdict (Yes/No). A 'No' triggers a second-chance rethink; a 'Yes,' or a turn cap, finalizes the output for computing the outcome-based reward. SVR-R1 is implemented with GRPO and an asynchronous multi-turn rollout framework and needs no external supervision or auxiliary critics. We evaluate SVR-R1 on vision-language reasoning benchmarks and show that it improves accuracy by a large margin over strong standard GRPO baselines. Training dynamics show decreasing reliance on verification-fewer verification turns, yet higher test accuracy-indicating that the gap between verification and generation narrows as the policy internalizes self-correction and chooses the most confident answer via our framework. SVR-R1 bridges the less explored intersection of inference-time self-refinement and RL training for VLMs, offering a simple yet effective recipe for bootstrapping multimodal reasoning. We will open-source \textbf{SVR-R1} to facilitate future research in VLMs.

AI.tldr: SVR-R1 is a multi-turn RL framework that uses a model's own binary self-verification (Yes/No) as a learning signal for multimodal reasoning. It improves accuracy over standard GRPO baselines on vision-language benchmarks without external supervision, and shows that the model internalizes self-correction over time.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between inference-time self-refinement and RL training for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and to leverage the model's own verification ability as a learning signal without external supervision or auxiliary critics.
AI.method: A multi-turn RL framework where the model proposes an answer, issues a binary self-verdict (Yes/No). A 'No' triggers a second-chance rethink; a 'Yes' or turn cap finalizes the output. Implemented with GRPO and an asynchronous multi-turn rollout framework.
AI.result: SVR-R1 improves accuracy by a large margin over strong standard GRPO baselines on vision-language reasoning benchmarks. Training dynamics show decreasing verification turns but higher test accuracy, indicating internalized self-correction.
AI.conclusion: SVR-R1 offers a simple yet effective recipe for bootstrapping multimodal reasoning by turning self-verification into an RL learning signal, narrowing the gap between verification and generation.

title: Learning from Local Walks on Dynamic Graphs with Bandit Feedback
summary: We study stochastic multi-armed bandits on dynamic graphs, where arms correspond to the vertices of a network with time-varying edges. In this setting, the learner is restricted to local movement, selecting only its current node or an immediate neighbor at each round. This constraint decouples best-arm identification from exploitation: even after the optimal arm is identified, the learner may remain unable to reach it through the evolving topology. We identify a process-agnostic structural condition, based on sliding-window mixing, that ensures the graph's intrinsic walk remains stable for both exploration and navigation. Under this regime, we analyze a family of local explore-then-commit algorithms and establish sublinear expected regret. Our framework includes a reward-aware strategy, for which we prove a worst-case safety theorem and a separate performance gain theorem.

AI.tldr: The paper studies stochastic multi-armed bandits on dynamic graphs where the learner can only move to neighboring nodes, and proposes a sliding-window mixing condition that enables sublinear regret for local explore-then-commit algorithms.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of multi-armed bandits on time-varying graphs where the learner's movement is locally constrained, which decouples identification of the optimal arm from the ability to reach it due to evolving topology.
AI.method: Identifies a process-agnostic structural condition based on sliding-window mixing that ensures stable graph walks; proposes a family of local explore-then-commit algorithms with reward-aware strategies; proves a worst-case safety theorem and a performance gain theorem.
AI.result: Establishes sublinear expected regret under the sliding-window mixing regime for the proposed local explore-then-commit algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The sliding-window mixing condition enables tractable regret analysis for bandit learning under local movement constraints on dynamic graphs, with both safety and performance guarantees.

title: Spectral Consistent Flow for One-step 3D Medical Image Translation
summary: We present Spectral Consistent Flow (SC-Flow), a 3D medical image translation framework with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) in the latent space. This approach reformulates medical image translation as a stochastic Brownian bridge process that directly constructs a mapping between source and target modalities by predicting the support regularized mean velocity field. To mitigate modality entanglement, over-smoothing, and artifacts induced by the implicit low-pass modulation of the latent average velocity, we introduce a Spectral Consistency Corrector that dynamically regularizes the evolution of the power spectral density via learnable frequency-domain gain modulation. This mechanism establishes an explicit bridge between spatial textures and spectral energy flow, enabling the model to recover fine-grained anatomical fidelity while maintaining global structural coherence. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate that SC-Flow delivers significantly more accurate, consistent, and robust performance across various translation scenarios.

AI.tldr: SC-Flow is a 3D medical image translation framework using a single latent-space function evaluation, modeling translation as a Brownian bridge with spectral consistency correction for high anatomical fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing medical image translation methods suffer from modality entanglement, over-smoothing, and artifacts due to implicit low-pass modulation of latent average velocity, lacking fine-grained anatomical detail preservation.
AI.method: SC-Flow reformulates translation as a stochastic Brownian bridge process in latent space (1-NFE), predicting a support-regularized mean velocity field, and introduces a Spectral Consistency Corrector that dynamically regularizes power spectral density evolution via learnable frequency-domain gain modulation.
AI.result: Achieves significantly more accurate, consistent, and robust performance across four datasets in various translation scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The spectral consistency mechanism effectively bridges spatial textures and spectral energy flow, recovering fine-grained anatomical fidelity while maintaining global structural coherence in 3D medical image translation.

title: From Checker to Forecaster: Code-Owned Evaluation of Model-Generated Strategic Routes Under Delayed Ground Truth
summary: Many evaluations of model outputs rely either on contracts checkable at evaluation time or on feedback that arrives within the operating loop. We study the complementary setting in which ground truth is delayed, censored, or private, so deterministic code cannot check correctness at scoring time and must instead issue a code-owned provisional forecast. RouteCast instantiates this regime for model-generated typed strategic routes: models propose candidate routes and structured factors; point-in-time evidence, reference classes, and deterministic transformations produce a provisional forecast-ranking; later outcomes evaluate the forecast. In a retrospective venture pilot on 21 binary-outcome cases (6 positive, 15 negative), the whole-packet RouteCast score showed preliminary retrospective discrimination (AUC 0.756, 95% CI [0.471,0.980]), while a blind LLM judge reached AUC 0.678 [0.419,0.897] and an identity-exposed LLM judge reached AUC 0.761 [0.515,0.944], consistent with recognition- or outcome-related leakage risk. A preregistered decomposition ablation on the same binary subset found that converting the identical inputs into typed staged routes was indistinguishable from the whole-packet score (Delta AUC = -0.144, 95% CI [-0.471,0.176]) and from a deterministic heuristic (Delta AUC = -0.089, 95% CI [-0.412,0.278]). The pilot establishes an auditable feasibility result and exposes failure modes; it does not establish prospective calibration, causal decision improvement, route-decomposition advantage, or cross-domain validity.

AI.tldr: RouteCast is a framework for scoring model-generated strategic routes when ground truth is delayed, censored, or private; it uses provisional forecasts from reference classes and deterministic transformations. A pilot on 21 binary-outcome cases showed discrimination (AUC ~0.76) comparable to LLM judges but with less leakage risk, though ablation found route decomposition didn't outperform simpler heuristics.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations rely on checkable contracts or in-loop feedback; this paper addresses the setting where ground truth is delayed, censored, or private, requiring provisional forecasts at scoring time.
AI.method: RouteCast ingests model-generated typed strategic routes and structured factors, applies point-in-time evidence, reference classes, and deterministic transformations to produce provisional forecast-rankings, which are later evaluated against observed outcomes.
AI.result: On 21 binary cases (6 positive, 15 negative): RouteCast AUC 0.756 [0.471,0.980]; blind LLM AUC 0.678 [0.419,0.897]; identity-exposed LLM AUC 0.761 [0.515,0.944]. Ablation: converting inputs to typed staged routes vs whole packet ΔAUC=-0.144 [-0.471,0.176]; vs deterministic heuristic ΔAUC=-0.089 [-0.412,0.278].
AI.conclusion: The pilot establishes an auditable feasibility result and exposes failure modes but does not establish prospective calibration, causal decision improvement, route-decomposition advantage, or cross-domain validity.

title: MemDecay: Region-Aware KV Cache Eviction for Efficient LLM Agent Inference
summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents accumulate heterogeneous context, including system instructions, plans, user turns, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and intermediate reasoning, whose key-value (KV) cache can become a major memory bottleneck. Existing eviction policies generally apply the same attention- or recency-based rule to every token, ignoring semantic structure already available to the agent orchestrator.
  We introduce MemDecay, a training-free, region-aware KV-cache eviction policy. MemDecay assigns tokens region-specific base priorities and decay rates, refreshes retention scores when tokens receive attention, and evicts the lowest-scoring pages under a fixed cache budget while allowing critical regions to be pinned. We also provide a procedure for calibrating decay rates from measured attention lifetimes.
  We evaluate MemDecay at approximately 450 and 1,700 token contexts using Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B. Across all settings, attention lifetimes differ by an order of magnitude across regions: system-token half-lives range from 148 to 189 decoding steps, compared with 14 to 16 for scratchpad tokens. Pinning preserves system-region facts at full-cache accuracy in every setting, while no baseline preserves more than 13 of 24. Region-aware retention remains effective as context grows, whereas recency-based retention collapses. Accumulated-attention retention performs better on unpinned content, however, and ablations identify attention-score normalization as the main limitation of the current formulation. These results establish semantic prompt structure as a robust signal for KV-cache management while clarifying how it should be combined with attention-based importance.

AI.tldr: MemDecay is a training-free, region-aware KV-cache eviction policy for LLM agents that assigns different priority and decay rates to tokens based on their semantic region (e.g., system instructions vs. scratchpad), outperforming uniform eviction baselines by preserving system facts at full-cache accuracy while reducing memory overhead.
AI.motivation: LLM agents accumulate heterogeneous context whose KV cache becomes a major memory bottleneck; existing eviction policies apply the same rule to every token, ignoring the semantic structure already available to the agent orchestrator.
AI.method: MemDecay assigns region-specific base priorities and decay rates, refreshes retention scores when tokens receive attention, and evicts the lowest-scoring pages under a fixed cache budget while allowing critical regions to be pinned. Decay rates are calibrated from measured attention lifetimes.
AI.result: Attention lifetimes differ by an order of magnitude across regions (system-token half-lives: 148-189 steps vs. scratchpad: 14-16 steps). MemDecay preserves system-region facts at full-cache accuracy in every setting; no baseline preserves more than 13 of 24. Region-aware retention remains effective as context grows, while recency-based retention collapses.
AI.conclusion: Semantic prompt structure is a robust signal for KV-cache management, though attention-score normalization remains the main limitation of the current formulation, suggesting it should be combined with attention-based importance.

title: Spectral Heat Flow for Conservative Token Condensation in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are costly at inference time because they must process long sequences of visual tokens. Existing token pruning methods often degrade under high compression by blindly discarding information, breaking spatial structure or collapsing diversity. We propose SpecFlow, a training-free framework that shifts the paradigm from destructive pruning to conservative condensation, strictly enforcing spatial coverage and statistical conservation to ensure stability. Treating visual tokens as nodes in a $k$NN graph, SpecFlow (i) computes a stable importance field via spectral heat flow to preserve structural coherence, (ii) allocates budgets via adaptive spatial partitioning to guarantee coverage, and (iii) aggregates discarded information into coreset sinks to maintain statistical conservation. The method is plug-and-play, requires no fine-tuning, and is compatible with FlashAttention. Experiments confirm that our SpecFlow outperforms SOTA methods across tasks, VLM architectures, and pruning ratios. Notably, LLaVA-1.5 with SpecFlow retains 95.6\% of original performance despite pruning 88.9\% of visual tokens, offering an exceptional efficiency-accuracy balance. Code is available at https://github.com/Lzy-dot/SpecFlow

AI.tldr: SpecFlow is a training-free framework that condenses visual tokens in VLMs via spectral heat flow, adaptive spatial partitioning, and coreset sinks, achieving superior performance-efficiency trade-offs (e.g., 95.6% performance retention with 88.9% token pruning).
AI.motivation: VLMs are computationally expensive at inference due to long sequences of visual tokens, and existing token pruning methods degrade under high compression by blindly discarding information, breaking spatial structure, or collapsing diversity.
AI.method: SpecFlow proposes a training-free framework with three components: (i) a stable importance field via spectral heat flow on a kNN graph to preserve structural coherence, (ii) budget allocation via adaptive spatial partitioning to guarantee coverage, and (iii) aggregation of discarded information into coreset sinks to maintain statistical conservation.
AI.result: SpecFlow outperforms SOTA methods across tasks, VLM architectures, and pruning ratios. LLaVA-1.5 with SpecFlow retains 95.6% of original performance despite pruning 88.9% of visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: SpecFlow shifts the paradigm from destructive pruning to conservative condensation, enforcing spatial coverage and statistical conservation. It is plug-and-play, requires no fine-tuning, and is compatible with FlashAttention, offering an exceptional efficiency-accuracy balance.

title: QwenPaw-Data: Bridging Facts, Methodology, and Execution for Autonomous Enterprise Data Analytics
summary: Enterprise data analysis is emerging as a distinct frontier for autonomous agents. Compared with general-purpose interaction and software engineering, it operates in an open, ambiguous, and continuously evolving environment. These characteristics call for a data-agent architecture that treats semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class system concerns. To this end, we introduce QwenPaw-Data, an agentic data system designed for enterprise intelligent data analysis. QwenPaw-Data consolidates heterogeneous assets from warehouses, dashboards, documents, interaction logs, and historical tasks into reusable, governable, and evolvable analysis assets, then turns natural-language requests into end-to-end analytical workflows spanning data understanding, retrieval, analysis, report generation, and decision support. Its architecture decomposes the problem into three collaborative subsystems: DataBridge provides trustworthy semantic grounding through interconnected metadata, knowledge, and trace graphs; Skill-Hub codifies expert analytical methodology into reusable and verifiable skills; and Host materializes these evidence and method assets into controllable, artifact-centric runtime execution. Across these subsystems, semantics, methods, traces, and feedback are continuously deposited back into the system, forming a self-evolving asset flywheel. Experiments on public benchmarks and real-world industrial BI workloads show that QwenPaw-Data improves both verifiable data access capability and higher-level analytical quality, offering a practical foundation for reliable, traceable, and continuously improving enterprise data agents.

AI.tldr: QwenPaw-Data is an agentic data system for enterprise data analysis that uses a three-subsystem architecture (DataBridge, Skill-Hub, Host) to treat semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class concerns, enabling natural-language-driven analytical workflows with self-evolving asset flywheel capabilities.
AI.motivation: Enterprise data analysis operates in an open, ambiguous, and continuously evolving environment, which differs from general-purpose interaction and software engineering. This calls for a data-agent architecture that treats semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class system concerns.
AI.method: The architecture decomposes the problem into three collaborative subsystems: DataBridge (trustworthy semantic grounding via metadata, knowledge, and trace graphs), Skill-Hub (codifies expert analytical methodology into reusable/verifiable skills), and Host (materializes evidence and method assets into controllable, artifact-centric runtime execution). A self-evolving asset flywheel continuously deposits semantics, methods, traces, and feedback back into the system.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks and real-world industrial BI workloads show improvements in both verifiable data access capability and higher-level analytical quality.
AI.conclusion: QwenPaw-Data offers a practical foundation for reliable, traceable, and continuously improving enterprise data agents.

title: Sharp Concentration Bounds for Bundle-Valued Statistics on Manifolds
summary: Many geometric statistics and manifold learning pipelines routinely produce observations -- such as tangent vectors or local frames -- whose natural home is a varying family of fibers attached to different points of a base manifold, rather than a single shared vector space. Forming empirical averages requires transporting these observations to a common reference fiber, thereby introducing curvature- and holonomy-driven effects that are absent from classical concentration theory. We develop a non-asymptotic concentration theory for such transported empirical means, deriving finite-sample, dimension-free Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type bounds via sharp Hilbert-space inequalities. When shortest paths to the reference point are non-unique, transport becomes path-dependent and introduces a deterministic holonomy bias; we isolate and quantify this bias through bundle curvature and loop geometry, with sharp closed-form formulas for the tangent bundle of a round sphere. The resulting bias-variance decomposition separates the stochastic fluctuation decaying at the classical $n^{-1/2}$ rate in sample size $n$, from a curvature-driven error floor that no amount of additional data can eliminate; minimax lower bounds confirm both terms are unavoidable. We further establish a robust median-of-means estimator achieving optimal rates under heavy tails and the central limit theorem in the reference fiber. Controlled experiments on the sphere validate all theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a non-asymptotic concentration theory for transported empirical means on manifolds, deriving Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type bounds, quantifying holonomy bias via bundle curvature, establishing a bias-variance decomposition with a curvature-driven error floor, and proving minimax lower bounds, robust median-of-means estimators, and a CLT in the reference fiber.
AI.motivation: Observations in geometric statistics (tangent vectors, local frames) live in fibers attached to different base manifold points, not a single vector space. Forming empirical averages requires transport to a common reference fiber, introducing curvature and holonomy effects absent from classical concentration theory — this gap motivates a new non-asymptotic theory.
AI.method: Sharp Hilbert-space inequalities are used to derive finite-sample, dimension-free Hoeffding- and Bernstein-type concentration bounds for transported empirical means. Holonomy bias is isolated via bundle curvature and loop geometry with closed-form formulas for the tangent bundle of a round sphere. A robust median-of-means estimator and CLT in the reference fiber are established; minimax lower bounds confirm both terms are unavoidable.
AI.result: A bias-variance decomposition separating stochastic fluctuation (decaying at n^{-1/2}) from a curvature-driven error floor that no amount of additional data can eliminate; minimax lower bounds proving both terms unavoidable; robust median-of-means estimator achieving optimal rates under heavy tails; CLT in the reference fiber.
AI.conclusion: Transporting geometric observations introduces unavoidable curvature-driven bias, fundamentally limiting estimation accuracy regardless of sample size; the theory provides sharp, verifiable predictions validated on the sphere.

title: Answer-Conditioned Chain-of-Thought Distillation for Few-Shot Industrial Vision with Small VLMs
summary: Deploying AI-based visual inspection in manufacturing is hard because requirements change often, new defect types appear, and large labeled datasets are rarely available. We propose answer-conditioned chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation for rapidly adapting small vision-language models (VLMs) to new industrial tasks using minimal labeled data. A frontier VLM receives each training image along with its correct label and generates a justified visual explanation. A 3B-parameter model is then fine-tuned on these reasoning-augmented examples via LoRA. By conditioning on correct answers, we ensure all training reasoning is directed toward the correct conclusion, which is critical because frontier models score as low as 24.1% on our hardest task. We validate on four industrial classification tasks spanning three image modalities using only 18 to 30 labeled images per task. Across 4 seeds per task (32 training runs), our method outperforms direct fine-tuning on all 16 seed-task combinations, with mean improvements of +1.7 to +4.4 percentage points. A controlled equal-budget experiment confirms the improvement comes from reasoning quality, not additional training steps. An unconditioned baseline demonstrates that with out answer-conditioning, wrong reasoning degrades performance by 17.8 percentage points. On weld radiograph classification, the fine-tuned 3B model outperforms GPT-4.1 by 10.0pp using just 24 training images.

AI.tldr: A method for rapidly adapting small VLMs to industrial visual inspection tasks using answer-conditioned chain-of-thought distillation from frontier models, achieving superior performance over direct fine-tuning with only 18-30 labeled images.
AI.motivation: Deploying AI-based visual inspection in manufacturing is challenging due to frequently changing requirements, emerging defect types, and scarcity of large labeled datasets.
AI.method: Proposes answer-conditioned chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation: a frontier VLM receives training images with correct labels to generate justified visual explanations, then a 3B-parameter model is fine-tuned on these reasoning-augmented examples via LoRA.
AI.result: Outperforms direct fine-tuning on all 16 seed-task combinations (mean improvements +1.7 to +4.4 pp), improves over unconditioned baseline by 17.8 pp, and a 3B model fine-tuned on 24 weld radiograph images outperforms GPT-4.1 by 10.0 pp.
AI.conclusion: Answer-conditioned CoT distillation enables effective few-shot adaptation of small VLMs for industrial inspection, with gains attributable to reasoning quality rather than additional training compute.

title: AdvNav: Behavior-Guided Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Despite progress in Embodied AI, Vision-and-Language Navigation systems remain vulnerable to adversarial visual disturbances. Most existing methods rely on white-box access to target model gradients, which is often unrealistic for real-world deployed systems and computationally exhaustive due to recursive backpropagation for optimization, limiting their applicability. While previous black-box methods predominantly target single-step, instantaneous decision tasks, they struggle to handle the task complexities and temporal dependencies. This highlights the need for a gradient-free attack method that can effectively disrupt the multistep sequential perception-action loop using only observable inputs and outputs. Therefore, we propose AdvNav, a behavior-guided black-box adversarial attack framework that disturbs an agent's first-person views during navigation. To construct an informative surrogate objective for effective optimization guidance in gradient-free search under the black-box setting, we design a dual-granularity behavior-based feedback, aggregating a trajectory-level performance score representing overall navigation degradation, an action-level reward score considering the potential decision risk, and a deviation indicator, all of which are extracted from the agent's self-output behaviors. This feedback guides a hybrid optimization strategy that heuristically tunes perturbation strength via adaptive updates and evolves noise spatial structure genetically, to iteratively discover the most disruptive noise configuration. Evaluated against Transformer-based HAMT and LLM-based MapGPT with two types of backbones on R2R dataset, AdvNav achieves 49.70/65.96/87.30% Attack Success Rate. The result demonstrates the effectiveness and generality of AdvNav, reveals critical perception vulnerabilities and offers insights for the design of future resilient VLN models.

AI.tldr: AdvNav is a black-box adversarial attack framework for Vision-and-Language Navigation that uses behavior-guided optimization (trajectory-level, action-level, and deviation feedback) with a hybrid evolutionary strategy to generate adversarial visual perturbations without access to model gradients, achieving 49.70-87.30% attack success rates on HAMT and MapGPT models.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial attacks on VLN systems require white-box gradient access (unrealistic for deployed systems) or target only single-step decisions, failing to handle the temporal dependencies and sequential perception-action loops inherent in navigation tasks.
AI.method: AdvNav uses a dual-granularity behavior-based feedback signal (trajectory-level performance score, action-level reward score, and deviation indicator) extracted from the agent's observable outputs to guide a hybrid optimization strategy combining adaptive perturbation strength updates and genetic noise evolution.
AI.result: Tested on Transformer-based HAMT and LLM-based MapGPT on R2R dataset, AdvNav achieves 49.70%, 65.96%, and 87.30% Attack Success Rate across configurations.
AI.conclusion: AdvNav reveals critical perception vulnerabilities in VLN models, demonstrating that effective black-box attacks can be mounted using only behavioral feedback, which offers insights for designing more resilient navigation agents.

title: AutoNorm: Understanding Adaptive Normalization in Transformers through Differentiable Gating
summary: Normalization is a critical component for stabilizing Transformer training, yet the choice between static strategies such as Layer Normalization (LN) and adaptive alternatives remains largely task-dependent. In this paper, we investigate a key optimization challenge in differentiable normalization gating. Our experiments show that, on relatively stationary vision tasks, the high gradient variance introduced by Gumbel-Softmax gating can hinder convergence of the routing mechanism, causing learned gates to underperform simple random selection. In contrast, on non-stationary language modeling and classification tasks, sustained gating diversity enables the model to learn more effective layer-wise normalization policies. Motivated by these observations, we propose AutoNorm-S (Stabilized), a training strategy that mitigates optimization instability through a gate-freezing schedule. AutoNorm-S achieves competitive or improved performance across multiple benchmarks, outperforming adaptive normalization baselines on NLP datasets, including PTB and SST-2, while remaining competitive on standard vision benchmarks.
