These results suggest that decoupling normalization selection from optimization noise provides a practical and principled approach for adaptive normalization in Transformer architectures.

AI.tldr: AutoNorm-S introduces a gate-freezing schedule to stabilize training when adaptively selecting normalization methods in Transformers, outperforming static LN on NLP tasks and matching it on vision benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Normalization choice in Transformers (static LN vs. adaptive) is task-dependent, and differentiable normalization gating suffers from high gradient variance that hinders convergence on stationary vision tasks.
AI.method: Proposes AutoNorm-S (Stabilized), which mitigates optimization instability in differentiable normalization gating through a gate-freezing schedule that decouples normalization selection from optimization noise.
AI.result: AutoNorm-S achieves competitive or improved performance across multiple benchmarks, outperforming adaptive normalization baselines on NLP datasets (PTB, SST-2) while remaining competitive on standard vision benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling normalization selection from optimization noise provides a practical and principled approach for adaptive normalization in Transformer architectures.

title: HyperBank: A Differentiable Bank of Classical Priors for Few-Shot Spheroid Microscopy Segmentation
comment: Accepted for publication in the IEEE Xplore ICIP 2026 Workshop Proceedings, Computational Optical Microscopy Satellite Workshop of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP), Tampere, Finland
summary: Few-shot spheroid segmentation must adapt to new cell lines, microscopes, and illumination conditions from only a small set of annotated images. While foundation few-shot segmenters can be accurate, their large opaque backbones make it difficult to understand which visual cues drive success or failure. We study this question with HyperBank, a differentiable bank of classical image-processing operators combining Frangi vesselness, a Sauvola threshold pyramid, structure-tensor responses, gradient magnitude, and Laplacian-of-Gaussian filters. HyperBank is fitted on the annotated support images and evaluated on disjoint held-out images across three independently acquired spheroid datasets. We treat it not as a general replacement for foundation models, but as a compact, interpretable few-shot microscopy pipeline and an analytic-prior probe of which classical cues carry the few-shot signal. The results show that, adapted on the same few annotated support images, a compact bank of analytic priors is competitive with, and on small-cluster, contrast-driven data can outperform, much larger foundation models, while those models remain stronger on externally sourced, texture-dominated spheroids. Leave-one-family-out ablations indicate that the useful few-shot signal is distributed across operator families and strengthened by support-set-tuned morphology.

AI.tldr: HyperBank, a differentiable bank of classical image-processing operators (Frangi, Sauvola, structure-tensor, etc.), achieves competitive few-shot spheroid segmentation vs. large foundation models on small, contrast-driven data, while providing interpretability; useful signal is distributed across operator families and boosted by tuned morphology.
AI.motivation: To understand which visual cues drive few-shot spheroid segmentation success/failure, as large opaque foundation models make this difficult; HyperBank serves as an interpretable analytic-prior probe.
AI.method: HyperBank: a differentiable bank of classical operators (Frangi vesselness, Sauvola threshold pyramid, structure-tensor, gradient magnitude, Laplacian-of-Gaussian) fitted on annotated support images and evaluated on held-out images across three spheroid datasets.
AI.result: HyperBank is competitive with and on small-cluster, contrast-driven data can outperform larger foundation models; foundation models remain stronger on externally sourced, texture-dominated spheroids.
AI.conclusion: Classical analytic priors can carry substantial few-shot signal; useful signal is distributed across operator families and strengthened by support-set-tuned morphology.

title: Are LLMs Ready for Scientific Discovery? A Capability-Oriented Benchmark for AI Scientists
summary: Existing benchmarks for scientific data analysis evaluate LLMs primarily on code execution or workflow completion, overlooking that scientific analysis serves to support distinct types of scientific claims: hypothesis exploration, statistical inference, mechanistic explanation, each with different assumptions and validity criteria. We introduce SDABench, a benchmark that reorganizes evaluation around six capabilities (descriptive, exploratory, inferential, predictive, causal, and mechanistic) across five domains (Biology, Chemistry, Environment, Geography, Physics). SDABench comprises 527 real-data instances (SDA-Real) and 6000 synthetic instances (SDA-Synth), each in both multiple-choice and open-ended formats, constructed through an automated pipeline. Evaluating 15 representative LLMs, we find that models handle descriptive analysis well but degrade sharply on tasks requiring assumption selection, latent-process modeling, or mechanistic reasoning. SDABench further provides a five-stage error analysis framework that locates where LLMs fail: more advanced models more reliably identify the relevant scope and variables, but still struggle to select appropriate analytical procedures, model variable relationships, and draw valid conclusions.

AI.tldr: SDABench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on scientific data analysis, reorganizing evaluation around six capabilities across five domains, finding that models perform well on descriptive tasks but struggle with assumption selection, latent-process modeling, and mechanistic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs on code execution or workflow completion, ignoring that scientific analysis serves to support distinct types of scientific claims (hypothesis exploration, statistical inference, mechanistic explanation) with different assumptions and validity criteria.
AI.method: The authors introduce SDABench, reorganizing evaluation around six capabilities (descriptive, exploratory, inferential, predictive, causal, mechanistic) across five domains, with 527 real-data instances and 6000 synthetic instances in both multiple-choice and open-ended formats, constructed via an automated pipeline. They also provide a five-stage error analysis framework.
AI.result: Evaluating 15 LLMs shows models handle descriptive analysis well but degrade sharply on tasks requiring assumption selection, latent-process modeling, or mechanistic reasoning. The five-stage error analysis reveals that advanced models better identify scope and variables but still struggle to select appropriate analytical procedures, model variable relationships, and draw valid conclusions.
AI.conclusion: SDABench fills a critical gap by evaluating LLMs on the diverse reasoning capabilities required for genuine scientific data analysis, revealing persistent weaknesses in higher-order analytical reasoning beyond basic description.

title: M+Adam: Low-Precision Training via Additive-Multiplicative Optimization
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). 45 pages
summary: Training with quantized weights can reduce costs but often results in degraded accuracy, especially when optimization is carried out in low precision, without storing high-precision copies. We identify a key failure mode: under low precision, standard optimizers can get stuck and not make progress, especially at large weight magnitudes due to coarse mantissa resolution. To overcome this, multiplicative updates have been previously proposed, in place of additive updates in standard optimizers. While successful under extremely low precision, such as under the logarithmic number system, they suffer from failures near zero and across sign changes. The failure modes of additive and multiplicative updates are therefore complementary. To exploit this, we propose M+Adam, which combines both update types: additive steps handle sign changes and small magnitudes, while multiplicative steps ensure progress at large magnitudes when additive updates are zeroed out under rounding. We prove monotone descent for M+Adam under standard smoothness assumptions. Across LLaMA-style pretraining with 60M-1B models, 1x-8x Chinchilla budgets, and using only BF16, FP8, and FP4 master weights, M+Adam consistently improves low-precision training.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that low-precision weight training degrades accuracy because additive optimizers stall at large magnitudes due to coarse mantissa resolution. To address this, it proposes M+Adam, which combines additive and multiplicative updates to handle sign changes, small magnitudes, and large magnitudes robustly. M+Adam achieves monotone descent and improves low-precision training across various model sizes and bit-widths (BF16, FP8, FP4).
AI.motivation: Low-precision training reduces costs but suffers accuracy degradation; standard optimizers (additive) stall under coarse mantissa resolution at large weight magnitudes, while purely multiplicative updates fail near zero and across sign changes; the complementary failure modes motivate a hybrid approach.
AI.method: Proposes M+Adam, a hybrid optimizer combining additive updates (for sign changes and small magnitudes) and multiplicative updates (for progress at large magnitudes where additive updates are zeroed out by rounding). Theoretical monotone descent is proven under standard smoothness assumptions.
AI.result: Consistent improvement over standard low-precision training across LLaMA-style models (60M-1B), 1x-8x Chinchilla budgets, and master weights in BF16, FP8, and FP4.
AI.conclusion: M+Adam effectively addresses the complementary failure modes of additive and multiplicative updates, enabling robust low-precision optimization without high-precision copies.

title: Incremental Online Scene Reconstruction by 3D Gaussian Triangulation
summary: Incremental scene reconstruction is essential for real-world applications. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting shows strong potential, most existing approaches require offline conversion of the optimized Gaussians into an intermediate implicit field for explicit mesh extraction, which hinders seamless integration with downstream tasks. To address this limitation, we propose a novel online framework that incrementally reconstructs and updates high-fidelity explicit meshes by directly triangulating a dense geometric Gaussian representation, which supports both high-quality rendering and incremental surface reconstruction. Moreover, we present a direct meshing algorithm that efficiently extracts and updates the mesh from the Gaussian set. To ensure mesh accuracy, we enforce a plane-based pulling constraint that dynamically aligns 3D Gaussian primitives to the approximated local surface. Furthermore, our framework significantly reduces memory and computational overhead during long-sequence processing by dynamically freezing fully optimized historical regions. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms conventional Gaussian-based methods on both rendering quality and reconstruction accuracy.

AI.tldr: An online framework for incremental scene reconstruction that directly triangulates dense geometric 3D Gaussians into explicit meshes, with a plane-based pulling constraint and dynamic freezing of optimized regions, outperforming existing Gaussian-based methods in both rendering and reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods require offline conversion of optimized Gaussians into an implicit field for mesh extraction, hindering seamless integration with downstream tasks. The authors aim to enable incremental, high-fidelity explicit mesh reconstruction directly from Gaussians.
AI.method: Proposes an online framework that (1) directly triangulates dense geometric Gaussian representations into explicit meshes, (2) uses a direct meshing algorithm for efficient extraction/updates, (3) enforces a plane-based pulling constraint to align Gaussians to local surfaces, and (4) dynamically freezes fully optimized historical regions to reduce memory/computation.
AI.result: Outperforms conventional Gaussian-based methods on public datasets in both rendering quality and reconstruction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed online framework enables seamless incremental explicit mesh reconstruction and high-quality rendering from 3D Gaussians without offline conversion, with reduced computational overhead for long sequences.

title: NVAITC AI Scientist: A Governed End-to-End Research System -- A Hypertension GWAS Case Study
summary: Agentic research systems are emerging as a new paradigm for coordinating scientific workflows beyond isolated model inference, code generation, or statistical analysis. However, deployment in institutional biomedical environments requires governed mechanisms for research planning, data access, workflow orchestration, evidence tracking, reproducibility, and human oversight. We present NVAITC AI Scientist (NAIS), a governed end-to-end agentic research system designed to support domain-general scientific workflows while keeping protected data within institutional privacy boundaries. NAIS integrates proposal review, execution planning, governed computational routing, reproducible workflow orchestration, evidence generation, and scientist-in-the-loop oversight. We validate NAIS in a real-world hypertension genome-wide association study (GWAS) using hospital-linked genotype and electronic health record (EHR) data from 286,422 individuals under an aggregate-only data policy. The agent planned cohort extraction, orchestrated GWAS execution, generated quality-control summaries, and drafted publication-oriented outputs. Human-AI review identified phenotype discrepancies and enabled iterative refinement of the hypertension definition. After reconciliation, the agent-orchestrated GWAS reproduced established hypertension loci, including FGF5, ATP2B1, CNNM2, FTO, and GRB14, with the strongest signal at FGF5 reaching $-\log_{10}(p) \sim 70$. As a secondary demonstration, NAIS also supported a drug-induced liver injury prediction workflow, achieving a multimodal graph neural network AUC of 0.842. These results demonstrate that governed agentic research systems can support scalable AI-assisted biomedical discovery while producing outputs comparable to expert-led workflows.

AI.tldr: NAIS is a governed end-to-end agentic research system that coordinates scientific workflows in institutional biomedical environments while keeping protected data within privacy boundaries. Validated on a real-world hypertension GWAS (286,422 individuals) and a drug-induced liver injury prediction task, it reproduced established genetic loci and achieved competitive performance, demonstrating scalable AI-assisted biomedical discovery with human oversight.
AI.motivation: Existing AI research systems typically operate as isolated tools (model inference, code generation, statistical analysis) and lack the governed, end-to-end orchestration required for deployment in institutional biomedical environments where data privacy, reproducibility, human oversight, and workflow tracking are critical.
AI.method: NAIS integrates proposal review, execution planning, governed computational routing (keeping data within institutional privacy boundaries), reproducible workflow orchestration, evidence generation, and scientist-in-the-loop oversight. It was validated on a hypertension GWAS using hospital-linked genotype and EHR data from 286,422 individuals under an aggregate-only data policy, and on a drug-induced liver injury prediction task using multimodal graph neural networks.
AI.result: In the GWAS, NAIS planned cohort extraction, orchestrated GWAS execution, generated QC summaries, and produced publication-oriented outputs. Human-AI review identified phenotype discrepancies enabling iterative refinement. The final analysis reproduced established hypertension loci (FGF5, ATP2B1, CNNM2, FTO, GRB14) with strongest signal at FGF5 reaching -log10(p) ~ 70. For DILI prediction, NAIS achieved a multimodal GNN AUC of 0.842.
AI.conclusion: Governed agentic research systems like NAIS can support scalable AI-assisted biomedical discovery while maintaining institutional privacy and producing outputs comparable to expert-led workflows.

title: modelDNA: Calibrated Lineage Verification and Merge Decomposition from Sampled Weight Fingerprints
summary: The lineage graph of open-weight language models is self-reported: Hugging Face's base_model metadata field is optional and unverified, and over 60% of Hub models document no parentage at all. Methods for detecting lineage from weights exist in the research literature, but each ships as paper code tied to one signal and one experiment; when a provenance dispute breaks, the analysis is redone by hand. This report describes modelDNA, a tool that fingerprints a model from roughly 100-300 MB of ranged HTTP reads (instead of a full 15 GB download for a 7B model), compares the fingerprint against a reference database of foundation models across four published signal families, and returns one of eight verdict classes with a calibrated probability, preferring honest abstention to confident error. On a benchmark of 15 real Hub models with org-documented parentage, judged against 8 candidate bases (13 positives, 107 hard negatives), the system achieves AUROC 1.0, zero false positives at its reporting threshold, and 13/13 correct top-1 parent attribution. The report's second contribution is merge decomposition. Every mainstream weight-merging method is (near-)linear per tensor, and fingerprint sample positions are deterministic functions of tensor identity, so a merged model's fingerprint is the same linear combination of its parents' fingerprints. Mixture weights can therefore be recovered from fingerprints alone by sum-to-one constrained least squares. Against merges with published mergekit configurations as ground truth, the method recovers a slerp merge's layer-interpolation curves at r = 0.999 and a dare_ties merge's mixture weights to within 0.011 of the published values, without downloading any weights beyond the fingerprints. All fingerprints, benchmarks, and the inferred lineage graph of 55 models are public and reproducible offline.

AI.tldr: modelDNA fingerprints language models from ~100-300 MB of partial downloads, identifies parent models with perfect accuracy (AUROC 1.0, zero false positives), and decomposes merged models' lineage via linear fingerprint analysis, recovering mixture weights within 0.011 of ground truth.
AI.motivation: The lineage graph of open-weight language models is unreliable because Hugging Face's base_model metadata is optional and unverified (>60% of models document no parentage). Existing detection methods are paper-specific, one-signal, and require manual reanalysis for each dispute.
AI.method: modelDNA fingerprints models via ~100-300 MB ranged HTTP reads (vs. full 15 GB downloads), compares against a database of foundation models across 4 signal families, outputs 8 verdict classes with calibrated probabilities. For merge decomposition, it exploits that weight-merging methods are (near-)linear per tensor and fingerprint positions are deterministic—so a merged model's fingerprint equals the linear combination of parents' fingerprints, solved via sum-to-one constrained least squares.
AI.result: On 15 real Hub models against 8 candidate bases (13 positives, 107 hard negatives): AUROC 1.0, zero false positives, 13/13 correct top-1 parent attribution. Merge decomposition recovers slerp interpolation curves at r=0.999 and dare_ties mixture weights within 0.011 of published values.
AI.conclusion: modelDNA enables efficient, accurate, and reproducible model provenance verification, including decomposition of merged models, without requiring full model downloads.

title: Effective Synthetic Image Detection via Noise Residual Clustering
summary: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made synthetic images remarkably realistic, posing security threats such as misinformation and fraud. It is significant to detect the synthetic image in the manner of passive and blind image authentication. Most existing detectors rely on supervised training with large labeled datasets, leading to high costs and degraded performance on unknown generative models. To attenuate such deficiencies, we propose a training-free detection method. Specifically, noise residual fingerprints are first extracted by a simple yet effective pre-trained Noiseprint++ model. Then multi-scale features are further extracted from such residual by a frozen Vision Transformer (ViT), followed by adaptive weighted fusion. Only a few real image samples are used needed to initialize the clustering centers for unsupervised K-Means, distinguishing real and synthetic images without training. Extensive evaluations on four benchmark datasets show that our proposed scheme achieves an average accuracy of 82.2%, outperforming the state-of-the-art detectors on generalization ability. Superior performance is gained on the popular diffusion type of synthetic images, and the effectiveness of each module is validated by ablation studies. Source code will be publicly available at https://github.com/multimediaFor/NoiseCluSID.

AI.tldr: Proposes a training-free synthetic image detection method using noise residual fingerprints from Noiseprint++, multi-scale features from frozen ViT, and unsupervised K-Means clustering with few real samples, achieving 82.2% average accuracy and outperforming state-of-the-art detectors.
AI.motivation: Synthetic images from generative AI pose security threats (misinformation, fraud). Existing supervised detectors require large labeled datasets, incur high costs, and generalize poorly to unknown generative models.
AI.method: (1) Extract noise residual fingerprints via pre-trained Noiseprint++ model; (2) Extract multi-scale features using a frozen Vision Transformer (ViT); (3) Apply adaptive weighted fusion; (4) Use few real image samples to initialize K-Means clustering centers for unsupervised detection of real vs. synthetic images — no training required.
AI.result: Average accuracy of 82.2% on four benchmark datasets; outperforms state-of-the-art detectors in generalization; superior on diffusion-type synthetic images; ablation studies validate each module.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free, unsupervised clustering approach effectively detects synthetic images with strong generalization, especially for diffusion model outputs.

title: OS-Pruner: Pruning Chains-of-Thought of Reasoning Models via Optimal Stopping
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in complex reasoning tasks through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. However, these models often exhibit "computational overthinking," generating redundant reasoning steps that increase latency and cost without improving accuracy. Recent studies suggest that CoT trajectories can be significantly pruned, yet existing methods often rely on forcing a static thinking budget, heuristic filtering, sub-optimal early exit via classification, or expensive re-training. In this paper, we introduce OS-Pruner, a lightweight plug-in framework that formulates chain-of-thought pruning as an optimal stopping problem. Given a reasoning prefix, OS-Pruner learns whether further reasoning is worth its token cost by optimizing an explicit utility that trades off final-answer accuracy against generated length. Our novel formulation enables the model to dynamically assess the sufficient point of termination for a reasoning chain. OS-Pruner is designed to be lightweight during both training and inference, and to provide users with fine-grained control over the reasoning-effort vs. accuracy trade-off. On diverse reasoning benchmarks and base models, OS-Pruner achieves 20-60\% reduction in generation length with minimal accuracy sacrifice.

AI.tldr: OS-Pruner is a lightweight plug-in framework that formulates chain-of-thought pruning as an optimal stopping problem, dynamically deciding when to stop reasoning to reduce generation length by 20-60% with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit "computational overthinking" in CoT reasoning, generating redundant steps that increase latency and cost without improving accuracy. Existing pruning methods rely on static budgets, heuristic filtering, sub-optimal early exit via classification, or expensive re-training.
AI.method: OS-Pruner formulates CoT pruning as an optimal stopping problem. Given a reasoning prefix, it learns whether further reasoning is worth its token cost by optimizing an explicit utility that trades off final-answer accuracy against generated length, enabling dynamic assessment of termination point.
AI.result: Achieves 20-60% reduction in generation length with minimal accuracy sacrifice across diverse reasoning benchmarks and base models.
AI.conclusion: OS-Pruner provides a lightweight, plug-in framework that offers fine-grained control over the reasoning-effort vs. accuracy trade-off, effectively reducing computational overthinking without requiring static budgets or expensive re-training.

title: Auditing Construct Overlap in Explainable Machine Learning: Evidence from Burnout-Depression Prediction Across Student Cohorts
summary: Explainable machine learning (XML) pipelines applied to composite mental health outcomes can produce apparently-robust, cross-population-stable risk hierarchies that are largely artefacts of how the outcome was constructed. We demonstrate this using an ElasticNet pipeline applied to 886 medical students at the University of Lausanne (primary cohort, 2022), validated across 2,580 longitudinal observations at three time points and 701 non-medical students from eight faculties; all three datasets share identical instruments. The pipeline produces a hierarchy in which trait anxiety and health satisfaction dominate wherever the outcome is measured, with Kendall $τ= 1.0$ for the top-two positions across all five evaluation sets and consistent transfer performance ($R^2$: 0.41-0.49). Two residualization experiments, which isolate shared variance between correlated variables via regression, reveal the mechanism: when trait anxiety (STAI-T) is residualized against the co-included depression subscale (CES-D, $r = 0.72$), model $R^2$ drops from 0.41 to 0.16 and STAI-T falls from rank 1 to rank 6; when burnout subscales are residualized against CES-D, $R^2$ collapses to 0.016. Prediction intervals average 35.4 units on a 0-100 scale (2.4 outcome standard deviations), independently ruling out individual-level deployment. The residualization protocol is the paper's transferable contribution: any XAI study combining correlated predictor and outcome constructs should apply this check before interpreting apparent stability as a finding.

AI.tldr: Explainable ML pipelines can produce artifactually stable risk hierarchies when applied to composite mental health outcomes, as demonstrated by an ElasticNet study where trait anxiety dominance vanished after residualization against correlated depression measures, and prediction intervals were too wide for individual-level use.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that apparently robust, cross-population-stable risk hierarchies from XAI pipelines on composite mental health outcomes can be artifacts of how the outcome was constructed, rather than reflecting genuine causal relationships.
AI.method: An ElasticNet pipeline was applied to 886 medical students (primary cohort), validated across 2,580 longitudinal observations and 701 non-medical students from eight faculties. Two residualization experiments isolated shared variance between correlated variables via regression. Prediction intervals were computed to assess individual-level deployability.
AI.result: Trait anxiety and health satisfaction dominated consistently (Kendall τ=1.0 for top-two positions across all sets, R²=0.41-0.49). After residualizing STAI-T against CES-D (r=0.72), R² dropped to 0.16 and STAI-T fell from rank 1 to 6. Residualizing burnout subscales against CES-D collapsed R² to 0.016. Prediction intervals averaged 35.4 units (2.4 SDs), precluding individual-level use.
AI.conclusion: XAI studies combining correlated predictor and outcome constructs should apply residualization checks before interpreting apparent cross-population stability as a genuine finding. The residualization protocol is the paper's transferable methodological contribution.

title: Traj-VLN: Learning Pixel-Space Interaction via Autoregressive Trajectory Generation
summary: Benefiting from the powerful priors embedded in large-scale pre-training data and the emerging commonsense reasoning ability, large language models (LLMs) have shown unprecedented generalization capabilities in many research fields. Recently, projecting visual embeddings into the language space via vision-language models (VLMs) to achieve sim-toreal and cross-scene generalization has become a prevailing paradigm in the field of Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE). VLN requires an embodied agent to navigate through unseen environments following natural linguistic instructions. We emphasize that a VLN task can be decomposed into a sequence of sub-tasks, each corresponding to a process of 3D spatial interaction with the environments described by instructions such as "walk to the end of the sofa and turn left." However, such spatial interactions involving moving into the image along the direction of depth sensing are puzzling for VLMs as they were predominantly trained on conversations with RGB images. Rather than incorporating depth or 3D geometric information-which VLMs rarely encounter during pretrainingwe propose an alternative approach: fine-tuning VLMs to learn navigation interactions directly in 2D pixel space through autoregressive trajectory generation. Given a linguistic instruction and historical observations, our model sequentially predicts a series of pixel coordinates, drawing a trajectory from the bottom center of the current observation. While prior work has proved that pixel-goal supervision outperforms learning of discrete actions, our experiments further verify that the supervision of pixel-space trajectory significantly enhances VLN performance. Moreover, we demonstrate that our flagship model achieves state-of-the-art level performance with relatively limited computational resources and training data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes fine-tuning VLMs to directly learn navigation interactions in 2D pixel space via autoregressive trajectory generation for VLN-CE, achieving SOTA performance with limited resources.
AI.motivation: VLMs are predominantly trained on RGB image conversations and struggle with 3D spatial interactions (e.g., depth perception) required in VLN-CE tasks. Rather than incorporating depth/3D information unfamiliar to VLMs, the authors aim to enable navigation learning directly in 2D pixel space.
AI.method: Fine-tuning VLMs to autoregressively predict pixel coordinates, drawing a trajectory from the bottom center of the current observation given linguistic instructions and historical observations. This formulates navigation as pixel-space trajectory generation rather than discrete action prediction or depth-informed approaches.
AI.result: Pixel-space trajectory supervision significantly outperforms pixel-goal supervision and discrete action learning. The flagship model achieves state-of-the-art performance with relatively limited computational resources and training data.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing VLN tasks into sub-tasks of 2D pixel trajectory generation is an effective alternative to incorporating 3D geometric information for VLMs, enabling strong sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization without requiring depth perception.

title: A Formal Hierarchical Architecture for Agentic Orchestration with Stack-Based Execution and Lazy Discovery
summary: The rapid expansion of capabilities in Large Language Model (LLM) agents has exposed a critical architectural bottleneck: when agents are given access to a flat, monolithic registry of tools, the model must evaluate hundreds or thousands of options simultaneously. This leads to decision-space explosion, context window saturation, and degraded routing accuracy. To address these limitations, this paper presents a hierarchical, skill-based architecture for agentic orchestration. Capabilities are organized as a rooted tree where internal nodes make routing decisions and leaf nodes execute deterministic tasks. The runtime enforces a single-step execution loop governed by a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack, giving the agent a form of memory akin to a Pushdown Automaton, therefore enabling it to track nested execution contexts and resume deterministically from any depth. Capability discovery follows a manifest-driven, lazy-loading protocol: only the immediate children of the active node are loaded, so memory and prompt costs scale with the explored path rather than the global registry. By replacing global memory with localized stack frames, the architecture prevents outputs from one execution branch from leaking into another, establishing the isolation guarantees required for deployment in regulated enterprise environments. We also discuss UPI Help, an AI-powered digital payments support product, as a motivating production deployment context. We provide a mathematical formalization of the orchestration state, detailed algorithmic analysis of the execution loop, and controlled benchmarks comparing flat and hierarchical routing under increasing tool catalogs, multi-step workflow pressure, and visible schema-token exposure per LLM call.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical, skill-based architecture for LLM agents that uses a rooted tree of capabilities with LIFO stack-based execution, manifest-driven lazy loading, and localized stack frames to overcome the limitations of flat tool registries, such as decision-space explosion and context window saturation.
AI.motivation: Flat, monolithic tool registries in LLM agents lead to decision-space explosion, context window saturation, and degraded routing accuracy when the number of available tools grows large, creating a critical architectural bottleneck.
AI.method: Capabilities are organized as a rooted tree (internal nodes route, leaf nodes execute); runtime uses a LIFO stack (Pushdown Automaton-like memory) for nested context tracking; manifests enable lazy-loading so only immediate children of the active node are loaded; localized stack frames isolate execution branches.
AI.result: Controlled benchmarks compare flat vs. hierarchical routing under increasing tool catalogs, multi-step workflow pressure, and visible schema-token exposure per LLM call, demonstrating improvements in routing accuracy and reduced context saturation.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical architecture with stack-based isolation and lazy loading provides scalability and memory isolation guarantees suitable for regulated enterprise deployments, as demonstrated in the UPI Help production context.

title: Modernizing HEBO: a robust Bayesian optimization baseline for practical heteroskedastic and non-stationary problems
summary: Bayesian optimization is increasingly used to guide data-efficient experimentation in chemistry, materials science, and related laboratory settings, but its practical performance depends strongly on how well surrogate-model assumptions match the geometry and noise structure of the underlying objective. We introduce tidyHEBO, a robust Bayesian optimization model inspired by heteroskedastic evolutionary Bayesian optimization (HEBO) for single-objective, sequential optimization. tidyHEBO reconstructs the HEBO design philosophy in BoTorch and revises surrogate training, output-warping selection, acquisition function evaluation, and Pareto-front search. We benchmarked tidyHEBO on synthetic functions, Olympus emulators, fully experimental reaction-optimization datasets, needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) materials problems, and Bayesmark hyperparameter optimization tasks. On these tasks tidyHEBO achieved competitive to superior performance and improvement in robustness across repeated optimization runs. We therefore propose tidyHEBO as a practical tool for sequential experimentations and a strong general-purpose benchmark for future Bayesian optimization research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces tidyHEBO, a robust Bayesian optimization model built on the HEBO framework using BoTorch, which improves surrogate training, output-warping selection, acquisition function evaluation, and Pareto-front search. It demonstrates competitive to superior performance with improved robustness across synthetic functions, experimental datasets, materials problems, and hyperparameter optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Bayesian optimization's practical performance depends heavily on how well surrogate-model assumptions match the geometry and noise structure of the objective; existing approaches often lack robustness across diverse experimental settings.
AI.method: tidyHEBO reconstructs the HEBO design philosophy in BoTorch, revising surrogate training, output-warping selection, acquisition function evaluation, and Pareto-front search.
AI.result: Competitive to superior performance and improved robustness across synthetic functions, Olympus emulators, experimental reaction-optimization datasets, needle-in-a-haystack materials problems, and Bayesmark hyperparameter optimization tasks.
AI.conclusion: tidyHEBO is proposed as a practical tool for sequential experimentation and a strong general-purpose benchmark for future Bayesian optimization research.

title: Water Reflection Detection Using Symmetric Attention
summary: Reflections of water pose a significant challenge for computer vision systems, as standard deep learning models frequently confuse objects with their mirror images, producing spurious false positives and negatives in tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation. As a result, detecting reflection axes in natural-water scenes is pivotal for reliable object detection and scene understanding. To mitigate this issue, we leverage the intrinsic imperfect reflective symmetry of water and introduce a Symmetry-Aware Water Reflection Detection Network, namely, SAWRD-Net, that couples dihedral group-equivariant convolutions with a matrix-decomposition decoder in an end-to-end framework. First, dihedral group convolutional layers extract geometry-consistent feature maps that explicitly encode both rotational and mirror symmetries. A Multi-scale Reflection Equivariant block then aggregates features across scales and employs a symmetric-attention mechanism to highlight reflection-relevant regions. The proposed matrix-decomposition decoder factorizes high-dimensional features into compact low-rank parameter and confidence spaces, after which the network directly regresses keypoints on the reflection axis. Then a robust principal component analysis fits the final axis. Evaluated on the largest available water reflection scene data set, SAWRD-Net achieves a true-positive rate of 0.890 against human annotations, outperforming all existing water reflection detectors.

AI.tldr: SAWRD-Net is a symmetry-aware deep network that uses dihedral group-equivariant convolutions and a matrix-decomposition decoder to detect reflection axes in water scenes, achieving a 0.890 true-positive rate on the largest water reflection dataset.
AI.motivation: Water reflections cause spurious false positives and negatives in standard computer vision tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation, so detecting reflection axes in natural-water scenes is critical for reliable scene understanding.
AI.method: The network couples dihedral group-equivariant convolutions (extracting rotation and mirror symmetry features) with a Multi-scale Reflection Equivariant block using symmetric-attention, and a matrix-decomposition decoder that factorizes features into low-rank parameter and confidence spaces for keypoint regression, followed by robust PCA for final axis fitting.
AI.result: SAWRD-Net achieves a true-positive rate of 0.890 against human annotations, outperforming all existing water reflection detectors on the largest available water reflection scene dataset.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging the intrinsic imperfect reflective symmetry of water via group-equivariant architectures enables superior water reflection axis detection, mitigating confusion in downstream vision tasks.

title: NextFund: A Unified Performance Tracking Platform for Agentic Portfolio Management
summary: Large language models (LLMs) based agents are beginning to participate in portfolio construction and market analysis, where decisions must be justified under evolving information and risk constraints. Current assessment practice, however, remains poorly aligned with this setting: many studies rely on static examinations or report only terminal portfolio returns, while the intermediate evidence, analyst judgments, and execution steps that produced those returns stay largely invisible. We introduce NextFund, an evaluation platform that makes financial-agent behavior observable under live market conditions. The platform couples time-consistent market access, coordinated multi-agent analysis, and persistent logging of the full decision path from observation to trade. Through an interactive Trading Arena, users can compare models across markets, inspect equity curves, and drill from leaderboard outcomes down to individual justifications. We present NextFund on Hong Kong, U.S., and China A-share equities, illustrating how inspectable decision histories enable fairer benchmarking and more actionable diagnosis. Our demo is available at https://paradoox.cn/nextfund/.

AI.tldr: NextFund is a transparent evaluation platform that makes LLM-based financial agents' decision-making observable under live market conditions through time-consistent market access, multi-agent coordination, and full decision-path logging.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of LLM-based financial agents is poorly aligned with real-world settings: studies rely on static exams or only report terminal portfolio returns, leaving intermediate evidence, analyst judgments, and execution steps invisible, which hinders fair benchmarking and actionable diagnosis.
AI.method: NextFund provides a platform with time-consistent market access, coordinated multi-agent analysis, persistent logging of the full decision path from observation to trade, and an interactive Trading Arena for comparing models across markets and drilling down from leaderboard outcomes to individual justifications.
AI.result: Demonstrated on Hong Kong, U.S., and China A-share equities, showing that inspectable decision histories enable fairer benchmarking and more actionable diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: Making financial-agent decision processes observable under live conditions improves evaluation fairness and diagnostic utility for LLM-based trading agents.

title: From Self-Attention to Connection Laplacian: A Unified Operator View of Transformers
summary: Self-attention is a ubiquitous primitive in modern sequence models, yet its operator-level geometry is only partially understood. We view a token sequence as a vector field over the token-position graph and identify attention as a connection walk: messages are aggregated by a nonnegative walk matrix while being transported along each edge by a learned linear map. Within this framework, we prove that single-head attention (SHA) is exactly a connection propagation step with constant transport, and that multi-head attention (MHA) is exactly a single edge-dependent connection walk whose effective transport is an attention-gated mixture of headwise transports. We further clarify the conditions under which the corresponding generator reduces to a random-walk connection Laplacian, highlighting the roles of stochasticity, reversibility, and metric-compatible transports. Empirically, we find that trained Transformers across scales (from 124M to 8B) and structures (encoder/decoder) exhibit geometric structure consistent with our theory: effective attention graphs converge to stable geometric operators in deeper layers, learned transports self-organize into approximate scaled isometries, and both phenomena strengthen consistently with scale. Overall, the paper provides a precise connection-walk formalism that links self-attention to classical geometric operators, along with a set of operator-level tools for analyzing transformer models from a geometric perspective.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes self-attention as a connection walk over a token-position graph, proving that single-head attention corresponds to a connection propagation step and multi-head attention to an edge-dependent connection walk. It establishes conditions under which the attention generator reduces to a random-walk connection Laplacian. Empirical analysis of trained Transformers (124M-8B) confirms that attention graphs stabilize to geometric operators in deeper layers and learned transports become approximate scaled isometries, with these phenomena strengthening at scale.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous geometric understanding of self-attention's operator-level structure, bridging the gap between the empirical success of Transformers and the limited theoretical understanding of attention as a geometric operator.
AI.method: Formalizes token sequences as vector fields over a token-position graph, models attention as a connection walk with nonnegative walk matrix and learned linear edge transports, proves theoretical equivalences between SHA/MHA and connection propagation/walk, and validates predictions through empirical analysis of trained Transformers across scales (124M-8B).
AI.result: SHA is exactly a connection propagation step with constant transport; MHA is an edge-dependent connection walk with attention-gated mixture of headwise transports. Under stochasticity, reversibility, and metric-compatibility conditions, the generator reduces to a random-walk connection Laplacian. Empirically, attention graphs converge to stable geometric operators in deeper layers, and learned transports organize into approximate scaled isometries, both strengthening with model scale.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a precise connection-walk formalism linking self-attention to classical geometric operators (connection Laplacians), offering operator-level theoretical tools and revealing consistent geometric structure in trained Transformers that scales with model size.

title: TriCons-Pose: Triangle-Invariant Geometric Consistency Learning for Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
summary: Category-level object pose estimation is a crucial yet challenging task in both academia and industry, and has achieved remarkable success by leveraging keypoint-based correspondence paradigms. However, most existing methods increasingly rely on stronger feature learning while overlooking whether the established correspondences are geometrically stable across diverse perturbations. This often results in fragile pose recovery under intra-class shape variations and occlusions. To tackle this challenge, we develop a novel Triangle-Invariant Geometric Consistency Learning for Category-Level Object Pose Estimation (TriCons-Pose) to anchor stable keypoints and aggregate pose-invariant cues, yielding reliable canonical mapping and accurate pose estimation. Specifically, a Structure-Consistent Keypoint Detector (SCKD) is designed to identify robust keypoints by enforcing cross-view structural consistency via normalized pairwise distance matching. Moreover, we propose a Pose-Invariant Geometric Aggregator (PIGA) to augment keypoint representations by injecting triangle-based pose-invariant descriptors into a local-to-global attention mechanism. The proposed framework is optimized using standard objective functions while incorporating an additional geometry consistency loss. Extensive experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25, and HouseCat6D datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: TriCons-Pose is a category-level object pose estimation method that uses triangle-invariant geometric consistency learning to identify stable keypoints and aggregate pose-invariant cues, achieving robust canonical mapping and accurate pose recovery under intra-class shape variations and occlusions.
AI.motivation: Existing keypoint-based correspondence methods for category-level pose estimation increasingly rely on stronger feature learning but overlook whether established correspondences are geometrically stable across diverse perturbations, leading to fragile pose recovery under intra-class shape variations and occlusions.
AI.method: Proposes (1) a Structure-Consistent Keypoint Detector (SCKD) that enforces cross-view structural consistency via normalized pairwise distance matching to identify robust keypoints, and (2) a Pose-Invariant Geometric Aggregator (PIGA) that injects triangle-based pose-invariant descriptors into a local-to-global attention mechanism to augment keypoint representations. Optimized with standard objectives plus a geometry consistency loss.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25, and HouseCat6D datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TriCons-Pose.
AI.conclusion: Triangle-invariant geometric consistency learning anchors stable keypoints and aggregates pose-invariant cues, yielding reliable canonical mapping and accurate pose estimation for category-level objects.

title: The Hidden Footprint: Making Storage a First-Class Metric for LLM Agent Evaluation
summary: LLM agent benchmarks measure task completion, reliability, and inference cost, but not the persistent data an agent run leaves on disk, including logs, context snapshots, checkpoints, and debug traces. We introduce AgentFootprint, a cross-framework benchmark of post-run agent storage footprint. Its serialization-aware metric suite measures total retention, channel composition, duplication, growth, compressibility, and conversation-history reconstructability. It addresses a measurement trap: naive byte-level measurement understates duplication by an order of magnitude because database paging and JSON escaping obscure repeated content. A fixed-trace control separates agent-generated logical volume from persistence-layer amplification: replaying the same trajectory through seven persisting frameworks yields a 6.7x spread. Under identical models, tools, and tasks, configurations with 100% accuracy differ by 15.7x in retained bytes, although their defaults support different recovery and audit capabilities. Three full-history configurations grow superlinearly on a repeated-observation stress task. Exported trajectories from 108 instance-normalized SWE-bench Verified submissions span three orders of magnitude per instance, with no detectable correlation with resolve rate. A content-addressed store reduces retention by 4.8x-32.7x while preserving every reconstructability score. These results establish persistent storage as a resource metric to report jointly with accuracy and reconstructability.

AI.tldr: AgentFootprint is a benchmark that measures the persistent storage footprint (logs, checkpoints, traces) of LLM agent runs, revealing huge disparities (up to 15.7x in retained bytes) across frameworks with identical accuracy, and showing that deduplication via content-addressed storage can reduce footprint 4.8–32.7x without losing reconstructability.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks focus on task completion, reliability, and cost, but ignore the persistent data (logs, snapshots, checkpoints, debug traces) left on disk, which affects storage, auditability, and reproducibility.
AI.method: Introduces AgentFootprint, a cross-framework benchmark with serialization-aware metrics (total retention, channel composition, duplication, growth, compressibility, reconstructability). Uses a fixed-trace control to separate agent-generated logical volume from persistence-layer amplification, and evaluates seven frameworks, SWE-bench submissions, and content-addressed stores.
AI.result: 7 frameworks replaying the same trajectory show a 6.7x storage spread; configurations with 100% accuracy differ by 15.7x in retained bytes; SWE-bench trajectories span three orders of magnitude per instance with no correlation to resolve rate; content-addressed store reduces retention 4.8–32.7x while preserving reconstructability.
AI.conclusion: Persistent storage is a crucial resource metric that should be reported alongside accuracy and reconstructability, as naive byte-level measurement significantly understates duplication.

title: LayerNorm as Implicit Gain Control in Looped Transformers
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Code available at https://github.com/clojure-finance/mythjure/tree/paper-v1
summary: In pre-LayerNorm looped transformers, LayerNorm inside the recurrent block acts as an implicit gain controller: by coupling the block's local Lipschitz constant inversely to the activation scale, it renders the recurrence Jacobian non-normal -- asymptotically contractive at every verified fixed point even where its operator norm exceeds 1 -- so the true stability budget is the spectral margin, not an operator-norm bound. That margin depletes as the carry $ρ\to 1$, and a minority of initializations never converge to a fixed point at all, so the diagonal carry constraint $ρ(\bar{A}) < 1$ is necessary but not sufficient for convergence of the full recurrence. Training experiments across six tasks, including a controlled ablation, reveal that the linear carry is not the depth-memory mechanism: gradient descent routes memory through the block's more expressive nonlinear recurrence and leaves the stability-constrained carry at rest -- the carry's role is stabilization, not memory. We characterize the boundary of this claim: on tasks with axis-aligned per-channel structure, gradient descent does recruit the carry. All results are derived analytically and verified in a from-scratch, CPU-scale implementation; verification at larger scale is needed.

AI.tldr: In pre-LayerNorm looped transformers, LayerNorm acts as an implicit gain controller that couples local Lipschitz constant inversely to activation scale, making recurrence Jacobian non-normal and contractive at fixed points. The linear carry's spectral radius < 1 is necessary but not sufficient for convergence; gradient descent routes memory through nonlinear recurrence, not the carry, except on axis-aligned per-channel tasks.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of LayerNorm and the linear carry (diagonal state matrix) in looped transformers, particularly regarding stability, convergence, and whether the carry serves as a memory mechanism or a stabilizer.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of Jacobian properties under pre-LayerNorm recurrence; training experiments across six tasks with controlled ablation to isolate the linear carry's role; verification in from-scratch CPU-scale implementation.
AI.result: LayerNorm creates non-normal Jacobian with contractive fixed points; spectral margin (not operator norm) determines stability. The linear carry constraint ρ(Ā) < 1 is necessary but insufficient for convergence. Gradient descent uses nonlinear recurrence for memory and keeps the carry at rest for stabilization, except on axis-aligned per-channel tasks.
AI.conclusion: The linear carry's primary role is stabilization, not depth-memory; the claim has a boundary condition on axis-aligned per-channel tasks. Larger-scale verification is needed.

title: TOLiD: Bridging the Architecture Gap in Vision Foundation Model to LiDAR Pretraining via Token Lifting for Distillation
comment: Accepted to The IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
summary: Cross-modal distillation from Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to LiDAR backbones has recently emerged as a self-supervised pretraining strategy that reduces reliance on dense point-wise annotation for 3D scene understanding. However, existing distillation pipelines typically treat the VFM as a frozen feature source and train a heterogeneous 3D backbone to match fixed image embeddings, forcing the student to bridge both the modality gap and the cross-architecture gap between dense ViT token representations and sparse 3D encoders. We propose TOLiD, a self-supervised pretraining method for LiDAR representation learning that addresses this gap by coupling a LiDAR backbone with a student Vision Transformer (ViT) initialized from a frozen VFM teacher and applying supervision over compatible patch-token representations. TOLiD converts the set of point features within each image patch frustum into a token using Frustum Pooling followed by Frustum Attention, and performs token-level distillation with visibility masking. For LiDAR-only deployment, we lift token features back to per-point representations using masked bilinear sampling to avoid patches that have limited LiDAR points. We extensively evaluate TOLiD on five heterogeneous LiDAR datasets and four cross-sensor adaptation pairs, demonstrating improved transfer with frozen backbones and lightweight heads.

AI.tldr: TOLiD is a self-supervised pretraining method that distills knowledge from Vision Foundation Models (ViT-based) into LiDAR backbones using frustum-based token-level alignment and visibility masking, enabling effective cross-modal and cross-architecture representation learning without dense annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-modal distillation from VFMs to LiDAR requires bridging both modality and cross-architecture gaps between dense ViT token representations and sparse 3D encoders, while treating the VFM as a frozen feature source.
AI.method: TOLiD couples a LiDAR backbone with a student ViT initialized from a frozen VFM teacher, converts point features within each image patch frustum into tokens via Frustum Pooling and Frustum Attention, performs token-level distillation with visibility masking, and lifts token features back to per-point representations using masked bilinear sampling for LiDAR-only deployment.
AI.result: Evaluated on five heterogeneous LiDAR datasets and four cross-sensor adaptation pairs, demonstrating improved transfer with frozen backbones and lightweight heads.
AI.conclusion: TOLiD effectively addresses cross-modal and cross-architecture gaps in LiDAR representation learning through compatible patch-token representations and frustum-based token distillation, reducing reliance on dense point-wise annotations.

title: STAMP: Provenance-Guided Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning for deep-search agents has largely focused on trajectory-level scoring -- outcome correctness, citation-aware rewards, and evidence coverage. Yet the actions that expose supporting documents receive no targeted credit, a gap we call the reward-credit mismatch. We propose STAMP, in which a reference-based verifier judges whether each cited document supports an entity or relation in a training-time evidence graph, and first-exposure attribution traces each supported citation back to the action that first surfaced it. This step credit is injected through sign-preserving advantage modulation, which redistributes advantage across steps without changing the trajectory-level reward or the relative ranking of trajectories within each group. On BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, and xbench-DS, STAMP improves the GRPO baseline by +2.0/+5.5/+3.0 points under matched SFT initialization, training data, and search tools, and composes with both outcome-only and citation-rubric base rewards. Component ablations confirm that the provenance-based credit signal and the sign-preserving advantage modulation each contribute to the gains.

AI.tldr: STAMP addresses the reward-credit mismatch in deep-search RL by providing step-level credit to actions that first surface supporting documents via reference-based verification and sign-preserving advantage modulation, improving GRPO by +2.0/+5.5/+3.0 on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, and xbench-DS.
AI.motivation: Existing RL for deep-search agents uses trajectory-level rewards (correctness, citation, coverage), but actions that expose supporting documents receive no targeted credit, creating a reward-credit mismatch.
AI.method: STAMP uses (1) a reference-based verifier to judge document support against an evidence graph, (2) first-exposure attribution tracing each supported citation to the action that first surfaced it, and (3) sign-preserving advantage modulation that redistributes advantage across steps without altering trajectory-level reward or group rankings.
AI.result: STAMP yields +2.0/+5.5/+3.0 points over GRPO baseline on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, and xbench-DS under matched settings, and composes with both outcome-only and citation-rubric rewards. Ablations confirm both provenance-based credit and sign-preserving modulation contribute.
AI.conclusion: Providing targeted step-level credit for document-surfacing actions via provenance attribution and sign-preserving advantage modulation significantly improves deep-search agent performance without altering trajectory-level reward structure.

title: Learning to Fine-tune Foundation Models under Resource Limitations
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, accepted and presented at ICMLCN 2026
summary: We study the problem of optimal continual fine-tuning for a pre-trained Foundation Model deployed at a resource-limited device. At each time slot, a new batch of training data arrives, and the controller is faced with two options: either use the data to fine-tune the model and incur a compute cost, or do not fine-tune the model and discard the data. After the decision, the performance of the current model is measured in terms of an application-specific performance metric such as classification accuracy. Our objective is to learn an optimal policy that determines \emph{when to fine-tune the model} on a single task (e.g., sentiment analysis), under a finite compute budget. We formulate this online decision-making problem as a constrained Markov Decision Process, where the system state captures three essential aspects: (\textit{i}) model's performance, (\textit{ii}) computational budget, and (\textit{iii}) data distribution relevance to historic data encountered up to that point. The transition to the next state is stochastic and therefore, we propose a reinforcement learning-based method to solve this problem, namely the \emph{actor-critic} algorithm. We also consider the special case where the performance of fine-tuning for a given model can be predicted or estimated prior to decision; in this case the problem becomes a Dynamic Programming one. Experiments with a large pre-trained model on a widely-used text classification dataset demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms fine-tuning approaches with the same compute budget by more than $4\%$ in terms of accuracy and achieves $97\%$ of full-parameter fine-tuning accuracy while requiring only $25\%$ of the fine-tuning steps.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning-based (actor-critic) method to determine when to fine-tune a pre-trained Foundation Model on a resource-limited device under a finite compute budget, formulating the problem as a constrained Markov Decision Process. The method achieves 97% of full-parameter fine-tuning accuracy while using only 25% of fine-tuning steps, outperforming baselines by >4% in accuracy.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of optimal continual fine-tuning for a pre-trained Foundation Model deployed at a resource-limited device, where the controller must decide at each time slot whether to fine-tune (incurring compute cost) or skip (discarding data) under a finite compute budget.
AI.method: Formulated as a constrained Markov Decision Process with state capturing (i) model performance, (ii) computational budget, and (iii) data distribution relevance. Solved via a reinforcement learning-based actor-critic algorithm. A special case with predictable fine-tuning performance is solved using Dynamic Programming.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms fine-tuning approaches with the same compute budget by more than 4% in accuracy and achieves 97% of full-parameter fine-tuning accuracy while requiring only 25% of the fine-tuning steps.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RL-based selective fine-tuning strategy is highly effective for resource-constrained continual learning, significantly reducing computation while maintaining accuracy close to full fine-tuning.

title: RED-Sphere: Hyperspherical Residual Edge Debiasing for Cross-Population Fundus Disease Domain Generalization
summary: Medical image classifiers are often trained within one source population, yet clinical deployment requires robustness to patients whose appearance, acquisition style, and disease prevalence differ from the source cohort. Existing fairness and robustness methods often require group supervision or treat appearance variation as an undifferentiated nuisance, which is insufficient when population-correlated low-level cues and lesion evidence share edge and texture structure. We study a strict source-only cross-population setting, where external populations are unseen during optimization, validation, scheduling, hyperparameter and model selection. We propose RED-Sphere, a plug-and-play robustness framework for image classification under unseen population shifts. It estimates shortcut-sensitive nuisance responses with an edge and feature energy prior, attenuates dominant responses through residual soft gating, regularizes masked nuisance views with counterfactual-inspired consistency and separation losses, and predicts labels with normalized spherical prototypes. It favours angular semantic evidence over source-correlated activation magnitude while preserving lesion structure. Although demonstrated on 2D Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscopy (SLO) fundus classification for Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) and Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), RED-Sphere is not tied to retinal anatomy: the same principle can be adapted with modality-specific nuisance priors wherever appearance shortcuts and semantic evidence are entangled. Under a strict White-only Harvard-FairVision protocol, RED-Sphere improves held-out macro-F1 across all 20 task and backbone comparisons, with average gains of 1.28 and 2.98 F1 points on AMD and DR. Gains in AUC and PR-AUC, visual diagnostics, ablations, and sensitivity analyses further support stronger external semantic alignment and more stable angular disease geometry.

AI.tldr: RED-Sphere is a plug-and-play robustness framework for medical image classification that improves cross-population generalization by suppressing shortcut-sensitive edge/texture features and enhancing angular semantic evidence, achieving consistent F1 gains across AMD and DR tasks under strict source-only settings.
AI.motivation: Medical image classifiers trained on one population fail to generalize to unseen populations due to appearance shifts (e.g., acquisition style, disease prevalence). Existing fairness/robustness methods require group supervision or treat appearance variation as undifferentiated nuisance, which is inadequate when population-correlated low-level cues and lesion evidence share edge/texture structure.
AI.method: RED-Sphere: (1) estimates shortcut-sensitive nuisance responses using an edge and feature energy prior; (2) attenuates dominant responses via residual soft gating; (3) regularizes masked nuisance views with counterfactual-inspired consistency and separation losses; (4) predicts labels with normalized spherical prototypes to favor angular semantic evidence over source-correlated activation magnitude.
AI.result: Under a strict White-only Harvard-FairVision protocol, RED-Sphere improves held-out macro-F1 across all 20 task/backbone comparisons, averaging +1.28 F1 on AMD and +2.98 F1 on DR. Gains in AUC, PR-AUC, visual diagnostics, ablations, and sensitivity analyses confirm stronger external semantic alignment and stable angular disease geometry.
AI.conclusion: RED-Sphere effectively handles unseen population shifts in a source-only setting without group supervision. While demonstrated on 2D SLO fundus classification (AMD and DR), the principle is generalizable to other modalities with appropriate nuisance priors where appearance shortcuts and semantic evidence are entangled.

title: The Path to Self-Evolving Clinical Systems: Scaling Medical Agents from Assistance to Autonomy
summary: The growing ability of large language models and vision language models to jointly interpret and reason over images and text is reshaping medical agents, moving them from task specific predictors toward autonomous systems that perceive, reason, plan, remember, and act in clinical environments. This work departs from the capability first perspective of existing literature and instead begins from clinical deployment, asking what tasks, contamination resistant benchmarks, and interactive training environments are required before medical agents can be trusted in practice. Medical agents are formalized as sequential decision making systems under partial observability, together with a three level autonomy taxonomy spanning assisted, cooperative, and fully autonomous operation. The field is organized along a unified scaling spine consisting of framework scaling, capability scaling, and environment scaling. Within this framework, clinical environment scaling, the integration of tools, data, and clinical gyms, is identified as the most actionable yet underexplored direction for agents operating in PACS, EHR, and FHIR ecosystems. Clinical self evolution, where agents improve through interaction with their environments rather than parameter scaling alone, is further positioned as a key research frontier, drawing insights from self improving agents, agent gyms, and test time compute scaling. Applications across radiology, pathology, ophthalmology, and hospital workflows are examined together with deployment challenges including hallucination, cascading failures, and fairness. By consolidating more than 300 references, with particular emphasis on advances from 2025 to 2026, this work provides a roadmap toward trustworthy, self improving medical imaging systems for real clinical practice.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deployment-first framework for medical agents (LLMs/VLMs) with a three-level autonomy taxonomy, a unified scaling spine (framework, capability, environment), and identifies clinical environment scaling and self-evolution as key frontiers toward trustworthy clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing literature takes a capability-first perspective; this work instead begins from clinical deployment requirements, asking what tasks, benchmarks, and training environments are needed before medical agents can be trusted in practice.
AI.method: Formalizes medical agents as sequential decision-making systems under partial observability with a three-level autonomy taxonomy (assisted, cooperative, fully autonomous). Organizes the field via a unified scaling spine (framework, capability, environment scaling) and identifies clinical environment scaling (PACS, EHR, FHIR ecosystems) as the most actionable direction.
AI.result: Clinical environment scaling—integrating tools, data, and clinical gyms—is identified as the most actionable yet underexplored direction. Clinical self-evolution (improvement through interaction rather than parameter scaling) is positioned as a key research frontier. Applications across radiology, pathology, ophthalmology, and hospital workflows are examined with deployment challenges including hallucination, cascading failures, and fairness.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a roadmap toward trustworthy, self-improving medical imaging systems for real clinical practice, consolidating >300 references with emphasis on 2025–2026 advances.

title: On the modality gap and the contrastive loss in multi-modal representation learning
summary: We study the modality gap in CLIP-style dual-encoder contrastive learning, where image and text embeddings remain misaligned despite being trained in a shared space. We argue that the gap is induced by a failure of the InfoNCE formulation with independent encoders. We conduct a uni-modal experiment with two independent encoders and identical initialization conditions and find that InfoNCE actively generates a gap at low temperatures. We provide a theoretical analysis of this phenomenon and show that the modality gap is indeed a mode-failure of InfoNCE, but only at low temperatures. We propose a simple modification called xNCE, which uses intermodal as well as intra-modality negative contrastive pairs. xNCE matches retrieval performance on MS-COCO while consistently reducing the gap even at low temperatures. Notably, xNCE improves zero-shot classification over the InfoNCE baseline across all benchmarks, whereas high-temperature InfoNCE and regularized InfoNCE both fail to do so, demonstrating that xNCE reduces the modality gap without sacrificing the discriminative geometry needed for transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that the modality gap in CLIP-style models (misalignment between image and text embeddings) is caused by InfoNCE loss at low temperatures, and proposes xNCE, which adds intra-modality negative pairs to bridge this gap while improving zero-shot classification performance.
AI.motivation: To understand and resolve the modality gap phenomenon in dual-encoder contrastive learning (e.g., CLIP), where image and text embeddings remain separated despite being trained in a shared space.
AI.method: The authors conduct uni-modal experiments with two independent encoders and identical initialization to isolate the gap phenomenon, provide theoretical analysis showing InfoNCE induces a gap at low temperatures, and propose xNCE—a modified loss that incorporates both inter-modal and intra-modal negative contrastive pairs.
AI.result: xNCE matches InfoNCE on MS-COCO retrieval while consistently reducing the modality gap at low temperatures. It also improves zero-shot classification across all benchmarks, unlike high-temperature InfoNCE or regularized InfoNCE.
AI.conclusion: The modality gap is a mode-failure of InfoNCE specific to low temperatures, and xNCE effectively reduces this gap without sacrificing the discriminative embedding geometry needed for transfer tasks.

title: Is Energy Guidance All You Need? Training-Free Norm Injection for Driving World Models
comment: Accepted to Robotics: Science and Systems 2026 Robot World Models Workshop
summary: Driving world models built on large video-diffusion backbones generate realistic scenes but are hard to control: enforcing a traffic norm typically means retraining the backbone or conditioning it on hand-built layouts. We ask whether controllability requires training at all. Our experiment shows that a rectified-flow driving world model, which jointly generates future video and a planned ego trajectory, can have its planned trajectory steered entirely at sampling time by differentiable energy functions that encode driving norms, without knowledge-specific retraining of the diffusion backbone. Concretely, we demonstrate that a world model built on Open-Sora 2.0 MM-DiT backbone can be steered to brake at a counterfactual target by injecting energy guidance at sampling time. However, we find that the generated video does not yet follow the steered trajectory through the backbone's joint self-attention and identify the cross-stream coupling as a crucial requirement for end-to-end-controllable rollouts.

AI.tldr: A rectified-flow driving world model with joint video-trajectory generation can be steered at sampling time via differentiable energy functions encoding driving norms, without retraining the diffusion backbone.
AI.motivation: Driving world models built on large video-diffusion backbones generate realistic scenes but lack controllability—enforcing traffic norms typically requires retraining the backbone or conditioning on hand-built layouts. The authors ask whether controllability can be achieved without any training.
AI.method: The authors use a rectified-flow driving world model that jointly generates future video and a planned ego trajectory, built on Open-Sora 2.0 MM-DiT backbone. At sampling time, differentiable energy functions encoding driving norms (e.g., braking at a counterfactual target) inject energy guidance to steer the planned trajectory without retraining the diffusion backbone.
AI.result: The world model can be steered to brake at a counterfactual target by injecting energy guidance at sampling time. However, the generated video does not yet follow the steered trajectory through the backbone's joint self-attention; cross-stream coupling is identified as a crucial missing requirement for end-to-end-controllable rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Controllability of driving world models can be achieved without retraining via sampling-time energy guidance, but full end-to-end control requires stronger cross-stream coupling between the video and trajectory generation streams in the backbone's joint self-attention.

title: SCALECUA: Scaling Computer Use Agents with Verifiable Task Synthesis and Efficient Online RL
summary: Computer use agents (CUAs) are emerging as a powerful interface for automating complex digital workflows through visual perception and GUI execution. Online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a key direction for scaling their capabilities. However, this paradigm is bottlenecked by verifiable data scarcity and online RL inefficiency. To break these barriers, we introduce ScaleCUA, a unified framework that scales online RL for CUAs via verifiable task synthesis and efficient training. At the data level, we design VeriGen, an end-to-end framework for generating verifiable RL tasks through iterative docker interactions and a multi-agent feedback loop. Scaled to 100+ concurrent agent workers via a shared docker interaction probe, this pipeline produces 24K+ verifiable tasks and nearly 3K high-quality RL tasks. To maximize sample efficiency, we propose Frontier Sampling, which tracks per-task capability and allocates rollouts to the current learning frontier. On the training side, we further design Visual Context Segmentation, a sliding window over recent visual context that balances rollout and training-engine pressure, yielding a 2.83x training speedup over step-wise decomposition. Together, ScaleCUA achieves 68.7% on OSWorld and 54.0% on ScienceBoard, establishing new state-of-the-art performance among open-source computer use agents. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/THUDM/SCALE-CUA.

AI.tldr: ScaleCUA is a unified framework for scaling online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for computer use agents (CUAs), introducing VeriGen for verifiable task synthesis (24K+ tasks), Frontier Sampling for efficient rollout allocation, and Visual Context Segmentation for 2.83x training speedup, achieving SOTA performance on OSWorld (68.7%) and ScienceBoard (54.0%).
AI.motivation: Online RLVR for CUAs is bottlenecked by verifiable data scarcity and online RL inefficiency.
