AI.method: (1) VeriGen: end-to-end verifiable task generation via iterative docker interactions and multi-agent feedback loop; (2) Frontier Sampling: per-task capability tracking for efficient rollout allocation; (3) Visual Context Segmentation: sliding window over visual context for 2.83x training speedup.
AI.result: 68.7% on OSWorld and 54.0% on ScienceBoard, establishing new SOTA among open-source CUAs.
AI.conclusion: ScaleCUA effectively breaks the data scarcity and inefficiency barriers in online RLVR for CUAs through scalable task synthesis and efficient training techniques, achieving SOTA performance.

title: Scaffold splits hide structural-frontier failures in ADMET models
summary: Molecular property models are commonly evaluated by holding out Bemis--Murcko scaffolds, yet a scaffold identifier is only one notion of chemical unfamiliarity. We introduce a label-free structural-frontier split that reserves the sparsest and most physicochemically remote scaffold groups, and evaluate it on six public experimental or curated ADMET tasks. Against a 70/10/20 scaffold control with identical acyclic grouping, the frontier inflates equally weighted primary error with a taskwise median of 87.0\% and a skew-sensitive mean of 130.3\% (descriptive task/seed bootstrap interval, 52.1--246.0\%). The mean falls to 75.9\% once BBB is removed; that endpoint is the one whose score ranking inverts at the frontier. A message-passing graph-network control still shows a large gap (mean 82.8\% over four tasks) and does not invert, so a low-capacity head does not explain the effect. We also test Multi-View Frontier Risk Extrapolation (\method), a count-adjusted tail-risk penalty over four molecular views, and treat it as a falsifiable probe. It changes normalized frontier error by only 0.16\% relative to empirical risk minimization for the perceptron head (interval, $-0.43$--0.84\%) and by $-1.9$\% for the graph network; three fixed robust-penalty controls are likewise inconclusive. Against the published Lo-Hi and DataSAIL splitters the frontier inflates error more on average, though no split is uniformly hardest. An audit of 31,561 marine natural products further shows that OOD status and agreement with legacy ADMET predictions depend on the molecular view, endpoint and teacher coverage. Split construction and label provenance are important evaluation constraints in their own right, and the tested training penalties do not resolve the frontier failures we observe.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a label-free structural-frontier split that reserves the sparsest and most physicochemically remote scaffold groups for molecular property model evaluation, showing that this split inflates error significantly (87-130% median/mean increase) compared to standard scaffold splits, and that robust training penalties like Multi-View Frontier Risk Extrapolation fail to resolve these failures.
AI.motivation: Standard Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits are insufficient for evaluating molecular property models because a scaffold identifier captures only one notion of chemical unfamiliarity. The authors seek to create a more challenging evaluation split that tests models on truly out-of-distribution (OOD) regions of chemical space.
AI.method: The authors design a label-free structural-frontier split that holds out the sparsest and most physicochemically distant scaffold groups. They evaluate this split across six ADMET tasks using both a perceptron head and a message-passing graph network. They also propose Multi-View Frontier Risk Extrapolation, a count-adjusted tail-risk penalty over four molecular views, as a falsifiable probe to test whether training penalties can address frontier failures.
AI.result: The frontier split inflates primary error by 87% (median) to 130.3% (mean) over standard scaffold splits; removing BBB reduces the mean to 75.9%. The graph network shows a mean 82.8% error increase over four tasks. The proposed Multi-View Frontier Risk Extrapolation penalty changes normalized frontier error by only 0.16% (perceptron) and -1.9% (graph network). The frontier split also inflates error more than published Lo-Hi and DataSAIL splitters on average.
AI.conclusion: Split construction and label provenance are critical evaluation constraints in molecular property modeling, and current training penalties (including the proposed one) do not resolve the OOD failures introduced by the structural-frontier split.

title: Toward Efficient Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation Using Only Low-Magnification Histopathological Images
summary: Whole-slide images (WSIs) provide rich tissue-level and cellular-level information, but storing and transmitting high-magnification pathology data is resource-intensive. Moreover, annotating WSIs at the pixel level is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Therefore, it is important to investigate whether low-magnification pathology images with limited annotations (i.e., image-level instead of pixel-level labels) can achieve performance comparable to high-magnification images. This paper presents a systematic benchmark study on weakly supervised histopathological image segmentation under different low-resolution storage settings. Starting from high-resolution image patches, we simulate lower-magnification inputs and reconstruct them to the original size using interpolation and deep learning-based reconstruction methods before applying the weakly-supervised segmentation pipeline. This framework enables a quantitative evaluation of how weakly supervised methods respond to different levels of resolution degradation. Experimental results show that reconstruction quality metrics alone are insufficient to predict downstream segmentation performance. In particular, the study identifies a critical degradation point where the localization of small-scale structures declines significantly. These findings provide practical guidance for designing efficient digital pathology storage systems while maintaining reliable automated analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/Dung-Dx/LowMagWSS

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks weakly supervised histopathological image segmentation under low-resolution settings, finding that reconstruction quality doesn't predict segmentation performance and identifying a critical degradation point for small-scale structures.
AI.motivation: WSIs are resource-intensive to store/transmit at high magnification, and pixel-level annotations are costly. The authors investigate whether low-magnification images with image-level labels can achieve comparable performance to high-magnification ones, aiming to guide efficient digital pathology storage design.
AI.method: The authors simulate lower-magnification inputs from high-resolution patches, reconstruct them to original size via interpolation and deep learning methods, then apply a weakly-supervised segmentation pipeline to evaluate how different resolution degradation levels affect performance.
AI.result: Reconstruction quality metrics alone are insufficient to predict downstream segmentation performance. A critical degradation point exists where localization of small-scale structures declines significantly.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide practical guidance for designing efficient digital pathology storage systems that balance compression with reliable automated analysis.

title: What We Talk About When We Talk About LLM Planning: Evidence for Two Distinct Planning Abilities
comment: 19 pages. Keywords: Reasoning, Automated Planning, Item Responses Theory, LLMs as Planner Research Area: NLP and Symbolic Reasoning Research Area Keywords: neurosymbolic, planning in agents, symbolic reasoning Contribution Types: Model analysis & interpretability
summary: When LLMs exhibit uneven performance across planning tasks, these gaps are often attributed to task difficulty. We argue that this explanation is incomplete, as task-level variation may reflect distinct latent planning competencies rather than differences along a single ability spectrum. We study this question on ACPBench-Hard by evaluating multiple LLM families under varying test-time reasoning budgets and applying a multidimensional item response theory model to uncover the latent competency structure underlying LLM planning. The analysis reveals two principal dimensions that shape planning performance: operational reasoning, the ability to evaluate local action applicability and immediate state transitions, and structural enumeration, the ability to reason about goal reachability and landmark structure. Operational reasoning improving under model scaling and longer reasoning traces, while structural enumeration remains comparatively insensitive. Our findings motivate competency-level evaluation of LLM planning, shifting the focus from whether models improve overall to which planning competencies improve, under what conditions, and why.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that uneven LLM performance across planning tasks stems from distinct latent competencies (operational reasoning and structural enumeration) rather than just task difficulty, using multidimensional IRT on ACPBench-Hard to reveal these two dimensions differ in their sensitivity to model scaling and reasoning budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing explanations attribute LLM planning performance gaps to task difficulty, but this is incomplete. The paper aims to show these gaps reflect distinct latent planning competencies rather than a single ability spectrum.
AI.method: Evaluated multiple LLM families on ACPBench-Hard under varying test-time reasoning budgets and applied a multidimensional item response theory (IRT) model to uncover latent competency structures.
AI.result: Two principal dimensions identified: (1) operational reasoning (evaluating action applicability and immediate state transitions) and (2) structural enumeration (reasoning about goal reachability and landmark structure). Operational reasoning improves with model scaling and longer reasoning traces; structural enumeration is insensitive to these factors.
AI.conclusion: Planning evaluation should shift from overall improvement to competency-level analysis—which competencies improve, under what conditions, and why.

title: To Answer or to Abstain: Mitigating Search-Agent Hallucinations via Abstention-Aware Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent advances in equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with search tools and outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) have achieved new state-of-the-art results on open-domain QA tasks. However, we argue that current training paradigms harbor a critical vulnerability: they predominantly reward correct answers but fail to penalize fabricated ones when retrieval fails, thereby implicitly exacerbating hallucinations. To address this, we propose Abstention-Aware Reinforcement Learning (AWA-RL), which dynamically shapes the abstention reward utilizing the model's query-specific prior capabilities and continuous on-policy training observations. We also introduce a novel metric, RA-F1, to measure the capability-reliability trade-off. Compared to non-abstaining baselines, AWA-RL boosts absolute precision by up to 10.3% and overall RA-F1 by 2.9%, with only marginal sacrifice in raw accuracy. These results confirm that AWA-RL successfully yields highly capable and reliable search agents. The code, data, and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/zfj1998/AWA-RL.

AI.tldr: AWA-RL introduces abstention-aware reinforcement learning to mitigate hallucinations in LLMs with search tools by penalizing incorrect answers when retrieval fails, achieving significant precision gains with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Current training paradigms for LLMs with search tools reward correct answers but fail to penalize fabricated ones when retrieval fails, implicitly exacerbating hallucinations.
AI.method: Proposes Abstention-Aware Reinforcement Learning (AWA-RL) that dynamically shapes abstention rewards using the model's query-specific prior capabilities and continuous on-policy training observations, along with a new metric RA-F1 for measuring capability-reliability trade-off.
AI.result: AWA-RL boosts absolute precision by up to 10.3% and overall RA-F1 by 2.9% compared to non-abstaining baselines, with only marginal sacrifice in raw accuracy.
AI.conclusion: AWA-RL successfully yields highly capable and reliable search agents by enabling appropriate abstention when retrieval is unreliable.

title: Detecting AI-Generated Video: A Vision-Language Dual-View Survey
summary: The evolving realism of AI-generated Videos (AIGC-V) is rapidly rendering traditional artifact-centric detection insufficient, necessitating a paradigm shift from low-level inspection to high-level semantic verification. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of AIGC-V detection, reframing the task as Factual Fidelity Verification, which asks whether the events, entities, and physical processes depicted in a video are consistent with real-world facts. To systematize this rapidly evolving field, we propose a Vision-Language Dual-View taxonomy that organizes existing methods into a hierarchical, four-layer landscape, spanning intrinsic cue analysis, spatiotemporal consistency modeling, cross-modal consistency reasoning, and language-guided world-level reasoning. This dual-view framing highlights a fundamental transition from artifact matching in traditional deepfake detection to evidence-based semantic verification enabled by vision-language models and agentic reasoning pipelines. Based on a systematic review of 221 works, we synthesize AIGC-V generation paradigms, survey the landscape of detection methods, and review evaluation metrics and benchmarks in line with proposed views. Finally, we discuss current challenges and identify promising directions toward robust, explainable, and trustworthy detection.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys AIGC-V detection by reframing it as Factual Fidelity Verification—checking video consistency with real-world facts. It proposes a Vision-Language Dual-View taxonomy across four layers (intrinsic cues, spatiotemporal consistency, cross-modal reasoning, world-level reasoning), reviews 221 works, and identifies challenges toward robust detection.
AI.motivation: Traditional artifact-centric deepfake detection fails against increasingly realistic AI-generated videos. A paradigm shift from low-level artifact inspection to high-level semantic verification is needed.
AI.method: Proposes a Vision-Language Dual-View taxonomy organizing detection methods into a four-layer hierarchy: (1) intrinsic cue analysis, (2) spatiotemporal consistency modeling, (3) cross-modal consistency reasoning, and (4) language-guided world-level reasoning. The survey systematically reviews 221 works across generation paradigms, detection methods, and benchmarks.
AI.result: Synthesizes AIGC-V generation paradigms, surveys detection methods organized by the dual-view taxonomy, and reviews evaluation metrics/benchmarks aligned with the proposed views.
AI.conclusion: Current challenges remain; promising directions include building robust, explainable, and trustworthy detection systems via vision-language models and agentic reasoning pipelines.

title: PREF-Gate: Provenance-Constrained Relational Evidence Fusion with Validation-Gated Selection for Graph Fraud Detection
summary: Relational fraud detection can exploit both label-free graph context and label-derived neighborhood evidence, but these two information sources obey different validity conditions. In particular, neighborhood risk becomes invalid when a queried node's own label, or any validation or test label, enters its construction. We formulate this issue as provenance-constrained relational evidence use and present PREF-Gate, an auditable decision framework with two fixed experts and a finite validation gate. The context expert uses attributes, one-hop means, feature residuals, and degree descriptors without labels. The evidence expert adds self-excluded, training-label-only neighborhood risk and empirical-Bayes summaries that expose support, uncertainty, availability, and shrinkage. Before test inference, the gate selects either expert or one of three pre-specified probability mixtures and fixes the decision threshold. On Amazon, YelpChi, and TFinance, using five identical stratified splits and 14 same-protocol methods, PREF-Gate obtains mean AUPRC values of 0.9085, 0.8104, and 0.8913. It selects the label-free expert on all Amazon and YelpChi splits and an evidence mixture on all TFinance splits. Thus, the main result is conditional rather than universal: label-derived relational evidence is useful only where held-out validation supports it. The framework couples competitive ranking performance with an explicit label-provenance contract, finite selection policy, failure accounting, and review-budget evaluation, providing an auditable knowledge-based decision pipeline for graph fraud detection.

AI.tldr: PREF-Gate is an auditable fraud detection framework that conditionally uses label-derived relational evidence only when held-out validation supports it, achieving high AUPRC across three datasets while enforcing a label-provenance contract.
AI.motivation: Relational fraud detection faces a provenance problem: label-free graph context and label-derived neighborhood evidence obey different validity conditions, and neighborhood risk becomes invalid when test/validation labels leak into its construction. Existing methods lack explicit handling of this issue.
AI.method: PREF-Gate uses two fixed experts (context expert using attributes, one-hop means, feature residuals, degree descriptors without labels; evidence expert adding self-excluded, training-label-only neighborhood risk and empirical-Bayes summaries) and a finite validation gate that selects either expert or one of three pre-specified probability mixtures before test inference, with a fixed decision threshold.
AI.result: On Amazon, YelpChi, and TFinance with 5 identical stratified splits and 14 same-protocol methods, PREF-Gate achieves mean AUPRC of 0.9085, 0.8104, and 0.8913. It selects the label-free expert on all Amazon/YelpChi splits and an evidence mixture on all TFinance splits.
AI.conclusion: Label-derived relational evidence is conditionally useful, not universally. The framework provides an auditable pipeline with explicit label-provenance contract, finite selection policy, failure accounting, and review-budget evaluation for graph fraud detection.

title: Multi-Scale Convolution with Optimal Transport Attention Effect on Multivariate Time Series
summary: The analysis of Multivariate Time Series (MTS) plays an important role in a lot of real-world practical applications, but it still remains some challenging problem about capturing multi-granularity structural patterns and suppressing noise appropriately. Multi-Scale Convolution with Optimal Transport Attention (MSC-OT) is proposed in this paper. MSC-OT is a useful architecture to optimize the attention mechanism. It combines multi-scale convolution with Sinkhorn optimal transport method based on inverted embedding. The inverted embedding approach embeds each variable as a token and allows the model to capture cross-variate relationships better. MSC-OT consists of two part: (1) Multi-Scale Convolution Enhancement, that applies multi-scale convolutions to attention score matrices based on inverted embedding, capturing local structural patterns in the variate-interaction space induced by compressed temporal representations; (2) Sinkhorn Optimal Transport Regularization, that formulates attention computation as an optimal transport problem and employs iterative matrix scaling to ensure balanced information flow across variates. Adaptive Fusion Strategy utilizes softmax-normalized learnable weights to dynamically combine base attention, convolution-enhanced, and OT-regularized scores. Experiments on widely-used datasets, including ETT, Electricity, Traffic, Solar-Energy, and Exchange-Rate, show that MSC-OT achieves well performance in both short-term and long-term forecasting tasks. Ablation experiments further validate the effectiveness of each proposed component and their synergistic contributions to improving prediction accuracy for multivariate time series forecasting.

AI.tldr: MSC-OT introduces a novel architecture combining multi-scale convolution and Sinkhorn optimal transport attention with inverted embedding to improve multivariate time series forecasting by capturing multi-granularity patterns and suppressing noise.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle to capture multi-granularity structural patterns and suppress noise appropriately in multivariate time series analysis.
AI.method: MSC-OT combines (1) Multi-Scale Convolution Enhancement for capturing local structural patterns in the variate-interaction space via inverted embedding, and (2) Sinkhorn Optimal Transport Regularization for balanced information flow across variates, fused adaptively via softmax-normalized learnable weights.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance on ETT, Electricity, Traffic, Solar-Energy, and Exchange-Rate datasets for both short-term and long-term forecasting; ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component.
AI.conclusion: MSC-OT effectively addresses multi-granularity pattern capture and noise suppression in MTS forecasting, validated across diverse real-world datasets.

title: MAC-Splat: Multi-Attribute Consistency for High-Fidelity Sparse-View Reconstruction
comment: Accepted to the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2026)
summary: Reconstructing high-fidelity 3D scenes from sparse-views remains a central problem in generalizable neural rendering. Existing generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods often exhibit geometric artifacts in sparse-view settings, since supervision based solely on 2D photometric losses cannot resolve depth and correspondence ambiguities. To address this issue, we propose MAC-Splat, a training framework built around direct 3D consistency supervision. MAC-Splat builds on the MASt3R geometric backbone and a frozen DINOv3 encoder to obtain semantically informed 2D correspondences, which serve as geometric anchors for 3D supervision. Using these anchors, we define the Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss. This objective jointly regularizes the 3D attributes of matched Gaussians, including their position, shape, and appearance, by enforcing agreement in a common world coordinate frame. The formulation is robust to outliers and respects the geometry of covariance matrices, which leads to stable training under sparse-view conditions. Experiments on ScanNet++ show that MAC-Splat outperforms strong baselines, with particularly large gains under different overlap regimes. In particular, it improves average PSNR over Splatt3R by more than 4.5 dB, reduces LPIPS, and maintains performance as the camera pose gap increases. These results indicate that a direct, multi-attribute 3D consistency objective, when combined with high-quality correspondences, is effective for addressing the ill-posed sparse-view reconstruction problem.

AI.tldr: MAC-Splat introduces a Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss using 3D correspondences from MASt3R and DINOv3 to supervise generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, significantly improving sparse-view 3D reconstruction (e.g., +4.5 dB PSNR over Splatt3R on ScanNet++).
AI.motivation: Existing generalizable 3DGS methods suffer from geometric artifacts in sparse-view settings because they rely solely on 2D photometric losses, which cannot resolve depth and correspondence ambiguities.
AI.method: MAC-Splat uses MASt3R as a geometric backbone and a frozen DINOv3 encoder to obtain semantically informed 2D correspondences, which serve as geometric anchors. A Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss jointly regularizes position, shape, and appearance of matched Gaussians in a common world coordinate frame, with robustness to outliers and respect for covariance matrix geometry.
AI.result: On ScanNet++, MAC-Splat outperforms strong baselines, improving average PSNR over Splatt3R by more than 4.5 dB, reducing LPIPS, and maintaining performance as camera pose gap increases, with particularly large gains under different overlap regimes.
AI.conclusion: A direct, multi-attribute 3D consistency objective combined with high-quality correspondences effectively addresses the ill-posed sparse-view reconstruction problem.

title: Heterogeneous Agent Cohorts for Safe Open-Ended Exploration with Runtime Constraint Memory
summary: LLM agents today are caught in an awkward bind. Lock them down with static safety instructions and they rarely venture beyond the obvious; give them free reign with tools and multi-agent debate, and safety violations quickly follow. Rather than forcing a single model to juggle both creativity and caution, we separate the concerns across specialized roles. A Disrupter generates unconventional proposals, a Validator enforces hard runtime checks at the tool gateway, and a Broker pulls in distant but relevant analogies. Failures are not discarded -- they are compiled, via MCTS, into compact, signed constraint patches we call Scars. These patches are cached locally and inherited by future cohorts, turning repeated failures into reusable, low-cost runtime constraints. In a spatial-semantic sandbox (N=20 runs, p<0.01), our cohort reaches remote targets where debate fails, the Validator prevents all executed breaches, and Scars reduce token consumption by 15.1% by avoiding redundant validator checks. Furthermore, credit-based Communication Allocation Scores (CAS) restrict outbound bandwidth, reducing overall token costs by 55.9% under resource constraints.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent framework (Disrupter, Validator, Broker) separates creativity and safety concerns, using MCTS-derived constraint patches (Scars) and credit-based communication limits to improve exploration, prevent safety breaches, and reduce token costs.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to balance creativity and safety — static instructions limit exploration, while unrestricted agentic freedom leads to safety violations.
AI.method: Three specialized roles: Disrupter (generates unconventional proposals), Validator (enforces runtime tool-use constraints), Broker (retrieves distant analogies). Failures are compiled via MCTS into signed constraint patches (Scars), cached and inherited across cohorts. Communication Allocation Scores (CAS) restrict bandwidth.
AI.result: In a spatial-semantic sandbox (N=20, p<0.01): agents reach remote targets where debate fails; Validator prevents all executed breaches; Scars reduce token consumption by 15.1%; CAS reduces total token costs by 55.9%.
AI.conclusion: Separating creative and safety roles with reusable failure-derived constraints and communication budgeting enables both safer and more exploratory LLM agent behavior at lower cost.

title: Policy-Driven CT-Agent: Modeling Phase-Aware Diagnostic Control for Clinically Consistent CT Reasoning
summary: Computed Tomography (CT) diagnosis often relies on dynamic selection of imaging phases, such as non-contrast, arterial, or venous phases, based on preliminary findings, clinical suspicion, and diagnostic guidelines. This phase-wise decision process is critical for reducing unnecessary radiation exposure while supporting timely staging and treatment planning. However, phase-selection protocols can vary across hospitals, regions, and guidelines, while most existing CT-based AI methods assume that all phases are available and focus on static tasks under a fixed imaging phase, failing to model whether additional phases are required. This limitation stems from heterogeneous multi-phase representations, the need for knowledge-guided phase control beyond visual cues, and the lack of supervision for phase-sufficiency decisions in existing datasets. To address these challenges, we propose Policy-Driven CT-Agent (PD-CTAgent) for clinically consistent CT phase selection and diagnostic reasoning. PD-CTAgent introduces a Clinical Structure Abstraction Module (CSAM) to harmonize heterogeneous CT phases into a unified, phase-aware evidence representation. Based on this representation, a Knowledge-Guided Diagnostic Control Model (KDCM) evaluates phase sufficiency and iteratively requests additional phases when necessary. The policy-driven agent design further allows PD-CTAgent to flexibly follow different institutional, regional, or guideline-specific diagnostic protocols. Together, PD-CTAgent bridges static CT analysis and real-world clinical workflows. Experiments on two public datasets, LIDC and MCT-LTDiag, and one private dataset demonstrate its effectiveness and clinical consistency. Code will be made public upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: PD-CTAgent is a policy-driven AI framework for dynamic CT phase selection and diagnostic reasoning that harmonizes heterogeneous multi-phase CT data, evaluates phase sufficiency using knowledge-guided control, and adapts to various clinical protocols, outperforming existing static methods on public and private datasets.
AI.motivation: Current CT-based AI methods assume all imaging phases are available and only handle static tasks under fixed phases, failing to model whether additional phases are needed. Phase-selection protocols vary across hospitals and guidelines, and there is no supervision for phase-sufficiency decisions in existing datasets.
AI.method: PD-CTAgent consists of two key modules: (1) Clinical Structure Abstraction Module (CSAM) harmonizes heterogeneous CT phases into a unified, phase-aware evidence representation; (2) Knowledge-Guided Diagnostic Control Model (KDCM) evaluates phase sufficiency and iteratively requests additional phases when needed. The policy-driven agent design enables flexible adherence to different institutional/guideline-specific protocols.
AI.result: Experiments on LIDC, MCT-LTDiag (public), and one private dataset demonstrate effectiveness and clinical consistency of PD-CTAgent.
AI.conclusion: PD-CTAgent bridges static CT analysis and real-world clinical workflows by enabling dynamic, policy-driven phase selection and reasoning that adapts to varying diagnostic protocols.

title: Mixture of Cognitive Experts in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) require strong reasoning over both visual and textual input. Recent work suggests that cognitive elements, especially diverse representations and metacognition, correlate with better performance. Many of the needed perceptual functions are already provided by specialized domain-specific computer vision models, which act as the perceptual subsystem for detecting objects, localizing them, inferring states, recovering spatial layout, and reading text. The key challenge is to integrate these multi-encoder experts into a trustworthy, interpretable, and coherent representation that improves verifiability and reduces hallucinations. This is difficult because vision-language questions span different cognitive levels, yet most LVLM pipelines apply the same perception-reasoning routing regardless of the demand of each query. We propose an evidence-driven multimodal reasoning framework that utilizes a Bloom-inspired taxonomy as a hierarchical reasoning protocol. The two-stage cognitive verbalization first produces a Literal Evidence Summary by decomposing expert outputs into short, atomic evidence statements. It then performs Bloom Verbalization to turn these evidence items into a staged reasoning trace, and a lightweight Reasoning Trace Module quantitatively analyzes the trace to make evidence usage and reasoning progression explicit. Through this integration, we observed several improvements in perception and reasoning abilities. Moreover, the trace module provides quantitative evidence that different queries induce different cognitive entry levels and evidence-use trajectories that enable fine-grained analysis.

AI.tldr: A Bloom's taxonomy-inspired framework that decomposes visual expert outputs into atomic evidence statements and produces staged reasoning traces for LVLMs, enabling explicit evidence usage analysis and improved interpretability.
AI.motivation: Current LVLM pipelines lack adaptive reasoning — they apply the same perception-reasoning routing regardless of query complexity. Integrating diverse domain-specific vision experts is challenging due to the need for trustworthy, interpretable, and coherent representations that reduce hallucinations.
AI.method: (1) Uses Bloom-inspired taxonomy as a hierarchical reasoning protocol; (2) Two-stage cognitive verbalization: first generates a Literal Evidence Summary (atomic statements from expert outputs), then performs Bloom Verbalization (staged reasoning trace); (3) A lightweight Reasoning Trace Module quantitatively analyzes the trace to make evidence usage and reasoning progression explicit.
AI.result: Improvements in both perception and reasoning abilities. The trace module reveals that different queries induce different cognitive entry levels and evidence-use trajectories, enabling fine-grained analysis.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-driven multimodal reasoning with explicit cognitive staging improves LVLM performance, verifiability, and interpretability, while providing quantitative insights into query-dependent reasoning dynamics.

title: Bringing Back Rule Induction to Fluid Intelligence Research? An Initial Validation of the ARC-AGI Benchmark in Humans
summary: Two competing perspectives on fluid intelligence (gf) measures propose that performance is primarily constrained either by working memory capacity or by the ability to induce novel relations. The first perspective is currently dominant in measurement, as evident from the use of a limited set of recurring rules, whereas the second perspective is reflected in many definitions but rarely present in measurement. The ARC-AGI benchmark predominantly requires rule induction and was proposed as a measure of gf for both humans and artificial systems. However, its psychometric properties have not yet been examined in human samples. We therefore investigated the psychometric characteristics and nomological network of ARC-AGI in a first study with 100 participants. A compilation of ARC-AGI items showed good psychometric properties and correlated substantially with figural fluid intelligence as measured by a figural reasoning test (\r{ho} = .63). Associations with figural originality were weak. These findings provide initial support for the validity of ARC-AGI as a measure of human fluid intelligence. Future research should include more rule induction tasks as well as additional multivariate covariates. This study is unusual by studying a task in humans that was initially designed for machines. We suggest systematically embedding AI benchmarks into the nomological network of human cognitive abilities to enable more systematic evaluation and interdisciplinary cooperation.

AI.tldr: This paper examines whether the ARC-AGI benchmark, originally designed for AI, serves as a valid measure of human fluid intelligence. A study with 100 participants finds ARC-AGI items have good psychometric properties and correlate substantially (ρ = .63) with figural fluid intelligence, supporting its validity as a measure of gf.
AI.motivation: Two competing views of fluid intelligence (gf)—working memory capacity versus rule induction ability—coexist, with the latter rarely operationalized in current tests. ARC-AGI, a benchmark requiring rule induction, was proposed as a gf measure but lacked psychometric evaluation in humans, motivating this study.
AI.method: 100 human participants completed a compilation of ARC-AGI items along with a figural reasoning test (figural fluid intelligence) and a measure of figural originality. Psychometric properties and the nomological network were analyzed via correlation analysis.
AI.result: ARC-AGI showed good psychometric properties and a substantial correlation with figural fluid intelligence (ρ = .63), while associations with figural originality were weak.
AI.conclusion: ARC-AGI is supported as a valid measure of human fluid intelligence, particularly emphasizing rule induction. Future work should include more rule induction tasks and multivariate covariates, and systematically embed AI benchmarks into the nomological network of human cognitive abilities.

title: The VC dimension of partial concept classes via Radon's theorem
summary:
Following Alon, Hanneke, Holzman, and Moran (FOCS 2021), we define a partial concept class (PCC) as a family of partial functions \(f: V\to\{0,1,\ast\}\); equivalently, its concepts partition the ground set into black ($f^{-1}(1)$), grey ($f^{-1}(\ast)$), and white parts ($f^{-1}(0)$). Its VC dimension is defined by shattering sets on which the value $\ast$ is not taken. We study two geometric PCCs in real Banach spaces, both with a margin \(δ>0\): expanded half-spaces, where the grey part is a strip of width at least \(δ\) adjacent to a half-space, and expanded balls, where the grey part is an annulus of width \(δ\) around a unit radius ball.
  Our main results are dimension-free upper bounds on the VC dimension of the PCC of expanded balls in \(L_p\parenthμ\), \(1\le p<\infty\), including the non-Euclidean and algorithmically particularly relevant case \(\ell^d_1\). These bounds depend on the margin and on the radii, but not on the ambient dimension or the underlying measure space. These are extensions of the work of Bourneuf, Charbit, and Thomassé (FOCS 2025) who studied the PCC of expanded balls in Euclidean space, that is, $\ell_2^d$. We also prove lower bounds on the VC dimension that match the upper bounds in terms of the margin parameter $δ$. Finally, we derive a Dense Neighborhood Lemma in \(L_p\)-spaces, again extending the known Euclidean results.
  Our method relies on the linearization of the distance through a map into a space of non-trivial Rademacher type, and then the use of a balanced signed-sum estimate, or a no-dimensional Radon theorem. The arguments rely on ideas from functional analysis that are clearly explained for the non-expert in that field.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the VC dimension of two geometric partial concept classes (PCCs) in real Banach spaces: expanded half-spaces and expanded balls with a margin δ. It provides dimension-free upper bounds on VC dimension for expanded balls in Lp spaces (1≤p<∞), including ℓ1, with matching lower bounds in δ. It also extends the Dense Neighborhood Lemma to Lp spaces, using linearization via Rademacher type spaces and balanced signed-sum estimates.
AI.motivation: To understand the combinatorial complexity (VC dimension) of geometric partial concept classes in general Banach spaces beyond Euclidean settings, particularly for algorithmically relevant non-Euclidean cases like ℓ1, and to establish dimension-free bounds that extend prior Euclidean results.
AI.method: The method linearizes distance via a mapping into a space of non-trivial Rademacher type, then applies a balanced signed-sum estimate or a no-dimensional Radon theorem. Functional analysis tools are used and explained for non-experts.
AI.result: Dimension-free upper bounds on the VC dimension of the PCC of expanded balls in Lp(μ) for 1≤p<∞, including ℓ1, depending only on margin δ and radii, not on dimension or measure space. Matching lower bounds in δ are proved. A Dense Neighborhood Lemma is extended to Lp spaces.
AI.conclusion: The work extends Euclidean PCC results for expanded balls to general Lp spaces, with tight bounds in the margin parameter, demonstrating that the combinatorial complexity remains dimension-free in these non-Euclidean settings.

title: Compositional Context Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Model for Complex Assembly Action Understanding from Videos
comment: Accepted by ICRA 2026. Video Understanding; Vision Language Model; Multi-modal LLM; Action Recognition; Assembly
summary: Assembly action understanding is a key enabler for effective human-robot collaborative assembly, yet it remains challenging due to subtle motions and fine-grained hand-object interactions. We adapt vision-language models (VLMs) to this challenging domain with Compositional Context Fine-Tuning (CCFT), a method that decomposes assembly actions into semantic elements (Verb, Object, Tool) and fine-tunes VLMs to recognize each action element using templated question-answering pairs. This approach ensures near-deterministic outputs. To enable efficient and effective multi-task learning under limited data, a Layer-Partitioned Alternating Training (LP-AT) method is presented, which assigns distinct model layers to recognize specific action elements through element-specific low-rank adapters. LP-AT alternates weight updates across element-specific adapters, reducing cross-task interference while enabling per-adapter hyperparameter optimization. Furthermore, we create HA-ViD-VQA and IKEA-ASM-VQA datasets from existing assembly video datasets. Extensive experiments on these datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong action recognition baselines while providing interpretable element-level predictions that can support diverse downstream applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Compositional Context Fine-Tuning (CCFT) and Layer-Partitioned Alternating Training (LP-AT) to adapt vision-language models for assembly action understanding by decomposing actions into Verb, Object, and Tool elements, outperforming baselines on HA-ViD-VQA and IKEA-ASM-VQA datasets.
AI.motivation: Assembly action understanding is challenging due to subtle motions and fine-grained hand-object interactions, yet it is critical for effective human-robot collaborative assembly.
AI.method: 1) Compositional Context Fine-Tuning (CCFT): decomposes assembly actions into semantic elements (Verb, Object, Tool) and fine-tunes VLMs using templated QA pairs. 2) Layer-Partitioned Alternating Training (LP-AT): assigns distinct model layers to recognize specific action elements via element-specific low-rank adapters, alternating weight updates to reduce cross-task interference.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms strong action recognition baselines on HA-ViD-VQA and IKEA-ASM-VQA datasets while providing interpretable element-level predictions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables effective multi-task learning under limited data and supports diverse downstream applications with interpretable element-level outputs.

title: Valid $\ne$ Necessary: Diagnosing Latent Inefficiency in Chain-of-Thought
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly advanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet it often incurs substantial computational costs due to over-reasoning: the generation of redundant, verbose, or irrelevant steps. While existing reasoning step evaluators effectively detect logical fallacies and factual errors, our analysis reveals a critical blind spot: they fail to penalize valid but inefficient reasoning steps that inflate token usage without contributing to the solution. To systematically diagnose this limitation, we introduce RIV-GSM8K, a diagnostic benchmark injected with five distinct types of inefficiencies, including circular reasoning and excessive decomposition. Diagnostic experiments reveal that state-of-the-art evaluators struggle to distinguish these inefficiencies from necessary reasoning. To address this gap, we propose CAID (Context-Aware Information Density), a training-free metric grounded in information theory that identifies low-utility steps. To validate the metric's practical utility, we apply it within PACE, a post-hoc compression strategy. Additional control experiments show that the gains of PACE are not explained by trivial pruning: compared with random step removal and PRM-based compression baselines, it preserves accuracy at substantially higher compression rates. Empirical results on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge demonstrate that PACE reduces token consumption by 31-53% while maintaining accuracy, confirming that CAID successfully distills informational froth from reasoning chains without compromising deductive validity.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that current reasoning step evaluators for LLMs fail to penalize inefficient (but valid) reasoning steps, introduces RIV-GSM8K (a benchmark with five inefficiency types), proposes CAID (a training-free metric to detect low-utility steps), and validates it via PACE (a compression strategy) that reduces token usage by 31-53% while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought prompting incurs high computational costs due to over-reasoning (redundant/verbose/irrelevant steps). Existing evaluators detect logical errors but fail to penalize valid yet inefficient reasoning steps that inflate token usage without contributing to the solution.
AI.method: The authors introduce RIV-GSM8K, a diagnostic benchmark with five inefficiency types (e.g., circular reasoning, excessive decomposition). They propose CAID (Context-Aware Information Density), a training-free metric based on information theory to identify low-utility steps, and apply it within PACE, a post-hoc compression strategy.
AI.result: State-of-the-art evaluators struggle to distinguish inefficiencies from necessary reasoning. PACE reduces token consumption by 31-53% on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge while maintaining accuracy, outperforming random step removal and PRM-based compression baselines.
AI.conclusion: CAID effectively distills informational froth from reasoning chains without compromising deductive validity, demonstrating that targeting informational density rather than logical validity alone improves efficiency in CoT reasoning.

title: LSTrans: Efficient Knowledge Transfer for Lightweight and Automated ECG Classification
summary: Deploying deep learning models for automated electrocardiogram classification on resource-constrained wearable devices remains challenging due to high computational costs. To address this, we propose LSTrans, a lightweight hybrid model designed for efficient and sensitive ECG analysis. LSTrans introduces a specialized 1D convolutional backbone with an interleaved layer architecture to capture both macroscopic rhythmic trends and microscopic morphological variations. This backbone is cascaded with a Transformer encoder to model long-range temporal dependencies, incorporating Low-Rank Adaptation across critical layers to compress the model and reduce the trainable parameter space. We further employ homogeneous and heterogeneous knowledge distillation to transfer diagnostic expertise from high-capacity teacher models to the student. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that LSTrans achieves a competitive balance between diagnostic sensitivity and resource efficiency, substantially reducing peak memory footprints and training latency during downstream adaptation. The source code is available for review at https://github.com/zyee00128/LSTrans4BIBM.

AI.tldr: LSTrans is a lightweight hybrid model (1D CNN + Transformer with LoRA) for ECG classification on wearable devices, using knowledge distillation to achieve efficient and sensitive arrhythmia detection with reduced memory and latency.
AI.motivation: Deploying deep learning models for automated ECG classification on resource-constrained wearable devices is challenging due to high computational costs.
AI.method: LSTrans uses a 1D convolutional backbone with interleaved layers to capture both macroscopic rhythmic trends and microscopic morphological variations, cascaded with a Transformer encoder for long-range temporal dependencies. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) compresses the model across critical layers, and homogeneous + heterogeneous knowledge distillation transfers expertise from teacher to student.
AI.result: LSTrans achieves a competitive balance between diagnostic sensitivity and resource efficiency, substantially reducing peak memory footprints and training latency during downstream adaptation on multiple benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: LSTrans demonstrates that lightweight hybrid architectures with knowledge distillation can enable practical, resource-efficient ECG analysis on wearable devices without compromising diagnostic sensitivity.

title: h-Flow: Flexible Flow-based Image Editing via Doob's h-Transform
summary: Editing images with pre-trained text-to-image flow models typically requires carefully balancing target alignment with the desired prompt and source consistency with the original image. Existing approaches either rely on inversion-based pipelines or heuristic source-to-target trajectory constructions, which often depend on architecture-specific designs or are sensitive to hyperparameters. In this paper, we propose h-Flow, a training-free and theoretically grounded flow-based editing framework. Inspired by Doob's $h$-Transform, we reformulate image editing as conditional generation under multiple terminal events corresponding to source consistency and target alignment. We first extend the classical $h$-Transform from SDE-based models to the deterministic RF framework by constructing an equivalent SDE with identical marginals. Within this formulation, we design dedicated $h$-functions for source consistency and target alignment, yielding closed-form reconstruction guidance and velocity-based semantic editing signals. We further introduce a velocity orthogonal decomposition to decouple reconstruction and editing directions, enabling a controllable trade-off between the two objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that h-Flow achieves effective, robust, and flexible editing across diverse scenarios. The code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: h-Flow is a training-free, theoretically grounded flow-based image editing framework that uses Doob's h-Transform to reformulate editing as conditional generation under multiple terminal events, achieving effective and robust editing across diverse scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing image editing methods with pre-trained text-to-image flow models require careful balancing between target alignment and source consistency, often relying on inversion-based pipelines or heuristic source-to-target trajectory constructions that are architecture-specific or hyperparameter-sensitive.
AI.method: Proposes h-Flow, which extends Doob's h-Transform from SDE-based models to deterministic Rectified Flow (RF) by constructing an equivalent SDE with identical marginals. Designs dedicated h-functions for source consistency and target alignment, yielding closed-form reconstruction guidance and velocity-based semantic editing signals. Introduces velocity orthogonal decomposition to decouple reconstruction and editing directions for controllable trade-off.
AI.result: Achieves effective, robust, and flexible editing across diverse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: h-Flow provides a training-free, theoretically grounded editing framework that overcomes limitations of prior methods and enables controllable trade-off between source consistency and target alignment.

title: Efficient Test-Time Optimization for Multi-Agent Proof Autoformalization
summary: Full-proof autoformalization bridges extensive mathematical proofs in natural language with formally validated reasoning, offering a pathway to elevate the ceiling of verifiable mathematical reasoning. Unlike statement-level formalization, proof autoformalization is a long-horizon challenge requiring coordination of claims, contexts, and dependencies across many proof steps, yet has only recently come under focused study. Current approaches either rely on costly model training or apply excessive, unguided repair at inference time. To this end, we introduce ToMap, a multi-agent framework that structures proof autoformalization as a Decomposer-Formalizer-Prover pipeline with efficient test-time optimization guided by formal verification and semantic rubrics for proof quality. Rather than distributing test-time compute across all agents, we perform bottleneck analysis and identify the Decomposer as the critical bottleneck: the quality of its atomic, self-contained proof units directly determines whether downstream agents can successfully formalize and prove each step. ToMap therefore treats the Formalizer and Prover as downstream executors and efficiently focuses test-time compute on Decomposer refinement. This refinement follows a loop inspired by GEPA, evolving prompts over candidate decompositions and using formal verification progress together with semantic proof rubrics to define a Pareto frontier that guides the next decomposition update. Experiments on ProofFlowBench show that ToMap improves over the best previous method by 19.0% when evaluated by both syntactic correctness and semantic faithfulness, while requiring lower test-time cost. Scaling analysis shows that most gains emerge within a few iterations of decomposition evolution, guiding test-time budget selection.

AI.tldr: ToMap is a multi-agent framework for proof autoformalization that uses a Decomposer-Formalizer-Prover pipeline with test-time optimization focused on decomposition quality, achieving 19.0% improvement over prior methods on ProofFlowBench.
AI.motivation: Proof autoformalization is a long-horizon challenge involving coordination across many proof steps, yet existing approaches rely on costly training or excessive unguided repair at inference time.
AI.method: ToMap employs a multi-agent Decomposer-Formalizer-Prover pipeline. Bottleneck analysis identifies the Decomposer as critical; test-time compute is focused on refining it via a GEPA-inspired loop with Pareto frontier guided by formal verification and semantic rubrics.
AI.result: ToMap surpasses prior methods by 19.0% on ProofFlowBench in both syntactic correctness and semantic faithfulness, with lower test-time cost. Most gains are achieved within few decomposition evolution iterations.
AI.conclusion: Targeted test-time optimization on decomposition quality is more effective than distributing compute uniformly, and the proposed framework offers a cost-efficient path for proof autoformalization.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Quadrature
comment: 17 pages (9 main text), 10 figures. Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026)
summary: Numerical integration is a cornerstone of various scientific computing applications, such as engineering simulations and model evidence computations in probabilistic machine learning. Bayesian Quadrature uses Gaussian process surrogates that explicitly encode structural assumptions about the integrand to obtain integral estimates with quantified uncertainty. These surrogates are predominantly based on stationary covariance functions, which results in model misspecification for integrands exhibiting nonstationary behavior. We tackle this issue through an adaptively growing, tree-based partition of the integration domain into local stationary models. Our method recombines the local integral estimates through a hierarchy of GP conditioning that reintroduces cross-subdomain correlations, while model selection criteria control the tree growth to avoid unnecessary partitioning. The resulting algorithm is simple, requires no MCMC, and adapts its evaluation budget to local integrand complexity. On benchmark integration problems and a model evidence computation for an epidemiological model, Hierarchical Bayesian Quadrature achieves substantial gains over standard Bayesian Quadrature on nonstationary integrands while matching its performance on stationary ones.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Bayesian Quadrature (HBQ) uses an adaptively growing tree-based partition of the integration domain into local stationary GP models, recombines estimates via GP conditioning, and outperforms standard BQ on nonstationary integrands while matching performance on stationary ones.
AI.motivation: Standard Bayesian Quadrature relies on stationary covariance functions, which leads to model misspecification for integrands exhibiting nonstationary behavior.
AI.method: An adaptively growing, tree-based partition of the integration domain into local stationary models, with recombination via hierarchical GP conditioning that reintroduces cross-subdomain correlations, and model selection criteria controlling tree growth.
AI.result: Substantial gains over standard Bayesian Quadrature on nonstationary integrands while matching its performance on stationary ones, demonstrated on benchmark problems and a model evidence computation for an epidemiological model.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical Bayesian Quadrature is simple, requires no MCMC, adapts its evaluation budget to local integrand complexity, and effectively handles nonstationarity without sacrificing performance on stationary integrands.

title: Calibrated e-CUSUM Decoding for Quantized Reasoning Models: Why Token Log-Probability Is the Wrong Observable for Decoding Monitors
summary: Low-bit quantization makes small reasoning models inexpensive to deploy but can degrade their chains of thought. This motivates decoder-side monitors that intervene when generation becomes unreliable. We show that a natural candidate, the centered token log-probability increment $\log p(w_t)+H_t$, is the wrong observable for this purpose. Under the model's own sampling law it is a mean-zero martingale by construction, so it measures sampling self-consistency rather than trajectory health and is nearly silent during confident repetition, where both $\log p(w_t)$ and entropy are close to zero. We introduce a training-free decoding controller that combines (i) a degeneration-aware alarm score fusing token uncertainty with explicit verbatim repetition and (ii) a calibrated e-process-inspired sequential detector. The raw product process is Ville-valid under a conditional-mean null, while the deployed CUSUM-floored statistic is treated as an empirical change detector because the score is history-dependent and autocorrelated. On GSM8K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B in FP16 and INT4, calibration turns a monitor that fires on 93--95% of generations into a selective detector of failing traces ($φ\approx 0.3$, precision $\approx 0.6$ against a 0.38 base rate). In this pilot, the controller reduces measured verbatim-degeneration signals and yields a positive but statistically inconclusive INT4 accuracy change from 63% to 69% (paired McNemar $p=0.18$, $n=100$), at a 28% token-budget cost. We also find that non-termination, rather than looping, is the dominant failure mode on GSM8K. The main contribution is methodological: an explanation of why centered token log-probability is inadequate for decoder monitoring and a calibrated, cautiously evaluated replacement.

AI.tldr: Centered token log-probability increments are mean-zero martingales under the model's own sampling law, making them poor monitors for decoding health. The paper proposes a training-free controller combining a degeneration-aware alarm score and a sequential detector, demonstrating improved detection of failing traces and modest accuracy gains on INT4 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K.
AI.motivation: Low-bit quantization degrades chains of thought in small reasoning models, motivating the need for decoder-side monitors that can intervene when generation becomes unreliable.
AI.method: A training-free decoding controller combining (i) a degeneration-aware alarm score that fuses token uncertainty with verbatim repetition detection, and (ii) a calibrated e-process-inspired sequential detector with CUSUM flooring, treated as an empirical change detector.
AI.result: Calibration reduces monitor firing from 93-95% to a selective detector of failing traces (φ≈0.3, precision≈0.6 against 0.38 base rate). INT4 accuracy improves from 63% to 69% (p=0.18, n=100) at 28% token-budget cost. Non-termination, not looping, is the dominant failure mode on GSM8K.
AI.conclusion: Centered token log-probability is theoretically inadequate for decoder monitoring; the proposed calibrated replacement offers a more reliable detection approach for low-bit quantization scenarios.

title: Weight-Adjusted Gradients Reveal Parameter Importance and Failure Modes in LLMs
summary: Understanding which parameters are influential in Large Language Models (LLMs) is central to improving their efficiency, reliability, and interpretability. We introduce Weight-Adjusted Gradients (WAG), a simple yet effective approach for estimating parameter importance that explicitly captures the interaction between model weights and first-order gradient information and identifies parameters that disproportionately influence model behavior, such as those responsible for collapse phenomena in LLMs. Across a range of models and settings, we show that WAG surfaces a tiny but critical subset of parameters whose modification leads to dramatic degradation in performance, a failure mode that existing importance metrics overlook. These findings reveal a previously underexplored interplay between weights and gradients, suggesting that parameter importance cannot be fully understood through either signal alone. The surprising effectiveness of WAG points to fundamental structural properties of trained networks and motivates new open questions about the role of zeroth-order and first-order information in deep learning. We demonstrate the practical utility of WAG across multiple applications, including expert allocation in mixture-of-expert architectures, parameter-specific unlearning, mixed-precision quantization, and layer selection for knowledge editing. Our results position WAG as a unified approach for analyzing, debugging, and controlling LLMs, and opens new directions for principled model-level interpretation.

AI.tldr: WAG (Weight-Adjusted Gradients) is a method for estimating parameter importance in LLMs by combining weights and gradients, revealing a tiny but critical subset of parameters whose modification severely degrades performance—a failure mode overlooked by existing metrics. It proves useful across multiple applications including MoE expert allocation, unlearning, quantization, and knowledge editing.
AI.motivation: Understanding which parameters are influential in LLMs is central to improving their efficiency, reliability, and interpretability. Existing importance metrics overlook certain failure modes where modifying a tiny subset of parameters leads to dramatic performance degradation.
AI.method: Weight-Adjusted Gradients (WAG) explicitly captures the interaction between model weights and first-order gradient information to estimate parameter importance.
AI.result: WAG surfaces a tiny but critical subset of parameters whose modification leads to dramatic degradation in performance—a failure mode existing metrics overlook. WAG reveals a previously underexplored interplay between weights and gradients.
AI.conclusion: Parameter importance cannot be fully understood through either weights or gradients alone. WAG serves as a unified approach for analyzing, debugging, and controlling LLMs, opening new directions for principled model-level interpretation. Its effectiveness points to fundamental structural properties of trained networks.

title: OmniX: Any-view and Any-time 4D Reconstruction via Feed-forward Trajectory Fields
comment: Accepted by ECCV 2026, project page: https://omnix4d.github.io/
summary: Previous feed-forward 4D reconstruction methods either predict per-frame static point clouds, ignoring foreground motion, or estimate point cloud trajectories while being limited to small camera motions. This restricts their ability to aggregate observations over time and reconstruct complete dynamic scenes under large viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, we propose OmniX, a feed-forward 4D reconstruction framework that predicts dense 3D point trajectories for every pixel from videos with large camera motion. OmniX decouples dynamic motion modeling from static geometry prediction and represents motion using a compact set of dynamic tokens. By leveraging the sparse and low-rank structure of 3D motion, these tokens generate trajectory fields for all pixels across all images while efficiently preserving global interactions. To facilitate training, we further build an automatic UE5-based 4D data engine and introduce a large-scale dataset containing 80K scenes and 1.28M multi-view videos with full geometric annotations. OmniX achieves state-of-the-art performance on dense 3D point trajectory prediction and 3D point tracking, while also demonstrating competitive results on video depth estimation and camera pose estimation.

AI.tldr: OmniX is a feed-forward 4D reconstruction framework that predicts dense 3D point trajectories from videos with large camera motion, achieving state-of-the-art performance on trajectory prediction and 3D point tracking.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward 4D reconstruction methods are limited by either ignoring foreground motion (per-frame static point clouds) or being constrained to small camera motions, restricting their ability to aggregate observations over time and reconstruct complete dynamic scenes under large viewpoint changes.
AI.method: OmniX decouples dynamic motion modeling from static geometry prediction, represents motion using compact dynamic tokens, leverages sparse and low-rank structure of 3D motion to generate trajectory fields for all pixels while preserving global interactions, and uses an automatic UE5-based 4D data engine with a large-scale dataset (80K scenes, 1.28M multi-view videos).
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on dense 3D point trajectory prediction and 3D point tracking, competitive results on video depth estimation and camera pose estimation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decoupling of motion and geometry, combined with compact token-based motion representation and large-scale synthetic data, effectively enables feed-forward 4D reconstruction under large camera motion.

title: Verifier-Guided Twelve-Tone Composition: A Generate-Verify-Repair Harness for Symbolic Music Generation
summary: Large language models can produce superficially legal twelve-tone scores that collapse into degenerate textures. We introduce a neuro-symbolic harness that wraps a language-model proposer in a generate-verify-repair-trace loop with symbolic verification. The complete pipeline improves event-local consistency without claiming whole-piece legality. Across 40 controlled tasks and four paired models, audited delivery yield rises from 13.3% under raw generation to 48.1% with the harness, which explicitly abstains otherwise. The pass rate of a narrower collision and serialisation-consistency check rises from 33.5% to 58.3%, while degeneracy remains near 0.05, including under exploratory adversarial prompting. A blinded evaluation by five experts also shows a descriptive aggregate preference for harness candidates over raw generation in adherence, perceived legality, coherence, and overall quality.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic harness combining LLM proposers with symbolic verification (generate-verify-repair-trace loop) improves twelve-tone score consistency from 13.3% to 48.1% audited delivery yield and from 33.5% to 58.3% pass rate on collision/serialization checks, with near-zero degeneracy (0.05) and expert preference for harness outputs.
AI.motivation: Large language models produce twelve-tone scores that appear legally structured but degenerate into chaotic textures; the paper aims to improve local consistency without claiming full legality.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic harness wrapping an LLM proposer in a generate-verify-repair-trace loop with symbolic verification, tested across 40 controlled tasks with four paired models.
AI.result: Audited delivery yield rose from 13.3% to 48.1%; pass rate for collision/serialization-consistency checks rose from 33.5% to 58.3%; degeneracy remained near 0.05 even under adversarial prompting; blind expert evaluation favored harness outputs.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic verification loop substantially improves event-local consistency in LLM-generated twelve-tone scores while maintaining low degeneracy, though it does not guarantee whole-piece legality.

title: When does distribution shift break graph neural networks calibration?
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications where distribution shift is un-avoidable. However, how such shifts affect model calibration, defined as the agreement between predictive confidence and actual accuracy, remains poorly understood, and existing graph calibration methods typically rely on labeled validation data from the deployment distribution. In this work, I present the first closed-form theoretical characterization of GNN calibration under distribution shift. I show that calibration is governed by a single scalar quantity that explicitly depends on structural changes between the source and target graphs, as well as feature quality. This characterization precisely identifies when a model becomes over-confident, under-confident, or remains calibrated, and directly yields the optimal temperature scaling strategy. I further extend the analysis to graph convolutional networks with symmetric normalization, multi-class classification, and covariate shift, and derive a theoretical upper bound on the expected calibration error. My analysis also reveals that, under homogeneous distribution shift, a single global temperature is theoretically optimal, providing a principled explanation for why more complex node-wise recalibration methods offer no additional benefit. Building on these theoretical insights, I propose STAC, a source-free, label-free calibration method. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks demonstrate substantial calibration improvements, while evaluations on five real-world graph datasets show that reliable calibration without target labels remains challenging despite the strong predictive power of the theory.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first closed-form theoretical characterization of GNN calibration under distribution shift, showing calibration depends on graph structural changes and feature quality. It introduces STAC, a source-free, label-free calibration method, with experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Despite increasing deployment of GNNs under distribution shift, how such shifts affect model calibration remains poorly understood, and existing calibration methods rely on labeled validation data from the target distribution, which is often unavailable.
AI.method: The author derives a closed-form theoretical characterization showing GNN calibration under shift is governed by a single scalar depending on structural changes and feature quality. The analysis is extended to GCNs with symmetric normalization, multi-class classification, and covariate shift, yielding a theoretical upper bound on expected calibration error. Based on these insights, STAC (a source-free, label-free calibration method) is proposed.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic benchmarks show substantial calibration improvements. However, evaluations on five real-world graph datasets reveal that reliable calibration without target labels remains challenging despite the theory's strong predictive power.
AI.conclusion: The theory precisely identifies when a model becomes over-confident, under-confident, or stays calibrated, and shows that under homogeneous distribution shift, a single global temperature is theoretically optimal, explaining why complex node-wise recalibration offers no extra benefit.

title: Align and Segment: Unsupervised Learning for Building Segmentation From Misaligned Labels
comment: main draft with references is 17 pages
summary: Supervised learning for image segmentation typically requires spatially aligned image and label sets. When images and labels originate from different sources, the pairing may be misaligned, which can significantly deteriorate the performance of the learned models. This is especially common in remote sensing, when aerial or satellite images are co-registered with labels from another source (e.g., OpenStreetMap). In this work, we propose a novel approach for training on misaligned labels, where we simultaneously learn the label alignment. Our align and segment (AnS) approach builds on the spatial transformer module to transform the misaligned labels using an affine transformation to provide a better learning target for a canonical semantic segmentation network. We prevent shortcut learning of misaligned labels in these semantic segmentation networks through a self-supervised regularization loss and show that it is complementary to data augmentation, especially for systematically misaligned training data. A decisive characteristic of our AnS approach is that it learns without requiring any golden labels. We experimentally show on both synthetic and real-world data from different cities that our approach enables high-quality building segmentation and precise label-image alignment at the same time. Code and derived datasets are available at https://github.com/venkanna37/align-and-segment

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Align and Segment (AnS) approach that simultaneously learns to align misaligned labels and perform semantic segmentation without requiring any golden labels, using a spatial transformer module and self-supervised regularization to prevent shortcut learning.
AI.motivation: Supervised learning for image segmentation requires spatially aligned image-label pairs, but in remote sensing, aerial/satellite images and labels from different sources (e.g., OpenStreetMap) are often misaligned, which significantly degrades model performance.
AI.method: The AnS approach uses a spatial transformer module to learn an affine transformation that aligns misaligned labels, feeding the transformed labels as a better learning target to a canonical semantic segmentation network. A self-supervised regularization loss prevents shortcut learning of misaligned labels, complementing data augmentation.
AI.result: Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data from different cities demonstrate that the approach enables high-quality building segmentation and precise label-image alignment simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: The AnS approach effectively addresses misaligned label-image pairs in remote sensing by jointly learning alignment and segmentation without requiring any ground-truth labels, with code and datasets publicly available.

title: AutoVSR: Automatic Visual-to-Symbolic Reasoning for Symbolic Expression Generation from Circuit Schematic
summary: Symbolic expressions can effectively characterize and predict circuit behavior, but deriving them directly from circuit schematics is challenging. This process requires accurate visual-to-symbolic construction of circuit structure from images and correct multi-step symbolic derivation, both of which impose strict correctness requirements. This work proposes AutoVSR, an automated framework for visual-to-symbolic generation of circuit expressions using Vision Language Models (VLMs). By reconstructing circuit diagrams into an executable intermediate representation (Executable IR) and leveraging a symbolic solver for reasoning, AutoVSR significantly improves the accuracy of symbolic expression generation. AutoVSR introduces two key innovations: an IR construction method guided by component rule retrieval and verification-based feedback, and a symbolic solver implemented as a planning agent equipped with a symbolic tool library for reliable multi-step derivation. Compared with end-to-end VLM approaches and specialized methods on the main symbolic expression generation task, AutoVSR achieves accuracy improvements of 30.01--59.45% and 41.96--51.84%, respectively. Moreover, AutoVSR surpasses closed-source state-of-the-art VLMs in inference cost and computational efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/LongfeiLi1/AutoVSR.

AI.tldr: AutoVSR is an automated framework that uses Vision Language Models to convert circuit diagrams into symbolic expressions by reconstructing them into an Executable IR and using a symbolic solver, achieving 30-59% accuracy improvements over end-to-end VLMs and 42-52% over specialized methods.
AI.motivation: Deriving symbolic expressions from circuit schematics is challenging due to the need for accurate visual-to-symbolic construction and correct multi-step symbolic derivation, both of which require high correctness.
AI.method: AutoVSR reconstructs circuit diagrams into an Executable IR using an IR construction method guided by component rule retrieval and verification-based feedback, then leverages a symbolic solver implemented as a planning agent with a symbolic tool library for reliable multi-step derivation.
AI.result: AutoVSR achieves accuracy improvements of 30.01-59.45% over end-to-end VLM approaches and 41.96-51.84% over specialized methods, while surpassing closed-source state-of-the-art VLMs in inference cost and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: AutoVSR significantly improves symbolic expression generation accuracy from circuit diagrams by combining VLMs with structured intermediate representation and symbolic reasoning, offering both performance and efficiency gains.

title: Lower Bound on the Cumulative Constrained Violation for the OGD+Projection algorithm for Constrained Online Convex Optimization (COCO)
summary: The problem of constrained online convex optimization is considered, where at each round, once a learner commits to an action $x_t \in \mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, a convex loss function $f_t$ and a convex constraint function $g_t$ that drives the constraint $g_t(x)\le 0$ are revealed. The objective is to simultaneously minimize the static regret and cumulative constraint violation (CCV) compared to the benchmark that knows the loss functions and constraint functions $f_t$ and $g_t$ for all $t$ ahead of time, and chooses a static optimal action that is feasible with respect to all $g_t(x)\le 0$. Currently, the best known algorithm is OGD+Projection algorithm of [Vaze and Sinha, 2025] that has simultaneous regret of $O(\sqrt{T})$ and CCV of $O(T^{1/3})$ for $d=2$ [Balasundaram et al., 2026], and simultaneous regret of $O(\sqrt{T})$ and CCV of $O(\sqrt{T})$ for any $d$ [Sarkar and Sinha, 2026]. In this paper, we show that the CCV of the OGD+Projection algorithm is $Ω(T^{\frac{d-1}{2d}})$. This is the first such lower bound result.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a lower bound of Ω(T^{(d-1)/(2d)}) for cumulative constraint violation (CCV) in the OGD+Projection algorithm for constrained online convex optimization, which is the first such lower bound result.
AI.motivation: To establish a lower bound for CCV in constrained online convex optimization using the OGD+Projection algorithm, addressing the gap between existing upper bounds and theoretical limits.
AI.method: The paper derives a lower bound analysis showing that the CCV of the OGD+Projection algorithm is Ω(T^{(d-1)/(2d)}), where d is the dimension of the action space.
AI.result: The CCV lower bound for OGD+Projection is Ω(T^{(d-1)/(2d)}), which is the first such lower bound; for d=2 this gives Ω(T^{1/4}), while the best known upper bound is O(T^{1/3}).
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies a gap between the lower bound Ω(T^{(d-1)/(2d)}) and existing upper bounds, suggesting that either the upper bound can be improved or a different algorithm is needed to achieve optimal CCV.

title: Learning To Focus: Anatomy-Guided Attention Regularization for Medical Image Classification
