summary: Medical image classification models are ideally expected to identify diagnostically relevant regions while making predictions, yet standard classification losses rarely provide spatial supervision. Explicit supervision via anatomical shape information, such as segmentation masks of task-relevant anatomy, has been shown to guide the network toward regions relevant to the target prediction. However, obtaining such masks incurs substantial manual annotation effort and computational overhead. With the advent of segmentation foundation models that exhibit strong localization of anatomical structures across diverse imaging modalities, we leverage this capability to extract anatomical shape priors without the burden of training a dedicated segmentation model. In this paper, we propose a new framework, Locus, an anatomical attention regularization framework that leverages pretrained segmentation foundation models to guide a classifier's attention toward diagnostically meaningful anatomical structures across diverse imaging modalities. Instead of enforcing pixel-wise alignment with the foundation-model-derived mask, we introduce a regularization term that adaptively balances attention between anatomical (foreground) and background regions, penalizing the classifier when background attention dominates. We validate Locus on eight diverse medical imaging datasets spanning dermoscopy, X-ray, histopathology, and cardiac MRI, showing consistent gains in classification performance alongside improved anatomically grounded attention.

AI.tldr: Locus is an anatomical attention regularization framework that leverages pretrained segmentation foundation models to guide classifier attention toward diagnostically relevant anatomical structures without requiring dedicated segmentation model training, achieving consistent classification gains across eight diverse medical imaging datasets.
AI.motivation: Medical image classifiers ideally should focus on diagnostically relevant regions, but standard classification losses lack spatial supervision. While anatomical shape information (e.g., segmentation masks) can guide networks, obtaining such masks requires substantial manual annotation and computational overhead. The authors aim to leverage segmentation foundation models to extract anatomical priors without training a dedicated segmentation model.
AI.method: The framework (Locus) uses pretrained segmentation foundation models to extract anatomical shape priors. Instead of pixel-wise alignment with the mask, it introduces a regularization term that adaptively balances attention between anatomical (foreground) and background regions, penalizing the classifier when background attention dominates.
AI.result: Validated on eight diverse medical imaging datasets (dermoscopy, X-ray, histopathology, cardiac MRI), showing consistent gains in classification performance alongside improved anatomically grounded attention.
AI.conclusion: Locus effectively improves classification performance and anatomical attention grounding across multiple imaging modalities by leveraging foundation model priors without the need for dedicated segmentation model training or pixel-wise alignment.

title: Compile, Then Page: Executable SOP Programs and a Capability-Gated Runtime for Procedural LLM Agents
summary: Enterprise agents must follow long-horizon, conditional, safety-critical standard operating procedures (SOPs). We compile machine-readable SOP constraints into executable pseudo-code and run them with a program-guided (PG) stack machine that pages the active frame while an LLM performs semantic execution. A three-arm SOPBench study across six models separates representation from runtime: compiled text never significantly hurts and gains up to 16.0 points where official prose underperforms. Runtime guidance is capability-gated. Two strong models independently show positive seven-domain PG contrasts (58:19 and 75:31 discordant pairs), whereas weak models are harmed. A full-program cursor ablation (active frame first, complete program retained) recovers much of the strong-model refusal gain; selective visibility adds a smaller improvement. Paired probe and audit measurements track this divide to spontaneous state discipline rather than reconstruction ability. On Bank the three primary arms rise from 70.4 to 86.4 to 92.8, with 100% refusal correctness. Practical guidance: compile first; enable active-frame paging only after a model-level discipline check.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SOPBench, a framework that compiles standard operating procedures (SOPs) into machine-readable pseudo-code executed by a program-guided stack machine with LLM-based semantic execution. Results show that compiled text representation improves performance (up to 16 points), runtime guidance benefits strong models but harms weak ones, and active-frame paging recovers refusal gains. Practical recommendation: compile first, then conditionally enable active-frame paging based on model discipline.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agents need to follow complex, long-horizon, conditional, and safety-critical SOPs, but existing LLM-based agents struggle with faithful adherence and safe refusal when SOP constraints are violated.
AI.method: Machine-readable SOP constraints are compiled into executable pseudo-code, executed by a program-guided (PG) stack machine with active-frame paging, where an LLM performs semantic execution. A three-arm SOPBench study (compiled text, official prose, baseline) across six models separates representation from runtime effects.
AI.result: Compiled text never significantly hurts performance and gains up to 16.0 points where official prose underperforms. Runtime guidance is capability-gated: strong models show positive PG contrasts (58:19 and 75:31 discordant pairs), weak models are harmed. Full-program cursor ablation recovers most refusal gain; selective visibility adds smaller improvement. On Bank, three arms rise from 70.4 → 86.4 → 92.8, with 100% refusal correctness.
AI.conclusion: Practical recommendation: compile SOP constraints first; enable active-frame paging only after verifying model-level discipline. The performance divide between strong and weak models is attributed to spontaneous state discipline rather than reconstruction ability.

title: Diachronic Sample Integration: Robust Tail-Risk Estimation with Generative Models
summary: Deep generative models are increasingly used as simulators for downstream decision-making under data scarcity, but in risk-sensitive applications their usefulness depends on rare adverse scenarios rather than typical samples. Standard generative objectives prioritize bulk distributional fidelity, leaving low-probability tails vulnerable to localized optimization noise and making tail-dependent functionals unstable under finite simulation budgets. We introduce Diachronic Sample Integration (DSI), a test-time inference framework that ensembles generated samples across checkpoints from a stochastic training trajectory. DSI targets a checkpoint-mixture distribution that averages checkpoint-specific tail fluctuations rather than relying on a single brittle endpoint. We formalize this mechanism through a finite-budget bias-variance theory. Empirically, across multivariate synthetic processes and high-frequency trading data, DSI substantially reduces tail-estimation error compared to single-checkpoint baselines under fixed simulation budgets, outperforming standard diffusion and state-of-the-art tail-aware baselines without modifying the generative objective.

AI.tldr: DSI is a test-time inference framework that ensembles generated samples across training checkpoints to improve tail estimation accuracy in downstream risk-sensitive applications, without modifying the generative objective.
AI.motivation: Standard generative models prioritize bulk distributional fidelity, causing low-probability tails to suffer from localized optimization noise. This makes tail-dependent functionals unstable under finite simulation budgets, which is problematic for risk-sensitive decision-making under data scarcity.
AI.method: Diachronic Sample Integration (DSI) ensembles generated samples across checkpoints from a stochastic training trajectory, targeting a checkpoint-mixture distribution that averages checkpoint-specific tail fluctuations instead of relying on a single brittle endpoint. A finite-budget bias-variance theory is used to formalize this mechanism.
AI.result: Across multivariate synthetic processes and high-frequency trading data, DSI substantially reduces tail-estimation error compared to single-checkpoint baselines under fixed simulation budgets, outperforming standard diffusion and state-of-the-art tail-aware baselines.
AI.conclusion: DSI effectively stabilizes tail functional estimates without modifying the generative objective, serving as a practical test-time framework for risk-sensitive applications.

title: Diversify Diffusion with Temperature Sampling and Variance-Corrective Time Shifting
summary: Diffusion models faithfully reproduce their training distribution, but also inherit its imbalances and leave rare or under-represented modes hard to reach. A natural inference-time remedy is to sample from the high-temperature target $p^{(γ)}_0(x) \propto p_0(x)^γ$ for $0 < γ< 1$, which flattens dominant modes and lifts rare ones. However, naive score scaling while correctly reweighting modes also inflates the per-mode variance, breaking the reverse diffusion process and degrading sample quality. We introduce variance-corrective time shifting, a training-free fix that queries the network at a shifted timestep and scales the resulting score by $γ$, canceling the variance inflation while preserving the mode reweighting. The correction turns simple temperature sampling into a practical diversity knob for pretrained diffusion and flow-matching backbones with no retraining, and we demonstrate consistent gains at minimal cost to sample quality and condition fidelity across DiT, Stable Diffusion and Motion Diffusion models. We further show that the timing of the temperature intervention enables coarse-to-fine control: high-noise stages drive compositional diversity across modes, while low-noise stages drive local appearance variation under a fixed composition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces variance-corrective time shifting, a training-free method that enables temperature sampling in diffusion models by canceling variance inflation while preserving mode reweighting, demonstrated on DiT, Stable Diffusion, and Motion Diffusion models with coarse-to-fine diversity control.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models inherit imbalances from their training data, making rare or under-represented modes difficult to sample. Temperature sampling ($p_0(x)^γ$ for $0<γ<1$) could flatten dominant modes and lift rare ones, but naive score scaling inflates per-mode variance, degrading sample quality.
AI.method: Variance-corrective time shifting: a training-free technique that queries the network at a shifted timestep and scales the resulting score by $γ$, canceling variance inflation while preserving mode reweighting. The timing of temperature intervention enables coarse-to-fine control (high-noise stages for compositional diversity, low-noise stages for local variation).
AI.result: Consistent diversity gains with minimal cost to sample quality and condition fidelity across DiT, Stable Diffusion, and Motion Diffusion models. Temperature sampling becomes a practical diversity knob for pretrained diffusion and flow-matching backbones with no retraining.
AI.conclusion: The proposed correction makes temperature sampling practical for pretrained diffusion models, enabling a simple diversity knob with coarse-to-fine control over sample diversity.

title: From Neural Network Decisions to Training Cases: An Exact Account via Case-Based Decision Theory
comment: Preprint. 15 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Includes appendix
summary: Neural networks increasingly guide decisions in high-stakes domains such as medical diagnosis, credit approval, and energy bidding. Audit in these settings requires case-level evidence: which training cases support an action and what outcomes they carried. Case-based decision theory (CBDT) formalizes this reasoning by aggregating outcome support from remembered cases. We show that an OLS action readout fitted on a fixed neural representation admits an exact case-based decomposition. Each action score is a weighted sum of training-case returns, with coefficients determined by empirical Gram geometry. We identify a sufficient regime for CBDT similarity semantics; outside it, the coefficients should generally be treated as signed Gram-geometric influence. The decomposition yields audit signals that trace scores to training cases, measure action coherence, and identify weak support. Across synthetic CBDT, PJM, Adult Income, and Default Credit tasks, the method recovers case-level preference structure and achieves the highest mean Top-30 consistency among compared attribution baselines, while remaining competitive on support reconstruction. The audit requires only fitting an OLS top-layer probe, without retraining the representation or accessing the original optimization trajectory; probe fidelity is measured by score reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an OLS probe on fixed neural representations yields exact case-based decompositions for auditing model decisions by tracing outcome support from training cases, achieving high attribution consistency across tasks.
AI.motivation: High-stakes AI decisions need case-level audit evidence (which training cases drove an action and their outcomes), but existing methods lack exact decompositions relating predictions to individual training-case returns.
AI.method: Proves that an OLS linear probe fitted on a fixed neural representation produces action scores that are weighted sums of training-case returns, with weights determined by empirical Gram geometry. Identifies regimes where these weights correspond to CBDT similarity semantics vs. signed Gram-geometric influence.
AI.result: Across synthetic CBDT, PJM, Adult Income, and Default Credit tasks, the method recovers case-level preference structure, achieves highest mean Top-30 consistency among baselines, and remains competitive on support reconstruction—all without retraining or accessing optimization trajectory.
AI.conclusion: OLS probe case-based decomposition is a simple, faithful audit tool providing case-level evidence (support tracing, coherence measurement, weak support identification) for neural network decisions in high-stakes domains.

title: Graph Neural Networks for RFID-Based Spatial Geometry Inference in Spatial AI Systems
comment: 38 pages, 10 figures. Introduces a Graph Neural Network framework for RFID-based spatial geometry inference using indoor floorplan semantics and digital twin representations
summary: Indoor spatial understanding remains a fundamental challenge for intelligent systems operating in physical environments. Traditional RFID localization techniques typically estimate positions of tags using signal strength measurements but fail to capture higher-order spatial relationships between objects and infrastructure. Recent work on RFID and wireless indoor localization has increasingly emphasized robust learning under noisy propagation, while recent graph-based localization methods demonstrate the value of relational modeling over isolated samples. This paper introduces a graph-based learning framework that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to infer spatial geometry from RFID observations. Rather than predicting isolated coordinates, the proposed system models relationships between RFID readings, antennas, and physical structures within an indoor floorplan. This framing is aligned with recent graph-based indoor positioning and graph construction literature, where topology is a first-class source of information for downstream inference. The approach integrates signal strength data, floorplan semantics, and spatial constraints into a graph representation where nodes correspond to RFID observations and edges encode proximity and contextual relationships. A GNN is then trained to predict geometric patterns such as linear trajectories, rectangular bounding regions, and movement paths of objects in space.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for indoor spatial understanding from RFID data. Instead of predicting isolated tag coordinates, the method models relationships between RFID readings, antennas, and floorplan structures using graph representations that encode signal strength, spatial semantics, and proximity. The GNN predicts geometric patterns like trajectories, bounding regions, and movement paths.
AI.motivation: Traditional RFID localization estimates positions from signal strength but fails to capture higher-order spatial relationships between objects and infrastructure. The paper aims to address this gap by using relational modeling to infer spatial geometry from RFID observations in indoor environments.
AI.method: The approach constructs a graph where nodes represent RFID observations and edges encode proximity and contextual relationships. It integrates signal strength data, floorplan semantics, and spatial constraints into this graph representation, then trains a GNN to predict geometric patterns such as linear trajectories, rectangular bounding regions, and movement paths.
AI.result: The system predicts geometric patterns including linear trajectories, rectangular bounding regions, and movement paths of objects in space, leveraging topology as a first-class information source for downstream inference.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based relational modeling via GNNs can effectively infer spatial geometry from RFID data, moving beyond isolated coordinate prediction to capture richer spatial relationships in indoor environments.

title: AU-Guided Synthetic Video Generation for Micro-Expression Recognition
summary: Micro-expression recognition is limited by the small scale, narrow demographic coverage, and restricted emotion labels of existing datasets. We introduce EquiME, a synthetic micro-expression dataset built from AU-guided image-to-video generation. EquiME contains 75K videos generated from 15K source face images across five target emotions, together with automatically inferred demographic metadata and video-quality measurements. We evaluate EquiME using frame-pair similarity, spatial variation, and no-reference perceptual-quality metrics, together with cross-dataset MER experiments on SAMM and CASME II. Models trained on EquiME achieve competitive cross-dataset performance on SAMM and CASME II and show comparatively low variation across the four evaluated architectures. This paper focuses on the dataset design, the structured AU-conditioning pipeline used for video generation, and the empirical evidence needed to assess EquiME as a synthetic MER resource. Project page: https://kirito-blade.github.io/me-vlm/

AI.tldr: EquiME is a large-scale synthetic micro-expression dataset (75K videos, 15K source faces, 5 emotions) built via AU-guided image-to-video generation, achieving competitive cross-dataset performance on SAMM and CASME II with low architectural variation.
AI.motivation: Existing micro-expression datasets suffer from small scale, narrow demographic coverage, and limited emotion labels, which restrict the generalization of MER models.
AI.method: EquiME is constructed using an AU-guided image-to-video generation pipeline, producing 75K videos from 15K source face images across five target emotions, with automatically inferred demographic metadata and video-quality measurements.
AI.result: Models trained on EquiME achieve competitive cross-dataset performance on SAMM and CASME II, with low variation across four evaluated architectures. The dataset is assessed via frame-pair similarity, spatial variation, and no-reference perceptual-quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: EquiME provides a scalable synthetic resource for micro-expression recognition, with empirical evidence supporting its utility for cross-dataset generalization, though this work focuses on dataset design and validation rather than downstream task innovation.

title: Predictive Divergence Masks for LLM RL
summary: Reinforcement learning for large language models (LLMs) typically relies on trust-region masks to stabilize off-policy updates. The dominant PPO-style approach uses the sampled-token importance ratio for two criteria: a proximity criterion, which asks whether the policy has moved too far from the behavior policy, and a direction criterion, which asks whether the update pushes it farther away. Recent work DPPO improves the proximity criterion by replacing PPO's ratio-based test with a probability divergence between the behavior and training policies. However, its direction criterion is still inherited from PPO. A token can be masked only when the sampled-token importance ratio moves away from one. We observe that this ratio-based direction criterion is a single-sample proxy that can disagree in sign with the change of the divergence that defines the proximity criterion. We therefore propose the predictive divergence mask, which asks whether the next policy-gradient step will increase or decrease the same divergence used by the trust region. For the discrete softmax policies used in LLM RL, we derive this prediction in closed form. Because production rollout engines expose only a truncated (top-K) view of the vocabulary, we develop two lightweight top-$K$ estimators for this prediction. Detailed analysis shows the divergence-based direction is better aligned with the realized change of the divergence than the sampled ratio, and the resulting masks improve RL training across model scales and precision settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes predictive divergence masks for LLM reinforcement learning, which replace PPO's ratio-based direction criterion with a divergence-based one that better aligns with the trust-region objective, improving training across model scales.
AI.motivation: PPO-style RL for LLMs uses trust-region masks with two criteria: proximity (has policy moved too far?) and direction (is the update pushing it further?). DPPO improved proximity using probability divergence, but its direction criterion still relies on a sampled-token importance ratio, which is a single-sample proxy that can disagree in sign with the divergence change used for proximity.
AI.method: The authors propose the predictive divergence mask, which predicts whether the next policy-gradient step will increase or decrease the same divergence used by the trust region. For discrete softmax policies, they derive this prediction in closed form. They also develop two lightweight top-K estimators for production rollout engines that expose only a truncated vocabulary view.
AI.result: The divergence-based direction is better aligned with the realized change of the divergence than the sampled ratio. The resulting masks improve RL training across different model scales and precision settings.
AI.conclusion: Replacing PPO's ratio-based direction criterion with a divergence-based predictive mask yields more consistent trust-region enforcement and improved LLM RL training performance.

title: X-GuideAR: An Augmented Reality Framework to Mitigate Radiation Exposure during Fluoroscopic Guidance
summary: Achieving optimal screw placement for orthopedic surgeries requires frequent alignment checks and multiple anatomical views under X-ray -- a process known as "fluoro-hunting" that increases radiation exposure to patients and surgical teams. This work introduces X-GuideAR, an augmented reality (AR) framework for identifying optimal X-ray views, aimed at reducing radiation exposure while ensuring accurate screw placement. To exemplify the benefits of X-GuideAR, we focus on S2 alar-iliac (S2AI) screw placement. Our system provides radiation-free guidance for view acquisition and drilling by generating synthetic X-ray previews that accelerate fluoro-hunting. Once the required anatomical views are identified using these previews, a real X-ray is acquired, and the preview of the drilling trajectory is augmented onto it, facilitating precise screw placement with minimal additional radiation. A preliminary study involving eight S2AI trajectories performed by an expert spine surgeon demonstrated a 62.3% reduction in the number of X-rays. Post-procedure evaluations showed that trajectories done with X-GuideAR supported an average safe screw diameter of 12.95 mm compared to 5.9 mm under the conventional workflow, suggesting improved bony containment and potential biomechanical benefit. X-GuideAR shows great potential to reduce radiation exposure and streamline S2AI screw placement, offering a promising direction toward safer and more efficient surgeries.

AI.tldr: X-GuideAR is an augmented reality framework that reduces radiation exposure during S2AI screw placement by generating synthetic X-ray previews to guide view acquisition, achieving a 62.3% reduction in X-ray usage and improved screw containment (12.95 mm vs 5.9 mm safe diameter).
AI.motivation: Reduce radiation exposure from "fluoro-hunting" (frequent X-ray checks during orthopedic screw placement) while maintaining or improving surgical accuracy.
AI.method: AR framework generating synthetic X-ray previews for radiation-free view acquisition guidance; once optimal views are identified via previews, a single real X-ray is taken and drilling trajectory is augmented onto it for precise placement.
AI.result: 62.3% reduction in number of X-rays; average safe screw diameter of 12.95 mm (X-GuideAR) vs 5.9 mm (conventional), indicating better bony containment.
AI.conclusion: X-GuideAR demonstrates strong potential to reduce radiation exposure and improve surgical efficiency and safety for S2AI screw placement.

title: StructAgent: Harness Long-horizon Digital Agents with Unified Causal Structure
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled increasingly capable digital agents for computer use. However, real-world tasks are often long-horizon and involve evolving contexts containing accumulated observations, intermediate edits, failed attempts, and partially completed executions. Existing agents typically operate over raw interaction history, making task progress difficult to interpret, verify, and recover, which ultimately limits reliable long-horizon execution. In this paper, we argue that addressing this challenge requires explicitly structuring both the agent's state and workflow around a unified causal representation of task progress. We present \textbf{StructAgent}, a state-centered framework that introduces a unified state for maintaining compact, verifiable task progress and a structured workflow that regulates progress through verifier-backed state transitions. Building on this design, StructAgent further enables explicit progress checkpointing, evidence-driven task completion, targeted failure recovery, and tool-supported execution, while ensuring that all progress updates remain grounded in verification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that StructAgent consistently improves a wide range of LLM and VLM backbones on long-horizon computer-use tasks. On OSWorld-Verified, it improves Qwen3.5-9B from 27.0\% to 46.9\% success rate and Qwen3.5-27B from 31.6\% to 62.2\%, while achieving a new open-source state of the art of 78.9\% with MiniMax-M3. Moreover, the same framework generalizes beyond desktop environments to Minecraft, demonstrating the generality of our design.

AI.tldr: StructAgent is a state-centered framework for long-horizon computer-use tasks that introduces a unified causal representation of task progress with verifier-backed state transitions, achieving significant improvements across LLM/VLM backbones (e.g., Qwen3.5-27B from 31.6% to 62.2% on OSWorld-Verified, and a new SOTA of 78.9% with MiniMax-M3) and generalizing beyond desktop to Minecraft.
AI.motivation: Existing digital agents operating over raw interaction history make task progress difficult to interpret, verify, and recover, limiting reliable long-horizon execution in evolving contexts with accumulated observations, intermediate edits, failed attempts, and partially completed executions.
AI.method: StructAgent is a state-centered framework with (1) a unified state maintaining compact, verifiable task progress, and (2) a structured workflow that regulates progress through verifier-backed state transitions, enabling progress checkpointing, evidence-driven task completion, targeted failure recovery, and tool-supported execution with grounded verification.
AI.result: On OSWorld-Verified, StructAgent improved Qwen3.5-9B from 27.0% to 46.9%, Qwen3.5-27B from 31.6% to 62.2%, and achieved 78.9% with MiniMax-M3 (new open-source SOTA). The framework also generalized to Minecraft environments.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly structuring agent state and workflow around a unified causal representation of task progress consistently improves LLM and VLM backbones on long-horizon computer-use tasks, with demonstrated generality beyond desktop environments.

title: Reliability Scaling Laws for Quantized Large Language Models
summary: Quantization is a powerful strategy to build capable and resource-efficient large language models (LLMs) by reducing the bitwidth of the parameters. While quantized LLMs achieve state-of-the-art performance on unperturbed inputs using standard predictive metrics, their performance on perturbed inputs, measured using reliability metrics, remains underexplored, despite its importance for reliable deployment. To address this gap, we first conduct a comprehensive reliability evaluation of quantized LLMs consisting of three key components: (1) Uncertainty: We assess the trustworthiness of LLMs quantized to 2, 3, 4, and 8 bits using six different quantization methods, employing established uncertainty metrics. (2) Calibration: We assess how well-calibrated the uncertainty estimates of quantized models are across model scales and bit precisions. (3) Robustness: We design character-level and word-level input perturbations to evaluate the reliability of quantized models under semantically-preserving variations in the inputs that arise in real-world applications. Second, we characterize how reliability scales with the total number of model bits. Our study reveals that while the performance scales monotonically with the total number of bits, the reliability scalings are nonlinear. A reliability peak occurs for 4-bit quantized models, indicating that quantizing moderately sized models offers the best reliability-efficiency trade-off. Additionally, our empirical findings reveal that quantization enhances the robustness of LLMs to natural input perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the reliability (uncertainty, calibration, robustness) of quantized LLMs across different bitwidths and quantization methods, finding that 4-bit quantization offers the best reliability-efficiency trade-off and that quantization enhances robustness to natural input perturbations.
AI.motivation: While quantized LLMs achieve state-of-the-art performance on unperturbed inputs using standard predictive metrics, their performance on perturbed inputs (reliability metrics) remains underexplored, despite its importance for reliable deployment.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive reliability evaluation of quantized LLMs with three components: (1) Uncertainty assessment using established metrics across 2, 3, 4, and 8-bit quantized models with six quantization methods; (2) Calibration evaluation across model scales and bit precisions; (3) Robustness evaluation using character-level and word-level input perturbations.
AI.result: Performance scales monotonically with total number of bits, but reliability scalings are nonlinear. A reliability peak occurs for 4-bit quantized models. Quantization enhances robustness of LLMs to natural input perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Moderately quantized (4-bit) models offer the best reliability-efficiency trade-off, and quantization can improve LLM robustness to natural perturbations.

title: Design Choices in Splitting-Based Self-Supervised Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
comment: 12 pages (main manuscript), 9 pages (supplementary material and figures)
summary: Self-supervised data splitting has emerged as a promising paradigm for sparse-view CT reconstruction, enabling training from incomplete measurements without fully sampled ground truth. However, the influence of key design choices, including partitioning strategy, preprocessing, and inference, remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce a unified framework that decomposes splitting-based reconstruction into these three components, enabling controlled comparison of existing methods and two incremental extensions: multi-partition splitting and an alternative inference strategy. Experiments on simulated LoDoPaB-CT data under independent and correlated noise, together with validation on the real-world 2DeteCT dataset, show that the optimal partitioning strategy strongly depends on the measurement noise structure. Lattice-based splitting performs favorably under independent noise, whereas angular masking is more robust under correlated noise and real measured data. Multi-partition splitting consistently improves over pure projection-wise splitting in several settings. Complementary perceptual and structural metrics, including LPIPS and HaarPSI, reveal differences between masking strategies that are less apparent from PSNR and SSIM alone. These results provide practical guidelines for designing self-supervised sparse-view CT reconstruction methods and highlight the limitations of common independence assumptions in realistic imaging environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unified framework for self-supervised data splitting in sparse-view CT reconstruction, decomposing it into partitioning, preprocessing, and inference components. Experiments show that lattice-based splitting works best under independent noise, while angular masking is more robust for correlated noise and real data. Multi-partition splitting and alternative inference strategies offer improvements, and perceptual metrics like LPIPS and HaarPSI reveal differences not captured by PSNR/SSIM alone.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand how key design choices (partitioning strategy, preprocessing, inference) influence self-supervised splitting-based sparse-view CT reconstruction, and to provide practical guidelines for method design under realistic noise conditions.
AI.method: A unified framework decomposing splitting-based reconstruction into three components (partitioning, preprocessing, inference), enabling controlled comparison of existing methods and two proposed extensions: multi-partition splitting and an alternative inference strategy.
AI.result: Optimal partitioning strategy depends on measurement noise structure: lattice-based splitting excels under independent noise, angular masking under correlated/real noise. Multi-partition splitting consistently improves over projection-wise splitting. Perceptual metrics (LPIPS, HaarPSI) reveal differences not captured by PSNR/SSIM alone.
AI.conclusion: Practical guidelines for designing self-supervised sparse-view CT reconstruction methods are provided, highlighting that common independence assumptions are often violated in realistic imaging environments, and emphasizing the need for noise-adaptive partitioning strategies.

title: Omni-Decision: A Progressive Evidence-State Agent System for Omni-Modal QA
summary: Omni-modal evidence-seeking QA requires agents to answer questions whose evidence is sparsely distributed across videos, audio, images, web pages, and computation results. Existing agentic multimodal systems often leave evidence in scratchpads, tool trajectories, or free-form histories, making it difficult to track what has been grounded, what remains missing, and when the evidence is sufficient to answer. We propose Omni-Decision, a training-free evidence-state system that turns omni-modal QA into a query-scoped evidence-closure process. For each query, Omni-Decision maintains a structured evidence state containing confirmed evidence, unresolved conflicts, fact and computation dependencies, and open evidence needs. A shared state view conditions planning, evidence acquisition, validation, repair, and finalization. Heterogeneous observations from media, web, computation, and verification modules are normalized, judged, and committed through deterministic state updates. This design enables targeted evidence acquisition, preserves sparse cross-modal cues, and provides inspectable control over repair and stopping. Omni-Decision achieves 45.6% accuracy on OmniGAIA and 58.3% on WorldSense, improving over the baselines by +27.3 and +30.2 percentage points, respectively. No-state ablations and trajectory audits further support the role of explicit evidence-state control in multi-step omni-modal evidence seeking.

AI.tldr: Omni-Decision is a training-free evidence-state system that converts omni-modal QA into a query-scoped evidence-closure process, achieving 45.6% on OmniGAIA and 58.3% on WorldSense, improving baselines by +27.3 and +30.2 percentage points respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic multimodal systems leave evidence in scratchpads, tool trajectories, or free-form histories, making it difficult to track what has been grounded, what remains missing, and when evidence is sufficient to answer questions whose evidence is sparsely distributed across videos, audio, images, web pages, and computation results.
AI.method: Maintains a structured evidence state per query containing confirmed evidence, unresolved conflicts, fact/computation dependencies, and open evidence needs. A shared state view conditions planning, acquisition, validation, repair, and finalization. Heterogeneous observations are normalized, judged, and committed through deterministic state updates.
AI.result: 45.6% accuracy on OmniGAIA and 58.3% on WorldSense, improving over baselines by +27.3 and +30.2 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: Explicit evidence-state control plays a crucial role in multi-step omni-modal evidence seeking, as supported by no-state ablations and trajectory audits.

title: Singular perturbations and hierarchical learning in two-layer neural networks
summary: We study the population gradient flow of an infinitely wide two-layer neural network learning a misspecified single-index model in high dimension. The two layers are optimized jointly, with a perturbative parameter tuning the relative training speed between the first and second layer. This setting was considered by Berthier, Montanari and Zhou in \cite{berthier2024learning}, who conjectured a hierarchical learning scenario with explicit timescales as the second layer is trained faster than the first. In this paper, we prove that the constant and linear components of the hidden link function are indeed recovered within the predicted timescales, at sharp explicit thresholds. We then analyze the onset of learning of the quadratic component and show that the components learned at earlier stages continue to influence the dynamics in an essential way. Our proof is based on quantitative approximation results for singularly perturbed flows evolving near a manifold defined by integral constraints. At a phenomenological level, we also show that the empirical measure of the weights displays singular behaviour when reaching the quadratic component of the hidden link, with a small fraction of neurons growing significantly while the remaining ones rearrange to preserve the components already learned.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously analyzes the population gradient flow dynamics of a two-layer neural network learning a misspecified single-index model in high dimensions, proving that constant and linear components of the hidden link function are recovered at predicted timescales, and characterizing the onset of quadratic component learning with singular behavior in the weight measure.
AI.motivation: To rigorously prove the hierarchical learning conjecture by Berthier, Montanari, and Zhou regarding the timescales at which different components of a misspecified single-index model are learned by a two-layer neural network with joint training and perturbative control of layer-wise training speed.
AI.method: Quantitative approximation results for singularly perturbed flows evolving near a manifold defined by integral constraints; analysis of the empirical measure of weights to capture singular behavior during quadratic component learning.
AI.result: Constant and linear components are recovered at sharp explicit thresholds matching predicted timescales; the quadratic component learning onset shows earlier-learned components continue to influence dynamics; the weight empirical measure exhibits singular behavior with a small fraction of neurons growing significantly while others rearrange to preserve already-learned components.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical learning scenario with explicit timescales is confirmed for constant and linear components, and the quadratic component learning exhibits rich dynamical phenomena including singular behavior in the weight distribution.

title: DP-Splat: Bayesian Nonparametric Complexity Control for Gaussian Splatting
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Code and experiment records: https://github.com/archiedong/dp-splat
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents scenes as finite mixtures of anisotropic Gaussians whose number of components $K$ is set by heuristic density control or user caps. Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting (VBGS) recast splat fitting as conjugate variational inference, but $K$ remains fixed. We replace the finite symmetric Dirichlet over mixture weights with a truncated stick-breaking Dirichlet-process prior -- and, as a theory-backed alternative, a sparse overfitted finite Dirichlet -- so that the number of occupied components adapts to the data while every update remains a closed-form coordinate-ascent step; a natural-gradient stochastic variant makes the per-step cost independent of the number of points. We give an exact monotonicity guarantee, a rigorous truncation-error bound correcting an anti-conservative large-$α$ approximation in common use, and an honest account of what the fitted number of components estimates. Empirically: (i) the effective complexity $\hat{K}$ adapts to scene complexity and recovers the true $K$ within $\pm 1$ on well-separated synthetic data with regime-appropriate concentration; (ii) a deconfounded comparison shows the DP prior's contribution is complexity selection, not per-component efficiency -- converged DP fits exceed single-pass fixed-$K$ VBGS by +2.7 dB at matched budgets yet tie an equally converged fixed-$K$ baseline, and on 3D scenes DP-Splat matches or exceeds VBGS's held-out color prediction with 5.9-7.6x fewer components; (iii) the posterior-predictive color variance is well calibrated on model-matched synthetic data; and (iv) the ordering suggested by exact-posterior asymptotics reverses under mean-field coordinate ascent: the DP prior resists over-splitting while the sparse finite mixture saturates its truncation, a gap between variational practice and posterior asymptotics documented across three orders of magnitude in $N$.

AI.tldr: This paper replaces the fixed number of Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting with a Bayesian nonparametric prior (Dirichlet process) that automatically adapts the number of components to the scene complexity, using closed-form coordinate-ascent updates and a natural-gradient stochastic variant. Theoretical guarantees and empirical results show complexity selection with 5.9-7.6x fewer components while matching or exceeding baseline performance.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods either use heuristic density control or fixed-K variational inference (VBGS) to determine the number of Gaussian components K, lacking a principled Bayesian mechanism for automatically adapting model complexity to the data.
AI.method: Replace the finite symmetric Dirichlet prior over mixture weights with a truncated stick-breaking Dirichlet-process prior (and a sparse overfitted finite Dirichlet alternative). The inference is done via closed-form coordinate-ascent variational updates with a natural-gradient stochastic variant that makes per-step cost independent of the number of points.
AI.result: (i) Effective complexity K̂ adapts to scene complexity, recovering true K within ±1 on synthetic data; (ii) DP prior's contribution is complexity selection, not per-component efficiency; (iii) posterior-predictive color variance is well calibrated; (iv) DP resists over-splitting while sparse finite mixture saturates truncation, showing a gap between variational practice and posterior asymptotics.
AI.conclusion: The Dirichlet-process prior provides principled automatic complexity selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting, achieving 5.9-7.6x fewer components than VBGS while matching or exceeding held-out color prediction quality, with theoretical guarantees on monotonicity and truncation error.

title: The Ebb and Flow of Multimodal Focus: Scheduling Visual Relay Windows for Grounded VLM Reasoning
summary: Vision-language models increasingly succeed on multimodal reasoning benchmarks, yet their visual evidence often becomes unstable once it enters the language stack, weakening evidence-grounded reasoning. To understand this fragility, we examine the internal dynamics of VLMs through a mechanistic lens and uncover a stable three-stage redistribution of multimodal attention focus across depth: an early question-conditioned organization, a critical middle visual-dominant relay, and a late return to answer formation. We operationalize the middle phase as the Visual Relay Window (VRW), and show that its geometry varies with task demand, is causally tied to grounded generation, and distinguishes unsupported answers from stronger reasoning trajectories. Guided by this internal rhythm, we propose TRACE, a task-adaptive inference-time control framework with lightweight trained modules. It reshapes relay allocation during prefill and preserves assembled visual support after handoff during decoding. Across four open-weight VLM backbones and seven benchmarks, TRACE delivers large gains on grounding-sensitive settings, improving them by 4.33 points on average and by up to 6.6 points, while also improving reasoning-heavy tasks. These results show that explicitly controlling multimodal focus across depth offers a unified and effective mechanism for strengthening evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: VLMs exhibit a stable three-stage internal attention rhythm across depth (question-conditioned → visual-dominant relay → answer formation). The middle Visual Relay Window (VRW) is critical for grounded reasoning, and the proposed TRACE framework reshapes relay allocation during prefill and preserves visual support during decoding, improving grounding-sensitive tasks by 4.33 points on average.
AI.motivation: VLMs' visual evidence becomes unstable once it enters the language stack, weakening evidence-grounded reasoning. The authors aim to understand and fix this fragility through mechanistic analysis.
AI.method: (1) Mechanistic analysis revealing a three-stage multimodal attention redistribution across depth; (2) Formalizing the middle phase as the Visual Relay Window (VRW); (3) Proposing TRACE, a task-adaptive inference-time control framework with lightweight trained modules that reshapes relay allocation during prefill and preserves visual support during decoding.
AI.result: Across 4 open-weight VLM backbones and 7 benchmarks, TRACE delivers gains of 4.33 points on average on grounding-sensitive settings, up to 6.6 points, while also improving reasoning-heavy tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly controlling multimodal focus across depth offers a unified and effective mechanism for strengthening evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning.

title: Infrared Organization and Critical Cognitive Field Formation in Transformer Dynamics
summary: Large language models exhibit remarkable emergent behaviors, yet the physical mechanism governing their collective dynamics remains poorly understood. Cognitive Field Theory predicts that learning reorganizes the time-scale density of states (TDOS) through the infrared accumulation of slow relaxation modes, thereby enhancing the memory self-energy, reducing the cognitive forgetting gap, and strengthening the collective susceptibility. Using publicly available Pythia language models, we extract relaxation spectra directly from Transformer layer Jacobians throughout training, network depth, and model scale, allowing the TDOS, memory self-energy, forgetting gap, memory kernel, and infrared critical exponent to be measured quantitatively. The measurements reveal progressive infrared accumulation of slow relaxation modes, producing an approximately flat infrared TDOS with \( ρ(λ)\simλ^{-0.1} \) and scale-free memory kernels \( K(t)\sim t^{-1}. \) The memory self-energy exhibits a pronounced transient maximum during early optimization before relaxing toward a metastable near-critical regime, corresponding to the smallest cognitive forgetting gap and the largest collective susceptibility predicted by Cognitive Field Theory. These observations provide quantitative experimental evidence that Transformer dynamics are governed by infrared collective organization. The reproducibility of the same dynamical behavior across training, network depth, and model scales suggests that infrared slow-mode organization represents a universal collective principle of Transformer dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper provides quantitative experimental evidence that Transformer dynamics are governed by infrared collective organization, with relaxation spectra extracted from Pythia language models revealing progressive infrared accumulation of slow relaxation modes, scale-free memory kernels, and a metastable near-critical regime consistent with Cognitive Field Theory predictions.
AI.motivation: The physical mechanism governing the collective dynamics of large language models remains poorly understood, despite their remarkable emergent behaviors.
AI.method: Using publicly available Pythia language models, the authors extract relaxation spectra from Transformer layer Jacobians throughout training, network depth, and model scale, measuring TDOS, memory self-energy, forgetting gap, memory kernel, and infrared critical exponent.
AI.result: Measurements reveal infrared accumulation of slow relaxation modes with approximately flat infrared TDOS (ρ(λ)∼λ^{-0.1}), scale-free memory kernels (K(t)∼t^{-1}), a pronounced transient maximum in memory self-energy during early optimization, and a metastable near-critical regime with minimal cognitive forgetting gap and maximal collective susceptibility.
AI.conclusion: Transformer dynamics are governed by infrared collective organization, and the reproducibility of this behavior across training, depth, and scale suggests infrared slow-mode organization is a universal collective principle of Transformer dynamics.

title: Unsupervised Detection of Entry and Exit Regions from Vehicle Trajectories for Camera-Agnostic Turning Movement Counts
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures; Supplementary Material: 7 pages, 3 figures
summary: Turning movement counts are essential for intersection-level traffic management, yet their collection remains predominantly manual due to the cost of per-camera region annotation. This paper presents an unsupervised pipeline that identifies entry and exit regions directly from raw vehicle trajectories extracted via object detection and multi-object tracking, requiring no manual annotation, camera calibration, or prior knowledge of intersection geometry. Unlike trajectory clustering methods that classify individual trajectories using pairwise similarity and must be re-executed on every new batch, the proposed pipeline clusters initial and terminal point locations to produce persistent spatial region polygons that classify future trajectories by point-in-polygon containment at linear cost. The pipeline comprises six sequential steps, each with configurable parameters evaluated through a systematic statistical analysis spanning 19,152 pipeline executions across 25 surveillance cameras capturing dense heterogeneous traffic in Bengaluru, India, and 10 sequences from the UA-DETRAC benchmark dataset. Both parametric and nonparametric testing frameworks identify three consistently significant parameters and yield an empirically grounded recommended configuration. Under this configuration, the pipeline achieves a median classification error of approximately 3% across all 25 cameras, including 16 held-out locations, with GEH values within accepted engineering thresholds. Compared with two trajectory clustering baselines, the proposed pipeline exhibits greater stability across camera views and lower computational cost, at the expense of higher median error. Extended evaluation demonstrates that calibration clips of at least 60 minutes and peak-traffic selection further improve region estimation quality.

AI.tldr: An unsupervised pipeline for turning movement counting that identifies entry/exit regions from raw vehicle trajectories using point clustering of initial/terminal locations, achieving ~3% median classification error across 25 cameras with no manual annotation or calibration needed.
AI.motivation: Turning movement counts are critical for intersection traffic management but are predominantly collected manually due to the high cost of per-camera region annotation. The authors aim to eliminate the need for manual annotation, camera calibration, and intersection geometry knowledge.
AI.method: The pipeline (1) extracts trajectories via object detection + multi-object tracking; (2) clusters initial and terminal point locations into spatial region polygons (entry/exit zones); (3) classifies future trajectories by point-in-polygon containment at O(1) cost. It has 6 sequential steps with configurable parameters, evaluated via 19,152 pipeline executions across 25 surveillance cameras (Bengaluru, India) and UA-DETRAC benchmark.
AI.result: Achieves ~3% median classification error across all 25 cameras (including 16 held-out locations), with GEH values within engineering thresholds. More stable than trajectory clustering baselines and computationally cheaper, though with higher median error. Calibration clips ≥60 min and peak-traffic selection improve estimation quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unsupervised pipeline enables practical large-scale turning movement counting without manual annotation, and the systematic statistical analysis identifies robust parameter configurations for real-world deployment.

title: Enhancing Query Efficiency for d-DNNF Representations Through Preprocessing
summary: In this paper, we investigate preprocessing techniques aimed at improving the efficiency of accessing models of propositional formulas represented in conjunctive normal form (CNF). We focus on three fundamental tasks: uniform sampling, direct model access, and model enumeration. Our analysis reveals that most state-of-the-art preprocessors, when they do not preserve formula equivalence, are generally unsuitable for these tasks. In contrast, we demonstrate that preprocessors which preserve model counts can be effectively leveraged, provided relevant preprocessing information is maintained. To validate our approach, we perform extensive experiments on a diverse suite of benchmarks from multiple domains. The experimental results show that our preprocessing methods are both efficient and robust, yielding significant performance improvements for model access queries when CNF formulas are compiled into d-DNNF representations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates preprocessing techniques for CNF formulas to improve efficiency of uniform sampling, direct model access, and model enumeration, finding that only model-count-preserving preprocessors with maintained preprocessing information are suitable, and demonstrating significant performance gains when formulas are compiled into d-DNNF representations.
AI.motivation: To improve the efficiency of accessing models of propositional CNF formulas for three fundamental tasks (uniform sampling, direct model access, model enumeration) by investigating suitable preprocessing techniques.
AI.method: The authors analyze state-of-the-art preprocessors, identify that only model-count-preserving preprocessors are suitable for these tasks (provided relevant preprocessing information is maintained), and perform extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks validating their approach.
AI.result: Preprocessing methods that preserve model counts, with maintained preprocessing information, yield significant performance improvements for model access queries when CNF formulas are compiled into d-DNNF representations; non-equivalence-preserving preprocessors are generally unsuitable for these tasks.
AI.conclusion: Model-count-preserving preprocessors can effectively improve model access tasks when preprocessing metadata is preserved, while non-equivalence-preserving preprocessors should be avoided for uniform sampling, direct model access, and model enumeration.

title: The Spectral Structure of Latent Treatment Effects
summary: Identifying heterogeneous treatment effects under unobserved confounding is central in observational causal inference. In proxy models with a discrete latent confounder, prior Synthetic Potential Outcomes (SPO) [Mazaheri-Squires-Uhler '25] recover the mixture of treatment effects through recursively constructed scalar moments. We show that this sequence is one projection of a more fundamental object. Under the same population factorization assumptions, there is an exact compressed observable operator: after projecting onto the shared proxy signal subspace, the difference of two treatment-arm quotient operators is similar to the diagonal matrix of latent treatment effects. Its eigenvalues are the latent effects; its lifted left eigenvectors, after anchor normalization, recover the target-proxy feature matrix and then the latent mixture proportions. Every scalar SPO moment is a bilinear functional of a power of this operator. The resulting estimator handles overcomplete proxy systems, replaces high-order scalar inversion with finite-dimensional spectral analysis, and admits high-probability first-order perturbation bounds for treatment effects, feature rows, and simplex-projected mixture weights.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Synthetic Potential Outcomes (SPO) framework by showing that the sequence of scalar moments used to recover heterogeneous treatment effects under unobserved confounding is a projection of a compressed observable operator. The operator's eigenvalues correspond to latent treatment effects, and its eigenvectors recover proxy feature matrices and mixture proportions. The approach handles overcomplete proxies, replaces high-order scalar inversion with spectral analysis, and yields perturbation bounds.
AI.motivation: To identify heterogeneous treatment effects in observational causal inference under unobserved confounding with a discrete latent confounder, improving upon prior SPO methods by providing a more fundamental operator-based view that handles overcomplete proxy systems.
AI.method: The paper defines a compressed observable operator by projecting onto the shared proxy signal subspace, then shows the difference of two treatment-arm quotient operators is similar to a diagonal matrix of latent treatment effects. Eigenvalues give latent effects; left eigenvectors (after anchor normalization) recover target-proxy feature matrix and mixture proportions. Spectral analysis replaces scalar moment inversion.
AI.result: The operator approach handles overcomplete proxy systems, replaces high-order scalar inversion with finite-dimensional spectral analysis, and admits high-probability first-order perturbation bounds for treatment effects, feature rows, and simplex-projected mixture weights.
AI.conclusion: The compressed observable operator perspective provides a more fundamental and robust framework for recovering heterogeneous treatment effects under unobserved confounding, with improved theoretical guarantees and broader applicability to overcomplete proxy settings.

title: Learning Anatomy-Grounded CT Vision-Language Representations with Organ-Hierarchical Report Knowledge
summary: Medical vision-language pretraining (VLP) from paired CT images and radiology reports enables scalable representation learning, but most existing methods align either whole scans with entire reports or local image regions with text fragments. These formulations underuse a key property of radiology reports: findings are organized around anatomical structures, with abnormalities described by organs, disease concepts, locations, and severity-related attributes. We propose OKA-CT, an organ-hierarchical knowledge-augmented framework for CT-report VLP. OKA-CT first converts free-text reports into organ-conditioned knowledge using radiology report parsing and LLM-assisted semantic structuring. The extracted hierarchy is used across two learning stages. Stage~1 injects anatomy-grounded evidence into the CT visual representation through fine-grained organ-conditioned supervision, while Stage~2 uses organ-specific report evidence to guide structured report-CT contrastive learning, where hierarchy-derived semantic soft targets treat non-paired cases with shared organ-level findings as weak semantic positives rather than uniform negatives. A lightweight query-based global branch further aggregates disease-relevant volumetric evidence for whole-scan representation. On CT-RATE and RAD-ChestCT datasets, OKA-CT achieves zero-shot abnormality diagnosis AUROCs of 84.9 and 72.2, outperforming prior CT VLP baselines. Retrieval and patch-occlusion analyses further show improved report-image alignment and stronger sensitivity to disease-associated anatomical regions.

AI.tldr: OKA-CT proposes an organ-hierarchical knowledge-augmented framework for CT-report vision-language pretraining that uses structured organ-level supervision and contrastive learning with semantic soft targets, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot abnormality diagnosis on CT-RATE and RAD-ChestCT datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing medical VLP methods underuse the key property of radiology reports where findings are organized around anatomical structures. Aligning whole scans with entire reports or local regions with text fragments fails to leverage organ-conditioned knowledge.
AI.method: OKA-CT converts free-text reports into organ-conditioned knowledge via radiology report parsing and LLM-assisted semantic structuring. Stage 1 injects anatomy-grounded evidence into CT visual representations via organ-conditioned supervision. Stage 2 uses organ-specific report evidence for structured report-CT contrastive learning with hierarchy-derived semantic soft targets that treat non-paired cases sharing organ-level findings as weak positives. A lightweight query-based global branch aggregates disease-relevant volumetric evidence.
AI.result: On CT-RATE and RAD-ChestCT, OKA-CT achieves zero-shot abnormality diagnosis AUROCs of 84.9 and 72.2, outperforming prior CT VLP baselines. Retrieval and patch-occlusion analyses show improved report-image alignment and stronger sensitivity to disease-associated anatomical regions.
AI.conclusion: Organ-hierarchical knowledge augmentation effectively improves CT-report representation learning by exploiting anatomical structure organization in radiology reports, leading to better zero-shot diagnosis and image-text alignment.

title: Comparative Analysis of GAT and BERT for Human-Like Playtesting
summary: Accurately modeling and understanding player experience is crucial for designing engaging puzzle games. To achieve this, a common approach involves collecting diverse user data to train predictive playtesting models that mimic player behavior. However, existing data-driven methods often lack the ability to capture the full range of player strategies and require extensive feature engineering and network architecture modeling. This limitation becomes particularly evident when new game mechanics or features are introduced, which necessitate continual adjustments to the models. To addrss these challenges, we propose a more generalized representation that reduces - or even eliminates - the need for ongoing feature-engineering maintenance. Specifically, we investigate two general-purpose network architectures: (a) a transformer-based model (BERT) and (b) a graph attention model (GAT), both of which are designed to effectively capture the relational structure of Candy Crush Saga (CCS) game boards. Our experiments compare these approaches to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) baselines, revealing better performance on challenging board configurations and underscoring the benefits of our generalizable representation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes general-purpose network architectures (BERT and GAT) to model player experience in puzzle games like Candy Crush Saga, reducing the need for feature engineering and outperforming CNN baselines on challenging board configurations.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven methods for modeling player experience in puzzle games struggle to capture the full range of player strategies, require extensive feature engineering and network architecture modeling, and need continual adjustments when new game mechanics or features are introduced.
AI.method: The authors investigate two general-purpose network architectures: a transformer-based model (BERT) and a graph attention model (GAT), both designed to capture the relational structure of Candy Crush Saga game boards, and compare them to CNN baselines.
AI.result: The proposed BERT and GAT models reveal better performance on challenging board configurations compared to Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) baselines.
AI.conclusion: A more generalized representation using transformer-based or graph attention architectures can reduce or eliminate the need for ongoing feature-engineering maintenance while achieving superior performance in modeling player experience for puzzle games.

title: The Singularity Space: A Generative Diffusion Framework for Signal Representation
summary: Generative models often represent signals as dense grids of amplitudes, blurring sharp transients that are crucial for the correctness of physical signals. We introduce Singularity Space, a generative framework that represents signals through complex-plane singularities, rooted in the classical pole-residue representation of meromorphic functions. We learn a latent space of physically constrained, per-signal singularity configurations to solve an inverse problem from degraded or partial observations. The framework has three key properties: interpretability, in which each generated singularity configuration corresponds to a set of physical parameters; structural stability, which mitigates Gibbs artifacts at discontinuities; and resolution-free output reconstruction on arbitrary grids without retraining or interpolation. Our framework employs a transformer-based diffusion model that directly predicts samples at complex-plane singularity coordinates, subject to geometric constraints during sampling. As a controlled test case for sharp-feature recovery, we evaluate our framework on 1D Burgers shocks, where each shock is represented by 32 predicted singularities (an $8\times$ reduction versus a 1024-point grid signal). Our framework preserves signal structure ($\text{TV ratio} \approx 1$) under unseen test-time observation noise, achieves a $4.2\times$ lower reconstruction error in zero-shot sub-resolution generalization than a grid-based baseline, and recovers physical parameters to $10^{-4}$ absolute error in-distribution. These results suggest that singularity-based representations may provide a practical foundation for other transient-dominated signals such as speech and biomedical signals, with potential extension to higher-dimensional domains.

AI.tldr: Singularity Space is a generative framework that represents signals via complex-plane singularities (pole-residue) rather than dense grids, using a transformer-based diffusion model to reconstruct signals from degraded observations with superior sharp-feature recovery, interpretability, and resolution-free output.
AI.motivation: Generative models that represent signals as dense grids blur sharp transients (e.g., discontinuities) that are essential for physically correct signals, motivating a representation that explicitly captures singularities.
AI.method: The framework learns a latent space of per-signal singularity configurations using a transformer-based diffusion model that directly predicts complex-plane singularity coordinates under geometric constraints, rooted in the classical pole-residue representation of meromorphic functions.
AI.result: On 1D Burgers shocks (32 singularities vs. 1024 grid points, 8× reduction), the method achieves TV ratio ≈ 1 under noise, 4.2× lower reconstruction error in zero-shot sub-resolution generalization versus grid baseline, and recovers physical parameters to 10⁻⁴ absolute error in-distribution.
AI.conclusion: Singularity-based representations offer a practical foundation for transient-dominated signals (e.g., speech, biomedical) and may extend to higher-dimensional domains, overcoming grid-based limitations in sharp-feature recovery.

title: EquiFusion: Kinematics-Agnostic Human Motion Prediction via Equivariant Latent Diffusion
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Visit our webpage at https://ceveloper.github.io/publications/equifusion/
summary: Existing Stochastic 3D Human Motion Prediction models are fundamentally constrained by hard-coding the skeleton kinematics, severely limiting generalization, preventing cross-dataset training, and requiring complex data retargeting. We introduce EquiFusion, the first kinematics-agnostic model to solve this bottleneck, implementing a latent diffusion model with a permutation equivariant architecture. EquiFusion treats the kinematics' connectivity as an explicit input parameter, ensuring its internal computations are inherently agnostic to joint ordering and graph structure. This novel design enables truly cross-dataset generalization to unseen kinematics and unlocks novel zero-shot directions, such as motion prediction from partial or occluded observations and targeted limb generation. EquiFusion achieves state-of-the-art results on major benchmarks, being up to 75% more compact than previous kinematics-specific methods, while achieving faster training and inference. EquiFusion thus establishes a new, flexible standard for robust human motion prediction. Model and training code are available at https://ceveloper.github.io/publications/equifusion/.

AI.tldr: EquiFusion introduces a kinematics-agnostic latent diffusion model with permutation equivariant architecture for 3D human motion prediction, enabling cross-dataset generalization, zero-shot capabilities (partial/occluded observations, targeted limb generation), and state-of-the-art results with 75% more compact models and faster training/inference.
AI.motivation: Existing stochastic 3D human motion prediction models are fundamentally limited by hard-coding skeleton kinematics, which restricts generalization, prevents cross-dataset training, and requires complex data retargeting.
AI.method: EquiFusion employs a latent diffusion model with a permutation equivariant architecture that treats kinematics connectivity as an explicit input parameter, making computations agnostic to joint ordering and graph structure.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on major benchmarks, is up to 75% more compact than prior kinematics-specific methods, and enables faster training and inference.
AI.conclusion: EquiFusion establishes a new, flexible standard for robust human motion prediction, enabling cross-dataset generalization and novel zero-shot applications.

title: Learning Residual Kinematic Corrections for Continuous Neural Decoding via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Decoding continuous three-dimensional (3D) motor imagery (MI) using non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) remains challenging due to signal variability and residual decoding errors. Deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural network--long short-term memory (CNN--LSTM) models can capture spatial and temporal dynamics for continuous kinematic decoding; however, systematic residual errors persist in predicted trajectories. We propose a two-stage decoding framework that applies reinforcement learning (RL) to perform residual kinematic correction on the outputs of a CNN--LSTM decoder (CNN--LSTM--RL). The RL agent is trained offline without direct EEG input and instead operates on predicted kinematic trajectories to optimize movement accuracy relative to target trajectories. Decoding performance was quantified using Pearson correlation coefficients ($r$) and Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE) along the $x, y$, and $z$ axes. Compared to CNN--LSTM applied alone, CNN--LSTM--RL improved the mean correlation from $0.5076$ to $0.7181$ ($p = 0.0005$) in 2D and from $0.6420$ to $0.7780$ ($p = 0.0059$) in VR, with relative gains of $41.5\%$ and $21.2\%$, respectively. Correspondingly, RMSE was reduced from $0.0890$ to $0.0532$ (2D, $p < 0.0001$) and from $0.0714$ to $0.0441$ (VR, $p < 0.0001$), representing relative reductions of $40.2\%$ and $38.2\%$. These findings demonstrate that this scalable framework enhances 3D BCI MI decoding by correcting kinematic errors via offline residual RL without extra neural data, advancing neurorehabilitation, prosthetics, and virtual interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage CNN-LSTM-RL framework that uses reinforcement learning to correct residual kinematic errors in EEG-based 3D motor imagery decoding, achieving significant improvements in correlation (up to 41.5% gain) and RMSE reduction (up to 40.2%) without additional neural data.
AI.motivation: Continuous 3D motor imagery decoding using non-invasive EEG-based BCIs is challenged by signal variability and persistent residual decoding errors in predicted trajectories, which limit the practical applicability of existing deep learning models.
AI.method: A two-stage framework combining CNN-LSTM for initial kinematic decoding followed by an RL agent trained offline (without direct EEG input) that operates on predicted kinematic trajectories to perform residual correction and optimize movement accuracy relative to target trajectories.
AI.result: CNN-LSTM-RL improved mean correlation from 0.5076 to 0.7181 (2D, +41.5%, p=0.0005) and from 0.6420 to 0.7780 (VR, +21.2%, p=0.0059). RMSE reduced from 0.0890 to 0.0532 (2D, -40.2%, p<0.0001) and from 0.0714 to 0.0441 (VR, -38.2%, p<0.0001).
AI.conclusion: The scalable RL-based residual correction framework enhances 3D BCI MI decoding without requiring additional neural data, with promising implications for neurorehabilitation, prosthetics, and virtual interaction.

title: Bandit PCA with Minimax Optimal Regret
summary: We study the bandit-feedback version of online principal component analysis (Bandit PCA): in each round $t = 1,\dots,T$, the adversary selects a $d \times d$ symmetric gain matrix $G_t$ with spectrum in $[0,1]$ and rank at most $r$; the learner simultaneously selects a unit vector $w_t \in S^{d-1}$ and receives the reward $w_t^\top G_t w_t$. The learner receives no other feedback, and aims to minimize the regret against the best unit vector in hindsight. This problem was introduced by Kotlowski and Neu (2019), who gave an algorithm with regret $O(d\sqrt{rT \log T})$ and showed the lower bound of $Ω(r\sqrt{T/\log T})$. We improve upon both of these bounds and essentially bridge the gap between them, establishing the minimax regret of order $r\sqrt{dT}$ up to polylogarithmic factors in $d$ and $T$. The upper bound is attained by a novel algorithm, which combines online mirror descent on the spectrahedron of (real) density matrices with a multiscale exploration scheme in which the eigenspaces with different spectral magnitudes are updated at different rates. For the lower bound, we construct an adaptive adversary that refines a hidden large-reward subspace based on the learner's actions, in such a way that low regret is impossible without estimating the subspace; as a result, lower-bounding the regret reduces to studying the arising subspace estimation problem. Finally, we discuss connections of Bandit PCA with adaptive-measurement quantum tomography.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Bandit PCA, establishes the minimax regret of order $r\sqrt{dT}$ (up to polylog factors), and bridges the gap between previous upper and lower bounds via a new algorithm combining online mirror descent on density matrices with multiscale exploration, and an adaptive adversary construction linking regret to subspace estimation.
AI.motivation: To resolve the gap between existing upper bound ($O(d\sqrt{rT\log T})$) and lower bound ($\Omega(r\sqrt{T/\log T})$) for Bandit PCA, and to establish the exact minimax regret for this problem.
AI.method: The upper bound is achieved by a novel algorithm combining online mirror descent on the spectrahedron of density matrices with a multiscale exploration scheme that updates eigenspaces at different rates based on spectral magnitudes. The lower bound uses an adaptive adversary that refines a hidden large-reward subspace based on learner actions, reducing regret lower-bounding to a subspace estimation problem.
AI.result: Established minimax regret of order $r\sqrt{dT}$ up to polylogarithmic factors in $d$ and $T$, improving upon both previous upper bound $O(d\sqrt{rT\log T})$ and lower bound $\Omega(r\sqrt{T/\log T})$.
AI.conclusion: The minimax regret for Bandit PCA is $r\sqrt{dT}$ (up to polylog factors), essentially closing the gap. The work also discusses connections to adaptive-measurement quantum tomography.

title: MED-DSLC: Multi-Expert-Domain Classification via Domain Supervision and Logit Calibration
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Code is available at https://github.com/Leonard-Zeng/MED-DSLC
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification by comparing image features with text prompts in a shared embedding space. A fundamental property underlying this capability is the global comparability of logits across arbitrary candidate classes. However, VLMs are often adapted to fine-grained domains using techniques such as LoRA. While this improves in-domain accuracy, out-of-domain accuracy degrades. This leads to a highly fragmented model ecosystem, with thousands of specialized models. Multi-Expert-Domain classification seeks to address this problem, by merging LoRAs trained independently on specialized domains. However, due to the independent training, the various domain experts no longer produce globally calibrated logits. As a result, when evaluating over the union of multiple domain-specific class sets, heterogeneous logit scales induce cross-domain interference and artificially high confidence for out-of-domain classes, inducing prediction errors. In this work, we identify domain supervision and cross-domain logit miscalibration as the key issue to scalable multi-domain zero-shot recognition.
