title: Benchmarking Edge Inference Strategies for Deep Learning Models in Industrial Machine Vision
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, accepted at IEEE COINS 2026. Preprint version; camera-ready version to appear in the conference proceedings
summary:
Edge deployment is often the preferred solution for industrial machine vision systems when low latency, data security, or limited connectivity are critical requirements. Several frameworks are available to optimise inference on edge devices; however, relatively few studies have systematically compared their inference-time performance under industrial deployment conditions.
  In this work, we present a comparative study of four widely used approaches for machine vision inference in industrial settings: plain PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, and TensorRT. The evaluation focuses on inference time, covers several CPU- and GPU-based hardware platforms, and includes both conventional convolutional neural networks and a transformer-based vision model. For the hardware platforms and models evaluated, the results show that OpenVINO achieves the lowest inference time on CPUs, while TensorRT achieves the lowest inference time on GPUs. However, TensorRT does not outperform plain PyTorch for the transformer-based model considered in this study.

title: Structure-Feature Aligned Graph Learning via Alternating Constrained Optimization
summary: We introduce a constrained two-view framework for node prediction that aligns structure-conditioned GNN embeddings with a structure-free feature prior learned by an anchor model. Conventional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) couple feature transformation and neighborhood aggregation, which renders them vulnerable to topology noise and heterophilous connections. To decouple this dependency, our framework utilizes an independent anchor network to capture intrinsic attribute features via a self-supervised reconstruction objective. Furthermore, we propose a Channel-Split Adaptive Gated GNN (CSAG-GNN) that dynamically routes representations between global spectral smoothing and local spatial discrimination through a node-wise gating mechanism. We propose a stable cyclic alternating optimization strategy to solve the resulting coupled bi-level objective, preventing mutual representation drift during training. Empirical results on both homophilous and heterophilous benchmarks show balanced performance gains and structural robustness over competitive baselines.

AI.tldr: A constrained two-view framework that decouples GNN feature transformation from neighborhood aggregation by using an anchor model for structure-free feature priors and a Channel-Split Adaptive Gated GNN with dynamic routing, trained via stable cyclic alternating optimization, achieving robust performance on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs.
AI.motivation: Conventional GNNs couple feature transformation and neighborhood aggregation, making them vulnerable to topology noise and heterophilous connections. The goal is to decouple this dependency for more robust node prediction.
AI.method: A constrained two-view framework: (1) an independent anchor network learns intrinsic attribute features via self-supervised reconstruction (structure-free prior); (2) Channel-Split Adaptive Gated GNN (CSAG-GNN) dynamically routes representations between global spectral smoothing and local spatial discrimination via a node-wise gating mechanism; (3) a stable cyclic alternating optimization strategy solves the coupled bi-level objective, preventing mutual representation drift.
AI.result: Balanced performance gains and structural robustness over competitive baselines on both homophilous and heterophilous benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decoupling framework with dynamic routing and stable optimization effectively addresses GNN vulnerability to noisy topology and heterophily, achieving robust and balanced performance across diverse graph structures.

title: Efficient Tuning Before Low-Bit Post-Training Quantization for Stochastic Gradient Descent-optimized Models
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems (TNNLS). Code available at https://github.com/xpxpxp2001xpxpxp/ETBQ
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses deep neural networks for deployment under limited memory and computational budgets. However, low-bit (i.e., 2-bit or 4-bit) PTQ often suffers from substantial performance degradation. Most existing PTQ methods operate on an unconstrained full-precision (FP) model and primarily address quantization errors through post-hoc reconstruction. We argue that low-bit PTQ accuracy is limited not only by post-quantization error minimization, but also by the quantization-error tolerance of a FP model itself. In this paper, we propose Efficient Tuning Before Quantization (ETBQ), a pre-conditioning tuning stage for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)-optimized models before PTQ. During tuning, the FP model is optimized under perturbations sampled from the error distributions of weight and activation quantization, guiding the model toward a loss-landscape region that is less sensitive to the subsequent PTQ. Unlike QAT, ETBQ does not train a fake-quantized deployment model, which is computationally and memory intensive. Instead, ETBQ outputs a FP model that can be used by any PTQ backend. Experiments on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, and Cityscapes provide consistent evidence that ETBQ improves low-bit PTQ across diverse tasks. Under W2A4 settings, e.g., ETBQ improves over naive PTQ by 2.14\% top-1 accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet and by 5.80\% mIoU on Cityscapes. Code is available at https://github.com/xpxpxp2001xpxpxp/ETBQ.

AI.tldr: ETBQ introduces a pre-conditioning tuning stage before PTQ that optimizes the FP model under simulated quantization error distributions, making it more tolerant to subsequent low-bit quantization without the heavy cost of QAT.
AI.motivation: Low-bit PTQ suffers from significant performance degradation, and existing methods focus on post-hoc error minimization while overlooking the inherent quantization-error tolerance of the FP model itself.
AI.method: ETBQ pre-conditions an SGD-optimized FP model by tuning it under perturbations sampled from weight and activation quantization error distributions, steering the model toward loss-landscape regions less sensitive to subsequent PTQ.
AI.result: Under W2A4 settings, ETBQ improves naive PTQ by 2.14% top-1 accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet and 5.80% mIoU on Cityscapes, with consistent gains across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, and Cityscapes.
AI.conclusion: ETBQ effectively bridges the gap between FP model training and PTQ by enhancing quantization robustness at the pre-tuning stage, offering a lightweight alternative to QAT that is compatible with any PTQ backend.

title: DiffEEG: A Self-Supervised Denoising Diffusion Model for Learning EEG Generic Representations
summary: Deep learning for EEG-based seizure detection faces critical challenges: severe annotation scarcity and extreme class imbalance, where ictal events comprise less than 10\% of clinical recordings. We present DiffEEG, a 9.6M-parameter self-supervised foundation model that addresses both limitations through denoising diffusion pre-training and reinforcement learning (RL)-based fine-tuning. Pre-trained on 1.3M unlabeled segments from the Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus (TUHSZ), DiffEEG learns generic neural representations via a 1D U-Net with multi-head self-attention. For downstream adaptation, a reinforced decision layer employs policy gradient optimization to directly maximize F1-score, prioritizing sensitivity to rare seizure events over overall accuracy. Under strict patient-wise evaluation (279 patients, Leave-One-Fold-Out), DiffEEG achieves 61\% accuracy and 59\% F1 for 4-class seizure subtyping, and 81\% accuracy with 85\% weighted F1 for binary detection, maintaining clinically viable seizure recall (59\%) despite extreme imbalance (6.7\% prevalence). Segment-level evaluation establishes an upper bound of 97.6\% accuracy, confirming strong architectural capacity. DiffEEG demonstrates that diffusion-based pre-training combined with metric-aware reinforcement learning enables clinically deployable seizure monitoring with minimal labeled data requirements.

AI.tldr: DiffEEG is a 9.6M-parameter self-supervised foundation model for EEG-based seizure detection that uses denoising diffusion pre-training on 1.3M unlabeled segments and RL-based fine-tuning to address annotation scarcity and class imbalance. It achieves 81% accuracy (binary detection) and 59% F1 (4-class subtyping) under strict patient-wise evaluation.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for EEG-based seizure detection faces critical challenges: severe annotation scarcity and extreme class imbalance, where ictal events comprise less than 10% of clinical recordings.
AI.method: A 9.6M-parameter self-supervised foundation model with denoising diffusion pre-training (1D U-Net + multi-head self-attention) on 1.3M unlabeled segments, followed by RL-based fine-tuning using policy gradient optimization to directly maximize F1-score.
AI.result: Under strict patient-wise evaluation (279 patients, Leave-One-Fold-Out): 61% accuracy and 59% F1 for 4-class seizure subtyping; 81% accuracy with 85% weighted F1 for binary detection; clinically viable seizure recall (59%) despite 6.7% prevalence; segment-level upper bound of 97.6% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: DiffEEG demonstrates that diffusion-based pre-training combined with metric-aware reinforcement learning enables clinically deployable seizure monitoring with minimal labeled data requirements.

title: Self-supervised training for high-resolution close-range multispectral remote sensing imagery
summary: Although self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a promising way to reduce annotation effort in close-range remote sensing, its effectiveness for high-resolution multispectral unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery remains underexplored due to limited data. This study evaluated SSL pretraining for precision agriculture using cm-scale multispectral drone imagery collected across multiple sensors, years, and regions. Transformer-based encoders were pretrained with Momentum Contrast v3 (MoCo-v3) and Masked Autoencoders on a harmonized dataset combining msuav500K with newly collected multi-year UAV imagery from agricultural fields in Finland. Pretraining used four spectral bands (Green, Red, Red-Edge, Near-Infrared) for cross-sensor compatibility. The models were evaluated on crop-weed semantic segmentation using the WeedMap dataset with 5--100% training data. The following two subsets served as downstream tasks: Task A (Germany, RedEdge-M), where all pretrained models were compared under partial and full fine-tuning, and Task B (Switzerland, Sequoia), where the best encoder from Task A was assessed. Our Swin Transformer pretrained with MoCo-v3 achieved the strongest performance on both tasks, surpassing the Swin Transformer model of Doornbos et al. pretrained on a pre-release of msuav500K. Our pretrained Swin Transformer further demonstrated cross-sensor and cross-region generalization. We additionally provide a public multi-year multispectral UAV dataset from Finland to support future research.

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates that SSL pretraining (particularly MoCo-v3 with Swin Transformer) effectively improves crop-weed segmentation in multispectral UAV imagery, achieving strong cross-sensor and cross-region generalization while reducing annotation requirements.
AI.motivation: SSL pretraining for high-resolution multispectral UAV imagery in precision agriculture remains underexplored due to limited data availability, despite its potential to reduce annotation effort.
AI.method: Transformer-based encoders (including Swin Transformer) were pretrained via MoCo-v3 and Masked Autoencoders on a harmonized dataset combining msuav500K with newly collected multi-year UAV data from Finland, using four spectral bands (Green, Red, Red-Edge, NIR). Evaluation was performed on crop-weed semantic segmentation using the WeedMap dataset across two tasks (Germany/RedEdge-M and Switzerland/Sequoia) with 5–100% training data.
AI.result: The Swin Transformer pretrained with MoCo-v3 outperformed all other models on both downstream tasks, including the prior Swin Transformer baseline by Doornbos et al., and demonstrated cross-sensor and cross-region generalization.
AI.conclusion: SSL with MoCo-v3 and Swin Transformer is an effective pretraining strategy for multispectral UAV-based precision agriculture, reducing annotation needs while achieving robust cross-domain performance. A public multi-year multispectral UAV dataset from Finland is also released.

title: Privacy-Aware Collaborative and Distributed Bayesian Optimization
summary: We propose a collaborative meta-learning framework for distributed Bayesian optimization matching centralized performance without raw-data exchange. We show gradient sharing leaks client observations, with leakage worsening as the search converges and queries concentrate near the optimum. We evaluate a differentially private defense and characterize its privacy-utility trade-off.

AI.tldr: A collaborative meta-learning framework for distributed Bayesian optimization achieves centralized performance without sharing raw data, though gradient sharing leaks client observations near the optimum; a differentially private defense is evaluated.
AI.motivation: To enable distributed Bayesian optimization that matches centralized performance without exchanging raw data, addressing privacy concerns in collaborative settings.
AI.method: Proposes a collaborative meta-learning framework for distributed Bayesian optimization; analyzes gradient sharing leakage, showing worsening leakage near the optimum; evaluates a differentially private defense mechanism.
AI.result: Gradient sharing leaks client observations, with leakage worsening as search converges and queries concentrate near the optimum. A differentially private defense is characterized with a privacy-utility trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative meta-learning enables distributed Bayesian optimization without raw-data exchange, but gradient privacy risks exist near the optimum; differential privacy offers a tunable defense.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for EO Regression Tasks: Building Height, Tree Canopy Height and Above-ground Biomass Estimation
summary: Earth Observation regression tasks such as building height, canopy height, and above-ground biomass estimation underpin critical applications in urban planning, forest monitoring, and climate policy, where both accuracy and reliability are critical. Yet most deep learning models yield only deterministic predictions, providing no indication of per-pixel reliability. These regression tasks are inherently challenging due to heterogeneous land surfaces, skewed target distributions, sensor noise, and signal saturation at high target values, making uncertainty (UC) estimation essential for reliable inference. We address this gap by modeling aleatoric uncertainty using year-long Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 MSI time series, proposing two complementary approaches: (i) Gaussian UC, which jointly predicts mean and standard deviation under a Gaussian assumption, and (ii) Quantile UC, which estimates the 10th, 50th, and 90th quantiles to capture asymmetric and heteroscedastic error distributions. Both models are evaluated on three representative EO regression tasks at 10 m spatial resolution. Results show that both approaches match or surpass deterministic benchmarks and existing global products, while delivering well-calibrated, interpretable, and operationally useful confidence estimates. Notably, both models outperform the current 10 m state-of-the-art uncertainty-aware model for canopy height estimation. Our implementation will be available at: https://github.com/RituYadav92/EO-Regression-Uncertainty-Estimation

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two uncertainty estimation approaches (Gaussian UC and Quantile UC) for Earth Observation regression tasks using Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 time series, achieving accurate and well-calibrated predictions for building height, canopy height, and above-ground biomass estimation at 10m resolution.
AI.motivation: Most deep learning models for EO regression tasks (building height, canopy height, AGB estimation) produce only deterministic predictions without per-pixel reliability indicators, yet these tasks face challenges from heterogeneous land surfaces, skewed distributions, sensor noise, and signal saturation, making uncertainty estimation essential for reliable inference.
AI.method: Two complementary uncertainty estimation approaches are proposed: (i) Gaussian UC, which jointly predicts mean and standard deviation under a Gaussian assumption, and (ii) Quantile UC, which estimates the 10th, 50th, and 90th quantiles to capture asymmetric and heteroscedastic error distributions. Both models use year-long Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 MSI time series as input.
AI.result: Both approaches match or surpass deterministic benchmarks and existing global products while delivering well-calibrated, interpretable, and operationally useful confidence estimates. Both models outperform the current 10m state-of-the-art uncertainty-aware model for canopy height estimation.
AI.conclusion: Modeling aleatoric uncertainty via time series EO data enables reliable per-pixel confidence estimates without sacrificing predictive accuracy, with quantile-based methods offering advantages for asymmetric error distributions common in EO regression tasks.

title: Fundamental Limitations of Fixed-Budget Best-Arm Identification
summary: In fixed-budget best-arm identification, also known as ranking and selection, an algorithm has a sampling budget to distribute across $K$ arms. Each sample provides noisy feedback about that arm's mean, and the goal is to identify the arm with the largest mean. A common performance benchmark is the static oracle: a non-adaptive strategy that knows the means in advance and chooses fixed sampling proportions to maximize the exponential decay rate of the probability of incorrect identification. Several adaptive algorithms have been constructed such that their sampling proportions converge to the static oracle proportions. However, it has remained open whether any algorithm could match the static oracle's error decay rate uniformly across all problem instances. We answer this in the negative. For any $K\ge 3$ and for rewards drawn from any one-parameter natural exponential family, we show that for any algorithm, there is at least one instance where the error decay rate is at most $\left(1 + \frac{\log(K)}{8}\right)^{-1}$ times that of the static oracle. This also answers the open question posed by Qin (2022), showing that fixed-budget best-arm identification does not admit a complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that no adaptive algorithm for fixed-budget best-arm identification can uniformly match the static oracle's error decay rate across all problem instances, answering an open question by Qin (2022).
AI.motivation: To determine whether any adaptive algorithm can achieve the static oracle's optimal error decay rate uniformly across all problem instances in fixed-budget best-arm identification, resolving an open question in the field.
AI.method: The authors prove a lower bound showing that for K≥3 arms and rewards from any one-parameter natural exponential family, any algorithm must have an error decay rate at most (1 + log(K)/8)^{-1} times the static oracle's rate on at least one instance.
AI.result: No algorithm can uniformly match the static oracle's error decay rate; the achievable rate is at least a factor of (1 + log(K)/8)^{-1} worse than the oracle on some instance.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-budget best-arm identification does not admit a complexity measure, answering the open question posed by Qin (2022).

title: Video Transformer for Remote Identity Document Hologram Detection
comment: Accepted to SMC2026 conference, 6 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables
summary: Remote identity authentification using Identification Documents has been a major challenge for several years. DeepFakes advent and the development of AI-guided tools helps fraudsters creating counterfeit ID Documents. Ensuring the authenticity of ID Documents has become a real clue in the seurization of remote authentification. This need is all the more pressing given the increasing digitization of administrative and transactional processes. To ensure widespread accessibility, the system should rely solely on video captured via mobile devices. In this specific context, confirming the authenticity of ID is a real challenge as many security features needs specific device like infrared sensor for instance. Among underutilized but promising security features, holographic printings hold a special place. Difficult to counterfeit, they produce distinctive visual effects according enlightment, making them both detectable in a video captured by a smartphone camera and difficult to imitate. In this paper, we propose a Remote Identity Document Verification System (RIDVS) and an approach based on a video transformer for detecting holograms in simple videos captured by smartphones. Our system is designed for a smartphone-based capture process, followed by a server-side verification. The hologram detection method builds on a robust model previously validated in a related research domain. We demonstrate that it outperforms existing SotA methods, achieving near-perfect accuracy even when trained on medium- to small-sized datasets. In particular, we report improvements of +26.86\% in Recall and +17.93\% in accuracy over the best MIDV-Holo baseline. This study includes several experiments that evaluate the model adaptation to frugality, both for training samples and computational resources.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Remote Identity Document Verification System (RIDVS) using a video transformer to detect holographic security features in ID documents captured via smartphone video. The method achieves near-perfect accuracy, outperforming existing SOTA methods with improvements of +26.86% in Recall and +17.93% in accuracy over the best MIDV-Holo baseline.
AI.motivation: Remote identity authentication using ID documents faces increasing challenges from DeepFakes and AI-guided counterfeiting tools. There is a pressing need for authenticating ID documents in digitized administrative processes, but existing systems often require specialized hardware. The authors aim to create an accessible system relying solely on smartphone-captured video.
AI.method: The proposed RIDVS uses a smartphone-based capture process with server-side verification. The hologram detection method employs a video transformer model, adapted from a previously validated model in a related domain. The system is designed to detect holographic printings, which produce distinctive visual effects under varying illumination, making them detectable in smartphone video.
AI.result: The method outperforms existing SOTA methods, achieving near-perfect accuracy even when trained on medium to small datasets. Specifically, it achieves +26.86% improvement in Recall and +17.93% improvement in accuracy over the best MIDV-Holo baseline. Experiments also evaluate model adaptation to frugality in both training samples and computational resources.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RIDVS with video transformer-based hologram detection is an effective and accessible solution for remote ID document authentication using only smartphone-captured video, achieving state-of-the-art performance while being resource-efficient.

title: Bet on Features: Anytime-Valid and Feature-Aware Auditing of Conditional Quantile Forecasters
summary: Black-box conditional quantile forecasts are widely used for sequential decisions under asymmetric costs, such as inventory planning in supply chain management. Once deployed, such forecasters must be monitored continuously as data streams drift and regimes change; this invalidates standard, fixed-horizon backtests for calibration. Further, existing backtests do not take into account that the notion of calibration is, in fact, information-dependent: forecasts can look calibrated to an auditor with coarse information while being miscalibrated to an auditor with richer information. We develop a distribution-free and game-theoretic testing framework for continuously auditing black-box conditional quantile forecasters with non-i.i.d. losses, such that the resulting evidence process is powerful against predictably chosen alternatives specified by the features available to the auditor. We first formalize notions of conditional quantile calibration when different sets of features are available to the auditor, establishing that the coarseness of the auditor's information set determines the hardness of the testing problem. We then identify the sets of alternatives for which the auditor can achieve power, and focusing on contextual bets linear in the features, we derive finite-time detection guarantees for such alternatives, all without an i.i.d. assumption. The resulting evidence processes are interpretable at the feature level, as they quantify fine-grained, "feature-aware" evidence for miscalibration. We empirically validate these methods on simulated and real data, finding that a popular time series forecaster (Chronos-2) is highly miscalibrated w.r.t. multiple relevant features.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a distribution-free, game-theoretic framework for continuously auditing black-box conditional quantile forecasters under non-i.i.d. losses, where calibration is information-dependent. It formalizes quantile calibration relative to different auditor feature sets, identifies powerful alternatives, provides finite-time detection guarantees without i.i.d. assumptions, and demonstrates that a popular forecaster (Chronos-2) is miscalibrated w.r.t. relevant features.
AI.motivation: Sequential decisions under asymmetric costs (e.g., inventory planning) rely on conditional quantile forecasts, which must be continuously monitored due to drifting data streams and regime changes. Existing fixed-horizon backtests are invalid in this setting and fail to account for the information-dependent nature of calibration (a forecast may appear calibrated with coarse information but miscalibrated with richer information).
AI.method: The authors develop a distribution-free, game-theoretic testing framework for continuous auditing of black-box conditional quantile forecasters with non-i.i.d. losses. They formalize conditional quantile calibration under different auditor feature sets, identify power-maximizing alternatives, focus on contextual bets linear in features, and derive finite-time detection guarantees without i.i.d. assumptions.
AI.result: The framework produces interpretable, fine-grained "feature-aware" evidence processes that quantify miscalibration at the feature level. Empirical validation on simulated and real data shows that the Chronos-2 time series forecaster is highly miscalibrated with respect to multiple relevant features.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables continuous, information-dependent auditing of quantile forecasts under drift, with finite-time guarantees and feature-level interpretability, revealing significant miscalibration in state-of-the-art forecasters like Chronos-2.

title: Towards Efficient Convolutional Neural Network for Embedded Hardware via Multi-Dimensional Pruning
comment: Author's accepted version. Published in Proceedings of the 60th ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC 2023)
summary: In this paper, we propose TECO, a multi-dimensional pruning framework to collaboratively prune the three dimensions (depth, width, and resolution) of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for better execution efficiency on embedded hardware. In TECO, we first introduce a two-stage importance evaluation framework, which efficiently and comprehensively evaluates each pruning unit according to both the local importance inside each dimension and the global importance across different dimensions. Based on the evaluation framework, we present a heuristic pruning algorithm to progressively prune the three dimensions of CNNs towards the optimal trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. Experiments on multiple benchmarks validate the advantages of TECO over existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/ntuliuteam/Teco.

AI.tldr: TECO is a multi-dimensional pruning framework that collaboratively prunes depth, width, and resolution of CNNs for efficient embedded execution, using a two-stage importance evaluation and heuristic pruning to achieve optimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.
AI.motivation: To improve execution efficiency of CNNs on embedded hardware by jointly pruning multiple dimensions (depth, width, resolution) rather than pruning them independently.
AI.method: A two-stage importance evaluation framework that assesses pruning units by both local importance within each dimension and global importance across dimensions, followed by a heuristic pruning algorithm that progressively prunes the three dimensions.
AI.result: Outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative multi-dimensional pruning achieves better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than prior methods, and the approach is validated across various benchmarks.

title: How to Tame Grokking: Representation Geometry as a Control Signal
summary: Grokking is a phenomenon in which neural networks initially memorize training data and only later exhibit strong generalization after prolonged optimization. Despite extensive recent study, the factors influencing the emergence and timing of grokking remain incompletely understood. We investigate the relationship between representation geometry and delayed generalization. We find that dimensionality collapse consistently precedes the onset of grokking in all evaluated settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce Geometric Dimensionality Regularization (GeomDR), a simple spectral regularizer that modifies the effective dimensionality of hidden representations during training. Across modular addition, modular division, and permutation composition tasks, GeomDR consistently alters grokking dynamics and can substantially accelerate the onset of generalization depending on the intervention schedule and target dimensionality. In several settings, grokking is accelerated by up to 52 times relative to standard AdamW training. Similar qualitative effects are observed in both multilayer perceptrons and transformers. Together, these results suggest that representation geometry can serve as an effective control signal for grokking and provide evidence that geometric interventions offer a practical approach for studying and influencing delayed generalization in neural networks.

AI.tldr: A study showing that dimensionality collapse precedes grokking, and introducing GeomDR—a regularizer that accelerates generalization by up to 52x by controlling hidden representation geometry.
AI.motivation: To understand the factors influencing the emergence and timing of grokking, specifically the relationship between representation geometry and delayed generalization.
AI.method: The authors observe dimensionality collapse before grokking, then propose GeomDR (Geometric Dimensionality Regularization), a spectral regularizer that modifies the effective dimensionality of hidden representations during training, tested on modular addition, division, and permutation composition tasks with MLPs and transformers.
AI.result: GeomDR consistently alters grokking dynamics; generalization is accelerated up to 52x relative to standard AdamW training, with similar effects across architectures.
AI.conclusion: Representation geometry is an effective control signal for grokking, and geometric interventions provide a practical approach for studying and influencing delayed generalization.

title: HyperGS: Fast and Generalizable Gaussian Video Representation
summary: Gaussian Splatting has emerged as an effective representation for video, but existing methods rely on per-video optimization. This leads to slow encoding and limits generalization across videos. To amortize this optimization, we propose HyperGS, a feedforward, optimization-free approach that directly predicts Gaussian representations from any video in a single forward pass, speeding up encoding and decoding by orders of magnitude while generalizing to out-of-distribution videos at higher resolutions. In HyperGS, we design a factorized spatiotemporal Transformer to extract tokens from video, and a learnable query-based Transformer to obtain 8-parameter Gaussian representations for each video frame. We find that naively predicting Gaussians across diverse videos induces a needle-like degeneration that collapses training, and address this with a rank-based geometric regularizer whose strength adapts dynamically to stabilize optimization. HyperGS achieves encoding at $10^4$--$10^5\times$ the speed of per-video Gaussian optimization at matched reconstruction quality while generalizing zero-shot to $720p$ video, enabling higher-resolution rendering without re-encoding. HyperGS improves PSNR by +2.9--3.1 dB over the prior video encoders on K400, SSv2, and UCF101 at a smaller video representation size. By predicting explicit 2D Gaussians in a single forward pass, HyperGS combines the fast, flexible rendering of Gaussian Splatting with the speed and generalization of feedforward prediction, advancing Gaussians as a practical direction for fast and generalizable video representation.

AI.tldr: HyperGS is a feedforward, optimization-free approach that directly predicts Gaussian representations from any video in a single forward pass, achieving 10^4-10^5× faster encoding than per-video optimization while improving PSNR by +2.9-3.1 dB and generalizing zero-shot to 720p video.
AI.motivation: Existing Gaussian Splatting methods for video rely on per-video optimization, leading to slow encoding and limited generalization across videos. HyperGS aims to amortize this optimization for fast, generalizable video representation.
AI.method: HyperGS uses a factorized spatiotemporal Transformer to extract tokens from video and a learnable query-based Transformer to predict 8-parameter Gaussian representations per frame. A rank-based geometric regularizer with adaptive strength stabilizes training against needle-like degeneration.
AI.result: HyperGS achieves encoding at 10^4-10^5× the speed of per-video Gaussian optimization at matched reconstruction quality, generalizes zero-shot to 720p video, and improves PSNR by +2.9-3.1 dB over prior video encoders on K400, SSv2, and UCF101.
AI.conclusion: By predicting explicit 2D Gaussians in a single forward pass, HyperGS combines the fast, flexible rendering of Gaussian Splatting with the speed and generalization of feedforward prediction, advancing Gaussians as a practical direction for fast and generalizable video representation.

title: A multi-scale feature enhanced graph neural network for fluid dynamics prediction in complex geometries
summary: Industrial design in fields such as vehicle and aerospace engineering often relies on large-scale numerical simulations to evaluate fluid dynamics performance, which can incur substantial computational costs. Deep neural networks have shown promise in improving simulation efficiency, especially graph neural networks (GNNs), which demonstrate great potential due to their flexibility with unstructured data. However, GNNs face challenges when dealing with tasks involving complex geometries and large-scale meshes. In this paper, we propose the Multi-scale Feature Enhanced Graph Neural Network (ME-GNN) to tackle these challenges. ME-GNN employs a graph neural network with a two-step message-passing mechanism to capture detailed local features effectively. Additionally, it integrates an Attention U-Net with uniform grid discretization, enabling the extraction of both fine and coarse features. The model also utilizes K-hop sampling to construct subgraphs, facilitating efficient training on large datasets while preserving detailed local features. We evaluated ME-GNN on three benchmark datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results: a relative L2 error of 0.0196 for the velocity field and 0.0556 for the surface pressure on ShapeNet-Car, a normalized mean squared error of 0.0033 for the flow field on AirfRANS, and a relative L2 error of 0.1416 for the surface pressure on DrivAerNet.

AI.tldr: ME-GNN is a multi-scale feature enhanced graph neural network that achieves state-of-the-art results in predicting fluid dynamics on complex geometries and large-scale meshes, using two-step message passing, Attention U-Net with uniform grid discretization, and K-hop sampling.
AI.motivation: Large-scale numerical simulations for fluid dynamics in vehicle and aerospace engineering are computationally expensive. While GNNs offer flexibility with unstructured data, they struggle with complex geometries and large-scale meshes, motivating the need for a more efficient and accurate approach.
AI.method: ME-GNN uses a two-step message-passing mechanism to capture local features, an Attention U-Net with uniform grid discretization to extract multi-scale (fine and coarse) features, and K-hop sampling to construct subgraphs for efficient training on large datasets while preserving local detail.
AI.result: On ShapeNet-Car: relative L2 error of 0.0196 (velocity) and 0.0556 (surface pressure). On AirfRANS: normalized mean squared error of 0.0033 (flow field). On DrivAerNet: relative L2 error of 0.1416 (surface pressure). All results are state-of-the-art on the respective benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ME-GNN effectively addresses GNN limitations on complex geometries and large-scale meshes, achieving superior performance across multiple fluid dynamics benchmarks, demonstrating its potential for efficient surrogate modeling in industrial design.

title: CFR-Net:Collaborative Feature Refnement Network for Medical Image Anomaly Detection
summary: Medical image anomaly detection remains challenging because networks pretrained on natural images often exhibit limited adaptability to medical images, where abnormal patterns appear as fine-grained local shifts, multi-scale contextual mismatches, and orientation-sensitive structural deviations. To address this, we propose the Collaborative Feature Refinement Network (CFR-Net), which combines shared teacher-student feature refinement before decoding with cross-space consistency after decoding. CFR-Net refines frozen teacher features and trainable student features using a Multi-Path Feature Refinement Module (MPFRM) with shared parameters, imposing common multi-path refinement rules on generic visual references and representations adapted to the medical domain, thereby mitigating domain discrepancy while modeling local, multi-scale, and orientation-sensitive feature characteristics. A variance-sensitive objective and dynamic ``homework set'' reorganization further support layer-adaptive consistency learning. Experiments on medical benchmarks show that CFR-Net achieves competitive anomaly classification and strong anomaly localization performance when trained on normal data.

AI.tldr: CFR-Net addresses medical image anomaly detection by using shared teacher-student feature refinement and cross-space consistency, achieving competitive classification and localization performance.
AI.motivation: Medical image anomaly detection is challenging because pretrained networks on natural images struggle with fine-grained local shifts, multi-scale contextual mismatches, and orientation-sensitive structural deviations in medical images.
AI.method: CFR-Net employs a Multi-Path Feature Refinement Module (MPFRM) with shared parameters to collaboratively refine frozen teacher features and trainable student features before decoding, plus cross-space consistency after decoding, with a variance-sensitive objective and dynamic "homework set" reorganization for layer-adaptive consistency learning.
AI.result: CFR-Net achieves competitive anomaly classification and strong anomaly localization performance on medical benchmarks when trained on normal data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CFR-Net effectively mitigates domain discrepancy between natural and medical image representations, enabling robust anomaly detection through collaborative refinement and consistency mechanisms.

title: CatRetriever: Contrastive Representation Learning for Slab-to-Bulk Retrieval in Generative Catalyst Discovery
summary: Inverse design is an emerging data-driven paradigm for efficiently navigating vast chemical spaces to discover new materials with targeted properties, and in the context of heterogeneous catalysis, surface generative models have recently advanced this goal by directly generating catalyst surface-adsorbate structures. However, these models typically operate at the slab level and do not provide the corresponding parent bulk structure, making it difficult to assess bulk-dependent properties such as formation energy, surface energy, crystallographic symmetry, and synthesizability. Here, we address this missing slab-to-bulk connection as a retrieval problem and introduce CatRetriever, a contrastive representation learning model that aligns slab and bulk crystal representations in a shared latent space. From a slab query, CatRetriever accurately retrieves plausible parent bulk candidates with R@1 > 91% and R@3 > 98% on both the in-distribution and holdout evaluation sets. We further extend the CatRetriever framework into an adsorption energy targeted bulk discovery pipeline that combines bulk retrieval, generative search space expansion, and adsorption energy distribution analysis. This workflow evaluates candidates by both structural compatibility with the query slab and their ability to access the target adsorption energy range across diverse surface environments. CatRetriever therefore provides a scalable route for connecting catalyst generative models with physically plausible and adsorption energy compatible bulk catalyst discovery.

AI.tldr: CatRetriever is a contrastive representation learning model that retrieves parent bulk structures from slab queries with high accuracy (R@1 > 91%, R@3 > 98%), enabling connection of surface generative models to bulk catalyst discovery and adsorption energy targeted screening.
AI.motivation: Existing surface generative models for catalyst design produce slab-level structures but lack corresponding parent bulk information, making it impossible to assess bulk-dependent properties such as formation energy, surface energy, symmetry, and synthesizability.
AI.method: The authors formulate slab-to-bulk mapping as a retrieval problem and develop CatRetriever, a contrastive representation learning model that aligns slab and bulk crystal representations in a shared latent space, enabling accurate retrieval of parent bulk candidates from slab queries. This is extended into an adsorption energy targeted discovery pipeline combining retrieval, generative search expansion, and adsorption energy distribution analysis.
AI.result: CatRetriever achieves R@1 > 91% and R@3 > 98% on both in-distribution and holdout evaluation sets for parent bulk retrieval from slab queries.
AI.conclusion: CatRetriever provides a scalable route to connect catalyst generative models with physically plausible and adsorption energy compatible bulk catalyst discovery, bridging the slab-to-bulk gap in inverse design for heterogeneous catalysis.

title: Vinci2: Providing Proactive Assistance in Continuous Egocentric Videos
summary: When should an intelligent assistant speak up without being asked? Continuous egocentric video offers rich, evolving context that enables a new form of assistance: one that is proactive rather than merely reactive. Yet existing approaches either wait passively for user queries or treat every detected event as requiring a response, without considering the user's history, current activity, or whether assistance would actually be welcome. We reframe proactive assistance as a context-dependent decision problem: the agent must not only perceive what is happening, but reason over accumulated temporal context to determine when and whether to intervene. To this end, we present Vinci2, a proactive egocentric assistance system that advances the on-device assistant Vinci from reactive response toward proactivity. On the evaluation side, we present EgoServe, the first large-scale benchmark for proactive assistance in continuous egocentric video. EgoServe comprises over 3,000 service instances organized along 4 temporal memory horizons, ranging from immediate safety alerts to long-term habit coaching, across 10 service categories. On the modeling side, we propose EgoMemo, a training-free, memory-augmented agent that maintains three complementary memory representations: multi-scale temporal summaries, a semantic knowledge graph, and visual embedding archives. At each timestep, EgoMemo performs retrieval-augmented reasoning to determine whether assistance is warranted and, if so, produces contextually grounded responses. Experiments demonstrate that EgoMemo establishes strong baselines on EgoServe while remaining competitive on existing egocentric benchmarks. Our benchmark and code are publicly available at \href{https://sitonggong.github.io/EgoServe-page/}{Vinci2}.

AI.tldr: Vinci2 introduces proactive egocentric assistance with EgoMemo (training-free, memory-augmented agent) and EgoServe (first large-scale benchmark with 3,000+ service instances across 4 temporal horizons and 10 categories).
AI.motivation: Existing intelligent assistants are either purely reactive (wait for user queries) or overly proactive (respond to every event without considering context, user history, or appropriateness). Continuous egocentric video offers rich temporal context that remains unexploited for deciding when and whether to proactively intervene.
AI.method: Proposes Vinci2, built on EgoMemo — a training-free, memory-augmented agent with three complementary memory representations: multi-scale temporal summaries, a semantic knowledge graph, and visual embedding archives. At each timestep, it performs retrieval-augmented reasoning to decide if assistance is warranted and produces contextually grounded responses. The EgoServe benchmark covers 4 temporal memory horizons (immediate safety alerts to long-term habit coaching) across 10 service categories with 3,000+ instances.
AI.result: EgoMemo establishes strong baselines on EgoServe and remains competitive on existing egocentric benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Proactive assistance in egocentric video can be effectively reframed as a context-dependent decision problem, and memory-augmented retrieval reasoning offers a viable path without requiring additional training.

title: Active Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
summary: Background: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables effective policies to be trained from large, previously collected datasets and subsequently improved through limited online interaction. This offline-to-online RL (O2O-RL) paradigm is particularly promising in nonstationary domains where interaction is costly or potentially hazardous. Standard O2O-RL pipelines train multiple candidate policies offline, evaluate them using off-policy or online evaluation, and then deploy and fine-tune the policy with the highest estimated value. However, as in offline pretraining, fine-tuning performance is highly sensitive to the choice of algorithm and hyperparameters, making it risky to commit to a single policy. Objectives: We study active policy selection for fine-tuning under a limited interaction budget in O2O-RL settings. To our knowledge, this is the first work to address this problem. Methods: We formulate the problem by identifying a fundamental trade-off between allocating online interactions to policy evaluation, which helps identify high-performing policies, and allocating them to fine-tuning, which improves policy performance. We then propose an approach that balances this trade-off by actively selecting policies for fine-tuning based on upper-confidence bounds on their future performance. These bounds are derived from locally linear performance forecasts fitted to observations obtained through online evaluation. Results: Across a diverse range of experiments, the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing O2O-RL baselines. Conclusions: Actively selecting and fine-tuning policies uses limited online interaction budgets more effectively than either committing to a single policy or dividing the budget equally among all policies. Our framework also advances offline RL toward practical deployment in real-world systems where online interaction is costly or risky.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an active policy selection framework for offline-to-online RL that optimally balances a limited online interaction budget between policy evaluation and fine-tuning, outperforming standard single-policy or equal-allocation baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard O2O-RL pipelines are sensitive to algorithm and hyperparameter choices when committing to a single policy for fine-tuning, making the selection process risky under limited online interaction budgets. No prior work had addressed active policy selection for fine-tuning in this setting.
AI.method: The authors formulate a trade-off between allocating online interactions to policy evaluation (identifying high-performing policies) vs. fine-tuning (improving policy performance). They propose an active selection approach using upper-confidence bounds derived from locally linear performance forecasts fitted to online evaluation observations.
AI.result: Across diverse experiments, the proposed approach consistently outperforms existing O2O-RL baselines, demonstrating more effective use of limited online interaction budgets than committing to a single policy or dividing the budget equally.
AI.conclusion: Active selection and fine-tuning of policies is more effective than standard O2O-RL approaches, and the framework advances offline RL toward practical deployment in real-world systems with costly or risky online interaction.

title: Parse, Search, and Confirmation: Training-Free Aerial Vision-and-Dialog Navigation with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning and Structured Spatial Memory
summary: In this paper, we tackle the Aerial Vision-and-Dialog Navigation (AVDN) task in the training-free setting for resource-efficient high-altitude UAV navigation.Naively applying MLLMs leads to unreliable navigation due to weak directional grounding and the lack of explicit spatial memory.To address these issues, we propose PSC-AVDN, a training-free framework that tightly couples a three-stage Parsing-Search-Confirmation reasoning pipeline with a Structured Spatial Memory (SSM).The parsing stage uses an LLM to convert ambiguous dialogue instructions into stable geometric directional and destination cues.A Search Chain-of-Thought (S-CoT) then performs stepwise target exploration under high-altitude observations, and a Confirmation Chain-of-Thought (C-CoT) conducts fine-grained verification around candidate regions to resolve visual ambiguity.Meanwhile, SSM integrates three complementary sources of spatial cues, including multi-scale visual observation, spatial visual memory, and structured geometric memory to provide global spatial context and long-horizon consistency.Extensive experiments on ANDH and ANDH-Full show that PSC-AVDN establishes new state-of-the-art performance in the training-free setting, matching or surpassing several finetuned methods.Code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/QY6616/PSC-AVDN

AI.tldr: PSC-AVDN is a training-free framework for Aerial Vision-and-Dialog Navigation that uses a Parsing-Search-Confirmation reasoning pipeline with Structured Spatial Memory to achieve state-of-the-art performance without training.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs applied to AVDN suffer from weak directional grounding and lack explicit spatial memory, leading to unreliable navigation. The goal is to achieve resource-efficient, training-free high-altitude UAV navigation.
AI.method: A three-stage Parsing-Search-Confirmation pipeline: (1) Parsing stage converts ambiguous dialogue into geometric directional/destination cues via LLM; (2) Search Chain-of-Thought (S-CoT) performs stepwise target exploration; (3) Confirmation Chain-of-Thought (C-CoT) does fine-grained candidate verification. SSM integrates multi-scale visual observation, spatial visual memory, and structured geometric memory for global spatial context.
AI.result: Establishes new state-of-the-art in training-free setting on ANDH and ANDH-Full benchmarks, matching or surpassing several finetuned methods.
AI.conclusion: Training-free PSC-AVDN effectively addresses directional grounding and spatial memory limitations, achieving competitive performance against finetuned approaches in aerial navigation.

title: Time-Lag-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling in PPVC Module Factories
comment: 10 pages,5 figures, UR by IEEE TII
summary: Prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction moves most building work into module factories, whose production floor operates as a flexible job shop. A major complication is decisive: long post-operation time-lags caused by concrete curing, watertightness ponding tests, and paint drying, during which a module is blocked while its workstation stays free. On benchmark instances grounded in an official national prefabrication guidebook, these lags inflate even the optimal reference makespan by about 67% on average, and ignoring them at decision time, then repairing to feasibility, is worse than every dispatching rule. We adapt a state-of-the-art dual-attention deep reinforcement learning solver through three minimally invasive, individually ablatable extensions: lag-aware dynamics with an admissible reward bound, two anticipatory lag feature channels, and liveness-masked operation- and station-type embeddings. With every extension disabled the implementation reproduces the original solver exactly, so all gains are attributable to the adaptations. We release a public, guidebook-grounded benchmark generator. On held-out instances the learned policy is the strongest solver-free scheduler: it reaches within about 4% of a constraint-programming reference and beats every dispatching rule and a genetic-algorithm metaheuristic, with its advantage widening under capacity contention, and a single size-mixed policy carries this lead across the trained range of factory sizes. It needs no solver, model, or license in the loop and re-plans within seconds of a disruption; where an exact solver can be deployed, that solver remains the quality ceiling, a boundary we map explicitly.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses long post-operation time-lags in prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction (PPVC) module factories, which operate as flexible job shops. These lags (from concrete curing, watertightness tests, paint drying) inflate makespan by ~67%. The authors adapt a dual-attention deep reinforcement learning solver with three extensions: lag-aware dynamics, anticipatory lag features, and liveness-masked embeddings. The learned policy beats dispatching rules and genetic algorithms, reaching within ~4% of a constraint-programming reference, and re-plans within seconds.
AI.motivation: To address the critical complication of long post-operation time-lags in PPVC module factories, which significantly degrade scheduling performance even when ignored and repaired, and to develop a solver-free, fast, and high-quality scheduling policy that does not rely on commercial solvers.
AI.method: Adapts a state-of-the-art dual-attention deep reinforcement learning solver with three minimally invasive, individually ablatable extensions: (1) lag-aware dynamics with admissible reward bound, (2) two anticipatory lag feature channels, and (3) liveness-masked operation- and station-type embeddings. A public benchmark generator grounded in an official national prefabrication guidebook is also released.
AI.result: The learned policy reaches within ~4% of a constraint-programming reference, beats all dispatching rules and a genetic-algorithm metaheuristic, with advantages widening under capacity contention. A single size-mixed policy carries this lead across the trained range of factory sizes. Exact solvers remain the quality ceiling, mapped explicitly.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRL-based approach is the strongest solver-free scheduler for PPVC flexible job shops with post-operation time-lags, offering high-quality, fast re-planning without requiring a solver or license in the loop.

title: Adaptive Routing for Efficient Diffusion Transformer-Based PNI Prediction
summary: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a critical prognostic factor in cholangiocarcinoma. However, its preoperative prediction from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains challenging due to subtle imaging features that extend beyond tumor boundaries into surrounding regions. Conventional convolutional neural networks are limited in capturing long-range spatial dependencies. Transformer-based architectures improve global modeling of volumetric MRI by aggregating spatially distributed contextual cues, yet capturing subtle and noise-sensitive patterns in peritumoral regions remains challenging. Diffusion-based classifiers offer an alternative formulation by leveraging denoising-based class scoring to better capture such subtle patterns. However, these approaches introduce substantial computational overhead due to the combination of transformer-based modeling and iterative denoising processes. To address these challenges, we formulate PNI prediction as a diffusion-based classification problem and implement the denoising network using a transformer-based representation. To improve computational efficiency, we introduce adaptive routing across attention heads, spatial tokens, and MLP width. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves an AUC of 0.731 with 257.57 GFLOPs.

AI.tldr: Proposes a diffusion-based classifier with a transformer backbone and adaptive routing (across attention heads, spatial tokens, and MLP width) to predict perineural invasion from MRI, achieving AUC 0.731 at 257.57 GFLOPs.
AI.motivation: PNI is a critical prognostic factor in cholangiocarcinoma but is difficult to predict preoperatively from MRI because subtle imaging features extend beyond tumor boundaries. CNNs lack long-range spatial modeling, transformers improve global context but struggle with subtle noise-sensitive peritumoral patterns, and existing diffusion classifiers add computational overhead. Thus, an efficient method is needed.
AI.method: Formulates PNI prediction as a diffusion-based classification problem using a transformer-based denoising network. Introduces adaptive routing across attention heads, spatial tokens, and MLP width to reduce computational overhead.
AI.result: Achieves AUC of 0.731 with 257.57 GFLOPs on the PNI prediction task.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diffusion-classifier with adaptive routing improves efficiency while maintaining competitive performance for PNI prediction from MRI.

title: HiFi-LLP: High-Fidelity, Low-Cost Latency Predictors with Confidence for Robust HW-NAS
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 2025 IEEE 38th International System-on-Chip Conference (SOCC)
summary: With deep neural networks (DNNs) increasingly deployed on edge devices, hardware (HW)-aware optimization techniques--such as HW-aware compression and HW-aware neural architecture search (HW-NAS)--have become essential. These methods rely on real feedback from the target hardware to tailor DNN architectures for efficient deployment. While the search can be parallelized, latency measurements via hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) remain a bottleneck due to their sequential nature. Recent approaches use latency predictors to replace costly HIL feedback, but challenges persist: (1) platform-specific predictors often require tens of thousands of samples, and (2) inaccurate predictions can mislead the NAS process. To address this, we introduce HiFi-LLP, a high-fidelity, low-cost latency predictor based on graph attention networks, augmented with a confidence metric. HiFi-LLP outperforms prior platform-specific predictors by up to 9 percentage points (p.p.) in the 10% accuracy bound and achieves a Spearman's rank correlation of up to 0.996 across six devices in the LatBench dataset. We further propose a hybrid NAS framework that routes low-confidence predictions to HIL, achieving up to 8.6$\times$ speedup compared to typical NAS while maintaining a competitive Pareto front.

AI.tldr: HiFi-LLP introduces a high-fidelity, low-cost latency predictor using graph attention networks with a confidence metric, achieving up to 0.996 Spearman correlation across six devices. A hybrid NAS framework routes low-confidence predictions to hardware-in-the-loop, delivering up to 8.6× speedup while maintaining a competitive Pareto front.
AI.motivation: Hardware-aware DNN optimization (e.g., HW-NAS) relies on latency feedback from target hardware via hardware-in-the-loop (HIL), which is a sequential bottleneck. Existing latency predictors are either platform-specific requiring tens of thousands of samples or suffer from inaccurate predictions that mislead NAS.
AI.method: HiFi-LLP: a graph attention network-based latency predictor augmented with a confidence metric. Additionally, a hybrid NAS framework is proposed that routes low-confidence predictions to actual HIL measurements, combining predictions with real feedback for reliability.
AI.result: HiFi-LLP outperforms prior platform-specific predictors by up to 9 p.p. in the 10% accuracy bound, and achieves Spearman's rank correlation up to 0.996 across six devices in LatBench. The hybrid NAS achieves up to 8.6× speedup over typical NAS while maintaining a competitive Pareto front.
AI.conclusion: HiFi-LLP provides an accurate, efficient alternative to costly HIL measurements for HW-NAS. The hybrid framework effectively balances speed and accuracy by using confidence-based routing, making hardware-aware DNN deployment more practical.

title: Training-Free Off-Screen Player Imputation for Broadcast-Based Spatial Football Analytics
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/nowayfootball/offscreen-impute
summary: Spatial football metrics such as pitch control assume access to the positions of all 22 players, yet the most widely available source of positional data -- the broadcast main camera -- shows only 10-16 of them at any moment. We quantify the resulting distortion with an open, reproducible benchmark: a simulated broadcast viewport applied to open full-pitch tracking data (Metrica Sports; three matches, one held out from method development). Ignoring off-screen players -- the visible-only baseline implied whenever a video-based game-state-reconstruction (GSR) pipeline adds no imputation layer -- inflates hidden-zone pitch-control error to 25.1-26.9 percentage points and a mean absolute control-share error of 11.1-13.4 points across the three matches. We then evaluate a ladder of training-free, online imputation baselines that use only observations from the match being analysed. The best overall on these decision-relevant metrics, role-anchored centroid voting (each visible player votes for the full-team centroid by subtracting its running role offset, attenuating the viewport-induced subset bias), roughly halves hidden-zone error (to 12.2-13.8 points) and cuts control-share error to 28-48% of the ignore policy at every viewport width from 36 m to 60 m in all three matches. For occlusions <=9.6 s -- the regime of the closest learned prior work -- it reaches binwise median position errors of 3.3-8.9 m; but 50-57% of hidden-player observations lie beyond that regime. Integrated end-to-end into a broadcast-video GSR pipeline, imputation moves a downstream possession-quality score (Space-Creation Index) by 15.6 and 17.2 points on two real World Cup broadcast windows, flipping the verdict class in one.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies pitch-control distortion from missing players in broadcast video (only 10-16 of 22 players visible), proposes role-anchored centroid voting as a training-free imputation method that roughly halves hidden-zone errors, and shows that imputation significantly changes downstream possession-quality metrics in real broadcast data.
AI.motivation: Spatial football metrics (e.g., pitch control) require all 22 player positions, but broadcast main camera typically shows only 10-16 players. Existing game-state-reconstruction pipelines often ignore off-screen players entirely, introducing unknown distortion. The paper aims to quantify this distortion and develop effective imputation methods that require no training data.
AI.method: The authors (1) create a simulated broadcast viewport benchmark using open full-pitch tracking data (Metrica Sports, three matches), (2) evaluate the "visible-only" baseline (no imputation), (3) propose a ladder of training-free online imputation baselines, with the best being role-anchored centroid voting—each visible player votes for the full-team centroid by subtracting its running role offset to attenuate viewport-induced subset bias, and (4) integrate the method into a broadcast-video GSR pipeline to test downstream impact on Space-Creation Index.
AI.result: Visible-only baseline: 25.1-26.9 percentage points hidden-zone pitch-control error, 11.1-13.4 points mean absolute control-share error. Role-anchored centroid voting roughly halves hidden-zone error (to 12.2-13.8 points) and reduces control-share error to 28-48% of the ignore policy across viewport widths 36-60m. For occlusions ≤9.6s, binwise median position errors are 3.3-8.9m; but 50-57% of occlusions exceed that duration. In real World Cup broadcast integration, imputation shifts Space-Creation Index by 15.6 and 17.2 points, flipping the verdict class in one case.
AI.conclusion: Ignoring off-screen players causes substantial pitch-control distortion. Simple training-free imputation (role-anchored centroid voting) significantly reduces error, and this matters for downstream decision-relevant metrics. The paper provides an open benchmark for future work.

title: From Global to Factor-Wise Expert Composition in Discrete Diffusion Models
summary: Discrete diffusion models offer a powerful framework for solving complex reasoning tasks, particularly through compositional generation, which combines multiple pre-trained experts to generalize beyond their individual training data. Recent theoretical corrections introduce time-dependent mixing weights to better align composed diffusion dynamics with the intended target. However, these methods are fundamentally limited by working on a per-sample basis, treating each generated state monolithically and ignoring the potential spatial or functional specializations of different experts. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing FactorDiff - a factor-wise composition framework for diffusion models. We posit that samples can be further decomposed into smaller factors, and propose a sampling process that dynamically routes each factor to the most relevant expert. We instantiate this framework with spatial/pixel-level compositions and validate it on the ARC-AGI benchmark, demonstrating that simple factor-specific routing consistently outperforms complex global scalar weighting schemes on tasks that require logical consistency and spatial disentanglement.

AI.tldr: FactorDiff is a factor-wise composition framework for discrete diffusion models that decomposes samples into smaller factors and dynamically routes each factor to the most relevant expert, outperforming per-sample global weighting schemes on the ARC-AGI benchmark for spatial/pixel-level tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing time-dependent mixing weight corrections for composed diffusion models operate on a per-sample basis, treating each generated state monolithically and ignoring potential spatial or functional specializations of different experts, which limits their effectiveness for tasks requiring spatial disentanglement.
AI.method: FactorDiff proposes decomposing samples into smaller factors (e.g., spatial/pixel-level components) and designing a sampling process that dynamically routes each factor to the most relevant expert, rather than applying global scalar weighting schemes.
AI.result: On the ARC-AGI benchmark, simple factor-specific routing consistently outperforms complex global scalar weighting schemes on tasks requiring logical consistency and spatial disentanglement.
AI.conclusion: Factor-wise composition is a more effective paradigm than per-sample global weighting for composed diffusion models, particularly for tasks with spatial or functional specializations, offering better alignment with the intended target distribution.

title: Single-Teacher View Augmentation: Enhancing Knowledge Distillation with Student-Guided Perturbations
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) typically relies on the fixed perspective of a single teacher, limiting the diversity of supervisory signals. While multi-teacher distillation addresses this by aggregating knowledge from multiple models, it incurs prohibitive computational and storage costs. To balance efficiency and diversity, recent research has focused on generating virtual views from a single teacher. However, existing methods face a trade-off: random perturbation approaches offer efficiency but lack controlled diversity, while structured augmentation methods require multi-stage training and incur linear parameter growth. We observe that this trade-off stems from a common design choice: using the teacher's strong but static features to generate views. Instead, we propose Shift-Augmented Knowledge Distillation (SAKD), a simple yet effective framework that leverages the student's evolving features as a dynamic condition for perturbation generation. This shift in perspective enables single-stage training while producing adaptive, diverse views through a parameter-free cyclic shift. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet demonstrate that SAKD consistently outperforms random perturbation methods and achieves accuracy on par with two-stage approaches, while using significantly fewer parameters and eliminating pre-training requirements.

AI.tldr: SAKD proposes a parameter-free cyclic shift method that uses the student's evolving features (instead of teacher's static features) as a dynamic condition for generating diverse views in knowledge distillation, achieving single-stage training with performance comparable to multi-stage methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-teacher distillation provides diverse supervision but is computationally expensive; existing single-teacher view generation methods face a trade-off between efficiency (random perturbation) and controlled diversity (structured augmentation with multi-stage training and parameter growth). This stems from using the teacher's strong but static features for view generation.
AI.method: Shift-Augmented Knowledge Distillation (SAKD) uses the student's evolving features as a dynamic condition for perturbation generation, employing a parameter-free cyclic shift mechanism to produce adaptive, diverse views in a single-stage training paradigm.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, SAKD consistently outperforms random perturbation methods and achieves accuracy comparable to two-stage approaches, while using significantly fewer parameters and eliminating pre-training requirements.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from teacher's static features to student's evolving features as the basis for view generation enables efficient, adaptive knowledge distillation with reduced computational overhead and no compromise on performance.

title: From Expressivity to Sample Complexity: Narrow Teachers for Transformers via C-RASP
summary: A theoretical understanding of Transformers is crucial to better understand the capacities and limitations of large language models (LLMs). There is much work analyzing the expressivity of attention-based models. By proposing handcrafted weights or using computational complexity arguments, a large amount of past theoretical works have sought to characterize which tasks are and which are not in the hypothesis class of Transformer models. However, little work investigates the learnability of such solutions. In this work, we make progress towards this goal. Inspired by recent loss landscape analysis work, we propose preliminary sample complexity bounds for learning C-RASP constructions with Transformers.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the theoretical understanding of Transformers, focusing on learnability rather than just expressivity. It proposes preliminary sample complexity bounds for learning C-RASP constructions with Transformers.
AI.motivation: Prior theoretical work has extensively analyzed the expressivity of Transformers (what tasks can be represented via handcrafted weights or complexity arguments), but little research investigates the learnability of such solutions—i.e., whether these solutions can actually be learned from data.
AI.method: The authors build on recent loss landscape analysis work to derive preliminary sample complexity bounds for learning C-RASP (a programming language for Transformer computations) constructions.
AI.result: The paper provides preliminary sample complexity bounds for learning C-RASP constructions with Transformers.
AI.conclusion: This work advances the theoretical understanding of Transformers by addressing the gap between expressivity and learnability, specifically for C-RASP constructions.

title: Technical Report on the CVPR 2026@AdvML Workshop Challenge
summary: Vision-language agents (VLAs) are increasingly used to interpret complex driving scenes and support safety-critical reasoning. This report presents the CVPR 2026@AdvML Workshop Challenge on adversarial multimodal attacks against autonomous-driving VLAs. Built on DriveLM-style multi-view visual question answering, the challenge represents each scene with six synchronized camera images and a structured collection of driving-related question-answer pairs. Participants generate adversarial images and suffix-only textual perturbations that induce model responses to deviate from reference answers while preserving image fidelity and limiting textual cost. The competition comprises two phases, with Phase II adding a hidden black-box model to assess transferability. We describe the task design, submission rules, evaluation protocol, and leaderboard results, and then examine five leading submissions for which technical reports were available. Across these reports, several recurring patterns emerge: image-side attacks are favored by the suffix penalty; scene-level, multi-view optimization is more effective than treating views in isolation; QA types and graph structure provide useful priors for allocating attack budget; feature-space objectives can improve black-box transfer; and typographic content embedded in camera images exposes a persistent vulnerability in driving VLAs. These findings provide a practical reference for future robustness evaluation and defense design in multimodal autonomous-driving systems.

AI.tldr: This report describes the CVPR 2026@AdvML Workshop Challenge on adversarial multimodal attacks against autonomous-driving VLAs. It presents the task design, evaluation protocol, and key findings from five top submissions, revealing that scene-level multi-view optimization, QA-type priors, feature-space objectives, and typographic vulnerabilities are central attack strategies.
AI.motivation: Vision-language agents (VLAs) are increasingly used for safety-critical driving scene interpretation, yet their robustness against adversarial attacks remains underexplored. This challenge was motivated by the need to systematically evaluate and understand vulnerabilities of multimodal autonomous-driving systems.
AI.method: Built on DriveLM-style multi-view VQA with six synchronized camera images per scene and structured QA pairs. Participants generated adversarial images and suffix-only textual perturbations to cause model responses to deviate from reference answers while preserving image fidelity and limiting textual cost. Phase II added a hidden black-box model to assess transferability.
AI.result: Five leading submissions analyzed. Key patterns: image-side attacks favored due to suffix penalty; scene-level multi-view optimization outperforms isolated view attacks; QA types and graph structure guide attack budget allocation; feature-space objectives improve black-box transfer; typographic content in camera images exposes persistent vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a practical reference for future robustness evaluation and defense design in multimodal autonomous-driving systems, highlighting specific attack strategies and persistent vulnerabilities that need to be addressed.

title: An Exact Instrument for State Usage in Selective State-Space Models, and the Input-Driven Migration It Reveals
summary: Selective state-space models such as Mamba route information through a bank of first-order modes whose input coupling is set by a learned selection mechanism. We give an exact instrument for measuring how a trained model uses these modes. Because the state matrix is diagonal, each channel's output decomposes exactly into per-mode contributions, and a per-(layer, channel, window) Gram tensor yields the exact output error of dropping any subset of modes, offline, at any budget. Validated against the reference implementation to a relative error of $2.3\times10^{-7}$ on the Mamba-1 family where it is exact, the instrument predicts a layer's deployed pruning error to a median relative deviation of $5\times10^{-7}$ over $4{,}464$ configurations, its floor set by the reconstruction. Applying the instrument across the Mamba-1 family (130M--2.8B), the deployed 7B Falcon-Mamba, and Mamba-2, we find that trained models re-allocate their state space with the input: which modes carry the signal migrates across contexts, and at the most affected layers a per-input oracle roughly halves the output error of a fixed mode set. Frozen-signal counterfactuals attribute the migration primarily to the input-dependent write map $B_t$; the timestep usually identified with selectivity carries almost none of it. Input-scheduled mode pruning on this measurement outperforms static, Hankel-based, and layer-adaptive rankings at every scale from 130M to the deployed 7B Falcon-Mamba, and at half the state budget it matches the unpruned model. Because the scheduler reads each window's mode usage from a first pass, this demonstrates realizable headroom; we claim no deployed compute or memory saving.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an exact instrument for measuring per-mode contributions in selective state-space models (Mamba), revealing that trained models dynamically re-allocate their state space based on input context—with the input-dependent write map B_t driving this migration, not the timestep—and demonstrates that input-scheduled mode pruning can match unpruned model performance at half the state budget.
